We investigate structural and contextual differences between stakeholder and product requirements, factors influencing acceptance, rejection, and approval with deviation, and the nature of stakeholder-to-product refinement. The results reveal systematic differences across abstraction levels and show that refinement complexity is driven primarily by architectural scope and missing contextual information rather than linguistic verbosity. We further derive a taxonomy of stakeholder-product mapping patterns and relate these patterns to differing refinement effort. The findings provide concrete insight into industrial requirements intake and refinement practices and identify actionable opportunities for improving intake validation, deviation management, and tool-supported contextual enrichment to support faster and more reusable automotive product development.

AI.tldr: A large-scale empirical study at Infineon analyzing 8,082 stakeholder requirements and 5,870 product requirements reveals that refinement complexity is driven by architectural scope and missing context rather than linguistic verbosity. The study identifies systematic differences across abstraction levels, a taxonomy of mapping patterns, and actionable insights for improving automotive requirements intake and deviation management.
AI.motivation: The automotive industry's shift to software-driven systems has increased complexity, yet limited empirical evidence exists on how stakeholder-level requirements are evaluated, refined, and transformed into product-level requirements in industrial practice. The authors seek to fill this gap with real-world data.
AI.method: A mixed-methods empirical study on an industrial dataset from Infineon, comprising 8,082 stakeholder requirements and 5,870 product requirements enriched with traceability links, decision outcomes, deviation rationales, and domain references. Combines quantitative analyses (requirement structures, decision distributions, mapping patterns) with qualitative analyses (rationales, referenced specifications, software/hardware artifacts).
AI.result: Systematic differences exist across abstraction levels between stakeholder and product requirements. Refinement complexity is primarily driven by architectural scope and missing contextual information, not linguistic verbosity. A taxonomy of stakeholder-to-product mapping patterns was derived, with patterns linked to differing refinement effort. Key factors influencing acceptance, rejection, and approval-with-deviation were identified.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide concrete, evidence-based insight into industrial requirements intake and refinement practices, and identify actionable opportunities for improving intake validation, deviation management, and tool-supported contextual enrichment to enable faster and more reusable automotive product development.

title: GeoXplain: On-the-Fly Visual Explanations for Weather Foundation Models
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to VISxClimate at IEEE VIS 2026
summary: Weather and climate foundation models produce high-dimensional forecasts whose learned relationships are difficult to inspect with static plots alone. GeoXplain is an interactive Python-based visualization toolkit for exploring geospatial attribution maps across climate variables, atmospheric pressure levels, and forecast time. The toolkit accepts attribution bundles containing attribution grids together with corresponding metadata and renders them in a notebook widget or browser with map and globe modes, linked timelines, pressure-level controls, target annotations, and optional physical-field overlays. We frame GeoXplain as a model-agnostic earth-system visualization toolkit and present the GeoXplain Aurora Adapter as its first computation backend. The adapter computes explanations for the Aurora foundation model, either in a local GPU process, through a GPU listener, or through a SLURM-backed listener, while preserving the same Python call site for analysts. It currently supports gradient saliency, Integrated Gradients, RISE, ViT-CX, multi-frame saliency and Integrated Gradients rollouts, and retrieval of ERA5 overlays. GeoXplain can be installed as a PyPI package with pip install geoxplain. The code is open-source and available at https://github.com/clemenskoprolin/geoxplain.

AI.tldr: GeoXplain is an interactive Python visualization toolkit for exploring geospatial attribution maps from weather/climate foundation models, featuring map/globe views, timeline controls, and pressure-level navigation, with a first backend adapter for the Aurora model supporting multiple explanation methods.
AI.motivation: Weather and climate foundation models produce high-dimensional forecasts with complex learned relationships that cannot be adequately inspected using static plots alone. There is a need for interactive, model-agnostic tools to explore geospatial attribution maps across multiple dimensions (climate variables, pressure levels, forecast time).
AI.method: GeoXplain provides an interactive Python-based visualization toolkit that accepts attribution bundles (attribution grids + metadata) and renders them in notebook widgets or browsers. It offers map and globe modes, linked timelines, pressure-level controls, target annotations, and optional physical-field overlays. The Aurora Adapter serves as the first computation backend, supporting gradient saliency, Integrated Gradients, RISE, ViT-CX, multi-frame saliency, Integrated Gradients rollouts, and ERA5 overlay retrieval. The adapter can run locally on GPU, through a GPU listener, or via SLURM-backed listener while maintaining a consistent Python API.
AI.result: GeoXplain is available as a PyPI package (pip install geoxplain) and is open-source on GitHub. It successfully enables interactive exploration of attribution maps for the Aurora foundation model across multiple explanation methods and deployment configurations.
AI.conclusion: GeoXplain fills a critical gap in explainability tooling for earth-system foundation models by providing an interactive, model-agnostic visualization framework that bridges attribution computation and exploratory analysis, with extensible backend support beginning with Aurora.

title: CSTutorBench: Benchmarking Small Language Models as Tutors for Block-Based Programming
summary: Large language models are increasingly explored as AI tutors, yet deploying them in K-12 settings raises concerns around privacy, cost, and reliance on proprietary models. Small language models (SLMs) offer a promising alternative, but selecting the right model for a specific educational context remains difficult, particularly when the target domain, such as block-based programming, is largely absent from model training data. We introduce CSTutorBench, a benchmark for evaluating language models as CS tutors in VEX VR, a block-based robotics environment. The benchmark comprises 17 scenario-based questions scored against a pedagogical rubric grounded in established tutoring and feedback research, with a human-in-the-loop LLM-as-judge pipeline for evaluation. Preliminary findings across 11 models (4B-120B parameters) reveal that models perform well on surface-level criteria such as vocabulary and tone but struggle with deeper pedagogical behaviors, particularly avoiding answer leakage and engaging with student debugging histories. In our sample, model family and instruction-tuning approach appear to be better predictors of tutoring quality than parameter count alone, though the small number of models limits the strength of this conclusion. A targeted prompt revision grounded in recent educational prompt engineering research improved scores for 10 of 11 models. These results underscore the value of context-specific, pedagogically grounded benchmarks for SLM selection in educational deployment.

AI.tldr: Introduces CSTutorBench, a benchmark for evaluating small language models as CS tutors in block-based programming (VEX VR). Tests 11 models (4B–120B params) across 17 scenario-based questions using a pedagogical rubric. Finds models handle surface features (vocabulary, tone) well but struggle with deeper pedagogy like avoiding answer leakage and using debugging history. Model family and instruction-tuning matter more than parameter count; targeted prompt engineering improved 10/11 models.
AI.motivation: SLMs are a cost-effective, privacy-preserving alternative to LLMs for K-12 AI tutoring, but selecting the right model is difficult—especially for domains like block-based programming that are underrepresented in training data. No existing benchmark specifically evaluates tutoring quality in this context.
AI.method: Created CSTutorBench: 17 scenario-based questions in VEX VR block-based robotics, scored with a pedagogical rubric (grounded in tutoring/feedback research) via a human-in-the-loop LLM-as-judge pipeline. Evaluated 11 models (4B–120B params), then applied a targeted prompt revision based on educational prompt engineering research.
AI.result: Models perform well on surface criteria (vocabulary, tone) but poorly on deeper pedagogy: avoiding answer leakage and engaging with student debugging histories. Model family and instruction-tuning approach better predict tutoring quality than parameter count. Prompt revision improved 10 of 11 models.
AI.conclusion: Context-specific, pedagogically grounded benchmarks are essential for informed SLM selection in educational deployment. Surface-level fluency does not guarantee effective tutoring; deeper pedagogical behaviors require deliberate evaluation and prompt design.

title: Text Distance from Nested and Hierarchical Repetitions: A Compression-Based Perspective
summary: We present a new method for structural sequence analysis grounded in Algorithmic Information Theory (AIT). At its core is the Ladderpath approach, which extracts nested and hierarchical relationships among repeated substructures in linguistic sequences -- an instantiation of AIT's principle of describing data through minimal generative programs. These structures are then used to define three distance measures: a normalized compression distance (NCD), and two alternative distances derived directly from the Ladderpath representation. Integrated with a $k$-nearest neighbor classifier, these distances achieve strong and consistent performance across in-distribution, out-of-distribution (OOD), and few-shot text classification tasks. In particular, all three methods outperform both gzip-based NCD and BERT under OOD and low-resource settings. These results demonstrate that the structured representations captured by Ladderpath preserve intrinsic properties of sequences and provide a lightweight, interpretable, and training-free alternative for text modeling. This work highlights the potential of AIT-based approaches for structural and domain-agnostic sequence understanding.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Ladderpath, a method from Algorithmic Information Theory that extracts nested, hierarchical substructures from sequences. It defines three distance measures — including normalized compression distance — and, combined with k-NN, outperforms gzip-based NCD and BERT on OOD and low-resource text classification tasks, offering a lightweight, interpretable, training-free alternative.
AI.motivation: To develop a structural sequence analysis method that captures intrinsic, hierarchical regularities in text without requiring training, providing robust performance especially under out-of-distribution and few-shot settings where deep learning models like BERT and simpler compression-based methods fall short.
AI.method: The Ladderpath approach, grounded in Algorithmic Information Theory, extracts nested and hierarchical repeated substructures from sequences by identifying minimal generative programs. From these representations, three distance measures are derived: (1) a normalized compression distance (NCD), and (2) two alternative distances based directly on the Ladderpath representation. These distances are used with a k-nearest neighbor classifier for text classification.
AI.result: All three Ladderpath-based distance measures achieve strong, consistent performance across in-distribution, out-of-distribution, and few-shot text classification tasks. Notably, all three outperform both gzip-based NCD and BERT under OOD and low-resource settings.
AI.conclusion: Ladderpath's structured representations preserve intrinsic sequence properties and provide a lightweight, interpretable, training-free alternative for text modeling. The work highlights the broader potential of Algorithmic Information Theory-based approaches for structural, domain-agnostic sequence understanding.

title: Geometry-Aware Infrastructure-Anchored Denoiser for UWB Sensing and Work-Zone Reconstruction
summary: Accurate work-zone geometry perception is critical for intelligent transportation systems, and ultra-wideband sensing offers a low-cost approach for infrastructure-aided reconstruction. However, outdoor UWB ranging is often degraded by non-line-of-sight propagation, burst noise, and long-tail errors, which can distort downstream spatial reconstruction. We present GAIA, a geometry-aware, infrastructure-anchored learning framework that couples temporal range modeling with latent anchor-layout estimation and deterministic distance projection. GAIA preserves range denoising as the supervised task while orienting the learned distances toward boundary-consistent reconstruction. We evaluate GAIA on a real-world outdoor UWB dataset with synchronized UWB, GNSS, and IMU measurements, and further test robustness using a real-data-calibrated stress-test simulator. GAIA achieves the lowest overall range MSE and highest polygon IoU among evaluated filtering-based and learning-based baselines, reducing MSE by 18.4% and improving polygon IoU by 15.5% over PoseMLP. These results show that geometry-aware range denoising provides an effective path toward spatially coherent work-zone reconstruction.

AI.tldr: GAIA is a geometry-aware, infrastructure-anchored learning framework that denoises UWB ranging data by coupling temporal range modeling with latent anchor-layout estimation and deterministic distance projection, achieving state-of-the-art work-zone reconstruction accuracy.
AI.motivation: Outdoor UWB ranging for work-zone perception suffers from NLOS propagation, burst noise, and long-tail errors that degrade spatial reconstruction. Existing methods lack explicit geometric consistency constraints linking range denoising to downstream reconstruction quality.
AI.method: GAIA couples temporal range modeling with latent anchor-layout estimation and deterministic distance projection. It preserves range denoising as the supervised task while orienting learned distances toward boundary-consistent reconstruction through explicit geometry-aware constraints.
AI.result: On a real-world outdoor UWB dataset and a calibrated stress-test simulator, GAIA achieves the lowest overall range MSE and highest polygon IoU among all baselines, reducing MSE by 18.4% and improving polygon IoU by 15.5% over PoseMLP.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-aware range denoising is an effective strategy for achieving spatially coherent work-zone reconstruction, outperforming both filtering-based and learning-based alternatives.

title: Abductive Corroboration of Probabilistic AI Models for Forensic Synthetic Media Detection
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) models, at their core, apply general learnings from broad datasets to individual circumstances using probabilistic behaviour. This inductive approach stands in contrast to deductive reasoning approaches which seek to prove conclusions from their premises. However, research has shown that deductive reasoning with AI models is a challenging problem and in the real-world it may not always be feasible. An alternative way forward is to leverage abductive reasoning, seeking to corroborate the output of multiple approaches to identify the most likely conclusion from the factual matrix. We apply this to synthetic media detection in forensic settings, and find we are able to disproportionately lower the risk of false positives to true positive recall. We also provide the first empirical evaluation of OpenAI's rollout of SynthID on synthetic images and evaluate how complementary different synthetic media detection approaches are.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using abductive reasoning—corroborating multiple detection approaches to infer the most likely conclusion—as a practical alternative to deductive reasoning for AI-based synthetic media detection in forensic contexts. It demonstrates that this approach disproportionately reduces false positives relative to true positive recall and provides the first empirical evaluation of OpenAI's SynthID on synthetic images, assessing complementarity among different detection methods.
AI.motivation: AI models operate inductively (probabilistic generalization from data), not deductively (proving conclusions from premises). Deductive reasoning with AI is challenging and often infeasible in real-world forensic settings. The authors are motivated to find a practical reasoning framework—abductive reasoning—that can improve reliability in synthetic media detection, particularly by mitigating false positives which are especially costly in forensic contexts.
AI.method: The authors apply abductive reasoning, which involves corroborating outputs from multiple independent synthetic media detection approaches to identify the most likely conclusion from the available factual evidence. They evaluate this framework empirically on synthetic image detection tasks, including a first-of-its-kind assessment of OpenAI's SynthID watermarking tool, and analyze the complementarity (orthogonality) of different detection modalities.
AI.result: The abductive reasoning approach disproportionately lowers the false positive rate compared to any reduction in true positive recall. Additionally, the empirical evaluation reveals how complementary different synthetic media detection approaches (including SynthID) are when used in combination.
AI.conclusion: Abductive reasoning offers a viable and effective framework for synthetic media detection in forensic settings, where deductive certainty is unattainable. Combining multiple detection methods through corroboration significantly improves reliability, particularly by suppressing false positives, and tools like SynthID can play a complementary role in a multi-modal detection strategy.

title: Scientific Code Search at Scale: A Multi-Domain Dataset and Benchmark
comment: Datasets and benchmarks publicly released on HuggingFace. Code released on GitHub
summary: Scientists increasingly rely on open-source tools to support their research workflows, yet discovering relevant software among over 600 million GitHub repositories remains challenging. Existing code search benchmarks focus on general software engineering tasks and fail to capture the domain-specific vocabulary and needs of scientific computing. We present a curated corpus of 5,264 high-quality, domain-classified scientific repositories spanning five NASA Science Mission Directorate divisions -- Earth Science, Astrophysics, Planetary Science, Heliophysics, and Biological & Physical Sciences -- enriched with cleaned READMEs, extracted topics, and additional context from crawled links. Building on this corpus, we introduce two novel information retrieval benchmarks: (1) a repository search benchmark with 219 expert-curated queries designed by domain scientists, and (2) a large-scale code snippet retrieval benchmark containing 117,950 code snippets and 119,720 queries across seven programming languages. Baseline evaluations on repository search reveal significant performance variation across scientific domains. Code snippet retrieval proves equally challenging, with substantial variation driven by differing documentation practices, coding standards, and programming language conventions across scientific communities. All datasets and benchmarks are publicly released on HuggingFace to support research on scientific tool discovery.

AI.tldr: A curated corpus of 5,264 domain-classified NASA scientific repositories is introduced, along with two novel IR benchmarks: repository search (219 expert queries) and code snippet retrieval (117,950 snippets, 119,720 queries across 7 languages). Baseline evaluations show significant performance variation across scientific domains, driven by differing documentation practices and coding conventions.
AI.motivation: Existing code search benchmarks target general software engineering and lack the domain-specific vocabulary and needs of scientific computing. Discovering relevant scientific software among 600M+ GitHub repositories is a major challenge for scientists.
AI.method: Curated a corpus of 5,264 NASA-aligned scientific repositories across five domains (Earth Science, Astrophysics, Planetary Science, Heliophysics, Biological & Physical Sciences), enriched with cleaned READMEs, extracted topics, and crawled link context. Constructed two IR benchmarks: (1) repository search with 219 domain-expert queries, and (2) code snippet retrieval with 117,950 snippets and 119,720 queries across seven programming languages. Baseline evaluations were conducted on both benchmarks.
AI.result: Repository search baselines exhibit significant performance variation across scientific domains. Code snippet retrieval is equally challenging, with substantial variation attributed to differing documentation practices, coding standards, and programming language conventions across scientific communities.
AI.conclusion: Scientific tool discovery via code search remains a difficult problem requiring domain-adapted approaches. The publicly released datasets and benchmarks on HuggingFace aim to catalyze further research into scientific information retrieval.

title: EvalLoop: A Methodology for Evaluation-Driven Iterative Improvement of Business AI Systems
summary: Teams deploying large language models in business contexts need evaluation systems, yet most treat evaluation as static model selection: run benchmarks, rank models, deploy the winner. This framing misses evaluation's primary value for production systems--diagnosing why a system underperforms and guiding what to fix. We present EvalLoop, a methodology for evaluation-driven iterative improvement. EvalLoop organizes evaluation around three mechanisms: (1) dimensional metric grouping that decomposes quality into business-relevant dimensions enabling orthogonal failure diagnosis; (2) failure mode classification that categorizes why outputs fail within weak dimensions, bridging diagnosis to action; and (3) a structured iteration workflow where each evaluation run varies one system variable and compares dimensional profiles before and after. We validate EvalLoop through a case study on sales intelligence briefing generation (10 models, 3 providers, 18 metrics, 5 dimensions, 3 iterations). Dimensional diagnosis identified that 69% of hallucination failures were prompt-induced interpretation errors--invisible in aggregate scoring. A targeted prompt fix improved the best model from 82.6% to 94.6% overall, with improvement concentrated in diagnosed dimensions (Content Accuracy +16.8pp, Synthesis Power +26.4pp). An undirected configuration change in a prior iteration produced zero impact, illustrating the cost of iterating without diagnosis. We additionally demonstrate that dimensional profiling enables deployment-specific model selection, and that a one-time blind human gate on a finalist panel (4 models, 16 cases) confirms dimensional rankings while resolving multi-criteria deployment trade-offs--a 94% reduction in review burden compared to evaluating the full design. EvalLoop is packaged as reusable artifacts (playbook, agent specification, template repository) for adoption by other teams.

AI.tldr: EvalLoop introduces a diagnostic evaluation methodology that decomposes LLM quality into business-relevant dimensions, classifies failure modes, and employs structured iteration to guide targeted fixes—demonstrating a 12pp improvement over undirected iteration in a sales intelligence case study.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation practices treat LLM evaluation as static model selection (benchmark → rank → deploy), ignoring evaluation's primary value in production: diagnosing underperformance causes and guiding corrective action. Teams waste effort on undirected iteration without understanding why systems fail.
AI.method: EvalLoop organizes evaluation around three mechanisms: (1) dimensional metric grouping that decomposes quality into orthogonal business-relevant dimensions for targeted diagnosis; (2) failure mode classification that categorizes why outputs fail within weak dimensions, linking diagnosis to actionable fixes; (3) a structured iteration workflow where each evaluation run varies exactly one system variable and compares dimensional profiles pre/post change. Validated via a case study on sales intelligence briefing generation (10 models, 3 providers, 18 metrics, 5 dimensions, 3 iterations). Also introduces deployment-specific model selection via dimensional profiling and a blind human gate for finalist adjudication.
AI.result: Dimensional diagnosis revealed 69% of hallucination failures were prompt-induced interpretation errors—invisible in aggregate scoring. A targeted prompt fix improved the best model from 82.6% to 94.6% overall, with Content Accuracy (+16.8pp) and Synthesis Power (+26.4pp) gains concentrated in diagnosed dimensions. An undirected prior iteration yielded zero impact. Dimensional profiling enabled deployment-specific model selection; a one-time blind human gate on a 4-model, 16-case panel confirmed dimensional rankings with 94% reduction in review burden vs. full-design evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation for production LLMs is fundamentally a diagnostic activity, not a selection activity. Dimensional decomposition and failure mode classification enable targeted, high-impact improvements that undirected iteration cannot achieve. Reusable artifacts (playbook, agent specification, template repository) are provided for adoption.

title: Perceived System Predictability: Scale Development and Application
summary: How predictable users perceive an interactive system to be shapes how they interpret, trust, and rely on it, yet HCI lacks both a precise conceptualization and a validated instrument for this perception. We address this gap by introducing perceived system predictability (PSP) as a user-centered construct grounded in uncertainty theory, distinguishing epistemic, aleatory, and effective predictability. We contribute (i) a theoretical framework that situates PSP relative to adjacent constructs such as trust and understanding, (ii) a 6-item PSP scale, derived from a 60-item pool through expert review and cognitive interviews, and validated in a shape-classifier study ($N=200$) that supports both a unidimensional and a three-factor hierarchical structure, and (iii) a sentiment-classifier study ($N=200$) that varies explanations and stochasticity, and relates PSP to the correctness of users' predictions of system behavior, trust, subjective information processing awareness, and need for cognition. We find that PSP and prediction correctness capture distinct aspects of users' mental models and that both can diverge: PSP itself predicts correctness, explanations shift PSP but not correctness, and increased stochasticity degrades correctness without lowering PSP. PSP thus goes beyond existing objective and subjective measures and offers a principled foundation for designing transparent and trustworthy interactive systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Perceived System Predictability (PSP) as a user-centered construct grounded in uncertainty theory, develops and validates a 6-item PSP scale across two studies (N=400 total), and demonstrates that PSP captures distinct aspects of users' mental models beyond prediction correctness, offering a principled foundation for designing transparent and trustworthy interactive systems.
AI.motivation: HCI lacks both a precise conceptualization and a validated instrument for measuring how predictable users perceive an interactive system to be, despite this perception shaping interpretation, trust, and reliance. The authors address this gap by grounding the construct in uncertainty theory.
AI.method: The authors (i) developed a theoretical framework situating PSP relative to trust and understanding; (ii) generated a 60-item pool, refined it through expert review and cognitive interviews, and validated a 6-item PSP scale in a shape-classifier study (N=200) testing unidimensional and three-factor hierarchical structures; and (iii) conducted a sentiment-classifier study (N=200) manipulating explanations and stochasticity, relating PSP to prediction correctness, trust, subjective information processing awareness, and need for cognition.
AI.result: PSP and prediction correctness capture distinct aspects of users' mental models and can diverge: PSP predicts correctness, explanations shift PSP but not correctness, and increased stochasticity degrades correctness without lowering PSP. The scale supports both unidimensional and three-factor (epistemic, aleatory, effective) hierarchical structures.
AI.conclusion: PSP goes beyond existing objective and subjective measures, providing a principled, empirically validated construct and instrument that captures users' perceived predictability distinct from actual prediction accuracy, enabling better design and evaluation of transparent, trustworthy interactive systems.

title: Foundation Models for Automatic CAD Generation
comment: Accepted as a book chapter in "Advances in Global Applied Artificial Intelligence" (G. A. Tsihrintzis, M. Virvou, N. G. Bourbakis, L. C. Jain, Eds.), authenticated version will be published in Springer series: Learning and Analytics in Intelligent Systems
summary: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable the automatic generation of parametric 3D designs from natural-language specifications. This chapter presents an empirical study of foundation models for automatic Computer-Aided Design (CAD) generation of mechanical parts, using a unified evaluation pipeline and a curated benchmark of 97 engineering design problems. We introduce LLMForge, a multi-model text-to-CAD framework integrating JSON-schema validation, analytic feature scoring, mesh synthesis, and multi-round iterative refinement, studied under two critique regimes. IterTracer uses a Phong-shaded ray-trace renderer with analytic visual metrics (silhouette IoU, hole visibility, edge clearance, aspect-ratio conformance) for lightweight geometry-aware feedback across rounds. IterVision replaces the analytic scorer with a VLM semantic critic (Qwen2.5-VL-72B) that evaluates rendered views via chain-of-thought visual reasoning, assessing spatial coherence and design intent. On a benchmark spanning four canonical geometry families (plates with holes and bolt circles, multi-feature boxes, flanged cylinders, and L-brackets), we evaluate seven foundation models: DeepSeek-V3.2, Qwen3-235B-A22B, Llama-3.3-70B, Gemma-3-27B, GLM-4.5, MiniMax-M2.1, and INTELLECT. Under IterTracer, the four highest-ranked models form a tight cluster (overall mean in [0.885, 0.890]) with 98.97% mesh success, showing that compact instruction-tuned models can match substantially larger systems. VLM-based critique in IterVision yields 100% watertight mesh generation on the leading model while surfacing systematic difficulty on rotationally symmetric geometries such as cylinders, where visual and semantic scoring diverge most. We discuss benchmark design, failure modes, CAD-oriented prompting, and implications for industrial workflows and scalable automated mechanical design.

AI.tldr: LLMForge is a multi-model text-to-CAD framework that evaluates seven foundation models on 97 mechanical design problems. Using analytic visual metrics (IterTracer) or VLM-based semantic critique (IterVision), top models achieve ~89% overall score with near-perfect mesh success, though VLM critique struggles with rotationally symmetric geometries like cylinders.
AI.motivation: To empirically evaluate how well foundation models (LLMs and VLMs) can automatically generate parametric 3D CAD designs from natural language specifications, and to understand the trade-offs between lightweight analytic feedback and VLM-based semantic critique for iterative refinement.
AI.method: LLMForge framework with JSON-schema validation, analytic feature scoring, mesh synthesis, and multi-round iterative refinement. Two critique regimes: IterTracer (Phong-shaded ray-trace renderer with silhouette IoU, hole visibility, edge clearance, aspect-ratio conformance metrics) and IterVision (Qwen2.5-VL-72B VLM with chain-of-thought visual reasoning). Evaluated seven models (DeepSeek-V3.2, Qwen3-235B-A22B, Llama-3.3-70B, Gemma-3-27B, GLM-4.5, MiniMax-M2.1, INTELLECT) across four geometry families using a curated 97-problem benchmark.
AI.result: Under IterTracer, top four models cluster tightly (mean score 0.885–0.890) with 98.97% mesh success, showing compact instruction-tuned models match larger systems. IterVision achieves 100% watertight mesh on the leading model but reveals systematic difficulty with rotationally symmetric geometries (cylinders), where visual and semantic scoring diverge most.
AI.conclusion: Foundation models are viable for automated parametric CAD generation with high mesh success rates. Compact models can rival larger ones. VLM-based semantic critique improves mesh quality but struggles with symmetric geometries, highlighting a key limitation. Findings have implications for benchmark design, CAD prompting, and industrial automation workflows.

title: Most LLM Conformity Needs No Speaker: Measuring the Speaker-Free Floor in Peer-Pressure Benchmarks
summary: LLM conformity is often used to describe cases where a model changes a correct answer toward a peer or group response. We show that most of this apparent conformity survives even after the peer is removed. The reason is a confound: standard conformity prompts mix two cues at once, the presence of a speaker and the repeated wrong answer itself. Existing benchmarks vary these cues together, so they cannot tell how much of the revision actually depends on the speaker. We introduce a no-source condition: the same asserted answer with the explicit speaker removed. Across six open-weight LLMs and seven QA and reasoning datasets, this condition alone causes harmful revision in $66.5\%$ of initially correct cases, compared with $10.3\%$ under a plain re-ask. The effect also remains when the repeated answer is paraphrased and when answer options are hidden in an open-ended setting. Source framing mainly modulates this floor: expert-panel framing raises it, while minimal person labels do not reliably raise it. When models flip, they are usually confidently wrong, and simple recalibration does not recover the original answer. Source attribution still matters, but it should be measured as an increment above this speaker-free floor. The methodological lesson is that conformity benchmarks should first measure what remains after the speaker is removed; without this step, benchmarks may mistake repeated text for social influence.

AI.tldr: LLM conformity is largely confounded by repeated wrong answers rather than genuine social influence; removing the speaker from prompts reveals that 66.5% of harmful revisions persist, suggesting benchmarks must isolate the effect of mere answer repetition from true conformity.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM conformity benchmarks conflate two cues — the presence of a speaker and the repeated wrong answer — making it impossible to disentangle whether models are genuinely conforming to social pressure or simply being misled by repeated text. The authors aim to isolate these factors.
AI.method: The authors introduce a "no-source" condition that presents the same asserted (wrong) answer but removes explicit speaker attribution. They evaluate six open-weight LLMs across seven QA/reasoning datasets, comparing revision rates under standard conformity prompts, plain re-ask, and speaker-free conditions. They also test paraphrased answers, open-ended settings, and various source-framing manipulations (expert panels, minimal person labels).
AI.result: The no-source condition alone causes harmful revision in 66.5% of initially correct cases, versus 10.3% under plain re-ask. Expert-panel framing raises this floor, while minimal person labels do not reliably do so. When models flip, they are confidently wrong, and simple recalibration fails to recover the original answer.
AI.conclusion: Conformity benchmarks should always include a speaker-free baseline to measure the effect of repeated text alone; without this, they risk mistaking mere repetition effects for social influence. Source attribution still matters but should be measured as an increment above this floor.

title: The Granularity Paradox: How Temporal Disaggregation Inflates In-Sample Fit and Compounds Out-of-Sample Error
summary: This paper explores the "Granularity Paradox" in time-series forecasting, wherein finer temporal disaggregation (e.g., Monthly to Weekly/Daily) improves in-sample diagnostics and dataset size (N), but degrades out-of-sample accuracy due to recursive error compounding over longer horizons (H). Conversely, coarse aggregation (Annual) eliminates recursive error propagation but reduces data available to estimators. We formalize this trade-off and benchmark 10 models - spanning naïve, statistical, machine learning, and deep learning architectures - across six granularities using a 13-year public procurement dataset. The empirical results reveal a non-monotonic threshold structure: recursive autoregressive and seasonal models degrade substantially under high-frequency forecasting (e.g., Holt-Winters reaches a Test R-squared of -151 and TPFE of 425.85% at the Daily grain), while the LSTM traces a U-shaped error curve, worsening from Monthly (19.66%) through Bi-Weekly (35.94%) before overcoming the error propagation penalty at Daily (TPFE of 4.35%, R-squared of 0.66). Linear Regression remains stable across all granularities (16.3-17.0% TPFE), confirming that the paradox is driven by recursive feedback topology, not model complexity. The results demonstrate that standard pointwise metrics (RMSE, MAE) systematically mask cumulative error propagation, and that evaluating forecasts without goal-dependent cumulative metrics produces misleading assessments of model adequacy. We introduce a consensus-dissensus diagnostic comparing the directional behaviour of pointwise metrics against cumulative TPFE across granularities, enabling the identification of models whose standard diagnostics mask systematic error propagation.

AI.tldr: Time-series forecasting faces a "Granularity Paradox": finer temporal granularity improves in-sample fit but degrades out-of-sample accuracy due to recursive error compounding. Benchmarking 10 models across six granularities reveals a non-monotonic threshold structure, with LSTM exhibiting a U-shaped error curve that eventually overcomes the propagation penalty at daily frequency. The paradox is driven by recursive feedback topology, not model complexity, and standard pointwise metrics systematically mask cumulative error.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by a practical tension in time-series forecasting: practitioners often assume finer temporal disaggregation (more data points) improves forecasts, but recursive multi-step forecasting at high frequencies compounds errors over long horizons, potentially degrading out-of-sample performance. The authors aim to formalize this trade-off, demonstrate that standard evaluation metrics (RMSE, MAE) fail to capture cumulative error propagation, and identify which model architectures are vulnerable to or robust against this paradox.
AI.method: The authors benchmark 10 models spanning naïve, statistical (e.g., Holt-Winters), machine learning (e.g., Linear Regression), and deep learning (e.g., LSTM) architectures across six temporal granularities (Annual, Quarterly, Monthly, Bi-Weekly, Weekly, Daily) using a 13-year public procurement dataset. They evaluate models using both standard pointwise metrics (RMSE, MAE, R-squared) and cumulative metrics (Total Percentage Forecast Error, TPFE). A novel "consensus-dissensus diagnostic" is introduced, comparing the directional behavior of pointwise metrics against cumulative TPFE across granularities to reveal when standard diagnostics mask systematic error propagation.
AI.result: A non-monotonic threshold structure emerges: recursive autoregressive and seasonal models degrade severely at high frequencies (Holt-Winters: Test R² = -151, TPFE = 425.85% at Daily). LSTM traces a U-shaped error curve — TPFE worsens from Monthly (19.66%) to Bi-Weekly (35.94%), then recovers at Daily (4.35%, R² = 0.66). Linear Regression remains stable across all granularities (16.3–17.0% TPFE), confirming the paradox is driven by recursive feedback topology rather than model complexity. Pointwise metrics systematically mask cumulative error propagation.
AI.conclusion: The Granularity Paradox is a structural phenomenon arising from the interaction between recursive forecasting architectures and temporal disaggregation, not model sophistication. Evaluating forecasts without goal-dependent cumulative metrics (e.g., TPFE) produces misleading assessments. The consensus-dissensus diagnostic offers a practical tool for identifying when standard model diagnostics conceal systematic error propagation, guiding practitioners toward architecture-appropriate granularity choices.

title: Evaluating calibrated refusal and safe usefulness in dual-use biology settings
summary: As AI agents are incorporated into life science workflows, the capabilities that speed discovery might also enable misuse. We present BioSecBench-Refusal, a benchmark for risk identification and refusal behavior for biological research tasks. The benchmark pairs 61 Routine tasks, legitimate analyses adapted from the published literature, with 46 Red-Team tasks, fictional scenarios that resemble real research but conceal a biosecurity hazard. Across 16 model-harness configurations, refusal rates ranged from 7\% to 74\% on Routine tasks and 1\% to 62\% on Red-Team tasks, with many configurations refusing legitimate Routine work at comparable or higher rates than concealed hazards. Refusals were most often triggered by provider API filters applied prior to agentic reasoning. However, models given room to reason showed the potential to identify more real threats. We release BioSecBench-Refusal as a tool for model developers to calibrate capability and caution for agentic biotech R\&D.

AI.tldr: BioSecBench-Refusal is a benchmark evaluating how AI agents handle biological research tasks, revealing that current models often refuse legitimate work at rates comparable to or higher than concealed biosecurity hazards, with most refusals triggered by API filters rather than agentic reasoning.
AI.motivation: As AI agents are increasingly integrated into life science workflows, their dual-use nature raises concerns: capabilities that accelerate discovery could also enable misuse. There is a need to systematically evaluate whether AI models can appropriately distinguish between legitimate biological research and potentially hazardous tasks.
AI.method: The authors constructed BioSecBench-Refusal, pairing 61 Routine tasks (legitimate analyses from published literature) with 46 Red-Team tasks (fictional scenarios resembling real research but concealing biosecurity hazards). They evaluated 16 model-harness configurations, measuring refusal rates across both task categories and analyzing whether refusals originated from provider API filters or from the model's own agentic reasoning.
AI.result: Refusal rates ranged from 7% to 74% on Routine tasks and 1% to 62% on Red-Team tasks. Many configurations refused legitimate Routine work at rates comparable to or exceeding those for concealed hazards. Most refusals were triggered by provider API filters applied before agentic reasoning. However, models given room to reason showed greater potential for identifying actual threats.
AI.conclusion: Current AI agent safeguards suffer from poor discrimination between legitimate and hazardous biological research tasks. The benchmark is released as a tool to help model developers better calibrate the balance between capability and caution in agentic biotech R&D.

title: Prompting Beats Fine-Tuning: Generative Expected Value Scoring for Statutory Term Retrieval
comment: Accepted to the ASAIL Workshop at ICAIL 2026
summary: Legal concepts in statutes are often expressed using vague terms, and practitioners frequently turn to case law to interpret them. We study the task of ranking case-law sentences by their usefulness for explaining a concept or target statutory term, using an established dataset of 26,959 sentences covering 42 U.S. Code concepts labeled into four explanatory-value categories. We compare two families of methods: (i) supervised fine-tuning of encoder-only models (ModernBERT) and (ii) zero-shot prompting of decoder-only models. We show that across all concepts and standard NDCG cutoffs, ModernBERT largely matches earlier BERT-family baselines. In contrast, prompting decoder-only models achieves the strongest overall effectiveness, with our best system surpassing all previously reported state-of-the-art results on this task.

AI.tldr: The paper compares supervised fine-tuning of encoder-only models (ModernBERT) and zero-shot prompting of decoder-only models for ranking case-law sentences by their explanatory value for vague statutory terms. ModernBERT matches prior BERT baselines, while prompting decoder-only models achieves new state-of-the-art results on a dataset of 26,959 sentences across 42 U.S. Code concepts.
AI.motivation: Statutory legal concepts often contain vague terms that require interpretation through case law. Practitioners need effective tools to identify the most explanatory case-law sentences for a given statutory term. Prior work established datasets and baselines for this ranking task, but there is room to explore whether modern architectures (ModernBERT encoder-only models and prompted decoder-only LLMs) can improve effectiveness.
AI.method: The paper compares two families of methods on a pre-existing dataset of 26,959 sentences covering 42 U.S. Code concepts, labeled into four explanatory-value categories: (i) supervised fine-tuning of encoder-only models, specifically ModernBERT; and (ii) zero-shot prompting of decoder-only large language models. Evaluation uses standard NDCG cutoff metrics across all concepts.
AI.result: ModernBERT largely matches the performance of earlier BERT-family baselines across all concepts and NDCG cutoffs. Zero-shot prompting of decoder-only models achieves the strongest overall effectiveness, with the best prompting system surpassing all previously reported state-of-the-art results on this task.
AI.conclusion: Decoder-only LLMs with zero-shot prompting are a superior approach for ranking case-law sentences by explanatory value compared to fine-tuned encoder-only models. ModernBERT offers no meaningful gains over earlier BERT variants for this task, suggesting that scaling decoder models and prompt engineering may be a more promising direction for legal-concept explanation tasks.

title: Agents with Feelings? Personality and Emotion in Multi-Agent Software Teams
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems for Software Engineering (SE) typically differentiate agents through roles and workflows, but little is known about how agents' behavioral profiles affect team performance. We investigate the impact of personality and emotion profiles on LLM agent teams using a psychology-informed framework that combines Big Five personality traits, basic emotions, SE-relevant work styles, and task roles. We evaluate 78 team-profile configurations across code generation and code review using four LLMs and 659 task instances. Results show that profile choice substantially affects both performance and team behavior. For code generation, the gap between the best and worst shared-profile configurations reaches 7.1-11.3 percentage points in pass@1 across models, while the best mixed-profile configuration outperforms the best shared-profile configuration in six of eight model-task settings. Profiles also influence collaboration dynamics and cost: fear and high-conscientiousness profiles increase revision activity, over-revision, and token usage without consistent performance gains. These findings identify agent profiles as an important design dimension in multi-agent SE systems, affecting not only task outcomes but also the efficiency of collaboration.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how personality and emotion profiles of LLM agents affect team performance in software engineering tasks. Using 78 team-profile configurations across code generation and review, the study finds profile choice significantly impacts performance (up to 11.3 pp gap), collaboration dynamics, and cost efficiency, with certain profiles like fear and high conscientiousness increasing revision activity without consistent performance gains.
AI.motivation: While multi-agent LLM systems for SE commonly differentiate agents by roles and workflows, the effect of agents' behavioral profiles (personality, emotions) on team outcomes remains unexplored. Understanding this dimension could unlock new ways to optimize agent team design.
AI.method: A psychology-informed framework combining Big Five personality traits, basic emotions, SE-relevant work styles, and task roles. 78 team-profile configurations were evaluated across code generation and code review tasks using four LLMs and 659 task instances, comparing shared-profile and mixed-profile team compositions.
AI.result: Profile choice substantially affects performance: pass@1 gaps of 7.1–11.3 pp between best/worst shared-profile configurations. Best mixed-profile configurations outperformed best shared-profile in 6/8 model-task settings. Fear and high-conscientiousness profiles increased revision activity, over-revision, and token usage without consistent performance gains.
AI.conclusion: Agent profiles represent a critical design dimension in multi-agent SE systems, influencing task outcomes, collaboration efficiency, and cost. Profile selection should be treated as a first-class design consideration alongside roles and workflows.

title: Depression Symptoms and Relational Patterns in 187k ChatGPT Histories
summary: Large language models are increasingly used as private, always-available conversational systems, but little is known about how people with depressive symptoms use them. Building on CSCW work on disclosure and peer support, we examine ChatGPT as an emerging informal support infrastructure: private, persistent, responsive, and available outside ordinary hours. We analyze 187,093 ChatGPT conversations from 766 participants who completed the PHQ-8, comparing those below the moderate-symptom threshold (score of 10) with those at or above it. Higher-PHQ participants used ChatGPT more for mental-health, interpersonal, loneliness, self-focused, and support-seeking conversations, with pronounced late-night and recurring month-level patterns. Their language contained more first-person singular pronouns and absolutist terms. They more often engaged ChatGPT in high-disclosure contexts, but professional redirection was not higher. Language-based prediction was modest and insufficient for screening (AUROC 0.591). We argue these histories should not be treated as clinical screening data but as evidence LLMs are increasingly used as informal support infrastructure.

AI.tldr: Analysis of 187K ChatGPT conversations from 766 PHQ-8-assessed participants reveals that users with elevated depressive symptoms engage more heavily in late-night, mental-health, and high-disclosure interactions, exhibiting distinct linguistic markers (first-person singular, absolutist terms). However, language-based screening proved insufficient (AUROC 0.591), leading the authors to argue these interaction histories should be viewed not as clinical data but as evidence that LLMs function as an emerging informal support infrastructure.
AI.motivation: Little is known about how individuals with depressive symptoms actually use LLMs like ChatGPT in real-world settings. The authors build on CSCW literature on disclosure and peer support to investigate whether ChatGPT serves as a novel informal support infrastructure — one that is private, persistent, always-available, and distinct from traditional peer-support channels. Understanding these usage patterns carries implications for design, policy, and whether such data should be leveraged for screening.
AI.method: The authors collected 187,093 anonymized ChatGPT conversation histories from 766 participants who completed the PHQ-8 depression screener. Participants were split at the moderate-symptom threshold (PHQ-8 ≥ 10). Analyses included: (1) comparative content analysis of conversation topics (mental health, interpersonal, loneliness, self-focused, support-seeking); (2) temporal pattern analysis (late-night usage, month-level recurrence); (3) linguistic analysis (first-person singular pronouns, absolutist terms, disclosure levels); (4) evaluation of professional redirection rates; and (5) a language-based machine-learning screening model assessed via AUROC.
AI.result: Higher-PHQ participants used ChatGPT significantly more for mental-health, interpersonal, loneliness, self-focused, and support-seeking conversations, with pronounced late-night and recurring month-level temporal patterns. Their language contained more first-person singular pronouns and absolutist terms, and they engaged more often in high-disclosure contexts. Professional redirection rates did not differ between groups. The language-based predictive model achieved an AUROC of only 0.591, well below clinically acceptable screening thresholds.
AI.conclusion: ChatGPT conversation histories should not be treated as clinical screening data given the poor predictive performance. Instead, these usage patterns constitute evidence that LLMs are increasingly functioning as informal support infrastructure for people experiencing depressive symptoms — serving as private, persistent, and always-available conversational partners outside of traditional clinical or peer-support channels. This reframing has important implications for how CSCW researchers and designers approach LLM-based systems.

title: Narrative World Model: Narratology-Grounded Writer Memory for Long-Form Fiction
comment: 23 pages, 4 figures; 9-page main text plus appendix. Preprint
summary: Long-form fiction writers need memory that answers multi-hop questions about evolving story state: who knows a secret and when they learned it, whether an event preceded the narration that revealed it, whether a setup paid off, and how a relationship shifted. General-purpose retrieval and agent-memory systems represent entities and facts but not the narratological structure these questions turn on, so they surface the wrong evidence or none at all. We introduce the Narrative World Model (NWM), a writer-memory system that pairs a narratology-grounded typed temporal-state graph with query-conditioned hybrid retrieval. To measure memory rather than the answerer, we read every system through a single held-constant Opus 4.8 reader over only that system's chapter-safe evidence, on a reproducible public corpus and a validated multi-hop benchmark, and we compare against the strongest existing temporal-knowledge-graph agent-memory framework, Graphiti/Zep (Rasmussen et al., 2025). NWM substantially and significantly outperforms this baseline on multi-hop narratological QA across both corpora, and far exceeds GraphRAG and flat retrieval. The advantage is representational rather than an artifact of extraction: it survives rebuilding the baseline with NWM's own extractor, and traces to its narratology-grounded structure and query-conditioned retrieval, not to graph size or extractor quality.

AI.tldr: The Narrative World Model (NWM) is a writer-memory system using a narratology-grounded typed temporal-state graph with query-conditioned hybrid retrieval, significantly outperforming existing temporal-KG agent systems on multi-hop narratological QA.
AI.motivation: Long-form fiction writers need memory systems that can answer complex multi-hop questions about evolving story state (secrets, chronology, setups/payoffs, relationship shifts). Existing retrieval and agent-memory systems represent entities and facts but lack the narratological structure needed to answer such questions, surfacing wrong or no evidence.
AI.method: The NWM pairs a narratology-grounded typed temporal-state graph with query-conditioned hybrid retrieval. It is evaluated by reading every system through a single held-constant Opus 4.8 reader over only chapter-safe evidence, using a reproducible public corpus and a validated multi-hop benchmark. Comparison is made against Graphiti/Zep (Rasmussen et al., 2025), the strongest existing temporal-knowledge-graph agent-memory framework.
AI.result: NWM substantially and significantly outperforms Graphiti/Zep on multi-hop narratological QA across both corpora, and far exceeds GraphRAG and flat retrieval. The advantage is representational (not an artifact of extraction): it persists when rebuilding the baseline with NWM's own extractor, and traces to narratology-grounded structure and query-conditioned retrieval rather than graph size or extractor quality.
AI.conclusion: A narratology-grounded representational structure is critical for multi-hop story-state QA in long-form fiction; NWM's typed temporal-state graph and query-conditioned retrieval provide a robust, generalizable advantage over entity/fact-based agent-memory systems.

title: The yes-no bias of large language models reflects answer order and wording, not shifts in moral judgment
summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly issue judgments read as binary verdicts, and a growing literature reports such judgments shifting under logically irrelevant changes of wording - among them an amplified yes-no bias on moral dilemmas, absent in humans. A single framing cannot say what such a shift is: in a yes/no question the word "no" is at once logical verdict, lexical token, and last-printed option. We introduce a psychometric battery that separates these: crossed symmetrization - every logically irrelevant factor flipped in balanced pairs - across a corpus of question forms. A graded rating across logically equivalent forms recovers a coherent internal moral scale: frontier models' stance $θ$ is nearly format-invariant (cross-form incoherence 0.12-0.21 on a $\pm 1$ axis); small open-weight models fail in model-specific ways. Forcing the verdict through yes/no overlays a decomposable artifact: an order bias toward the last-printed option - opposite to classic human primacy - plus a lexical pull toward the word "no"; the artifact is substantial only in the Claude models (story-averaged -0.32 to -0.86), $\approx 0$ for GPT-5.5 and Gemini, and shrinks under extended reasoning. The word and the verdict share one token; swapping the words for arbitrary labels separates them, and the verdict-attached logical bias proves $\approx 0$ for every frontier model, while model-specific label and order attachments remain: the models are not drawn toward rejecting - the pull follows the printed surface, not the verdict it carries. A minimal model, $P = σ((θ\pm m)/s)$, summarizes any such artifact by a framing susceptibility m and a moral decisiveness s, measurably distinct from sampling temperature. The battery applies unchanged to any dilemma set and binary format: measuring what a model values requires crossing the frames of the question, not asking once.

AI.tldr: LLMs show framing-induced verdict shifts on moral dilemmas, but these are decomposable artifacts (order bias toward last option + lexical pull toward "no"), not genuine moral inconsistency. A crossed symmetrization psychometric battery reveals frontier models have coherent internal moral scales, with artifact magnitude varying by model family and shrinking under extended reasoning.
AI.motivation: Prior work reports LLM judgments on moral dilemmas shift under logically irrelevant wording changes (e.g., amplified yes-no bias). However, a single yes/no framing conflates logical verdict, lexical token, and serial position, making it impossible to diagnose what drives the shift. The authors aim to disentangle these confounds.
AI.method: Crossed symmetrization: every logically irrelevant factor (order, lexical label, response format) is flipped in balanced pairs across a corpus of question forms. This yields (1) a graded rating scale recovering an internal moral stance θ, and (2) decomposition of binary yes/no artifacts into order bias (last-option preference), lexical bias (pull toward "no"), and label-attached logical bias. A minimal model P = σ((θ ± m)/s) captures framing susceptibility m and moral decisiveness s.
AI.result: Frontier models (GPT-5.5, Gemini, Claude) show near-format-invariant moral stance θ (cross-form incoherence 0.12–0.21 on ±1 axis). Small open-weight models fail model-specifically. Yes/no forcing adds artifacts: substantial in Claude (−0.32 to −0.86), ≈0 for GPT-5.5 and Gemini, shrinking under extended reasoning. When labels are arbitrary symbols, verdict-attached logical bias ≈0 for all frontier models — the pull follows printed surface, not verdict content. Parameters m and s are distinct from temperature.
AI.conclusion: Measuring what an LLM values requires crossing the frames of the question, not asking once. The crossed-symmetrization battery cleanly separates a model's stable moral stance from format-induced artifacts, and applies unchanged to any dilemma set and binary format.

title: Exogenous Dropout: A Simple, Strong Baseline for Corruption-Robust Time Series Forecasting with Covariates
summary: Time series forecasters that use exogenous covariates are fragile in deployment: when those covariates are noised, temporally misaligned, or missing, strong exogenous-fusion and exogenous-adapted models can degrade far above the endogenous-only floor. We study whether such robustness requires specialized architectures, or whether it can be obtained through a simple training intervention. We propose exogenous dropout, a model-agnostic method that randomly zeros whole exogenous channels during training. Across electricity-price forecasting, reservoir hydrology, and meteorology, exogenous dropout substantially improves robustness under Gaussian noise, temporal misalignment, and fully missing channels, while preserving clean accuracy. Applied to a dual-correlation network, it yields the most robust model in our experiments, outperforming a deliberately strong bounded architectural foil, BoundEx, which combines a learnable gate, a fallback residual to the endogenous backbone, and per-channel exogenous FiLM modulation. Architecture-by-dropout ablations, gate-behavior diagnostics, and a representation-level bound show that explicit architectural boundedness is not necessary for this robustness: an unbounded model trained with exogenous dropout is more robust than the bounded model in every domain. We release a corruption-robustness benchmark and recommend exogenous dropout as a simple, strong baseline for future work on time series forecasting with covariates.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Exogenous Dropout, a simple, model-agnostic training intervention that randomly zeros entire exogenous covariate channels during training. It demonstrates that this method yields superior robustness to corrupted covariates (noise, misalignment, missingness) compared to specialized bounded architectures, across electricity, hydrology, and meteorology forecasting tasks.
AI.motivation: Time series forecasters relying on exogenous covariates are brittle in deployment — when covariates are noised, temporally misaligned, or missing, model performance can degrade severely, even falling below endogenous-only baselines. The authors investigate whether robustness to such covariate corruption requires specialized bounded architectures or can instead be achieved via a simple training intervention.
AI.method: Exogenous Dropout: during training, entire exogenous covariate channels are randomly zeroed out with some probability. This is compared against a deliberately bounded architectural baseline called BoundEx, which incorporates a learnable gate, a fallback residual connection to the endogenous backbone, and per-channel FiLM modulation. The study evaluates both approaches under Gaussian noise, temporal misalignment, and fully missing channels across three domains: electricity-price forecasting, reservoir hydrology, and meteorology.
AI.result: Exogenous dropout substantially improves robustness under all corruption types while preserving clean-data accuracy. When applied to a dual-correlation network, it produces the most robust model overall, outperforming the specialized bounded BoundEx architecture. Ablation studies, gate-behavior diagnostics, and representation-level bound analyses reveal that explicit architectural boundedness is unnecessary — the unbounded model with exogenous dropout is more robust than the bounded model in every domain tested.
AI.conclusion: Robustness to covariate corruption does not require specialized bounded architectures; a simple exogenous dropout training intervention suffices and generalizes across domains and model architectures. The authors release a corruption-robustness benchmark and recommend exogenous dropout as a strong, simple baseline for future work on time series forecasting with covariates.

title: ShadowProbe: Language-Extensible Detection of Hidden Algorithmic Complexity Vulnerabilities
summary:
Algorithmic Complexity Vulnerabilities (ACVs) arise when adversarial inputs trigger worst-case execution behavior, causing severe performance degradation or Denial-of-Service conditions. A key but underexplored source is shadow complexity: non-trivial computational costs hidden inside seemingly benign standard library APIs. Because these costs are invisible at call sites, attackers can exploit them to induce unexpected superlinear runtime behavior. Existing ACV detectors often rely on fuzzing, symbolic execution, or hybrid analysis, but they are usually language-specific, require substantial manual effort to construct harnesses, and depend on heavy runtime instrumentation.
  We present ShadowProbe, a scalable and language-extensible framework for discovering ACVs through lightweight static analysis, automated reconstruction of execution contexts, and Large Language Model (LLM) assisted test generation. ShadowProbe uses a structured multi-stage pipeline: it statically screens for candidate functions guided by shadow-complexity signals, reconstructs minimal executable contexts from project-level symbols, and synthesizes size-controlled inputs to probe worst-case behavior. It then validates candidates using execution-time measurements and robust statistical growth inference, separating true algorithmic blowups from runtime noise such as garbage collection and JIT compilation effects.
  We evaluate ShadowProbe on the WISE benchmark, where it consistently improves analysis efficiency over existing approaches. We further apply it to large-scale systems including CPython, the JDK, Zig, Rustc, and vLLM, uncovering many previously unknown ACVs, many of which have been confirmed and partially remediated by maintainers. These results show that ShadowProbe can identify hidden algorithmic risks across diverse real-world codebases.

AI.tldr: ShadowProbe is a scalable, language-extensible framework that detects Algorithmic Complexity Vulnerabilities (ACVs) from "shadow complexity" in standard library APIs by combining lightweight static analysis, automated context reconstruction, and LLM-assisted test generation, validated through statistical growth inference on execution-time measurements.
AI.motivation: ACVs from shadow complexity—hidden superlinear costs inside seemingly benign standard library APIs—are underexplored because existing detectors are language-specific, require heavy manual harness construction, and depend on expensive runtime instrumentation. A more automated, scalable, and language-agnostic approach is needed.
AI.method: ShadowProbe employs a multi-stage pipeline: (1) static screening for candidate functions using shadow-complexity signals, (2) automated reconstruction of minimal executable contexts from project-level symbols, (3) LLM-assisted synthesis of size-controlled inputs to probe worst-case behavior, and (4) validation via execution-time measurements with robust statistical growth inference to distinguish genuine algorithmic blowups from noise (e.g., GC, JIT).
AI.result: On the WISE benchmark, ShadowProbe consistently improves analysis efficiency over existing approaches. Applied to CPython, JDK, Zig, Rustc, and vLLM, it uncovered many previously unknown ACVs, with numerous confirmed and partially remediated by maintainers.
AI.conclusion: ShadowProbe demonstrates that lightweight static analysis combined with LLM-assisted test generation can effectively and scalably identify hidden algorithmic risks across diverse, real-world codebases, offering a practical alternative to heavier fuzzing and symbolic execution methods.

title: Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration
summary: Multi-hop question answering and retrieval-augmented reasoning require selecting evidence passages that are jointly useful for answering a query. However, most retrievers still score passages independently or make locally supervised sequential decisions, which can fail when evidence usefulness depends on compatibility among passages. LLM-based set selection can model such interactions, but its computational cost limits practical use. We address this gap by formulating multi-hop retrieval as query-set compatibility scoring and propose a set-level retrieval framework. Our training objective teaches retrievers to rank complete and compatible evidence sets above incomplete, noisy alternatives, making set scoring more robust to variable-length and partially noisy contexts. We instantiate the framework with two complementary set scorers: ParaSet, a lightweight late-interaction scorer that applies self-attention over precomputed bi-encoder embeddings for fast candidate-set exploration, and SetCE, a cross-encoder-based reranker trained with the same set-level objective. Experiments on various multi-hop QA benchmarks show that set-level compatibility learning improves retrieval performance and downstream QA task performance. We further show that the proposed set-level retrievers not only outperform document-level retrievers, but also exhibit complementary retrieval characteristics: combining their outputs yields stronger performance than simply retrieving more passages from a single document-level retriever.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes reformulating multi-hop retrieval as query-set compatibility scoring, training retrievers to rank complete evidence sets above incomplete/noisy ones. It introduces two complementary set scorers—ParaSet (lightweight late-interaction) and SetCE (cross-encoder reranker)—that together outperform traditional document-level retrievers on multi-hop QA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing retrievers score passages independently or make locally supervised sequential decisions, failing when evidence usefulness depends on inter-passage compatibility. LLM-based set selection captures these interactions but is computationally prohibitive. A practical, set-aware retrieval approach is needed.
AI.method: The authors formulate multi-hop retrieval as query-set compatibility scoring with a set-level training objective that ranks complete, compatible evidence sets above incomplete or noisy alternatives. They instantiate this with two models: (1) ParaSet, a lightweight late-interaction scorer using self-attention over precomputed bi-encoder embeddings for fast candidate exploration; (2) SetCE, a cross-encoder reranker trained with the same set-level objective.
AI.result: Set-level compatibility learning improves both retrieval performance and downstream QA accuracy across multiple multi-hop QA benchmarks. The two set-level retrievers outperform document-level retrievers and exhibit complementary characteristics—combining their outputs yields stronger performance than simply retrieving more passages from a single document-level retriever.
AI.conclusion: Set-level retrieval with compatibility scoring effectively addresses the limitations of independent passage scoring for multi-hop reasoning, and the complementary nature of ParaSet and SetCE enables further gains through their combination.

title: What Do AI Agents Actually Change? An Empirical Taxonomy of Mutation Patterns in Performance-Improving Pull Requests
summary: AI coding agents are black boxes: we cannot inspect how they generate code, but we can inspect what they change. This distinction matters for search-based software engineering (SBSE), where techniques such as genetic improvement (in the performance-optimisation application we study) depend on mutation operators that reflect how code is actually transformed. Fewer than 1% of the 33,596 agent PRs in AIDev-pop target performance, making each case a rare window into otherwise opaque agent behaviour. We classify 1,254 performance-relevant diff hunks from 216 of these PRs, spanning five agent systems, against the 18-category syntactic mutation taxonomy of Even-Mendoza et al. (2025) using a dual-LLM intersection pipeline. Three categories dominate: name modification (37.0%), object creation (26.4%), and type change (22.7%), a profile markedly different from prior GI corpora where no change accounted for 84%. Each agent's deployed system commits to a distinctive mutation vocabulary, and each performance strategy activates a largely disjoint category subset. Agent identity and target strategy are therefore informative priors that narrow the effective SBSE operator space. Replication package: https://github.com/5uper6rain/ssbse-challenge-2026

AI.tldr: AI coding agents exhibit systematic, identifiable mutation patterns when optimizing code for performance. By classifying 1,254 performance-relevant diff hunks from 216 agent PRs across five systems, the authors find three dominant mutation categories (name modification, object creation, type change) that differ sharply from prior genetic improvement corpora. Agent identity and target strategy serve as informative priors for narrowing the SBSE operator space.
AI.motivation: AI coding agents are opaque in how they generate code, yet search-based software engineering (SBSE) techniques like genetic improvement depend on mutation operators that reflect real code transformations. With fewer than 1% of 33,596 agent PRs in AIDev-pop targeting performance, each case is a rare opportunity to study agent behavior empirically. The authors aim to characterize the syntactic mutation vocabulary that agents actually deploy, providing evidence to guide SBSE operator design.
AI.method: The study uses the AIDev-pop dataset of 33,596 agent-generated PRs, isolating 216 PRs with 1,254 performance-relevant diff hunks across five agent systems. These hunks are classified against the 18-category syntactic mutation taxonomy of Even-Mendoza et al. (2025) using a dual-LLM intersection pipeline, where two language models independently label each hunk and only agreed-upon classifications are retained, ensuring annotation reliability.
AI.result: Three mutation categories dominate: name modification (37.0%), object creation (26.4%), and type change (22.7%). This profile contrasts sharply with prior GI corpora where the "no change" category accounted for 84% of mutations. Each agent system exhibits a distinctive mutation vocabulary, and each performance strategy (e.g., caching, algorithmic optimization) activates a largely disjoint subset of mutation categories. Agent identity and target strategy thus act as informative priors that significantly narrow the effective SBSE operator space.
AI.conclusion: Agent-specific and strategy-specific mutation profiles provide actionable priors for designing SBSE mutation operators, moving beyond generic taxonomies. The dual-LLM annotation pipeline offers a scalable method for empirical analysis of agent behavior through observable code changes rather than unobservable generation processes.

title: Plainbook: Data Science, in Plain Language
summary:
Jupyter Notebooks have become widely adopted in data science, as they allow the sharing of reproducible computational analysis. They are, however, accessible only to people who understand computer code. To reach the broader audience of scientists interested in data analysis and computation, but unfamiliar with code, we introduce Plainbook, notebooks centered on natural language rather than code.
  Plainbook is based on two principles: promote the natural language descriptions, and verify the values. In plainbook, the natural language descriptions are preserved, rather than the resulting code; the code is generated automatically from the cell descriptions. As natural language is read top to bottom, Plainbook adopts a linear execution semantics, in which cells are guaranteed to be executed in the order in which they appear; there is no "hidden state" or out-of-order execution as in Jupyter. To allow users who may not understand code to verify the correctness of the computation, we have built into Plainbook verification mechanisms centered on values and value inspection. These include mechanisms that focus on individual cells, akin to unit tests, as well as global mechanisms. Both the linear execution semantics, and the verification mechanisms, are underpinned by a snapshot kernel that caches execution states and makes execution and verification efficient.

AI.tldr: Plainbook reimagines computational notebooks by centering on natural language descriptions instead of code, with automatic code generation, linear execution semantics, and built-in verification mechanisms to make data analysis accessible to non-programmers.
AI.motivation: Jupyter Notebooks have become standard in data science for sharing reproducible analysis, but they remain inaccessible to scientists who lack programming skills. The authors aim to bridge this gap by creating a notebook system that preserves natural language as the primary artifact rather than code, democratizing computational analysis for a broader scientific audience.
AI.method: Plainbook operates on two core principles: (1) natural language descriptions are preserved as first-class entities, with code generated automatically from cell descriptions, and (2) value verification mechanisms are built in for correctness checking. The system enforces linear execution semantics — cells execute strictly top-to-bottom with no hidden state or out-of-order execution. Verification includes both per-cell mechanisms (akin to unit tests) and global mechanisms. A snapshot kernel underpins the system, caching execution states to make both execution and verification efficient.
