AI.result: The paper introduces Plainbook as a functional system with linear execution guarantees, automatic code generation from natural language, and efficient verification via snapshot caching. The system enables non-coders to engage in reproducible computational analysis with mechanisms for verifying correctness without understanding the underlying code.
AI.conclusion: Plainbook demonstrates that computational notebooks can be redesigned around natural language rather than code, making data science more inclusive. The combination of linear execution semantics, automatic code generation, and value-centered verification, supported by a snapshot kernel, provides a viable path toward accessible and trustworthy computational analysis for non-programmers.

title: FirstResearch: Auditable Question Formation for LLM Scientific Discovery Agents
summary: LLM systems for scientific discovery increasingly assist with ideation, literature synthesis, experiment planning, and report generation, but the first research question they propose can remain difficult to audit: it may sound plausible without exposing the mechanism, falsifier, or assumption that a scientist should inspect. We introduce FirstResearch, a first-principles research-question formation framework for scientific LLM agents whose core artifact is a structured Research Question Certificate. The certificate records primitive definitions, assumptions, a mechanism model, a tension or contradiction, a falsifiable hypothesis, a minimal decisive test, and a failure update rule, making the proposed question inspectable before downstream execution. On ten LLM-agent research topics, FirstResearch outperforms controlled prompt-level baselines inspired by AI co-scientist, Agent Laboratory, and AI Scientist-v2 under a primary DeepSeek-blind-judge protocol. A Gemini-2.5-Flash independent-judge rescore of the same 40 baseline packages preserves the system-level ranking, with FirstResearch scoring 4.86/5 versus 4.38/5 for the strongest baseline and Pearson agreement of 0.865 on average score. A one-repeat ablation checkpoint further suggests that the certificate-centered core is the strongest component: certificate-only scoring reaches 4.90/5 under DeepSeek and 4.88/5 under Gemini, while removing certificates drops below 1/5 under both judges. These results are preliminary and use LLM judges rather than human domain experts, but they support a narrow scientific-discovery claim: explicit derivation constraints are a promising mechanism for making LLM-generated scientific questions more auditable. Code, prompts, saved outputs, and reproduction scripts are available at https://github.com/louiswang524/FirstResearch.

AI.tldr: FirstResearch introduces a structured "Research Question Certificate" that constrains LLM scientific agents to generate auditable research questions by explicitly recording definitions, assumptions, mechanisms, falsifiable hypotheses, and failure update rules. The system outperforms baselines under LLM-judge evaluation, with the certificate component proving essential.
AI.motivation: LLM systems for scientific discovery can propose research questions that sound plausible but lack inspectable components (mechanisms, falsifiers, assumptions), making them difficult for scientists to audit before committing to downstream execution.
AI.method: FirstResearch is a first-principles framework centered on a structured Research Question Certificate containing: primitive definitions, assumptions, a mechanism model, a tension/contradiction, a falsifiable hypothesis, a minimal decisive test, and a failure update rule. Evaluation used ten LLM-agent research topics, comparing against prompt-level baselines from AI co-scientist, Agent Laboratory, and AI Scientist-v2. Primary judging used DeepSeek-blind-judge protocol, with an independent Gemini-2.5-Flash rescore. An ablation study isolated the certificate component.
AI.result: FirstResearch scored 4.86/5 versus 4.38/5 for the strongest baseline under the Gemini independent judge, with Pearson agreement of 0.865. Ablation showed certificate-only scoring reached 4.90/5 (DeepSeek) and 4.88/5 (Gemini), while removing certificates dropped below 1/5 under both judges.
AI.conclusion: Explicit derivation constraints — operationalized through the Research Question Certificate — are a promising mechanism for making LLM-generated scientific questions more auditable. Results are preliminary and rely on LLM judges rather than human domain experts.

title: Prompt Robustness Is Task-Dependent: Comparing Objective and Belief-Style Questions in LLM Evaluation
summary: Survey-style evaluations of large language models often treat a prompted response as a measure of a model's values or beliefs. This assumption is particularly fragile when responses are read as evidence of political values, social attitudes, or beliefs. We ask whether prompt robustness differs between objective questions with fixed answers and subjective questions that ask for opinions or values. We evaluate four instruction-tuned model families on three objective datasets (MMLU, ARC, and CulturalBench) and three subjective datasets (Political Compass Test, ValueBench, and World Values Survey). For each question/statement, we apply multiple types of prompt changes, such as variations in wording, framing, and format, and measure whether the model gives the same answer across variants. Using a binomial generalized estimating equation, we find significant effects of model, dataset, prompt category, and their interactions. The dataset type effect is also significant, and the interaction between dataset type and prompt category is large. These results show that prompt robustness depends on the question type, the prompt change, and the model.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether prompt robustness differs between objective questions (with fixed correct answers) and subjective questions (asking for opinions/values) across four instruction-tuned LLM families. Using multiple prompt variations and a binomial GEE analysis, the authors find that robustness significantly depends on question type, prompt category, model, and their interactions — with especially large interaction effects between dataset type and prompt category.
AI.motivation: Survey-style evaluations often treat LLM responses as evidence of political values or social beliefs, yet this assumption is fragile because responses may shift under trivial prompt variations. The authors aim to systematically test whether prompt robustness differs between objective factual questions and subjective opinion/value questions — a distinction largely unexamined in prior work.
AI.method: Four instruction-tuned model families are evaluated on three objective datasets (MMLU, ARC, CulturalBench) and three subjective datasets (Political Compass Test, ValueBench, World Values Survey). For each question, multiple prompt variations are applied — spanning wording changes, framing shifts, and format differences — and answer consistency across variants is measured. A binomial generalized estimating equation (GEE) is used to model the effects of model, dataset, prompt category, dataset type, and their interactions on response stability.
AI.result: Significant main effects are found for model, dataset, prompt category, and dataset type (objective vs. subjective). The interaction between dataset type and prompt category is large and significant, indicating that different types of prompt changes affect objective and subjective questions differently. Overall, prompt robustness is contingent on the interplay of question type, the nature of the prompt perturbation, and the specific model.
AI.conclusion: Prompt robustness is not a uniform property of LLMs but varies systematically with question type and prompt manipulation. This undermines the practice of treating single-prompt survey responses as reliable indicators of model values or beliefs, particularly for subjective questions. Evaluators should account for prompt sensitivity when interpreting LLM outputs as evidence of attitudes or opinions.

title: Empirical Minimal-Realisation Compression of Deep Neural Networks via Controllability-Observability Tests
summary: Deep neural networks often contain substantial hidden-state redundancy, but most compression methods operate directly on weights, neurons, or quantised representations without explicitly characterising the dynamical role of internal states. This paper proposes a controllability-observability framework for empirical state-order reduction of deep neural networks. By viewing a trained network as a depth-indexed nonlinear dynamical system, we construct data-driven reachability, observability, and balanced Gramians from hidden-state snapshots and output Jacobians. The resulting A/B/C tests estimate layer-wise reachable, observable, and jointly reachable--observable ranks. These ranks are then used not only as diagnostic measures of hidden-state redundancy, but also as actual compressed layer widths for realised reduced networks. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 compare the proposed balanced realisation against projection-based reduction, unstructured pruning, structured pruning, low-rank SVD, dynamic INT8 quantisation, and linear baselines. On MNIST, a four-layer SiLU DNN is reduced from state order 1024 to 277, giving 72.95% state compression and 73.48% parameter compression, while maintaining 95.45% accuracy compared with 96.60% for the full model. On CIFAR-10, a larger SiLU DNN is reduced from state order 4608 to 1339, giving 70.94% state compression and 83.09% parameter compression, while preserving accuracy from 54.45% to 54.44% and reducing CUDA inference latency by approximately 3X. The results show that balanced reachable-observable ranks provide a principled empirical minimal-realisation criterion for designing compact neural architectures with little or no loss in accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a control-theoretic framework for compressing deep neural networks by identifying and removing hidden-state redundancy through reachability, observability, and balanced Gramians, achieving 70–73% state compression and up to 83% parameter reduction while maintaining accuracy on MNIST and CIFAR-10, with a ~3× inference latency improvement.
AI.motivation: Deep neural networks contain substantial hidden-state redundancy, but existing compression methods (pruning, quantization, low-rank factorization) operate directly on weights or representations without characterizing the dynamical role of internal states. The authors argue that a principled framework based on controllability and observability from systems theory can provide a more theoretically grounded criterion for determining minimal network width.
AI.method: The authors model a trained DNN as a depth-indexed nonlinear dynamical system. They compute data-driven reachability Gramians (from forward-pass hidden-state snapshots), observability Gramians (from output Jacobians via backpropagation), and balanced Gramians (via simultaneous diagonalization). These yield A/B/C tests that estimate layer-wise reachable rank, observable rank, and jointly reachable–observable rank. These ranks serve both as diagnostic measures and as the actual compressed layer widths for reduced networks. The approach is compared against projection-based reduction, unstructured/structured pruning, low-rank SVD, INT8 quantization, and linear baselines on MNIST and CIFAR-10.
AI.result: On MNIST, a 4-layer SiLU DNN was reduced from state order 1024 to 277 (72.95% state compression, 73.48% parameter compression) with 95.45% accuracy vs. 96.60% full model. On CIFAR-10, a larger SiLU DNN was reduced from 4608 to 1339 (70.94% state compression, 83.09% parameter compression), preserving accuracy (54.45% to 54.44%) and achieving ~3× reduction in CUDA inference latency. The balanced realization consistently outperformed all competing methods.
AI.conclusion: Balanced reachable–observable ranks provide a principled, empirical minimal-realization criterion for designing compact neural architectures with negligible accuracy loss. The framework bridges dynamical systems theory and practical neural network compression, offering both diagnostic insight into hidden-state redundancy and actionable reduced architectures.

title: Privilege and confidentiality in generative AI workflows
summary: Generative AI (GenAI) systems store and process client data in three distinct ways: in the model's parameters through training and memorisation, in the context window during a live session, and in knowledge databases for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Each mode creates different and often counter-intuitive risks to confidentiality and legal professional privilege, and each calls for specific governance responses. Drawing on the first English and American decisions to address privilege and generative AI, UK and Munir v Secretary of State for the Home Department and United States v Heppner, on the orthodox privilege authorities against which those decisions must be read, and on recent computer science research, we explain the three modes of data storage and processing in terms accessible to practitioners and analyse the legal consequences of each. We then situate the analysis within the regulatory framework governing solicitors in England and Wales and within the ordinary principles of professional negligence, arguing that the standard of effective information governance (and with it the benchmark against which negligence and misconduct will be measured) is changing. Although we write primarily for SRA-regulated practitioners, our data-governance analysis is framed to extend to any jurisdiction in which the protection of privilege or professional secrecy depends on demonstrable confidentiality. The ultimate aim of this article is to help legal services professionals understand salient data leakage risks in GenAI systems and thereby facilitate a more responsible deployment of GenAI on client data and other sensitive material.

AI.tldr: Generative AI systems process client data in three modes—model parameters, context windows, and RAG databases—each posing distinct risks to confidentiality and legal privilege. This paper explains these mechanisms, analyzes legal consequences through recent case law, and argues that the standard for information governance in legal practice is evolving to require responsible GenAI deployment.
AI.motivation: Legal professionals increasingly use GenAI tools without fully understanding how client data is stored and processed, creating underappreciated risks to confidentiality and legal professional privilege. The authors aim to bridge the gap between computer science and legal practice to enable responsible deployment.
AI.method: The authors employ a doctrinal legal methodology combined with technical analysis. They analyze two recent foundational cases (UK and Munir v Secretary of State for the Home Department; United States v Heppner) alongside orthodox privilege authorities, and synthesize recent computer science research on GenAI data storage to produce a practitioner-accessible framework for understanding and governing these risks.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that each of the three data-processing modes (training/memorization, context windows, and RAG databases) generates distinct and often counter-intuitive confidentiality risks requiring tailored governance responses. The standard of effective information governance is demonstrably shifting, raising the benchmark against which professional negligence and misconduct will be measured, particularly for SRA-regulated solicitors.
AI.conclusion: The standard for information governance in legal practice is changing. Practitioners must understand the specific data-leakage risks posed by different GenAI processing modes to meet evolving duties of confidentiality and privilege protection. The framework extends beyond England and Wales to any jurisdiction where privilege depends on demonstrable confidentiality.

title: SCOReD: Student-Aware CoT Optimization for Recommendation Distillation
summary:
Chain-of-thought (CoT) distillation in the recommendation domain is a necessary precursor to RL training, but raw teacher traces are ill-suited to this task. Large teachers approach the recommendation task with unusually high reasoning uncertainty, repeatedly rechecking their answers without revising them; supervised fine-tuning on such traces produces verbose students that never revise their initial guess. Furthermore, due to the novelty of the recommendation domain, the teacher's reasoning traces are highly out-of-distribution for the small student LLM.
  We propose Student-Aware CoT Optimization for Recommendation Distillation (SCOReD), a CoT optimization framework tailored to recommendation that first parses each teacher trace into typed segments and uses the student LLM's attention to score the importance of each segment. Then SCOReD dynamically selects a per-segment edit (KEEP / REWRITE / FUSE / PRUNE) based on the output length and comparative log probability lift of the answer given the edit as per the student. Therefore, SCOReD prunes redundant sections of the reasoning trace while preserving information-dense sections and adapts raw teacher traces to the student's output distribution. Training on SCOReD-optimized CoTs provides a cleaner learning signal to the student model and improves over baseline SFT by 1.56% NDCG and 1.9% Recall@5, while reducing reasoning length by 27.3%.

AI.tldr: SCOReD is a CoT optimization framework for recommendation distillation that uses student attention to score trace segments and applies dynamic edits (KEEP/REWRITE/FUSE/PRUNE), improving NDCG by 1.56%, Recall@5 by 1.9%, and reducing reasoning length by 27.3%.
AI.motivation: Raw teacher CoT traces are problematic for recommendation distillation: (1) teachers exhibit high reasoning uncertainty with redundant rechecking without revising, leading to verbose students; (2) teacher traces are out-of-distribution for smaller student LLMs due to the novelty of the recommendation domain.
AI.method: SCOReD parses teacher traces into typed segments, scores each segment's importance using the student LLM's attention weights, and dynamically selects per-segment edits (KEEP, REWRITE, FUSE, or PRUNE) based on output length constraints and comparative log probability lift of the answer given each edit as evaluated by the student model.
AI.result: SCOReD-optimized CoTs yield +1.56% NDCG and +1.9% Recall@5 over baseline SFT, while reducing reasoning trace length by 27.3%.
AI.conclusion: Student-aware CoT optimization that prunes redundant segments while preserving information-dense ones and adapting traces to the student's distribution provides a cleaner learning signal, outperforming standard SFT on raw teacher traces.

title: The Cathedral and the Bazaar of Software Vulnerabilities: From the NVD to the CNAs
summary: For decades, the National Vulnerability Database (NVD), the "Cathedral", has been the reference source for vulnerability information for downstream research and industry tasks, e.g., software update prioritization. An emerging "Bazaar" of diverse CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) has created many alternative and sometimes diverging sources. We conduct a systematic analysis of divergence in Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) metrics covering the NVD and the public CNAs. We also check for self-divergence: two identical textual descriptions of CVEs with identical CWEs are rated differently by the same CNA. The odds of diverging are widespread, not uniform and sometimes unexpected. The assessment of Attack Complexity, User Interaction, and Impact are the major metrics where divergence happens. To understand the root causes, we perform a qualitative study by reaching out to the NVD and other CNAs (both open sources and proprietary products). We also discussed the findings at the CVSS Special Interest Group of FIRST, the community responsible for maintaining and evolving the CVSS standard. The key insights are that while something might be due to human errors, in some cases diverging is actually the right thing to do and might require changes in the way CVEs are generated industry-wide, in other cases explaining divergence requires access to additional FAQs. The good news is that the situation is improving since 2025, the bad news is that if one downloads the whole NVD (or another CNA dataset) from several years and uses it for predictions, the models trained on one source do not reliably generalize to a different source (accuracy can drop by 40%). We discuss the implications for practice and research.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes systematic divergences in CVSS vulnerability scoring between the NVD "Cathedral" and the emerging "Bazaar" of diverse CNAs, finding widespread, non-uniform inconsistencies—especially in Attack Complexity, User Interaction, and Impact metrics—attributable to human error, legitimate contextual differences, and undocumented guidance. Models trained on one source suffer up to 40% accuracy drops when applied to another.
AI.motivation: The NVD has long been the single authoritative source for vulnerability information, but the proliferation of CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs) under the federated CVE Program has created multiple, potentially diverging data sources. No prior work systematically quantifies or explains these divergences, despite their critical implications for downstream tasks like software update prioritization, security metrics, and machine learning models trained on vulnerability data.
AI.method: A mixed-methods approach: (1) quantitative systematic analysis of CVSS metric divergences between NVD and public CNAs across the entire CVE corpus, including a novel check for self-divergence (same CNA scoring identical CWE-description pairs differently); (2) qualitative study via direct outreach to NVD, open-source and proprietary CNAs, and presentation/discussion at the CVSS Special Interest Group (SIG) of FIRST, the CVSS standards body.
AI.result: Divergence is widespread and non-uniform across CNAs and metrics. Attack Complexity, User Interaction, and Impact sub-scores are the primary loci of disagreement. Some divergence stems from human error, but some is legitimate—contextual factors and unpublished FAQs explain cases where differing scores are correct. Self-divergence (identical textual descriptions, identical CWEs, same CNA, different scores) was observed. A practical ML experiment showed accuracy drops of up to 40% when models trained on one CNA's data are tested on another's. The situation is improving post-2025.
AI.conclusion: The federated CNA model introduces inherent, partially legitimate divergence in vulnerability scoring. This has serious consequences for ML-based vulnerability prediction and industry processes that assume a single ground truth. Recommendations include industry-wide changes to CVE generation, public release of CNA-specific scoring FAQs, and caution when using multi-source NVD data for training predictive models.

title: PERSONAJUDGE: Simulating Individual Human Preference Judgments with Evaluator-Specific Demonstration Data
summary: Large language models increasingly serve as judges in AI evaluation, but current approaches rely on consensus preferences that ignore individual evaluator variation. We propose a novel simulation approach that combines categorical judgments with evaluator-specific auxiliary data--retrospective reasoning traces and interface telemetry--to enable LLM-based simulation of individual evaluators via in-context learning. We conduct a systematic empirical study of this approach using multi-facet data from 32 trained annotators across 4,200 preference judgments in a 4 x 4 x 4 factorial design. Our key findings: (1) The simulation approach achieves up to 9.9 percentage point improvements over the Base Judge; (2) Reasoning traces provide the largest gains with higher collection efforts, while interface telemetry often hurts rather than helps performance despite being cheaper to collect. (3) Simulation difficulty is systematic, predicted by an evaluator's neutral usage (most clearly on Helpfulness) and divergence from consensus; the neutral-usage tendency--rather than simulatability itself--is the cross-task-stable property (r = 0.728). These results establish both the potential and limits of evaluator-specific auxiliary data for personalized evaluation, offering methodological insights for scaling individual aware AI assessment.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes simulating individual human evaluators in AI assessment by augmenting LLM judges with evaluator-specific auxiliary data (reasoning traces and interface telemetry) via in-context learning. Experiments with 32 annotators across 4,200 judgments show up to 9.9pp improvement, with reasoning traces being most beneficial and telemetry often detrimental. Simulation difficulty is systematically predicted by evaluator neutrality and consensus divergence.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-as-judge paradigms rely on aggregate consensus preferences, ignoring systematic individual variation among human evaluators. Personalized evaluation that captures individual annotator behavior is needed for more fine-grained, fair, and representative AI assessment.
AI.method: A simulation framework that combines categorical preference judgments with two types of evaluator-specific auxiliary data: (1) retrospective reasoning traces (written justifications), and (2) interface telemetry (behavioral signals like response times, scroll patterns). These are fed into an LLM via in-context learning to simulate individual evaluators' judgments. A 4×4×4 factorial design systematically varies factors across 32 trained annotators and 4,200 judgments.
AI.result: (1) Simulation improves over a consensus-based Base Judge by up to 9.9 percentage points. (2) Reasoning traces yield the largest performance gains but are costlier to collect; interface telemetry often degrades performance despite lower collection costs. (3) Simulation difficulty is systematic: predicted by an evaluator's neutral-usage rate (especially on Helpfulness) and divergence from consensus. Neutral-usage tendency is cross-task-stable (r = 0.728), representing a stable evaluator trait rather than a simulation artifact.
AI.conclusion: Evaluator-specific auxiliary data shows clear promise for personalized LLM-based evaluation, but its effectiveness varies systematically by data type and evaluator characteristics. The stability of neutral-usage tendency across tasks offers a practical signal for identifying hard-to-simulate evaluators, pointing toward scalable individual-aware AI assessment methodologies.

title: Memory in the Loop: In-Process Retrieval as ExtendedWorking Memory for Language Agents
summary: Language agents run a loop - observe, reason, act - but the memory they reason over sits outside it: a store queried at most once per turn. We study the regime where memory moves inside the loop, read and written on every step. The obstacle has always been latency: networked stores answer in tens to hundreds of milliseconds, and in-loop retrieval can inflate end-to-end latency by up to 83x when retrieval is expensive. Prior work manages that cost rather than questioning it: serving-layer scheduling hides it, "memory-first" designs ration retrieval to once per turn. We argue latency is a property of where the store lives, not the in-loop pattern: an in-process store answers in ~100us, three orders of magnitude below the network regime, and at that speed the per-step tax collapses. By the extended-mind thesis's parity principle, a store fast enough to be constantly and directly available becomes extended working memory, not a tool the agent merely consults. The premise is causal: holding a fixed per-turn memory-latency budget and varying only the store's answer speed, redundant actions rise monotonically with latency - 0.0 of 12 at in-process speed, 7.2 of 12 at a 110ms cloud round trip (gpt-5-nano, gpt-5-mini; exact permutation p=0.0079). We demonstrate the regime end-to-end: across four GPT-5-class models under a bounded window, recall improves from 0/5 to 3.6-4.8/5 with in-loop memory, store ops at p50 80-165us - though an instructed restate-every-reply baseline also solves it perfectly, at a token cost that grows with the working set. The store never lost a fact in any run (244 of 244 writes kept); every miss traces to the agent's read policy, not the store. Our measurements also relocate the bottleneck: the dominant per-step cost is embedding (~200-400ms over the network); pairing the in-process store with a small local embedder returns the complete operation to a measured ~40us.

AI.tldr: Moving memory inside the agent loop from an external networked store to an in-process store collapses per-step latency from tens/hundreds of milliseconds to ~100μs. This transforms memory from a tool consulted occasionally into extended working memory, eliminating redundant actions and dramatically improving recall. The bottleneck shifts from store access to embedding generation, which can be further reduced with a local embedder (~40μs).
AI.motivation: Current language agents keep memory outside the execution loop, querying it at most once per turn due to network latency (tens to hundreds of milliseconds). In-loop retrieval would enable richer reasoning but has been avoided because it inflates end-to-end latency by up to 83×. Prior work accepts this constraint, hiding latency via scheduling or rationing retrieval. The authors argue this is an architectural limitation, not an inherent one: changing where the store lives eliminates the latency barrier entirely.
AI.method: The paper proposes an in-process memory store that answers in ~100μs, three orders of magnitude faster than networked stores. The core experiment holds a fixed per-turn memory-latency budget while varying only store answer speed, demonstrating a causal relationship: redundant actions increase monotonically with latency (0/12 at in-process speed vs. 7.2/12 at 110ms cloud round-trip, p=0.0079). The approach is evaluated end-to-end across four GPT-5-class models under a bounded window, measuring recall performance (0/5 without in-loop memory vs. 3.6–4.8/5 with it) and operational latency (p50 80–165μs). The paper also pairs the in-process store with a small local embedder, reducing the dominant per-step embedding cost from ~200–400ms to ~40μs.
AI.result: (1) In-process store latency: p50 of 80–165μs, three orders of magnitude below network stores. (2) Causal latency–redundancy link: redundant actions rise from 0/12 to 7.2/12 as latency increases to 110ms (significant at p=0.0079). (3) Recall improvement: from 0/5 to 3.6–4.8/5 across GPT-5-class models. (4) Reliability: 244/244 writes preserved with zero store-side loss; all misses attributed to agent read policy. (5) Full-stack optimization: in-process store + local embedder achieves ~40μs end-to-end, shifting the bottleneck away from both storage and embedding.
AI.conclusion: Latency is a property of store location, not the in-loop memory pattern. An in-process store fast enough for constant, direct availability constitutes extended working memory (per the extended-mind thesis's parity principle), not merely a consulted tool. The bottleneck consequently shifts to embedding generation, solvable with local embedders, enabling genuinely tight agent–memory coupling without latency penalties.

title: ResonatorLM: Causal Resonant Field Mixing for Efficient Long-Context Language Modelin
summary: Contemporary language models are dominated by the transformer architecture, which leverages self-attention mechanisms to enable more efficient, parallelized training across a wide set of documents and corpora. This has allowed transformers to effectively model data across a wide range of modalities and contexts. However, transformers, along with their conventional counterparts such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs), often struggle to maintain efficiency when processing long contexts. We introduce ResonatorLM, a new mechanism that replaces attention with a physics-derived alternative. ResonatorLM treats token sequences as a single, driven one-dimensional latent field and replaces attention dot products with causal functions of damped resonators. We implement ResonatorLM on a traditional network architecture and test it on standard long-context modeling tasks. We find that in a small, 6M matched setting, training and prefill speedups increase with sequence length, decode speed reaches 6.47x compared to that of a standard, optimized transformer at 32K tokens, and accuracy reaches 61.31 percent (compared to 55.32 percent) on WikiText.

AI.tldr: ResonatorLM replaces self-attention with physics-inspired damped resonator functions, treating token sequences as a driven 1D latent field. In a 6M-parameter setting, it achieves up to 6.47× decode speedup over transformers at 32K tokens and improves WikiText accuracy to 61.31% (vs. 55.32% for transformers).
AI.motivation: Transformers, RNNs, and CNNs struggle with computational efficiency when processing long context sequences. The authors seek an alternative to self-attention that scales better with sequence length while maintaining or improving accuracy.
AI.method: The authors propose ResonatorLM, which treats the token sequence as a single, driven one-dimensional latent field. Instead of computing attention dot products between all token pairs, it employs causal functions derived from damped resonators — a physics-inspired mechanism that governs how information propagates and interacts along the sequence.
AI.result: In a matched 6M-parameter setting: (1) training and prefill speedups increase with sequence length; (2) decode speed reaches 6.47× compared to an optimized standard transformer at 32K tokens; (3) WikiText accuracy reaches 61.31% versus 55.32% for the transformer baseline.
AI.conclusion: ResonatorLM demonstrates that physics-derived resonator mechanisms can serve as a viable and efficient replacement for self-attention in language models, offering significant speedups and improved accuracy on long-context tasks, particularly as sequence length grows.

title: Learning to Control LLM Agent Harnesses with Offline Reinforcement Learning
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are usually improved by changing prompts, models, or hand-written workflows, while the execution harness around the model is treated as fixed infrastructure. We argue that this harness is itself a learnable control layer. We formalize harness operation as a finite-horizon Harness MDP, where a lightweight controller selects structural execution actions while the LLM executor remains frozen. The controller is trained from offline rollouts using advantage-weighted regression with only terminal task-rubric rewards. We also separate final task quality from a post-hoc Harness Maturity Score, which measures whether the harness follows reliable execution patterns rather than only whether the final answer is correct. This separation gives a finite-buffer view of harness learning: final-quality gains require high-return support in the offline buffer, while process behavior can shift whenever it aligns with advantage-weighted actions. Across six controlled domains and two public-benchmark adapters, the learned controller consistently improves verification behavior and selectively improves final task quality, with the largest gains on adapted tau-bench retail, adapted AgentBench DB-Bench, and coding with a calibrated structural verifier. Ablations against behavior cloning and Forced CHECK show that the gains are not explained by imitation or by simply adding checks. These results identify harness control as a learnable layer for frozen LLM agents, while showing that offline support limits when better process control becomes better final answers.

AI.tldr: LLM agent execution harnesses can be treated as learnable control layers. The authors formalize this as a Harness MDP, train a lightweight controller via offline advantage-weighted regression using terminal task-rubric rewards, and introduce a separate Harness Maturity Score to measure reliable execution patterns. The learned controller improves verification behavior and selectively boosts task quality across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current approaches to improving LLM agents focus on prompt engineering, model fine-tuning, or manually designed workflows, while treating the execution harness (the structural scaffolding that orchestrates agent actions) as fixed infrastructure. The authors argue this harness is itself an underexplored, learnable component that can be optimized independently of the frozen LLM to improve agent reliability and task performance.
AI.method: The authors formalize harness operation as a finite-horizon Harness MDP, where a lightweight controller selects structural execution actions (e.g., when to verify, retry, or branch) while the underlying LLM executor remains frozen. The controller is trained from offline rollouts using advantage-weighted regression (AWR) with only terminal task-rubric rewards — no intermediate supervision. They also decouple final task quality from a post-hoc Harness Maturity Score, which measures whether the harness follows reliable execution patterns independently of answer correctness, providing a finite-buffer perspective on harness learning.
AI.result: Across six controlled domains and two public-benchmark adapters (tau-bench retail, AgentBench DB-Bench, and coding with a calibrated structural verifier), the learned controller consistently improves verification behavior. Final task quality improvements are selective: gains occur when the offline buffer contains high-return support. Ablations against behavior cloning and a "Forced CHECK" baseline confirm that improvements are not attributable to mere imitation or naive insertion of verification steps.
AI.conclusion: Harness control is a viable, learnable layer for frozen LLM agents. However, offline data support constrains when better process control translates into better final answers — process behavior can shift whenever aligned with advantage-weighted actions, but final-quality gains require high-return trajectories in the offline buffer.

title: Full-range Binary Classifier Calibration for Stable Model Updates in Production
summary: Detection models running in adversarial environments face a malicious distribution that drifts rapidly while the benign distribution stays comparatively stable, so teams retrain and redeploy constantly to stay ahead of new threats. Retraining tends to change the output prediction scores, which breaks downstream users of the model. For these security-oriented models we need consistent false-positive rate (FPR) across all output values, whereas standard probability-calibration methods target class probability rather than an FPR contract. We introduce a method built on top of existing calibration primitives that targets the whole FPR curve, giving scores a consistent FPR meaning across deployments. On one held-out split, the observed relative FPR error was at most 2.3% from 10% down to 0.1% FPR and 7.2% at 0.01% FPR. The shipped artifact remains under 200 KB in measurements across calibration sets from 1K to 10M benign samples.

AI.tldr: A calibration method is proposed that ensures consistent false-positive rate (FPR) across model retraining deployments for security-oriented detection models, achieving ≤2.3% relative FPR error down to 0.1% FPR with a compact artifact under 200KB.
AI.motivation: Security detection models operating in adversarial environments require frequent retraining due to rapidly drifting malicious distributions. Retraining alters prediction scores, which disrupts downstream consumers that depend on score stability. Standard probability calibration targets class probabilities, not FPR consistency. The need is for a calibration method that guarantees a stable FPR contract across deployments, so that a given score always corresponds to the same FPR.
AI.method: The authors introduce a method built atop existing calibration primitives that explicitly targets the entire FPR curve rather than class probabilities. This ensures that output scores carry a consistent FPR interpretation across different model deployments and retraining cycles.
AI.result: On a held-out split, the relative FPR error was at most 2.3% from 10% down to 0.1% FPR, and 7.2% at 0.01% FPR. The shipped calibration artifact remains under 200 KB across calibration set sizes ranging from 1K to 10M benign samples.
AI.conclusion: The proposed FPR-targeted calibration method effectively provides stable, deployment-consistent false-positive rates for security-oriented models, solving a practical problem where standard probability calibration falls short.

title: Quantifying and Expanding the Theoretical Capacity of Late-Interaction Retrieval Models
summary: Late-interaction retrieval models that use the MaxSim similarity function have shown strong empirical performance, often outperforming single-vector dense and sparse retrieval models. Despite these empirical findings, little is known about the theoretical representation power of MaxSim and how it compares to other retrieval approaches. This paper shows by construction that MaxSim similarity can exactly replicate the inner product between any two non-negative k-sparse vectors with possibly infinite dimension, requiring only O(k) representation space. Moreover, there exist similarities that MaxSim can express while standard vector inner products with the same representation space cannot. Leveraging our theoretical framework, we introduce Signed MaxSim which allows late-interaction models to exactly replicate any real-valued inner product, something we prove standard MaxSim is not capable of. We also show that MaxSim can act as an aggregation of soft-OR operations and as an evaluator of logical expressions in positive Conjunctive Normal Form. Our findings show that MaxSim is at least as capable as standard vector inner products for any non-negative vectors and our extension, Signed MaxSim, is as capable for any vectors. Both similarities possess additional capabilities that inner product cannot replicate, marking one of the first theoretical justifications and quantifications of late-interaction methods. Our theoretical findings are supported empirically: on a retrieval task featuring queries with negations, Signed MaxSim improves out-of-domain performance significantly over a standard ColBERT/MaxSim baseline with nDCG@10 increasing from 0.597 to 1.000 under a vocabulary shift and from 0.008 to 0.788 on negation-only queries.

AI.tldr: The paper provides a theoretical analysis of MaxSim similarity in late-interaction retrieval, proving it can exactly replicate inner products between non-negative sparse vectors with O(k) space, introduces Signed MaxSim to handle real-valued inner products, demonstrates MaxSim can evaluate logical expressions in positive CNF, and empirically validates Signed MaxSim's significant improvements on negation queries.
AI.motivation: Despite strong empirical performance of late-interaction retrieval models (e.g., ColBERT) using MaxSim, there is a lack of theoretical understanding regarding MaxSim's representation power and how it compares to standard inner product-based retrieval. The authors aim to fill this theoretical gap.
AI.method: The authors use constructive proofs to establish MaxSim's representational capacity: (1) showing MaxSim exactly replicates inner products between non-negative k-sparse vectors using O(k) space; (2) proving MaxSim can express similarities that standard inner products cannot; (3) introducing Signed MaxSim, which extends MaxSim via sign-decomposed embeddings to handle real-valued inner products; (4) demonstrating MaxSim as soft-OR aggregation and CNF logical expression evaluation. Empirical validation uses retrieval tasks with negation queries, comparing Signed MaxSim against standard ColBERT/MaxSim baselines.
AI.result: Theoretically, MaxSim can replicate any non-negative k-sparse inner product and express similarities beyond inner product's capacity. Standard MaxSim cannot replicate arbitrary real-valued inner products. Signed MaxSim overcomes this limitation. Empirically, on negation queries, Signed MaxSim improved nDCG@10 from 0.597→1.000 under vocabulary shift and 0.008→0.788 on negation-only queries, substantially outperforming the ColBERT/MaxSim baseline.
AI.conclusion: MaxSim is at least as capable as standard vector inner products for non-negative vectors; Signed MaxSim extends this to all real-valued vectors. Both possess additional expressive capabilities beyond inner products. This provides one of the first theoretical justifications for late-interaction methods, with strong empirical support on negation-aware retrieval.

title: From Conversation to Contribution: Characterizing Coding Agent in Open-Source Software
summary: AI coding assistants such as GitHub Copilot and Cursor have evolved from code-suggestion tools into conversational collaborators, enabling vibe-coding workflows in which developers guide AI-generated code through natural-language dialogue. Although researchers have increasingly recognized the importance of AI coding agents and begun examining their impact on open-source development, a comprehensive understanding of how developers' chat-based interactions with AI relate to subsequent open-source development and collaboration remains limited. This hinders efforts to effectively design, evaluate, and govern AI-assisted open-source software development. To address this gap, we collected 13,360 AI conversation sessions comprising 79,172 user messages from 1,356 OSS repositories, linked them to repository development histories, and complemented this analysis with a targeted developer survey. We find heavier AI use in smaller, less mature, and less collaborative repositories. After AI adoption, projects tended to show more active contributors and lower contributor concentration (p < .001), although communication remained highly concentrated. Code Writing was the dominant chat purpose, and nearly all AI chat sessions were followed by subsequent commits. We find no broad deterioration in code-quality signals or pull request merging rates. However, developers perceive others' AI-generated code as harder to maintain than their own (p = .029) and view AI as lowering barriers to OSS contribution. While most developers (68%) are willing to share their chat, concerns remain around appearing incompetent, increasing reviewer burden, and exposing ideas to competitors. These findings provide a large-scale empirical characterization of AI-assisted OSS contribution and offer practical insights for designing and governing responsible vibe-coding practices in open-source development.

AI.tldr: A large-scale empirical study analyzing 13,360 AI conversation sessions across 1,356 OSS repositories reveals that AI coding assistants are used most heavily in smaller, less mature projects, correlate with more active contributors and lower contributor concentration post-adoption, and do not degrade code quality or PR merge rates — though developers perceive others' AI-generated code as harder to maintain and express concerns about reviewer burden and idea exposure.
AI.motivation: Despite the rapid evolution of AI coding assistants from autocomplete tools into conversational collaborators ("vibe-coding"), there is a lack of comprehensive empirical understanding of how developers' chat-based interactions with AI relate to subsequent open-source development practices, collaboration dynamics, and code outcomes. This gap impedes informed design, evaluation, and governance of AI-assisted OSS development.
AI.method: The authors collected 13,360 AI conversation sessions (79,172 user messages) from 1,356 OSS repositories, linked them to corresponding repository development histories (commits, pull requests, contributor metrics), and conducted a complementary targeted developer survey. They performed quantitative analysis on pre/post-AI-adoption metrics, chat purpose classification, and code-quality signals complemented by perceptual survey data.
AI.result: Key findings include: (1) heavier AI use in smaller, less mature, less collaborative repositories; (2) post-adoption projects showed significantly more active contributors and lower contributor concentration (p < .001), though communication remained concentrated; (3) Code Writing dominated chat purposes, with nearly all sessions followed by commits; (4) no broad deterioration in code-quality signals or PR merge rates; (5) developers rated others' AI-generated code as harder to maintain than their own (p = .029) and viewed AI as lowering contribution barriers; (6) 68% of developers are willing to share chats, but concerns persist about appearing incompetent, reviewer burden, and competitive exposure.
AI.conclusion: The study provides the first large-scale empirical characterization of AI-assisted OSS contribution, demonstrating that while AI tools lower barriers to entry without broadly harming code quality, they introduce subtle social and maintenance challenges. The findings offer actionable insights for designing tools, workflows, and governance policies that support responsible vibe-coding practices in open-source ecosystems.

title: VisTCP: A Visualization Framework to Construct Knowledge-Graph-Based Representation for Traditional Chinese Painting
summary: Structured representation can characterize semantic objects and relationships in images. It provides a possible effective way for the semantic understanding of Traditional Chinese Paintings (TCPs) to better support archaeology and art history research. However, most image-oriented structured representation methods perform poorly on TCPs, due to two major challenges: 1) the objects and events of TCPs exhibit substantial differences from modern natural images, which results in semantic misunderstandings of TCPs; and 2) it is difficult to achieve accurate identification of ancient objects and events in TCPs, even for domain experts.In this paper, we propose VisTCP, a visualization framework that combines a TCP-oriented intelligent model and expert knowledge, which enables art historians to achieve trustworthy structured representations of TCPs in a human-in-the-loop manner. Firstly, we conduct a pilot study with three domain experts to build a semantic taxonomy of TCPs. Then, expert-annotated data are used to train a TCP-oriented structured representation model, which can automatically extract meaningful objects and their relationships in TCPs. To inform users of the model uncertainty, we design a joint embedding visualization view to show the differences between expert annotations and model predictions. This allows users to refine the structured representation based on their domain knowledge, enabling iterative optimization of the model. Finally, we conduct a case study, a usage scenario, and expert interviews on a real dataset to demonstrate the effectiveness of VisTCP in supporting the structured representation and semantic understanding of TCPs.

AI.tldr: VisTCP is a visualization framework that integrates a domain-specific AI model with expert knowledge through a human-in-the-loop approach to generate trustworthy structured representations of Traditional Chinese Paintings, addressing semantic understanding challenges in art history research.
AI.motivation: Traditional Chinese Paintings (TCPs) pose significant challenges for structured representation because existing image-oriented methods fail due to substantial semantic differences from natural images and the inherent difficulty in accurately identifying ancient objects and events, even for domain experts. A solution is needed to support archaeology and art history research through better semantic understanding.
AI.method: The authors first conducted a pilot study with three domain experts to build a semantic taxonomy of TCPs. Expert-annotated data were then used to train a TCP-oriented structured representation model that extracts objects and their relationships. A joint embedding visualization view was designed to reveal model uncertainty by showing differences between expert annotations and model predictions, enabling iterative human-in-the-loop refinement. The framework was evaluated through a case study, a usage scenario, and expert interviews on a real dataset.
AI.result: The case study, usage scenario, and expert interviews demonstrated that VisTCP effectively supports the structured representation and semantic understanding of TCPs, enabling art historians to achieve trustworthy results through iterative model refinement informed by uncertainty visualization.
AI.conclusion: VisTCP successfully combines an intelligent TCP-oriented model with expert knowledge via uncertainty-aware visualization and human-in-the-loop interaction, providing a viable approach for structured representation of culturally specific artworks that resist conventional image analysis methods.

title: Akashic: A Low-Overhead LLM Inference Service with MemAttention
summary: Recent LLM-based agent systems continuously accumulate context across multi-turn interactions, tool invocations, and cross-session workflows. Replaying the full history for every request quickly becomes impractical: long contexts increase prefill cost, may exceed context limits, and often bury task-relevant evidence in irrelevant content, degrading both serving efficiency and output quality. We propose Akashic, a low-overhead memory system built around MemAttention, which organizes context into bounded chunks and models semantic relationships across chunks, preserving cross-chunk evidence without repeatedly rewriting the full history. Akashic further applies hardware-software co-designed memory placement to co-locate likely co-retrieved chunks, reducing retrieval fragmentation and I/O overhead. Across four representative workloads and three model sizes, Akashic improves task accuracy by up to 10.2 points, throughput by up to 1.21x, and sustainable request rate by up to 1.88x over strong prior memory baselines.

AI.tldr: Akashic is a memory system for LLM agents that uses MemAttention to organize context into bounded chunks with cross-chunk semantic modeling, combined with hardware-software co-designed memory placement, achieving improvements in accuracy, throughput, and sustainable request rate over prior baselines.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agent systems suffer from continuously accumulating context across multi-turn interactions, tool invocations, and cross-session workflows. Replaying the full history per request becomes impractical due to high prefill costs, context length limits, and task-relevant evidence being buried in irrelevant content, degrading both serving efficiency and output quality.
AI.method: Akashic introduces MemAttention, which organizes context into bounded chunks and models semantic relationships across chunks to preserve cross-chunk evidence without rewriting the full history. Additionally, it employs hardware-software co-design for memory placement, co-locating likely co-retrieved chunks to reduce retrieval fragmentation and I/O overhead.
AI.result: Across four representative workloads and three model sizes, Akashic improved task accuracy by up to 10.2 points, throughput by up to 1.21×, and sustainable request rate by up to 1.88× compared to strong prior memory baselines.
AI.conclusion: Akashic demonstrates that bounded-chunk memory organization with cross-chunk semantic modeling, combined with co-designed memory placement, effectively addresses the long-context scalability challenges in LLM agent systems, delivering substantial gains in accuracy, efficiency, and throughput.

title: Revisiting the Relation Between Language Model Perplexity and ASR Word Error Rate for Modern End-to-End Speech Recognition
summary: Language model (LM) perplexity (PPL) has historically been used as a proxy for automatic speech recognition (ASR) word error rate (WER), with prior work reporting an approximately linear relation in log-log space. Modern end-to-end ASR systems challenge this assumption because they already contain internal language modeling capacity, are often evaluated without external language models, and can now be combined with neural LMs and large language models (LLMs) through different recognition strategies. This paper revisits the relation between PPL and WER for modern ASR systems. We study whether external LMs still improve current end-to-end ASR systems, whether the PPL-WER relation remains linear in log-log space, how encoder context length affects this relation, and how LLM perplexities fit into the trend observed for standard neural LMs. We further investigate internal language modeling (ILM) in attention-based encoder-decoder systems and show that ILM subtraction changes the observed PPL-WER relation, indicating that the decoder's internal LM must be considered when interpreting the effect of external LM quality.

AI.tldr: The paper revisits the relationship between LM perplexity (PPL) and ASR word error rate (WER) for modern end-to-end systems, finding that while the log-linear PPL-WER relation largely holds, factors like encoder context length, ILM subtraction, and LLM integration complicate the traditional assumption.
AI.motivation: Prior work established an approximately log-linear relationship between LM PPL and ASR WER, but modern end-to-end ASR systems — which have internal LM capacity, are often evaluated without external LMs, and can integrate neural LMs and LLMs via diverse recognition strategies — challenge this assumption. A systematic re-examination is needed.
AI.method: The authors empirically study external LM effects on current end-to-end ASR systems, analyze the PPL-WER relationship in log-log space across various settings, examine the impact of encoder context length, evaluate how LLM perplexities fit alongside standard neural LMs, and investigate internal language modeling (ILM) in attention-based encoder-decoder architectures, including the effect of ILM subtraction on the PPL-WER relation.
AI.result: External LMs still improve modern end-to-end ASR systems. The PPL-WER relation remains approximately linear in log-log space, though encoder context length modulates this relationship. LLM perplexities follow a distinct trend compared to standard neural LMs. ILM subtraction significantly alters the observed PPL-WER relation, demonstrating that the decoder's internal LM must be accounted for when interpreting external LM quality effects.
AI.conclusion: The log-linear PPL-WER relationship persists in modern ASR but is nuanced by architectural factors. Critically, the decoder's internal LM must be considered when evaluating external LM impact, as ILM subtraction changes the PPL-WER dynamic; neglecting this leads to misinterpretation of external LM quality benefits.

title: AdaStop: Cost-Aware Early Stopping for DNN Test Selection
summary: Existing methods for testing deep neural networks (DNNs) primarily prioritize test inputs likely to reveal model faults under a fixed labeling budget. In practice, choosing that budget is difficult: too little testing misses failures, while too much incurs unnecessary labeling costs. This work studies the stopping problem in DNN testing. We formulate testing as a cost--benefit decision process in which labeling an input incurs cost $c$ and discovering a fault yields value $v$. Based on this formulation, we introduce \textit{AdaStop}, a framework that estimates the marginal fault discovery rate during testing and stops labeling when the estimated rate falls below the threshold $τ= c/v$. Experiments across multiple datasets, architectures, and selection strategies show that $65$--$84\%$ of faults can be discovered using only $9$--$31\%$ of the labeling budget.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AdaStop, a framework that frames DNN testing as a cost-benefit decision process. It estimates the marginal fault discovery rate and stops labeling when that rate drops below a threshold defined by the cost-labeling ratio (c/v). Experiments show 65–84% of faults can be found using only 9–31% of the labeling budget.
AI.motivation: Existing DNN testing methods assume a fixed labeling budget, but in practice, determining the right budget is challenging: undertesting misses failures, while overtesting wastes labeling resources. No principled stopping criterion exists for DNN testing.
AI.method: Testing is formulated as a cost–benefit decision process where labeling costs c per input and finding a fault yields value v. AdaStop estimates the marginal fault discovery rate during testing and applies an optimal stopping rule: halt labeling when the estimated rate falls below the threshold τ = c/v.
AI.result: Across multiple datasets, architectures, and input selection strategies, AdaStop discovers 65–84% of total faults while using only 9–31% of the full labeling budget.
AI.conclusion: AdaStop provides an effective, principled stopping criterion for DNN testing that significantly reduces labeling costs while retaining high fault discovery, making it a practical solution for real-world testing scenarios where labeling budgets are uncertain.

title: aiAuthZ: Off-Host, Identity-Bound Authorization for AI Agents
summary: AI agents issue tool calls on the basis of text they cannot verify, so any party who controls part of the context can forge the appearance of authority. I evaluate 15 contemporary language models against eight attack scenarios derived from a published corpus of real agent incidents and find that refusal varies from 100% down to 38% across fully evaluated models; the most expensive model refused only half of the attacks despite a twentyfold price spread. I present aiAuthZ, an authorization gateway that moves the safety decision off the agent's host. Before a tool call executes, the gateway verifies caller identity with a per-message HMAC-SHA256 signature bound to a single-use nonce and a timestamp window, and it evaluates a role-based and argument-level policy that the agent can neither read nor modify. Every decision joins a SHA-256 hash-chained audit log, and each accepted message yields an HMAC-authenticated QR receipt that achieves 94% mean verification across eight transmission channels, with zero forgeries accepted in 25 wrong-key trials. With the gateway in place, residual attack success falls to 0% for all 15 models at no more than 0.03 ms of added decision latency. On the AgentDojo banking suite, aiAuthZ blocks all seven attacker-directed tool calls the evaluated agents emit, at the cost of one legitimate first-time payment, while a spotlighting baseline allows two injections to succeed. Across nine in-scope case studies from the same incident corpus, aiAuthZ blocks nine of nine, against four of nine for a policy baseline without identity binding. The gateway does not prevent a model from being deceived; it prevents a deceived model from acting beyond the verified user's authority on every call routed through it. The implementation and all experiments are released at https://github.com/Sports-Vision-Inc/aiAuthZ.

AI.tldr: Presents aiAuthZ, an authorization gateway that prevents compromised/decoyed AI agents from executing unauthorized tool calls by enforcing identity-bound, per-message HMAC signatures, role-based policies, and hash-chained audit logging. Testing across 15 LLMs shows attacks drop from 38-100% refusal variation to 0% success, with 0.03ms added latency.
AI.motivation: AI agents issue tool calls based on unverified text, allowing any party controlling part of the context to forge authority. Existing models show inconsistent refusal rates (100% down to 38%), and the most expensive model refused only half of attacks despite a 20x price spread. No existing solution moves the safety decision off the agent's host with cryptographic identity binding.
AI.method: aiAuthZ gateway architecture: (1) per-message HMAC-SHA256 signature bound to single-use nonce and timestamp window for caller identity verification; (2) role-based and argument-level policy evaluation that the agent cannot read or modify; (3) SHA-256 hash-chained audit log for all decisions; (4) HMAC-authenticated QR receipts achieving 94% mean verification across 8 transmission channels. Evaluated against 8 attack scenarios from published real agent incidents on 15 contemporary LLMs, plus AgentDojo banking suite and 9 in-scope case studies.
AI.result: Refusal rates across 15 models varied from 100% to 38% without the gateway; the most expensive model refused only 50% of attacks. With aiAuthZ: 0% residual attack success across all 15 models at ≤0.03ms added latency. On AgentDojo banking suite: blocks all 7 attacker-directed tool calls (cost: 1 legitimate first-time payment) vs. spotlighting baseline allowing 2 injections. In 9 case studies: aiAuthZ blocks 9/9 vs. policy-baseline-without-identity-binding blocking only 4/9. Zero forgeries accepted in 25 wrong-key QR trials.
AI.conclusion: aiAuthZ does not prevent models from being deceived but prevents deceived models from acting beyond verified user authority on every routed call. Moving authorization decisions off the agent host with cryptographic identity binding eliminates residual tool-call injection attacks that variable model-level refusal cannot reliably address.

title: CMDR: Contextual Multimodal Document Retrieval
comment: Accepted by ECCV 2026; project page: https://cmdr-bench.github.io/
summary: Multimodal document retrieval aims to retrieve relevant pages while preserving both textual and visual content from the original document. However, existing benchmarks primarily evaluate simple lexical or semantic matching, and most methods encode pages independently. Consequently, they overlook the contextual information in the document required to resolve queries that aggregate information across multiple pages. In this paper, we introduce CMDR and CMDR-Bench, a new multimodal document retrieval task and benchmark that require modeling document context. To address this challenge, we propose CMDR-Embed, a contextual multimodal embedding framework that explicitly incorporates document context by jointly encoding multiple pages and deriving page-level embeddings from a shared contextual representation. Furthermore, we introduce CMCL, a contextual multimodal contrastive learning objective that effectively trains CMDR-Embed by balancing contextual modeling with page-level discriminability. Experiments demonstrate that CMDR-Embed significantly outperforms non-contextual embeddings, highlighting the importance of context-aware multimodal embeddings for advancing document retrieval.

AI.tldr: Introduces CMDR, a contextual multimodal document retrieval task and benchmark, along with CMDR-Embed, a framework that jointly encodes multiple pages to incorporate document context, and CMCL, a contrastive learning objective balancing contextual modeling with page-level discriminability.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal document retrieval benchmarks only evaluate simple lexical or semantic matching, and most methods encode pages independently, ignoring cross-page contextual information needed for queries that aggregate information across multiple pages.
AI.method: Proposes CMDR (task/benchmark) requiring document context modeling; CMDR-Embed, a contextual multimodal embedding framework that jointly encodes multiple pages to derive page-level embeddings from a shared contextual representation; and CMCL, a contextual multimodal contrastive learning objective that balances contextual modeling with page-level discriminability.
AI.result: CMDR-Embed significantly outperforms non-contextual embedding baselines, demonstrating the critical importance of context-aware multimodal embeddings for document retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Context-aware multimodal embeddings are essential for advancing document retrieval performance, especially for queries requiring cross-page information aggregation.

title: Articulating Assumptions in AI-Generated Scientific Analyses through Task Decomposition
summary: Scientific results produced by LLM generated analysis code must be understandable and reproducible. However, uncertainty can arise at different stages of the process, both in the original natural language specification and in the generated implementation. As a result, even executable code may not provide a clear understanding of which quantities are being computed or which assumptions determine the final results. To address this challenge, we introduce quantity grounded semantic differencing, a multi-agent framework for analyzing and comparing scientific programs generated by LLMs. The framework assigns code generation, execution, tracing, and validation to separate agents, allowing it to reconstruct how key output quantities are produced and to identify differences between the intended analysis and the implemented code. We also introduce a module that inspects ambiguities in the initial user instruction and suggests alternative rewrites before code generation. Its modular design enables application to different scientific domains by replacing domain specific resources while preserving the same workflow. We validate the framework on representative collider physics analyses. The results demonstrate that the modular task decomposition enhances both transparency and reliability relative to the previous single prompt approach, while enabling substantially smaller models to execute the complete workflow.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multi-agent framework for analyzing and comparing LLM-generated scientific code by grounding semantic differences in output quantities, enhancing transparency and reproducibility in computational science.
AI.motivation: LLM-generated scientific analysis code often suffers from opacity: even when executable, it is unclear which quantities are being computed and which assumptions shape results, due to ambiguities in both the natural language specification and the generated implementation. This undermines reproducibility and scientific trust.
AI.method: The authors introduce a quantity-grounded semantic differencing framework that decomposes the workflow across specialized agents: one for code generation, another for execution, a third for tracing, and a fourth for validation. This enables reconstruction of how key output quantities are produced and identification of mismatches between intended analysis and implementation. An additional module inspects ambiguities in user instructions and proposes rewritten specifications prior to code generation. The architecture is modular, allowing domain adaptation by swapping domain-specific resources while preserving the core workflow.
AI.result: Validated on collider physics analyses, the multi-agent decomposition demonstrates improved transparency and reliability over a single-prompt baseline, while enabling substantially smaller models to execute the entire workflow successfully.
AI.conclusion: Modular task decomposition into specialized agents significantly improves the interpretability and trustworthiness of LLM-generated scientific code, reducing the barrier to entry for model size and facilitating cross-domain application.

title: Nested Episodic State Topology (NEST): A Graph-Theoretic Architecture of Cognitive States
summary: We present NEST (Nested Episodic State Topology), a foundational graph-theoretic representational ontology for modeling cognition as structured state formation and transformation rather than as a finished empirical model. Concepts, episodes, percepts, and task contexts are represented as typed, weighted graphs whose nodes may carry internal subgraph payloads; edges are typed under six relation classes -- causal, containment, temporal, associative, evidential, and spatial. Durable belief graphs are separated from capacity-limited working-memory graphs that may host transient non-belief content. WM-belief grounding, conflict catalogs, and belief-update operators specify how transient structure is tested against stored knowledge and how belief is revised. A reusable operator toolkit -- activation, graph-property functionals, working-memory transitions, awareness and trajectory functionals, and belief update -- organizes the formal core. Derived diagnostics such as fragmentation, involvement, signed evaluation, coherence, and active conflict define familiar phenomena in the same ontology; self-related processing is modeled through designated self-image subgraphs within belief. Subsequent sections instantiate this core without new primitives: phenomena signatures, a task-instantiation schema for action selection and failure modes, and compatibility mappings that embed ACT-R, Soar, Sigma, the Common Model of Cognition, Global Workspace Theory, semantic networks, Theory-Theory, and chunking as constrained regions of one language. Mappings constitute the culminating technical section; discussion addresses scope, limitations, and open research directions. The contribution is intentionally foundational: a transparent representational substrate for later empirical, computational, and domain-specific work.

AI.tldr: NEST (Nested Episodic State Topology) introduces a graph-theoretic ontology for modeling cognition as structured state formation and transformation, employing typed, weighted graphs with nested subgraphs and six relation classes, separate belief and working-memory graphs, and a reusable operator toolkit — all designed as a foundational representational substrate rather than a finished empirical model.
AI.motivation: To provide a transparent, foundational representational substrate for cognitive modeling that unifies disparate cognitive architectures and phenomena within a single graph-theoretic language, enabling later empirical, computational, and domain-specific work to build upon a common ontology.
AI.method: The paper constructs a formal ontology using typed, weighted directed graphs with internal subgraph payloads. It defines six edge-type classes (causal, containment, temporal, associative, evidential, spatial), separates durable belief graphs from capacity-limited working-memory graphs, and specifies grounding, conflict, and belief-update operators. A toolkit of reusable operators (activation, graph-property functionals, WM transitions, awareness/trajectory functionals, belief update) forms the formal core. Compatibility mappings embed ACT-R, Soar, Sigma, the Common Model of Cognition, Global Workspace Theory, semantic networks, Theory-Theory, and chunking as constrained regions of the NEST language.
AI.result: The paper delivers a complete formal ontology with derived diagnostics (fragmentation, involvement, signed evaluation, coherence, active conflict) that define familiar cognitive phenomena within the same language. It provides phenomena signatures, a task-instantiation schema for action selection and failure modes, and rigorous compatibility mappings demonstrating that major cognitive architectures and theories can be expressed as constrained regions of NEST without introducing new primitives.
AI.conclusion: NEST succeeds as a foundational contribution — a transparent representational substrate that does not claim to be a finished model but rather establishes a common formal language for unifying cognitive architectures, with explicit discussion of scope, limitations, and open research directions for subsequent empirical and computational development.

title: ArtisanCAD: An Industrial-Level CAD Agent with Expert-Grounded Knowledge Distillation
summary: Computer-aided design (CAD) for industrial components requires long-horizon procedural modeling, robust feature dependencies, editable parametric geometry, and production-grade B-Rep execution. Existing text-to-CAD methods have made promising progress in generating CAD programs from natural-language descriptions, but they still struggle when user prompts are ambiguous, underspecified, or only describe high-level design intent. They also rarely exploit expert procedural knowledge naturally available in industrial workflows, such as CATIA operation recordings, macro logs, drawing notes, and engineering descriptions. We present \algname, a skill-guided industrial CAD agent with expert-grounded knowledge distillation. The core of \algname is CAD intermediate representation (CAD-IR), an executable procedural representation that encodes parameters, ordered operations, MCP tool bindings, dependencies, generated entities, and verification rules. CAD-IR plays two key roles: it first serves as the carrier for distilling expert CAD procedures into reusable parameterized skills; then it provides a procedural scaffold that turns vague or intermediate-level prompts into complete executable CAD operations. \algname retrieves expert-derived skills, instantiates and revises CAD-IR, executes the resulting procedure through a dedicated CATIA-MCP backend, and uses multi-view visual feedback for iterative refinement, and finally generates production-ready B-Rep models. On the Text2CAD benchmark, CAD-IR improves generation from intermediate prompts by reducing mean Chamfer Distance from $14.83$ to $9.88$, showing its ability to bridge ambiguous textual intent and executable CAD construction. On four complex automotive components, CAD-IR enables expert CATIA recordings to be distilled into reusable skills, allowing \algname to generate editable CATIA-native B-Rep models for new variant requests.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a CAD agent that distills expert industrial workflows into reusable parameterized skills via a CAD Intermediate Representation (CAD-IR), enabling robust generation of editable, production-grade B-Rep models from ambiguous or high-level text prompts, with significant improvements on the Text2CAD benchmark and real automotive components.
AI.motivation: Existing text-to-CAD methods fail with ambiguous or underspecified prompts and do not leverage expert procedural knowledge (e.g., CATIA recordings, macro logs, engineering notes) available in industrial settings. Industrial CAD demands long-horizon procedural modeling, robust dependencies, editable parametric geometry, and B-Rep execution — capabilities current methods lack.
AI.method: The proposed system, a skill-guided agent, centers on CAD-IR: an executable procedural representation encoding parameters, ordered operations, MCP tool bindings, dependencies, generated entities, and verification rules. CAD-IR serves dual roles: (1) distilling expert CAD procedures into reusable parameterized skills, and (2) providing a procedural scaffold that expands vague prompts into complete executable operations. The agent retrieves relevant skills, instantiates/revises CAD-IR, executes via a CATIA-MCP backend, and iteratively refines using multi-view visual feedback.
AI.result: On the Text2CAD benchmark, CAD-IR reduced mean Chamfer Distance from 14.83 to 9.88 for intermediate prompts. On four complex automotive components, expert CATIA recordings were successfully distilled into reusable skills, enabling generation of editable CATIA-native B-Rep models for new variant requests.
AI.conclusion: CAD-IR with expert-grounded knowledge distillation bridges the gap between ambiguous textual design intent and executable CAD construction, producing industrial-grade, editable B-Rep models by effectively leveraging recorded expert workflows as parameterized skills.

title: BaFCo: A Document Understanding Benchmark for Complex Bangla Form Comprehension
