comment: Accepted at the 19th European Conference on Computer Vision (ECCV), 2026
summary: Document comprehension is a challenging yet impactful task for Multimodal Large Language Models, especially as these systems see growing adoption in real-world, human-centric applications. However, this adoption is limited for low-resource languages such as Bangla due to the scarcity of high-quality annotated data. To address this gap, we introduce BaFCo, a benchmark dataset for Bangla form comprehension with a focus on Document Layout Analysis (DLA) and Key Information Extraction (KIE). BaFCo curates 200 multi-page complex Bangladeshi government forms, sourced from across diverse sectors including agriculture, education, banking, and land management. To accurately capture the structural and contextual complexity of these forms, we define a fine-grained annotation schema comprising 26 types of form entities, along with a separate coarse form entity set consisting of 5 types. We evaluate the latest MLLMs from the ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Qwen, and Kimi series using zero-shot and chain-of-thought prompts under both low and high reasoning setups. Our results reveal limitations in current MLLMs' ability in comprehending Bangla forms, particularly in accurately localizing highly granular form entities. Our dataset and code is available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Mausul/bafco

AI.tldr: BaFCo is a benchmark dataset for Bangla form comprehension, containing 200 multi-page government forms with fine-grained annotations (26 entity types). It evaluates state-of-the-art MLLMs on Document Layout Analysis and Key Information Extraction, revealing significant limitations in localizing granular form entities in low-resource Bangla documents.
AI.motivation: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly used for document comprehension in human-centric applications, but adoption is hindered for low-resource languages like Bangla due to scarce high-quality annotated data. Existing benchmarks focus predominantly on high-resource languages, leaving a critical gap for evaluating Bangla document understanding.
AI.method: The authors introduce BaFCo, a benchmark dataset of 200 multi-page complex Bangladeshi government forms from agriculture, education, banking, and land management sectors. They define a fine-grained annotation schema with 26 form entity types and a coarse-grained schema with 5 types. Latest MLLMs (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Qwen, Kimi series) are evaluated using zero-shot and chain-of-thought prompting under both low and high reasoning setups on two tasks: Document Layout Analysis (DLA) and Key Information Extraction (KIE).
AI.result: Current state-of-the-art MLLMs exhibit notable limitations in comprehending Bangla forms. Models particularly struggle with accurately localizing fine-grained (highly granular) form entities, revealing a performance gap in low-resource document understanding scenarios.
AI.conclusion: BaFCo fills a critical benchmark gap for low-resource Bangla document comprehension. The evaluation results demonstrate that existing MLLMs are not yet robust in handling Bangla form documents, underscoring the need for improved multilingual and low-resource document understanding capabilities.

title: Learnable Weighting of Intra-Attribute Distances for Categorical Data Clustering with Nominal and Ordinal Attributes
summary: The success of categorical data clustering generally much relies on the distance metric that measures the dissimilarity degree between two objects. However, most of the existing clustering methods treat the two categorical subtypes, i.e. nominal and ordinal attributes, in the same way when calculating the dissimilarity without considering the relative order information of the ordinal values. Moreover, there would exist interdependence among the nominal and ordinal attributes, which is worth exploring for indicating the dissimilarity. This paper will therefore study the intrinsic difference and connection of nominal and ordinal attribute values from a perspective akin to the graph. Accordingly, we propose a novel distance metric to measure the intra-attribute distances of nominal and ordinal attributes in a unified way, meanwhile preserving the order relationship among ordinal values. Subsequently, we propose a new clustering algorithm to make the learning of intra-attribute distance weights and partitions of data objects into a single learning paradigm rather than two separate steps, whereby circumventing a suboptimal solution. Experiments show the efficacy of the proposed algorithm in comparison with the existing counterparts.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a graph-inspired unified distance metric for categorical data clustering that properly distinguishes nominal and ordinal attributes while preserving ordinal order relationships. It integrates distance weight learning and data partitioning into a joint optimization framework to avoid suboptimal solutions, and demonstrates superior performance over existing methods.
AI.motivation: Existing categorical clustering methods treat nominal and ordinal attributes identically when computing dissimilarity, ignoring the inherent order information in ordinal values. Furthermore, they fail to exploit the interdependence between nominal and ordinal attributes. These limitations lead to suboptimal clustering performance, motivating a unified approach that respects ordinal semantics and captures attribute interactions.
AI.method: The authors adopt a graph-based perspective to model the intrinsic differences and connections between nominal and ordinal attribute values. They propose a unified intra-attribute distance metric that handles both subtypes while preserving ordinal order. A new clustering algorithm is then introduced that jointly learns intra-attribute distance weights and data partitions within a single learning paradigm, rather than treating them as separate sequential steps.
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing clustering methods on categorical data, validating the effectiveness of both the unified distance metric and the joint learning framework.
AI.conclusion: By respecting ordinal order and modeling nominal-ordinal interdependence through a graph-inspired unified metric, and by jointly optimizing distance weights with clustering assignments, the proposed method achieves superior clustering quality and avoids suboptimal solutions inherent in two-stage approaches.

title: The Balkanization of Execution-Security Research for AI Coding Agents: Isolation, Access Control, and Time-of-Check-to-Time-of-Use Vulnerabilities
comment: 18 pages, 15 figures, 6 tables. Systematizes 39 execution-security papers (2023-2026) into 17 verified categories. Machine-readable corpus and verification script released as a supplementary artifact
summary: AI coding agents now read repositories, call tools, and execute shell commands with limited human oversight, and a fast-growing body of work studies whether the execution layer around them is actually safe. That literature is scattered. Papers on sandbox isolation, capability and access control, policy enforcement, time-of-check-to-time-of-use (TOCTOU) races, Model Context Protocol (MCP) threats, identity delegation, execution provenance, network egress control, and static analysis of agent-generated code are published independently and rarely cite one another. We systematize 39 papers published between 2023 and 2026 into 17 categories, each verified directly against its source. The same verification protocol also confirms four disclosed, patched CVEs directly affecting production agent harnesses. Reading across categories surfaces five cross-cutting gaps that no single paper addresses. (1) Isolation architectures and capability models are almost never evaluated against one another on a shared benchmark. (2) Policy-enforcement studies report failure rates from 69% to 98% of real denylists, yet no isolation paper re-evaluates its own defense under that adversarial setting. (3) TOCTOU and MCP threats are analyzed as separate literatures despite both being instances of the same state-validation problem. (4) Every enforcement mechanism assumes an honest policy author, leaving policy-authoring error itself unaddressed. (5) Benign but out-of-scope agent actions occurring at rates up to 17.1% under realistic prompting are addressed by no access-control or capability paper in the corpus. Existing broader surveys of agentic AI security discuss sandboxing only as one item among many defenses, leaving execution security without a dedicated systematization. This paper is written to fill that gap. We conclude with a research agenda directed at the five gaps.

AI.tldr: A systematization of 39 papers (2023–2026) on AI coding agent execution security, categorizing them into 17 types, identifying five cross-cutting gaps in the literature, and proposing a research agenda to address them.
AI.motivation: The literature on execution-layer safety for AI coding agents is fragmented across disjoint sub-areas (sandboxing, capability control, TOCTOU, MCP threats, etc.) with minimal cross-citation. Prior agentic AI security surveys treat sandboxing as one of many defenses, leaving execution security without a dedicated systematization.
AI.method: Systematization of 39 papers (2023–2026) into 17 categories, each verified directly against its source through a verification protocol. The same protocol confirmed four disclosed, patched CVEs affecting production agent harnesses. Cross-category reading surfaces five gaps through comparative analysis.
AI.result: Five cross-cutting gaps identified: (1) no shared benchmark for isolation vs. capability models; (2) policy-enforcement failure rates of 69–98% against denylists are never used to re-evaluate isolation defenses; (3) TOCTOU and MCP threats remain separate literatures despite shared state-validation roots; (4) no work addresses policy-authoring error; (5) benign out-of-scope actions (up to 17.1% rate) are unaddressed by any access-control or capability paper.
AI.conclusion: Execution security for AI coding agents lacks coherence as a field. The paper fills the gap with a dedicated systematization and outlines a research agenda targeting the five identified gaps, including shared benchmarks, adversarial re-evaluation, unified state-validation models, and handling of benign scope violations.

title: Faithful or Findable? Evaluating LLM-Generated Metadata for RDF Dataset Search
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, accepted at SynthIR @ SIGIR 2026
summary: Dataset search depends heavily on metadata, making LLM-generated metadata a consequential form of synthetic content in retrieval systems. We study six metadata-generation settings for RDF datasets, ranging from simple rewriting to profile-grounded and agentic graph-based generation, and evaluate them jointly for retrieval effectiveness and faithfulness. Unconstrained metadata rewriting delivers the strongest retrieval gains over the original metadata, but it is also the least faithful, showing that search improvements can be driven by unsupported semantic expansion. More grounded settings substantially improve faithfulness, and profile-grounded rewriting provides the most balanced trade-off between retrieval effectiveness and grounding. These findings position synthetic metadata as a system-level IR problem in which effectiveness, provenance, and trust must be evaluated together.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates six LLM-based metadata generation methods for RDF datasets, finding that unconstrained rewriting yields the best retrieval but lowest faithfulness, while profile-grounded rewriting offers the best balance between effectiveness and trustworthiness.
AI.motivation: Dataset search systems rely on metadata quality, yet LLM-generated synthetic metadata introduces a trade-off between retrieval effectiveness and faithfulness that has not been systematically studied. The authors aim to characterize this trade-off across different generation strategies for RDF datasets.
AI.method: Six metadata-generation settings are compared, spanning a spectrum from simple rewriting to profile-grounded and agentic graph-based generation. Each setting is evaluated jointly on two axes: retrieval effectiveness (search performance improvements over original metadata) and faithfulness (semantic fidelity to the source dataset).
AI.result: Unconstrained metadata rewriting achieves the strongest retrieval gains over original metadata but exhibits the lowest faithfulness, indicating that search improvements can stem from unsupported semantic expansion. More grounded approaches substantially improve faithfulness, with profile-grounded rewriting providing the most balanced effectiveness–grounding trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic metadata must be treated as a system-level information retrieval problem where effectiveness, provenance, and trust are evaluated jointly rather than independently.

title: Detecting Vulnerability-Inducing Commits via Multi-Stage Reasoning with LLM-Based Agents
summary: Detecting vulnerability-inducing commits (VICs) at submission time is critical for improving the security and reliability of software systems. However, this task is highly challenging because it requires reasoning about the semantic impact of code changes from heterogeneous information sources, including code diffs, commit messages, and the surrounding contextual code. Existing approaches often struggle to fully capture these complex interactions, resulting in limited detection performance. In this paper, we propose VIC-RAGENT, an LLM-based multi-agent framework for effective and explainable vulnerability detection. VIC-RAGENT leverages multiple specialized agents to provide complementary perspectives, including structural analysis, intent understanding, and vulnerability inspection. To further improve detection reliability, the framework employs a multi-stage reasoning process that progressively refines candidate vulnerabilities through preliminary inspection, reanalysis, and a final decision stage. Experimental results on a real-world dataset across multiple LLMs demonstrate that VIC-RAGENT consistently outperforms baselines, including Direct, CoT, and CodeAgent. Compared to the strongest baseline, VIC-RAGENT achieves 1.2-1.7x higher F1-scores across different models. Overall, VIC-RAGENT offers a robust, explainable, and practical solution for detecting VICs in modern software development workflows.

AI.tldr: VIC-RAGENT is an LLM-based multi-agent framework that detects vulnerability-inducing commits using specialized agents for structural analysis, intent understanding, and vulnerability inspection, combined with a multi-stage reasoning process. It achieves 1.2-1.7x higher F1-scores than baselines.
AI.motivation: Detecting vulnerability-inducing commits at submission time is critical for software security but highly challenging due to the need to reason about semantic impacts across heterogeneous sources (code diffs, commit messages, surrounding context). Existing approaches fail to capture these complex interactions, leading to limited detection performance.
AI.method: VIC-RAGENT is an LLM-based multi-agent framework with three specialized agents (structural analysis, intent understanding, vulnerability inspection) providing complementary perspectives. It employs a multi-stage reasoning process: preliminary inspection, reanalysis, and final decision, progressively refining candidate vulnerabilities for improved reliability and explainability.
AI.result: On a real-world dataset across multiple LLMs, VIC-RAGENT consistently outperforms baselines (Direct, CoT, CodeAgent). It achieves 1.2-1.7x higher F1-scores compared to the strongest baseline across different models.
AI.conclusion: VIC-RAGENT provides a robust, explainable, and practical solution for detecting vulnerability-inducing commits in modern software development workflows.

title: Designing Computerized Gait Analysis for Pediatric Care: Clinician Perspectives on Sensing, Workflow, and Care Environments
summary: Computerized gait analysis (CGA) serves as an essential diagnostic tool for evaluating neuromuscular, musculoskeletal, and neurological disorders in children, from cerebral palsy to muscular dystrophy. By enabling objective and comprehensive gait analysis, CGA supports timely clinical interventions that can significantly improve pediatric mobility outcomes and quality of life. Yet pediatric gait analysis introduces unique design considerations often underexplored in existing CGA research, as children's ongoing development shapes assessment requirements. To understand how CGA technologies can be designed for pediatric care, we conducted a qualitative study with 12 pediatric clinicians and one system designer who routinely work with CGA. Participants identified child-specific challenges including managing heightened sensory sensitivities to wearable devices, accommodating body proportions in sensor placement and calibration, and maintaining patient engagement during data collection. Clinicians also articulated needs for workflow adaptations and expressed interest in extending gait analysis beyond controlled laboratory settings into naturalistic environments such as playgrounds and schools, where children's authentic movement patterns emerge. Drawing from these clinician perspectives, we present design recommendations for pediatric-centered CGA that address sensing modalities suitable for sensory-sensitive children and approaches for capturing gait data across diverse care environments. Our findings contribute to the broader challenge of adapting clinical technologies to meet the distinct needs of pediatric populations.

AI.tldr: A qualitative study with 13 participants (12 pediatric clinicians, 1 system designer) identifies child-specific challenges in computerized gait analysis (CGA), including sensory sensitivities, body proportion issues, and engagement difficulties. The paper proposes design recommendations for pediatric-centered CGA systems suitable for both clinical and naturalistic environments.
AI.motivation: Existing CGA research underexplores the unique design considerations required for pediatric populations, where children's ongoing physical and neurological development fundamentally shapes assessment requirements. Current systems are largely designed for adults and fail to account for child-specific needs.
AI.method: A qualitative study involving semi-structured interviews or similar methods with 12 pediatric clinicians and one system designer who routinely use CGA in practice. Thematic analysis of clinician experiences and articulated needs was performed to surface design challenges and requirements.
AI.result: Three key child-specific challenges were identified: (1) managing heightened sensory sensitivities to wearable devices, (2) accommodating varying body proportions in sensor placement and calibration, and (3) maintaining patient engagement during data collection. Clinicians also expressed need for workflow adaptations and extending CGA capabilities into naturalistic environments (playgrounds, schools) where authentic movement patterns emerge.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes design recommendations for pediatric-centered CGA, including sensing modalities appropriate for sensory-sensitive children and methods for capturing gait data across diverse care settings. The findings address the broader challenge of adapting clinical technologies for pediatric populations.

title: Synthetic Consumer Insight Generation with Large Language Models
summary: Modern data-driven marketing relies on large amounts of consumer data, yet collecting such data can be costly, time-consuming, and difficult to scale. This research examines whether large language models (LLMs) can be used to generate synthetic consumer data for projective techniques, a set of methods designed to elicit consumer associations, emotions, wants, and needs. We test LLM-generated responses across multiple projective tasks, LLMs, prompting strategies, and temperature settings, and compare them with human responses from a primary research study on perceptions of city tourism destinations. Human and LLM responses were analyzed using linguistic measures, diversity and concentration metrics, topic models, and top-term analyses. The results show substantial overlap between human and LLM responses in broad topics and associations, but also important differences in style, linguistic structure, and the way diversity is generated. Recommendations are given on how to best utilize LLMs for generating synthetic consumer data, how model and prompt choices shape response quality, and on recognizing the limitations of LLM synthetic consumer data generation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether LLMs can generate synthetic consumer data for projective marketing techniques, comparing LLM outputs with real human responses. Results show topical overlap but stylistic and structural differences, with practical recommendations for using LLMs in consumer data generation.
AI.motivation: Collecting real consumer data for marketing research is costly, time-consuming, and difficult to scale. The authors explore whether LLMs can serve as a viable alternative for generating synthetic responses to projective techniques, which are commonly used to elicit subconscious consumer associations, emotions, and needs.
AI.method: The study tests LLM-generated responses across multiple projective tasks, varying LLMs, prompting strategies, and temperature settings. These synthetic responses are compared against human responses from a primary study on city tourism destination perceptions. Both human and LLM outputs are evaluated using linguistic measures, diversity and concentration metrics, topic models, and top-term analyses.
AI.result: Substantial overlap exists between human and LLM responses in broad topics and associations. However, notable differences emerge in linguistic style, structural properties, and the mechanisms by which diversity is produced. Model choice and prompt design significantly shape response quality.
AI.conclusion: LLMs show promise for synthetic consumer data generation in projective techniques but come with important limitations. The authors provide actionable recommendations on optimal LLM usage, prompt engineering, and temperature settings, while cautioning researchers to recognize where synthetic responses diverge from genuine human data.

title: NAVER LABS System Re-implementation for the IWSLT 2026 Instruction-Following Task
summary: We re-implement the NAVER LABS IWSLT 2025 instruction-following pipeline for the IWSLT 2026 Shared Task (constrained condition, short audio track), adapting it to the mandated components: SeamlessM4T-v2-large as the speech encoder and Qwen3-4B-Instruct as the LLM backbone. The three-stage approach projector alignment, text-only LoRA pre-training, and multimodal merging is preserved from the original design. We additionally construct 100k synthetic instruction-following examples across ten speech-centric task types (10k per task) from the provided corpora, suitable for further Stage 3 fine-tuning. Our primary model achieves COMET 0.781 on EN-ZH speech translation and BERTScore-F1 0.346 on English SQA on the MCIF benchmark.

AI.tldr: The paper adapts the NAVER LABS IWSLT 2025 instruction-following pipeline for the IWSLT 2026 Shared Task, replacing components with SeamlessM4T-v2-large and Qwen3-4B-Instruct, and constructs 100k synthetic instruction-following examples across ten speech tasks.
AI.motivation: To adapt a proven instruction-following speech pipeline to new mandated components (SeamlessM4T-v2-large encoder, Qwen3-4B-Instruct LLM) for the IWSLT 2026 Shared Task constrained condition, while generating sufficient synthetic training data for speech-centric instruction following.
AI.method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) projector alignment between speech encoder and LLM, (2) text-only LoRA pre-training, and (3) multimodal merging. Additionally, 100k synthetic instruction-following examples are constructed across 10 speech-centric task types (10k each) from the provided corpora for further Stage 3 fine-tuning.
AI.result: The primary model achieves COMET 0.781 on EN-ZH speech translation and BERTScore-F1 0.346 on English SQA, evaluated on the MCIF benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The re-implemented pipeline, adapted to the mandated components and augmented with large-scale synthetic instruction-following data, yields competitive baseline performance for the IWSLT 2026 Shared Task across speech translation and spoken question answering.

title: Breaking Structural Isolation: Scalable Graph Clustering via Community-Aware Sampling and Structural Entropy
comment: Accepted to the Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment (VLDB 2026). 18 pages, 15 figures, 15 tables
summary: Unsupervised graph clustering is a fundamental technique for uncovering underlying semantic patterns in large-scale networks. Although Graph Contrastive Learning has demonstrated promising performance, existing methods often suffer from the "structural isolation" issue during mini-batch training, making it challenging to capture cohesive community structures that characterize the global topological distribution. To address these challenges, we propose SCISE, a Scalable unsupervised graph Clustering framework that preserves structural Integrity by synergizing community-aware sampling with constrained Structural Entropy. Specifically, we first introduce the Structural Entropy Community Constraint operator (SECC), which optimizes structural information within a constrained solution space to mitigate community fragmentation and enhance partition cohesion. Second, to prevent global information loss during batch training, we design a Community-Aware Sampling Expansion (CSampE) mechanism that incorporates the community context of target nodes into sampling batches, effectively breaking structural barriers and preserving topological integrity. Finally, we devise a Structural Contrastive Learning (StructCL) module that refines edge weights based on intra-batch structural similarity, guiding the encoder to learn representations in a higher-order structural space. Extensive experiments on six mainstream benchmark datasets demonstrate that SCISE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms, with ablation studies and robustness analyses further validating its effectiveness and reliability for real-world large-scale graphs.

AI.tldr: SCISE is a scalable unsupervised graph clustering framework that addresses the "structural isolation" problem in mini-batch contrastive learning by integrating community-aware sampling, constrained structural entropy optimization, and structural contrastive learning to preserve global topological integrity.
AI.motivation: Existing graph contrastive learning methods for unsupervised clustering suffer from "structural isolation" during mini-batch training — the batch sampling process fragments the global community structure, making it difficult to capture cohesive clusters that reflect the true topological distribution of the graph.
AI.method: SCISE introduces three key components: (1) Structural Entropy Community Constraint (SECC), which optimizes structural information within a constrained solution space to reduce community fragmentation; (2) Community-Aware Sampling Expansion (CSampE), which enriches mini-batches with community context of target nodes to preserve topological integrity; and (3) Structural Contrastive Learning (StructCL), which refines edge weights based on intra-batch structural similarity to learn representations in a higher-order structural space.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on six mainstream benchmark datasets show SCISE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms, with ablation studies and robustness analyses validating its effectiveness and reliability for real-world large-scale graphs.
AI.conclusion: By synergizing community-aware sampling with constrained structural entropy, SCISE effectively mitigates structural isolation and community fragmentation in mini-batch graph contrastive learning, offering a scalable and robust solution for unsupervised graph clustering.

title: Unicode TAG-Block Concealment of Tool-Metadata Payloads in the Model Context Protocol: An Approval-View Fidelity Gap Across Three Independent Server Implementations
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables, 5 listings. Real-protocol proof-of-concept, 8 techniques across 3 independently developed MCP server libraries with 32 of 32 cross-library outcome cells agreeing, and 0 of 25 baseline false positives on a benign corpus. Data, harness, and fail-closed verifier released as a supplementary artifact
summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the dominant way coding agents discover and invoke external tools. A server advertises each tool through a tools/list handshake that returns a name, a natural-language description, and a JSON input schema. The client renders this metadata once, in a one-time approval dialog, and then injects it verbatim into the model's context on every subsequent turn. Nothing in the protocol requires the rendered approval view and the bytes delivered to the model to match. We isolate that gap as a single structural mechanism, concealment encoding, and show with a model-free, protocol-free analysis that Unicode's TAG block (U+E0000 to U+E007F) has no assigned glyph in any mainstream terminal, chat, or IDE renderer, so a payload written in it is absent from what a human reviewer sees while surviving byte-for-byte into the model's tokenizer. We then measure whether this mechanism actually defeats today's client-side defenses, building a proof-of-concept that speaks the real MCP JSON-RPC/stdio protocol against a genuine client and server. Across 5 distinct MCP metadata surfaces we implement 8 concrete techniques with a deterministic, protocol-level harness. All 8/8 techniques deliver an attacker-controlled payload into the model's context, 4/8 evade a representative string-matching sanitizer, and exactly as the mechanism analysis predicts, only the TAG-block encoding (1/8) is invisible in the human approval view while still reaching the model verbatim. MCP forces re-approval for 0/8 techniques even under a time-of-check to time-of-use rug-pull. To test whether these outcomes are a property of the protocol or an artifact of one server codebase, we re-implement the catalogue against 3 independently developed Python MCP server libraries and find total agreement across all 32 cross-library outcome cells. The baseline sanitizer flags 0 of 25 benign descriptions.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a structural vulnerability in the Model Context Protocol (MCP): the metadata rendered to a human reviewer during tool approval can differ from what is injected into the model's context. Using Unicode TAG block characters (U+E0000–U+E007F), which have no visible glyph in mainstream renderers, attackers can craft payloads that are invisible to human reviewers but survive byte-for-byte into the model's tokenizer. Across 8 techniques on 5 MCP surfaces, tested against real clients/servers and 3 independent server libraries (32 cross-library outcome cells), the TAG-block encoding is the only method that is both invisible in the approval UI and delivered verbatim to the model, with no re-approval triggered.
AI.motivation: MCP is the dominant protocol for coding agents to discover and invoke tools, yet its design contains a gap: the one-time approval dialog renders metadata for human review, but the same metadata injected into the model context on every turn is not required to match. This gap—termed "concealment encoding"—enables supply-chain or server-side attackers to hide malicious payloads from human reviewers while still reaching the model, undermining the trust model of tool approval.
AI.method: The authors (1) formalize the gap as "concealment encoding" through a model-free, protocol-free structural analysis; (2) identify Unicode TAG block characters as a mechanism invisible in terminals, chat UIs, and IDEs; (3) build a proof-of-concept using real MCP JSON-RPC/stdio against genuine client/server; (4) implement 8 concrete techniques across 5 MCP metadata surfaces; (5) test against a representative string-matching sanitizer; (6) validate against 3 independently developed Python MCP server libraries with 32 cross-library outcome cells; and (7) benchmark the baseline sanitizer against 25 benign descriptions.
AI.result: All 8/8 techniques deliver attacker-controlled payloads into the model's context. 4/8 evade string-matching sanitization. Only TAG-block encoding (1/8) is invisible in the human approval view while reaching the model verbatim. 0/8 techniques trigger MCP re-approval under time-of-check to time-of-use conditions. Results are fully consistent across all 3 server libraries (32/32 cells agree). The baseline sanitizer achieves 0 false positives on 25 benign descriptions.
AI.conclusion: The MCP protocol lacks a binding between what is displayed to the human reviewer and what reaches the model, creating a systemic vulnerability. Concrete mitigations are needed: cryptographic binding of rendered-to-delivered content, normative restrictions on Unicode control/metadata blocks in tool descriptions, or architectural changes to eliminate the gap entirely.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Cross-Modal Remote Sensing Image-Text Retrieval via Evidential Learning
summary: In cross-modal remote sensing image-text retrieval (CMRSITR), test-time remote sensing (RS) images and textual descriptions may deviate from well-curated benchmark conditions due to sensor- and atmosphere-related image degradations and text-side RS-vocabulary heterogeneity. Under such non-ideal conditions, existing CMRSITR methods may produce unreliable retrieval results because they perform retrieval with full certainty for each query and do not distinguish the varying uncertainty across queries. To address this issue, we propose an evidential learning-based CMRSITR (ELC) method for uncertainty-aware retrieval. During the training phase of ELC, evidential learning (EDL) is employed to model the inter-modal correspondences between RS images and textual descriptions as Dirichlet distributions, from which the uncertainty of each query can be obtained. Based on the EDL outputs, uncertainty-correctness alignment learning (UCL) is introduced to align the estimated uncertainty with retrieval correctness, encouraging high uncertainty for incorrect retrieval and low uncertainty for correct retrieval. Furthermore, intra-modal relationship learning (RL) distills the intra-modal similarity structure from pretrained mentor encoders for the trainable encoders, thereby making the Dirichlet distributions modeled by EDL more discriminative. In the test phase of ELC, the estimated uncertainty is compared with a threshold determined by a fixed deferral ratio, where low-uncertainty queries are directly returned and high-uncertainty queries are refined by RS-aware test-time augmentation (RS-TTA). Experimental results demonstrate that ELC achieves competitive retrieval performance compared with state-of-the-art CMRSITR methods and provides stronger robustness under the evaluated RS-specific degradations, including sensor- and atmosphere-related image perturbations and RS-vocabulary heterogeneity.

AI.tldr: ELC introduces evidential deep learning to CMRSITR, modeling inter-modal correspondences as Dirichlet distributions to quantify query uncertainty. High-uncertainty queries are deferred and refined via RS-aware test-time augmentation, while low-uncertainty ones are returned directly. Uncertainty-correctness alignment and intra-modal relationship learning further improve robustness against RS-specific image degradations and vocabulary heterogeneity.
AI.motivation: Existing CMRSITR methods produce unreliable results under non-ideal conditions (sensor/atmosphere-related image degradations, RS-vocabulary heterogeneity) because they treat every query with full certainty and cannot distinguish varying uncertainty across queries.
AI.method: ELC has three training components: (1) Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) models image-text correspondences as Dirichlet distributions to estimate query-wise uncertainty; (2) Uncertainty-Correctness Alignment Learning (UCL) aligns estimated uncertainty with retrieval correctness (high uncertainty for wrong, low for correct); (3) Intra-modal Relationship Learning (RL) distills intra-modal similarity from pretrained mentor encoders to make Dirichlet distributions more discriminative. At test time, queries with uncertainty below a threshold (set by a fixed deferral ratio) are returned directly; high-uncertainty queries are refined via RS-aware test-time augmentation (RS-TTA).
AI.result: ELC achieves competitive retrieval performance against state-of-the-art CMRSITR methods and demonstrates stronger robustness under RS-specific degradations, including sensor- and atmosphere-related image perturbations and RS-vocabulary heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ELC framework effectively addresses uncertainty in CMRSITR by combining evidential learning with uncertainty-aware test-time strategies, enabling reliable cross-modal retrieval under realistic, non-ideal remote sensing conditions.

title: Can Large Language Models Generate Observability-Aware Code?
summary: Recent advances in coding agents have enabled the generation of increasingly complex software systems. While existing evaluations primarily focus on functional correctness, production systems must expose failure evidence to support observability. In this paper, we present a systematic study of observability in agent-generated systems. We examine whether agents can reconstruct source-level diagnostic semantics by restoring observability artifacts in 10 open-source and 8 industrial repositories. We also evaluate whether these artifacts translate into effective fault signals at runtime through 200 generated microservice systems deployed on Kubernetes with 13 injected faults. Our results reveal a consistent gap between diagnostic semantics at the source level and fault signals (i.e., explicit, fault-specific evidence) at runtime. At the source level, agents partially recover observability artifacts but struggle to capture key diagnostic semantics. At runtime, generated systems expose fault signals for only a small fraction of failures (up to 13.99\%), despite the presence of logging, suggesting that the generated observability artifacts may lack the failure-specific semantics needed to effectively expose faults. We further introduce an observability-oriented skill, which can serve as a guidance to improve both diagnostic semantics and fault-signal exposure, but the gains remain limited, indicating that the gap is not easily addressed. More broadly, our findings suggest that current evaluations focusing primarily on functional correctness may overlook observability as an important dimension of practical software quality.

AI.tldr: A systematic study revealing that coding agents struggle to generate effective observability artifacts—while they partially recover logging and diagnostic code at the source level, these artifacts fail to produce meaningful fault signals at runtime (only up to 13.99% of failures exposed). An observability-oriented skill offers limited improvement, highlighting a gap in current evaluations that prioritize functional correctness over practical operational quality.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of code generation agents focus almost exclusively on functional correctness, overlooking whether agent-generated systems can support observability—the ability to expose failure evidence at runtime. In production systems, observability (logging, metrics, tracing) is critical for debugging and reliability, yet no prior work has systematically studied whether agents can produce code with adequate diagnostic semantics.
AI.method: The authors conduct a two-level empirical study: (1) Source-level analysis: examining whether agents can reconstruct observability artifacts (logging, error handling, etc.) by comparing agent-generated code against ground truth in 10 open-source and 8 industrial repositories. (2) Runtime-level analysis: generating 200 microservice systems, deploying them on Kubernetes, injecting 13 fault types, and measuring whether the generated observability artifacts produce explicit fault-specific signals. They also introduce and evaluate an observability-oriented skill as a mitigation.
AI.result: At the source level, agents partially recover observability artifacts but fail to capture key diagnostic semantics. At runtime, generated systems expose fault signals for only a small fraction of failures (up to 13.99%), despite the presence of logging code, indicating that generated artifacts lack failure-specific semantics. The introduced observability-oriented skill yields only limited gains, suggesting the gap between diagnostic semantics and effective fault signals is not easily addressed.
AI.conclusion: Current code generation benchmarks that focus solely on functional correctness miss observability as a critical dimension of practical software quality. The gap between generating observability artifacts and producing effective runtime fault signals is substantial and not trivially resolved, pointing to a need for new evaluation frameworks and training objectives that incorporate operational observability requirements.

title: BlossomPsy: A User-Centric AI System for Adaptive and Engaging MBTI Personality Assessments
summary: There has been growing public interest in understanding personality traits and emotional characteristics, as such knowledge helps individuals better accept themselves and manage negative emotions. While professional personality scales remain the standard tool for assessment, they are often perceived as tedious or inaccessible to the general public. AI-driven systems can make assessments more accessible, but it is difficult to balance user engagement with predictive consistency in existing works. We tackle this challenge by introducing BlossomPsy, a user-friendly AI-driven MBTI assessment system. MBTI, a widely recognized but psychometrically debated personality framework, serves as the foundation for many recent systems. BlossomPsy integrates multi-turn dialogue and photo-based questions to enhance user engagement while supporting confidence-aware predictions. By combining deep learning, multi-armed bandit algorithms, and control theory, the system dynamically adapts to users' responses. In particular, photo-based questions are designed to increase interactivity and provide additional user information, thereby improving prediction confidence. Experiments involving both human volunteers and large language models (LLMs) provide preliminary evidence that BlossomPsy can produce stable predictions, with higher reported user satisfaction compared to MBTI-M (Chinese version), while maintaining comparable consistency with the reference scale.

AI.tldr: BlossomPsy is an AI-driven MBTI assessment system that uses multi-turn dialogue and photo-based questions with confidence-aware, dynamically adaptive predictions, achieving stable results and higher user satisfaction than a baseline MBTI test.
AI.motivation: Existing personality assessments are either professionally rigorous but tedious (scales) or engaging but predictively inconsistent (existing AI systems). The authors aim to bridge this gap by creating an accessible, engaging system that maintains predictive reliability.
AI.method: BlossomPsy integrates deep learning, multi-armed bandit algorithms, and control theory to dynamically adapt questions based on user responses. It employs multi-turn dialogue and photo-based questions to boost interactivity and extract additional user information, enabling confidence-aware MBTI predictions.
AI.result: Experiments with human volunteers and LLMs showed that BlossomPsy produces stable predictions with higher user satisfaction than MBTI-M (Chinese version), while maintaining comparable consistency with the reference scale.
AI.conclusion: BlossomPsy demonstrates that an AI-driven personality assessment can successfully balance user engagement and predictive consistency, offering a practical alternative to traditional scales for public use.

title: Beyond Static Evaluation: Building Simulation Environments for Scalable Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: As Large Language Models (LLMs) evolve into autonomous agents, traditional static evaluation fails to capture multi-step decision-making. We introduce AgenticAI-Supervisor, an API and UI-driven RL Gym environment that decouples environment creation from scalable execution. By moving to verifiable execution outcomes, the platform generates high-fidelity traces and applies multi-dimensional reward shaping. Critically, our framework mitigates reward hacking through rigorous internal state validation and testing. This work provides a first look at our platform's core capabilities through a Customer Support Agent case study demonstrating a consistent closed-loop feedback for model optimization. Future work will focus on advanced features such as Computer Use, Tool Use, automated "stumping", and edge-case generation.

AI.tldr: AgenticAI-Supervisor is an RL Gym environment for LLM agents that enables verifiable execution, multi-dimensional reward shaping, and reward hacking mitigation, demonstrated through a customer support case study.
AI.motivation: Traditional static evaluation benchmarks cannot adequately assess LLMs operating as autonomous agents, which require evaluating multi-step decision-making processes rather than single-turn outputs.
AI.method: The platform provides an API/UI-driven RL Gym environment that decouples environment creation from scalable execution, generates high-fidelity execution traces, applies multi-dimensional reward shaping, and implements rigorous internal state validation to mitigate reward hacking.
AI.result: A Customer Support Agent case study demonstrates consistent closed-loop feedback for model optimization, offering an initial validation of the platform's core capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides foundational infrastructure for training and evaluating LLM agents. Future directions include Computer Use, Tool Use, automated "stumping," and edge-case generation.

title: Population-Level Profiling of DSM-5 Depressive Symptoms Among Self-Reported ADHD and ASD Users on Twitter: An Exploratory Study Using Advanced NLP and Statistical Analysis
summary: Background: Depression frequently co-occurs with ADHD and autism spectrum disorder (ASD), but population-level differences in symptom expression between these groups remain underexplored. Objective: We examined whether social media users with ADHD and ASD differ in how they express DSM-5 depressive symptoms in their tweets, and whether differences persist across varying levels of depressive-content filtering. Methods: We analysed 1,282,437 tweets from 792 users (622 ADHD; 170 ASD) with self-reported diagnoses on Twitter. Tweets were pre-filtered for depressive relevance using zero-shot NLI, then classified into nine DSM-5 symptoms using MentalRoBERTa fine-tuned on ReDSM5. Profiles were mean-centered per user. We applied L1-penalised logistic regression with cross-validation to distinguish ADHD from ASD users, complemented by Pearson correlations for symptom co-occurrence, and tested robustness across five filtering thresholds using bootstrapping. Results: MentalRoBERTa achieved macro-F1 of 0.901 on a held-out set, outperforming the original ReDSM5 benchmark. ADHD vs ASD classification yielded stable but modest performance (cross-validated ROC-AUC 0.645-0.653). Cognitive issues, sleep issues, appetite change, and fatigue leaned toward ADHD, while suicidal ideation and anhedonia leaned toward ASD. A largely shared symptom co-occurrence structure emerged between groups; no pair met our criterion for a robust disorder-specific difference. Conclusions: Population-level differences in depression-related language between ADHD and ASD social media users were consistently observed across thresholds, reflecting reproducibility rather than clinical validity. Findings are exploratory and do not establish differing phenomenology at the individual level.

AI.tldr: This study analyzed depression-related tweets from users with ADHD and ASD, finding modest but stable linguistic differences (ADHD leaning toward cognitive/somatic symptoms, ASD toward suicidal ideation/anhedonia), but largely shared symptom co-occurrence structures, suggesting reproducibility without clinical validity.
AI.motivation: Depression frequently co-occurs with both ADHD and ASD, yet population-level differences in how depressive symptoms are expressed between these neurodevelopmental groups remain underexplored. Understanding these differences could inform screening, digital phenotyping, and tailored interventions.
AI.method: Analyzed 1,282,437 tweets from 792 self-identified Twitter users (622 ADHD, 170 ASD). Tweets were pre-filtered for depressive relevance using zero-shot NLI, then classified into nine DSM-5 symptoms via MentalRoBERTa fine-tuned on ReDSM5. User-level symptom profiles were mean-centered. L1-penalized logistic regression with cross-validation distinguished ADHD from ASD users; Pearson correlations assessed symptom co-occurrence. Robustness was tested across five filtering thresholds using bootstrapping.
AI.result: MentalRoBERTa achieved macro-F1 of 0.901 on held-out data, surpassing the ReDSM5 benchmark. ADHD vs. ASD classification was modest but stable (ROC-AUC 0.645–0.653). Cognitive issues, sleep issues, appetite change, and fatigue leaned toward ADHD; suicidal ideation and anhedonia leaned toward ASD. Symptom co-occurrence structures were largely shared, with no robust disorder-specific differences detected.
AI.conclusion: Depression-related language differences between ADHD and ASD users were consistently observed across thresholds, reflecting reproducibility rather than clinical validity. Findings are exploratory and do not establish differing phenomenology at the individual level.

title: Parameter-Free Encoders Remain Viable for RDB Foundation Models
comment: ICML 2026 Workshop on Foundation Models for Structured Data
summary: Given a relational database (RDB) storing heterogeneous tabular information, how can we predict missing (or future) values in some target column of interest? As the space of potential targets is vast across enterprise settings, it is preferable to avoid learning a new model from scratch each time there is a new prediction task. Frozen foundation models based on RDB-specific encoders provide a viable solution, but ideal design remains an open question. On the one hand, it has recently been argued that certain parameter-free subgraph encoders combined with single-table foundation models can achieve near SOTA performance, with no RDB-specific pre-training required. Meanwhile, other contemporary studies advocate for parameterized encoders pre-trained to exploit observable labels for learning task-specific representations. To address this ambiguity, we analyze RDB encoder properties specifically when labels are present as inputs, proving limitations on the potential efficacy of trainable encoder parameters. As empirical validation, we demonstrate that considerably simpler parameter-free encoders are still capable of strong performance across many relevant benchmarking tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether parameter-free subgraph encoders can match the performance of parameterized encoders pre-trained on RDB data for tabular prediction tasks, theoretically proving limitations of trainable parameters when labels are input features, and empirically validating that simpler parameter-free encoders achieve strong results across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Resolve the ambiguity between two competing approaches to RDB foundation models: parameter-free subgraph encoders + single-table models versus parameterized encoders pre-trained with task-specific labels. The goal is to determine whether RDB-specific pre-training and trainable encoder parameters are genuinely necessary.
AI.method: The authors conduct a theoretical analysis of RDB encoder properties when labels are available as inputs, proving formal limitations on the efficacy of trainable encoder parameters. They then perform empirical validation by benchmarking simple parameter-free encoders against parameterized counterparts across multiple relevant tabular prediction tasks.
AI.result: The theoretical analysis establishes that trainable encoder parameters have bounded utility when labels are present as inputs. Empirical results confirm that considerably simpler parameter-free encoders achieve strong, competitive performance across many benchmarking tasks.
AI.conclusion: Parameter-free subgraph encoders combined with single-table foundation models represent a viable, simpler alternative to parameterized RDB-specific pre-trained encoders, challenging the necessity of complex trainable architectures for relational database prediction tasks.

title: Withdrawability in Fiat-Shamir with aborts constructions
summary: This article presents an extension of the work performed by Liu, Baek and Susilo on withdrawable signatures to the Fiat-Shamir with aborts paradigm. We introduce an abstract construction, and provide security proofs for this proposal. As an instantiation, we provide a concrete withdrawable signature scheme based on a no-hint, full-t Dilithium-style Fiat-Shamir with aborts construction; adapting to production ML-DSA (with hints) introduces a small epsilon term.

AI.tldr: The paper extends Liu, Baek, and Susilo's withdrawable signatures to the Fiat-Shamir with aborts paradigm, providing an abstract construction with security proofs and a concrete instantiation based on a Dilithium-style (no-hint, full-t) scheme, with notes on adapting to ML-DSA.
AI.motivation: To extend the concept of withdrawable signatures — which allow a signer to provably invalidate previously issued signatures — into the lattice-based, post-quantum setting enabled by the Fiat-Shamir with aborts paradigm, thereby providing post-quantum secure constructions with this advanced functionality.
AI.method: The authors propose an abstract (generic) construction of withdrawable signatures within the Fiat-Shamir with aborts framework and provide formal security proofs. They then instantiate this with a concrete scheme built on a no-hint, full-t Dilithium-style Fiat-Shamir with aborts construction, and discuss the adaptation to the production ML-DSA standard (which uses hints), noting the introduction of a small epsilon degradation in the security bound.
AI.result: A provably secure abstract construction for withdrawable signatures in the Fiat-Shamir with aborts setting, along with a concrete lattice-based instantiation. The adaptation to ML-DSA (with hints) introduces only a minor epsilon term in the security analysis.
AI.conclusion: Withdrawable signatures can be successfully realized in the Fiat-Shamir with aborts paradigm, yielding post-quantum constructions. The Dilithium-style instantiation is practical, and the transition to the standardized ML-DSA comes at negligible security cost.

title: Learn to Pool: Lightweight Fine-Tuning for Flexible Multi-Vector Compression
summary: Late interaction models have shown strong generalization capabilities, often outperforming much larger dense embedding models. One challenge to their widespread deployment is the large number of token vectors they produce per document and the associated storage and memory costs. Pooling tokens at inference time has shown great promise to reduce the vector count with limited effects on retrieval accuracy. Large-scale pooling-aware training has demonstrated even more impressive results at high compression rates. We propose lightweight fine-tuning as a practical alternative and find that even minimal pooling-aware training with k-means yields broad gains over inference-only pooling, shows evidence of transfer across pooling methods and datasets, and - with multi-factor training - produces a single model effective across different compression levels. Our strongest model outperforms the unpooled baseline on BEIR SciFact across pool factors 1-6, implying a vector compression rate of 83% at no cost to retrieval accuracy.

AI.tldr: Lightweight fine-tuning with pooling-aware training (including k-means pooling) enables late interaction models to achieve high vector compression rates (up to 83%) without sacrificing retrieval accuracy, outperforming inference-only pooling and offering transferability across pooling methods and compression levels.
AI.motivation: Late interaction models (e.g., ColBERT) achieve strong retrieval performance but suffer from high storage and memory costs due to producing many token vectors per document. While pooling at inference time reduces vector counts, it can degrade accuracy. The authors seek a practical, low-cost training alternative to large-scale pooling-aware training that still yields strong compression–accuracy trade-offs.
AI.method: The authors propose lightweight fine-tuning for pooling-aware adaptation of late interaction models. They explore minimal training with k-means pooling, investigate transferability across different pooling methods and datasets, and introduce multi-factor training to produce a single model that works well across multiple compression levels (pool factors). Comparisons are made against inference-only pooling and unpooled baselines.
AI.result: Lightweight pooling-aware fine-tuning with k-means yields broad improvements over inference-only pooling. The approach shows evidence of transfer across pooling methods and datasets. Multi-factor training produces a single model effective at various compression levels. The strongest model outperforms the unpooled baseline on BEIR SciFact across pool factors 1–6, achieving 83% vector compression with no loss in retrieval accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight fine-tuning is a practical and effective alternative to large-scale pooling-aware training for compressing late interaction models. It enables significant storage reductions without sacrificing accuracy and offers flexibility through transferable and multi-factor training capabilities.

title: SCOPE: Leveraging Subgoal Critiques for Code Generation
summary:
Code generation with large language models (LLMs) remains unreliable because generated programs can appear correct while still violating key semantic requirements in the natural language specification. Existing feedback-based methods improve over coder-only generation, but they often rely on unstructured critique or execution signals that do not explicitly identify what the code is semantically missing. We present SCOPE, a prover-initialized subgoal critic for code generation. SCOPE adapts a Lean-oriented prover model to produce three parseable feedback fields for downstream code generation: subgoals, gap analysis, and a robustness checklist. Our approach combines supervised fine-tuning, process-aligned reinforcement learning (RL), and feedback-guided inference, with two complementary rewards during RL: a dense reward for structured critique quality and a sparse reward based on whether the critique improves the coder's execution score.
  Experiments show that SCOPE improves over the compared feedback baselines. On LiveCodeBench V6, SCOPE achieves 39.4% pass@1, compared with 36.6% for Reflexion and 20.6% for the coder-only baseline. On BigCodeBench (Hard), it reaches 42.6%, surpassing Reflexion at 36.5% and coder-only generation at 34.5%. Further analysis shows that SCOPE's gains are concentrated in tasks with concrete semantic constraints and that its code corrections are more localized than Reflexion's.

AI.tldr: SCOPE is a code generation framework that uses a Lean-prover-initialized model to produce structured feedback (subgoals, gap analysis, robustness checklist) for improving LLM code generation. Trained with supervised fine-tuning and process-aligned RL with dual rewards, SCOPE outperforms baselines like Reflexion on LiveCodeBench V6 (39.4% vs 36.6% pass@1) and BigCodeBench Hard (42.6% vs 36.5%), with gains concentrated on tasks requiring concrete semantic constraints.
AI.motivation: LLM-generated code often appears syntactically correct but violates semantic requirements in the natural language specification. Existing feedback methods (Reflexion, etc.) rely on unstructured critique or execution signals that fail to explicitly identify what the code is semantically missing, limiting their effectiveness for reliable code generation.
AI.method: SCOPE (Subgoal Critic with Prover Initialization) adapts a Lean-oriented prover model to generate three structured feedback fields: (1) subgoals — decomposing the specification into verifiable sub-tasks, (2) gap analysis — identifying what semantic requirements the generated code fails to satisfy, and (3) a robustness checklist. Training combines supervised fine-tuning, process-aligned RL with two complementary rewards — a dense reward for structured critique quality and a sparse reward based on whether the critique improves the coder's execution score — and feedback-guided inference.
AI.result: On LiveCodeBench V6, SCOPE achieves 39.4% pass@1 vs. 36.6% (Reflexion) and 20.6% (coder-only). On BigCodeBench Hard, SCOPE reaches 42.6% vs. 36.5% (Reflexion) and 34.5% (coder-only). Gains are concentrated in tasks with concrete semantic constraints, and SCOPE's code corrections are more localized than Reflexion's.
AI.conclusion: Structured, prover-initialized feedback (subgoals, gap analysis, checklist) provides more effective guidance for code generation than unstructured critique, particularly for semantically-constrained tasks. The dual-reward RL training strategy successfully aligns the critic to produce actionable, improvement-driving feedback.

title: DS-MTNet:Structured Multi-Task EEG Decoding for Human-Machine Collaboration
summary: Current human-machine collaboration (HMC) systems rely on environment-facing sensors to observe visible actions and scene states, but the internal perceptual, intention-related, and state-related processes of operators remain insufficiently integrated into machine perception. Electroencephalography (EEG) provides a non-invasive, time-resolved modality to capture neural activity associated with these processes and can serve as an additional sensing channel in HMC. However, HMC-relevant EEG evidence is often mixed in continuous recordings. Existing EEG decoding methods usually target task-specific classification or aggregate prediction, so multiple HMC-relevant readouts are rarely organized in a unified EEG representation. To address this gap, this paper proposed the Decomposed-Source Multi-Task Network (DS-MTNet), a structured multi-task EEG decoding framework. DS-MTNet integrated three streams, namely EEG waveforms, task-routed source embeddings, and temporal-spectral power features, into reusable slots and used dual gating mechanisms to route task-specific components. The model was tested on a sustained-attention driving EEG dataset with three representative readouts: lane-departure-related epochs for environmental-event processing, steering-response stage for response preparation, and reaction-time-defined alertness state for internal state. DS-MTNet achieved the best mean performance among traditional, single-task deep, and multi-task EEG baselines, with the most robust gains observed for steering-response stage decoding. Ablation and interpretability analyses suggested that DS-MTNet jointly decoded multiple readouts and organized event-related, response-related, and state-related EEG evidence in a unified source-slot representation. These findings provide a computational step toward incorporating operator-related neural evidence into machine perception in HMC.

AI.tldr: DS-MTNet is a multi-task EEG decoding framework that unifies three HMC-relevant neural readouts (environmental-event processing, response preparation, and internal alertness state) using decomposed-source embeddings and dual gating, achieving superior performance over baselines on a sustained-attention driving dataset.
AI.motivation: Current HMC systems only capture visible actions and scene states via environment-facing sensors, while operators' internal perceptual, intentional, and state-related neural processes remain unintegrated. EEG offers a non-invasive window into these processes, but existing decoding methods perform task-specific classification without organizing multiple HMC-relevant readouts into a unified representation.
AI.method: DS-MTNet employs a three-stream architecture: (1) EEG waveforms, (2) task-routed source embeddings, and (3) temporal-spectral power features. These streams are integrated into reusable slots, and dual gating mechanisms route task-specific components. The framework was evaluated on three representative readouts: lane-departure-related epochs (environmental-event processing), steering-response stage (response preparation), and reaction-time-defined alertness state (internal state).
AI.result: DS-MTNet achieved the best mean performance against traditional methods, single-task deep learning, and multi-task EEG baselines. The most robust gains were in steering-response stage decoding. Ablation and interpretability analyses confirmed that the model jointly decodes multiple readouts and organizes event-related, response-related, and state-related EEG evidence within a unified source-slot representation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework represents a computational advance toward integrating operator-related neural evidence into machine perception for HMC, demonstrating that a structured multi-task approach with source-slot representations can effectively unify heterogeneous EEG readouts.

title: Beyond the Leaderboard: A Synthesis of Tool-Use, Planning, and Reasoning Failures in Large Language Model Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly evaluated on their ability to use tools, plan multi-step tasks, coordinate with other agents, and operate over extended horizons. Reported benchmark gains often obscure recurring failure modes documented across otherwise unrelated evaluation efforts. This paper synthesizes 27 benchmark, taxonomy, and audit papers (2023-2026), spanning 19 distinct benchmarks, into a cross-cutting taxonomy of agent limitations. To our knowledge, this is the first synthesis that integrates evidence across tool use, planning, long-horizon reasoning, multi-agent coordination, safety, and measurement validity into a single, unified taxonomy of LLM agent limitations. We identify six failure clusters: (1) tool invocation and parameter-level errors, (2) planning and constraint-satisfaction failures, (3) long-horizon degradation from context accumulation, (4) multi-agent coordination failures, (5) safety and security failures under adversarial or underspecified conditions, and (6) measurement validity problems. The taxonomy was derived iteratively by grouping independently reported error categories into themes corresponding to distinct stages of the agent reasoning-to-action pipeline. Across the literature, we find that failures compound nonlinearly with task length, that strong performance on individual sub-tasks does not reliably translate into end-to-end success, and that additional scaffolding does not consistently improve reliability. At the same time, substantial progress has been demonstrated in single-turn tool use, short-horizon web navigation, and narrowly scoped coding tasks.

AI.tldr: A cross-cutting taxonomy of LLM agent failures synthesized from 27 papers (2023–2026) across 19 benchmarks, identifying six failure clusters: tool errors, planning failures, long-horizon degradation, multi-agent coordination breakdowns, safety/security vulnerabilities, and measurement validity issues. Failures compound nonlinearly with task length, and strong sub-task performance does not reliably translate to end-to-end success.
AI.motivation: Reported benchmark gains on LLM agent capabilities often obscure persistent, recurring failure modes documented across disparate evaluation efforts. No prior work had integrated evidence across the full agent reasoning-to-action pipeline into a single unified taxonomy of limitations.
AI.method: A synthesis review aggregating findings from 27 benchmark, taxonomy, and audit papers (2023–2026) covering 19 distinct benchmarks. The taxonomy was derived iteratively by grouping independently reported error categories into themes mapped to distinct stages of the agent reasoning-to-action pipeline.
AI.result: Six failure clusters identified: (1) tool invocation and parameter-level errors, (2) planning and constraint-satisfaction failures, (3) long-horizon degradation from context accumulation, (4) multi-agent coordination failures, (5) safety and security failures under adversarial/underspecified conditions, and (6) measurement validity problems. Failures compound nonlinearly with task length; strong sub-task performance does not reliably yield end-to-end success; additional scaffolding does not consistently improve reliability. Progress was noted in single-turn tool use, short-horizon web navigation, and narrowly scoped coding tasks.
AI.conclusion: LLM agent evaluation must move beyond aggregate benchmark scores to systematically account for compounding, cross-cutting failure modes. Future work should target the observed nonlinear degradation in multi-step settings and the gap between sub-task proficiency and holistic task success.

title: Do It Right! A Methodology for Successful NLP System Development
summary: Natural language processing (NLP) is a common method for supplying data to clinical research and decision making by extracting information from electronic medical records. Numerous textbooks and tutorials describe specific algorithms and applications for text processing, yet algorithmic knowledge is only one ingredient of a successful NLP project. Drawing on the available literature, this paper presents a stepwise approach that applies the Systems Development Life Cycle (SDLC) to projects that rely on data extraction through language processing.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a stepwise framework that applies the Systems Development Life Cycle (SDLC) to NLP projects in clinical settings, emphasizing that successful NLP implementation requires more than just algorithmic knowledge.
AI.motivation: While NLP is widely used to extract information from electronic medical records for clinical research and decision-making, existing resources focus predominantly on algorithms and applications. There is a gap in guidance on the broader project management and lifecycle aspects necessary for successful NLP deployment in healthcare.
AI.method: The authors draw on available literature to map the Systems Development Life Cycle (SDLC) — a structured software engineering framework — onto NLP projects that involve data extraction via language processing, presenting it as a stepwise approach.
AI.result: The paper provides a structured, phased methodology for planning and executing clinical NLP projects, integrating technical NLP tasks within the broader SDLC framework to improve project outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Algorithmic proficiency alone is insufficient for successful clinical NLP projects; adopting a systematic lifecycle approach like the SDLC can address the organizational, design, and implementation challenges inherent in healthcare text processing initiatives.

title: InvWeaver: Deductive Feedback for Invariant Synthesis in Interacting-Loop Programs
summary: Loop invariant inference is a fundamental yet challenging problem in program verification. Recent LLM-aided guess-and-check techniques have shown strong performance on single-loop programs, but they often struggle with programs containing multiple interacting loops. This paper presents InvWeaver, a neuro-symbolic framework for synthesizing invariants for such programs. The key idea is to expose inter-loop dependencies and propagate proof obligations through a combination of loop-level abstraction, obligation-guided inference, and weakest-precondition-based refinement. We evaluate InvWeaver on a comprehensive benchmark suite, including a newly curated dataset derived from classic algorithms. Experimental results show that InvWeaver substantially outperforms existing invariant inference methods, solving 72 out of 82 multi-loop benchmark problems and maintaining strong performance on single-loop tasks.

AI.tldr: InvWeaver is a neuro-symbolic framework that infers loop invariants for multi-loop programs by exposing inter-loop dependencies through abstraction, obligation-guided inference, and weakest-precondition refinement. It solves 72/82 multi-loop benchmarks, substantially outperforming existing methods.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-aided guess-and-check techniques perform well on single-loop programs but struggle with programs containing multiple interacting loops due to the difficulty of reasoning about inter-loop dependencies.
AI.method: InvWeaver combines three techniques: (1) loop-level abstraction to expose inter-loop dependencies, (2) obligation-guided inference to propagate proof obligations across loops, and (3) weakest-precondition-based refinement to iteratively strengthen candidate invariants.
AI.result: On a comprehensive benchmark suite including a newly curated dataset of classic algorithms, InvWeaver solves 72 out of 82 multi-loop problems and maintains strong performance on single-loop tasks, substantially outperforming existing invariant inference methods.
AI.conclusion: The neuro-symbolic approach of exposing and reasoning about inter-loop dependencies is highly effective for multi-loop invariant synthesis, significantly advancing the state of the art in automated program verification.

title: MSCENet: A Multi-Scale Correlation Enhanced Network for Anomaly Detection
summary: In the field of multivariate time series anomaly detection, against the backdrop of increasing data complexity and complex dependencies across multiple temporal scales, traditional methods often struggle to simultaneously capture temporal dynamic features and intricate inter-series correlations. To address this, we propose an innovative framework, MSCENet, which leverages advanced spatio-temporal learning and multi-scale learning techniques to enhance detection accuracy. MSCENet includes a fine-grained temporal convolution module that captures complex temporal dependencies through dilated convolutions, enabling the detection of both short- and long-term patterns. Additionally, the framework models inter-series relationships as a graph structure, using Mixhop graph convolutions to adaptively capture spatial dependencies across varying time scales. To support robust anomaly detection, the multi-scale gated convolution module in MSCENet integrates spatial and temporal attributes through gated mechanisms, facilitating the detection of subtle variations across multiple scales. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets: SMD, PSM, and SWaT. It provides an adaptable and high-performance solution for anomaly detection in complex time series data environments.

AI.tldr: MSCENet is a multivariate time series anomaly detection framework that combines fine-grained temporal convolution, Mixhop graph convolution for inter-series spatial dependencies, and multi-scale gated convolution to capture subtle variations across temporal scales, achieving strong performance on SMD, PSM, and SWaT datasets.
AI.motivation: Traditional multivariate time series anomaly detection methods struggle with increasing data complexity and fail to simultaneously capture temporal dynamic features and intricate inter-series correlations across multiple temporal scales.
AI.method: MSCENet employs three core components: (1) a fine-grained temporal convolution module using dilated convolutions to capture both short- and long-term temporal dependencies; (2) a graph structure modeling inter-series relationships with Mixhop graph convolutions to adaptively capture spatial dependencies across varying time scales; (3) a multi-scale gated convolution module that integrates spatial and temporal attributes through gated mechanisms to detect subtle multi-scale variations.
AI.result: The framework was experimentally evaluated on three real-world datasets — SMD, PSM, and SWaT — demonstrating adaptable and high-performance anomaly detection in complex time series environments.
AI.conclusion: MSCENet provides an adaptable, high-performance solution for anomaly detection in complex multivariate time series data by effectively integrating spatio-temporal and multi-scale learning.

title: Beyond Refusal: A Same-Lineage Study of Aligned and Abliterated LLMs for Vulnerability Analysis
summary: Large language model (LLM)-assisted software security operates at a difficult boundary: the vulnerability-analysis terminology needed for legitimate code review, triage, and repair can closely resemble terminology associated with misuse. Existing safety and cybersecurity evaluations are difficult to interpret in this setting because they often compare unrelated model families, thereby conflating safety behavior with differences in architecture, scale, training data, and deployment. To isolate this factor, we study safety state: whether refusal behavior remains intact (Aligned) or has been refusal-ablated (Abliterated) within same-lineage models. We ask how this safety state affects defensive utility across software-security workflows. We compare aligned instruction-tuned models with publicly released refusal-ablated descendants from two model families, Gemma and Qwen. We evaluate Aligned and Abliterated states on vulnerability detection, CWE attribution, vulnerable-line localization, root-cause localization, and executable patch validation. We further treat prompt wording as a controlled framing dimension: prompts begin with neutral code-review language, add authorization context, and vary the density of cybersecurity terminology. In a Gemma-based Java/Vul4J repair-validation study, Abliterated achieves higher early-stage validation rates, with 67.8%, 65.0%, and 32.8% of patches judged usable, successfully applied, and successfully compiled, respectively, compared with 29.9%, 24.9%, and 9.0% for Aligned. In the Qwen pair, Abliterated improves localization performance, increasing line-level F1 from 2.08% to 3.91% and Top-1 accuracy from 4.10% to 6.95%. These findings suggest that evaluations of LLM-based security assistants should jointly measure whether models respond, whether their usable responses are correct, and whether their outputs remain actionable across the engineering workflow.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how the "safety state" of LLMs—specifically whether refusal behavior is intact (Aligned) or removed (Abliterated)—affects their utility in software security workflows. Comparing aligned models against refusal-ablated variants within the same model families (Gemma and Qwen), the authors find that abliterated models consistently outperform aligned ones on tasks like vulnerability detection, localization, and patch validation, suggesting that safety mechanisms may impede legitimate security assistance.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM safety evaluations conflate refusal behavior with differences in architecture, scale, and training data by comparing unrelated model families.
