This makes it difficult to assess whether safety alignment genuinely impairs performance on legitimate software security tasks. The authors isolate "safety state" as a controlled variable by comparing aligned and refusal-ablated versions of the same base models.
AI.method: The authors compare Aligned (instruction-tuned) and Abliterated (refusal-ablated) versions of two model families—Gemma and Qwen—across five software security tasks: vulnerability detection, CWE attribution, vulnerable-line localization, root-cause localization, and executable patch validation. They also control for prompt framing by varying neutral code-review language, authorization context, and density of cybersecurity terminology.
AI.result: In Gemma-based Java/Vul4J repair-validation, Abliterated achieved substantially higher patch usability: 67.8% judged usable, 65.0% successfully applied, and 32.8% compiled, versus 29.9%, 24.9%, and 9.0% for Aligned. In the Qwen pair, Abliterated improved line-level localization F1 from 2.08% to 3.91% and Top-1 accuracy from 4.10% to 6.95%.
AI.conclusion: Evaluations of LLM-based security assistants must jointly assess whether models respond, whether usable responses are correct, and whether outputs remain actionable across the engineering workflow. Safety alignment mechanisms can significantly degrade defensive utility, and evaluation frameworks should account for this trade-off.

title: The Impact of Security and Privacy Controls on Users' Emotional Engagement with Generative AI Chatbots
comment: Accepted at the 35th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 2026). 20 pages, 7 tables, 2 figures
summary: Chatbots powered by generative AI (e.g., OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google's Gemini) are increasingly being appropriated for emotional support and companionship. These tools offer a suite of security and privacy (S&P) controls, including model training opt-outs and memory toggles, yet how the presence of these controls influences users' attitudes toward emotionally sensitive disclosure remains understudied. We conducted a mixed-methods vignette study with 354 U.S. participants to examine how S&P controls influence users' willingness to engage with generative AI chatbots for emotional support, their perceptions of how protected they are when using these systems, and their perceptions of how effective the chatbots are for providing support. Controls enabling deletion of disclosures had the largest positive impact: these offerings outperformed technically sophisticated controls such as local-only processing and model training opt-outs, where participants expressed difficulty understanding the underlying mechanisms. Yet trust remains fragile, and participants often doubted S&P controls would function as promised. We conclude with actionable recommendations informed by our results to bridge users' comprehension gaps, build credible assurances, and properly calibrate barriers for users in distress.

AI.tldr: A mixed-methods vignette study (n=354) examining how security and privacy controls (deletion, local processing, training opt-outs) affect users' willingness to disclose emotionally sensitive information to AI chatbots, finding that simple deletion controls outperform technically sophisticated ones due to comprehension gaps, and that trust in these controls remains fragile.
AI.motivation: Generative AI chatbots are increasingly used for emotional support, yet how the presence of S&P controls (model training opt-outs, memory toggles, deletion) shapes users' willingness to engage in emotionally sensitive disclosure is understudied. Understanding this is critical for designing systems that users can trust with vulnerable personal information.
AI.method: Mixed-methods vignette study with 354 U.S. participants. Participants were presented with hypothetical scenarios involving generative AI chatbots for emotional support, varying the presence and type of S&P controls (deletion, local-only processing, model training opt-outs), and their attitudes toward disclosure, perceived protection, and perceived chatbot effectiveness were measured.
AI.result: Controls enabling deletion of disclosures had the largest positive impact on user willingness, perceived protection, and perceived effectiveness — outperforming technically sophisticated controls like local-only processing and model training opt-outs. Participants struggled to understand the mechanisms behind complex controls. Trust remains fragile, with users often doubting that S&P controls would function as promised.
AI.conclusion: Designers should prioritize comprehensible, credible S&P controls — particularly deletion — over technically sophisticated but poorly understood mechanisms. Actionable recommendations include bridging comprehension gaps, building credible assurances, and carefully calibrating barriers for users in distress.

title: Controlling Tool Use with Heading-Specific Activation Steering
summary: Tool-augmented large language models extend their capabilities beyond parametric knowledge through external tools, but tend to invoke them unnecessarily. We investigate whether tool-use decisions have any stable internal representation that can be extracted and manipulated, a question that is non-trivial given that tools exist entirely in context at inference time and have no direct encoding in model weights. We show that steering vectors extracted from heading-anchors positions exert bidirectional causal control over tool-invocation behavior across five open-source models and three domains, suppressing unnecessary tool use most effectively in domains where parametric reasoning suffices. However, geometric analysis reveals that this causal effectiveness does not correspond to clean linear structure: tool-invocation steps exhibit diffuse, bimodal alignment with the suppression vector rather than the consistent negative alignment a linear encoding account would predict, and different tool types recruit largely distinct internal signatures with low cross-tool feature overlap. We hypothesize these geometric properties are indicative of the non-parametric nature of tools, and distinguish tool-use steering vectors from those extracted for parametrically grounded concepts. The relationship between this geometric irregularity and the observed causal effectiveness remains an open question.

AI.tldr: Tool-invocation steering vectors can causally suppress unnecessary LLM tool use, but their internal geometry is diffuse and bimodal rather than linearly clean, suggesting a distinct representational signature for non-parametric (contextual) concepts versus parametrically grounded ones.
AI.motivation: LLMs augmented with tools often invoke them unnecessarily. The authors investigate whether tool-use decisions have stable internal representations that can be extracted and manipulated, despite tools existing only in inference-time context with no direct encoding in model weights.
AI.method: Steering vectors are extracted from heading-anchor positions across five open-source models and three domains. The vectors are used to causally intervene on tool-invocation behavior. Geometric analysis examines alignment patterns, bimodality, and cross-tool feature overlap.
AI.result: Steering vectors exert bidirectional causal control over tool invocation, most effectively suppressing unnecessary use where parametric reasoning suffices. However, tool-invocation steps show diffuse, bimodal alignment with suppression vectors rather than consistent negative alignment. Different tool types recruit largely distinct internal signatures with low cross-tool overlap.
AI.conclusion: The geometric irregularity (diffuse, bimodal structure with low cross-tool overlap) likely reflects the non-parametric nature of tools, distinguishing these steering vectors from those for parametrically grounded concepts. The link between this geometric irregularity and causal effectiveness remains unexplained.

title: RPAM: A Principled Metric for Evaluating Associations in Language Models with High Predictive Validity in Downstream Outputs
summary: Language models (LMs) exhibit problematic biases, such as stereotypes. Effectively analyzing and mitigating such biases requires accurate and generalizable evaluation methods of the underlying associations. Some existing approaches focus on downstream metrics that analyze associations in generated text. Since generated text content can vary drastically across LMs, such metrics often require specialized evaluation datasets, which limits the generalization of such downstream metrics. In contrast, upstream metrics examine LMs at the fundamental level of embeddings or continuation probabilities, enabling principled association analyses across LMs. Yet, to date, no upstream metric for generative LMs has uncovered a strong relationship with real-world associations, including those measured in generated text. To address this gap, we introduce the Relative Probability Association Metric (RPAM), an association evaluation metric for generative LMs. For three LMs of different quality of language generation and purpose (Mistral-7B-Instruct, Mistral-7B, and GPT-2) and well-studied evaluation datasets (WEAT-WS, Bellezza, WS-353, and SST2), we find a strong relationship between upstream RPAM measurements and corresponding implicit and explicit associations observed in humans, as well as biases measured downstream with LM-specific tasks, outperforming prior record values where applicable.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RPAM (Relative Probability Association Metric), an upstream evaluation metric for measuring biases in generative language models via continuation probabilities. RPAM demonstrates strong correlation with both human-observed associations and downstream bias measurements, outperforming prior methods across three LMs (Mistral-7B-Instruct, Mistral-7B, GPT-2) and four evaluation datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing bias evaluation methods are limited: downstream metrics analyzing generated text lack generalizability across LMs due to content variability and require specialized datasets, while upstream metrics (embedding/probability-based) have failed to establish strong correlations with real-world associations. The paper addresses this gap by seeking an upstream metric that reliably reflects both human associations and downstream bias measurements.
AI.method: The authors propose RPAM, which computes relative probability associations from generative LMs' continuation probabilities. Rather than analyzing generated text directly, RPAM operates at the fundamental probability distribution level, comparing relative likelihoods of different token continuations to quantify association strengths. The metric is evaluated across three LMs (Mistral-7B-Instruct, Mistral-7B, GPT-2) on four datasets (WEAT-WS, Bellezza, WS-353, SST2), measuring correlation with human implicit/explicit associations and downstream LM-specific bias tasks.
AI.result: RPAM demonstrates a strong relationship with both implicit and explicit human associations, as well as downstream bias measurements from LM-specific tasks. It outperforms prior record values where applicable, establishing the first upstream metric for generative LMs that reliably connects to real-world associations.
AI.conclusion: RPAM fills a critical gap by providing a generalizable upstream metric that does not depend on generated text content, enabling principled association analyses across generative LMs. Its strong correlation with human associations and downstream bias measurements validates its utility for analyzing and mitigating stereotypes in language models.

title: Code-Level Cost Function Generation for Spatial Image Steganography Using RAG-Enhanced Large Language Models
summary: Designing cost functions of adaptive steganography traditionally requires extensive manual tuning, while deep learning methods lack interpretability. Although large language models (LLMs) offer an automated alternative via evolutionary generation, they often violate domain specific mathematical constraints due to a lack of explicit domain knowledge. To address this problem, we propose a novel evolutionary system focused on exploiting Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhanced LLMs for the automatic code-level generation of spatial steganography cost functions. This system incorporates a core Self Evolving RAG (SE-RAG) module, wherein a Code Semantic Signature (CSS) translates procedural code into aligned queries, retrieving explicit guidance from static literature and dynamic experience knowledge bases to steer the LLM generation process. A dedicated feedback mechanism then continuously refines the dynamic knowledge base with successful optimization strategies. Extensive experiments on the BOSSBase and BOWS2 datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently achieves higher steganographic security than existing automatically designed methods, and increases the average code execution rate by 46.3% while reducing the search cost by 26.1%, thereby highlighting the effectiveness, efficiency, and potential of combining LLMs with domain-specific knowledge in the field of automatic steganographic algorithm generation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SE-RAG, a retrieval-augmented generation system for automatically evolving spatial steganography cost functions at the code level, achieving higher security, 46.3% higher code execution rate, and 26.1% lower search cost than prior automatic methods.
AI.motivation: Manual design of steganography cost functions is labor-intensive, deep learning methods are opaque, and LLM-based evolutionary generation often produces mathematically invalid code due to missing domain knowledge. There is a need for an automated approach that respects domain-specific mathematical constraints.
AI.method: The authors propose an evolutionary system with a Self-Evolving RAG (SE-RAG) module. A Code Semantic Signature (CSS) converts procedural code into aligned queries to retrieve explicit guidance from two knowledge bases: a static literature base and a dynamic experience base. A feedback mechanism continuously updates the dynamic base with successful optimization strategies, constraining LLM generation to produce mathematically valid cost functions.
AI.result: On BOSSBase and BOWS2 datasets, the framework achieves superior steganographic security over existing automatically designed methods, boosts average code execution rate by 46.3%, and reduces search cost by 26.1%.
AI.conclusion: Combining LLMs with domain-specific knowledge via RAG effectively bridges the gap between automated generation and mathematical validity in steganography cost function design, offering both improved security and computational efficiency.

title: Inject or Navigate? Token-Efficient Retrieval for LLM Analysis of Transactional Legal Documents
summary: Answering questions over a set of transactional legal documents is most simply done by injecting the whole corpus into the LLM's context window on every query. That baseline maximises retrieval recall, but its token footprint scales with the corpus rather than the question, and long-context degradation scales with it. We report what it took to replace full-corpus injection in a legal-document analysis system, comparing it against two structured retrieval modes over our proprietary structure-aware chunking: embedding retrieval (NAVEMBED) and LLM navigation over a compact structured index (NAVINDEX). On a 20-question benchmark with verified ground-truth answers, a position-bias-controlled, reference-anchored pairwise judge scored semantic retrieval with reranking tied with injection on 16 of 18 document-bound questions (injection preferred on 2) while attending to 17.3x fewer input tokens (a general-text-embedding (GTE) configuration reaches 29.9x at a lower tie rate); both modes were judged tied on the 2 out-of-scope controls. NAVINDEX was judged tied on all 18 at a 1.61x smaller total token footprint, a ~56x smaller answering context, and 25% lower dollar cost. We derive a closed-form caching-crossover rule: cached injection is cheaper in dollars only while the corpus stays below roughly ten times the retrieval payload. Scope and uncertainty are quantified in Section 8.

AI.tldr: The paper compares full-corpus injection against two structure-aware retrieval methods (embedding-based and LLM navigation over a compact index) for answering questions over transactional legal documents, finding that structured retrieval matches injection quality with dramatically lower token usage and cost, except when the corpus is very small relative to retrieval payload.
AI.motivation: Full-corpus injection into an LLM's context window maximizes recall but suffers from linear token scaling with corpus size and long-context degradation. The authors seek to determine whether structured retrieval methods can match injection quality while drastically reducing token footprint and cost in legal document QA systems.
AI.method: The authors benchmark three approaches on a 20-question set with verified ground-truth answers over transactional legal documents: (1) full-corpus injection (baseline), (2) NAVEMBED — embedding-based semantic retrieval with reranking over proprietary structure-aware chunking, and (3) NAVINDEX — LLM navigation over a compact structured index. Evaluation uses a position-bias-controlled, reference-anchored pairwise judge. They also derive a closed-form caching-crossover rule for cost comparison.
AI.result: NAVEMBED tied with injection on 16 of 18 document-bound questions (injection preferred on 2) while using 17.3x fewer input tokens (a GTE variant reached 29.9x). NAVINDEX tied on all 18 with a 1.61x smaller total token footprint, ~56x smaller answering context, and 25% lower dollar cost. Cached injection is only cheaper when the corpus stays below roughly 10x the retrieval payload size.
AI.conclusion: Structured retrieval methods can replace full-corpus injection in legal document QA with negligible quality loss and substantial efficiency gains. The caching-crossover rule provides a practical decision boundary for when to prefer cached injection versus retrieval-based approaches.

title: DebugTracker: Lightweight Process Evidence for Classroom Debugging
summary: Debugging exercises are often assessed from final code and test outcomes, yet these artifacts hide how students reproduced failures, formed hypotheses, inspected evidence, edited code, and verified fixes. We present DebugTracker, a Visual Studio Code extension that records lightweight debugging-process evidence for classroom tasks. DebugTracker separates uncoached Evaluation Mode traces from coached Training Mode traces, stores append-only JSONL events, and exports timeline and Markdown reports for human review. The prototype records test commands, editor and debugger metadata, student checkpoints, source snapshots, optional image evidence, human labels, and optional AI-assisted practice feedback. DebugTracker is largely language-agnostic: it captures process evidence through standard VS Code mechanisms rather than language-specific tooling, although debugger evidence depends on the relevant VS Code language extension. We validate the prototype with debugging tasks in Python, TypeScript, and Java, 16 automated checks, and an 11-case manual trial matrix spanning packaged VSIX installation and three operating systems.

AI.tldr: DebugTracker is a VS Code extension that captures lightweight, language-agnostic debugging-process evidence — including test runs, editor actions, debugger metadata, and student checkpoints — supporting both uncoached evaluation and coached training modes with human-reviewable timeline and Markdown exports.
AI.motivation: Traditional assessment of debugging exercises relies solely on final code and test outcomes, which conceals the rich process data of how students reproduce failures, form hypotheses, inspect state, edit code, and verify fixes. There is a need for tooling that captures this intermediate debugging-process evidence to enable more insightful pedagogical assessment.
AI.method: The authors built DebugTracker as a VS Code extension that records append-only JSONL events, separates uncoached Evaluation Mode from coached Training Mode traces, and captures test commands, editor/debugger metadata, checkpoints, source snapshots, optional image evidence, human labels, and optional AI-assisted feedback. It relies on standard VS Code mechanisms for language-agnostic capture, with debugger evidence depending on the relevant language extension. Validation included tasks in Python, TypeScript, and Java, 16 automated checks, and an 11-case manual trial matrix across packaged VSIX installation on three operating systems.
AI.result: The prototype was validated with debugging tasks across three languages (Python, TypeScript, Java), passed 16 automated checks, and was successfully trialed in 11 manual cases spanning VSIX installation on three operating systems, demonstrating cross-language and cross-platform feasibility.
AI.conclusion: DebugTracker demonstrates that lightweight, language-agnostic capture of debugging-process evidence within VS Code is feasible, enabling richer assessment of student debugging practices beyond final-code inspection. The dual-mode design (evaluation vs. training) and exportable reports make it suitable for both classroom grading and guided practice scenarios.

title: GlassTENG: Self-Powered Triboelectric Nanogenerator based Sensing of Pulse, Jaw, and Upper Facial Activity from Everyday Glasses
summary: Smart glasses maintain near-continuous skin contact at multiple arterial and muscular sites, making them a promising platform for physiological sensing. In practice, though, two factors make sustained daily wear and longitudinal deployment impractical for the quantified self: the discomfort of prolonged sensor-skin contact (e.g., gels and adhesives) and the sensor power demands that increase battery size, weight, and maintenance burden. We present GlassTENG, an ultra-low-power sensor that embeds three custom-fabricated triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) into a glasses frame at the angular artery on the nasal bridge, the superficial temporal artery on an extended arm, and the temporalis muscle at the temple. Each GlassTENG sensor is self-powered in transducing mechanical energy to electrical energy and consumes 1.36 $μ$W per sensor at the analog front-end. GlassTENG enables simultaneous capture of arterial pulse waveforms, jaw kinematics (e.g., clenching, tapping, eating), and upper facial activity (e.g., blinking, eyebrow movement). In a 20-participant user study, we achieve 93.8% accuracy across six jaw and upper facial activities and estimate heart rate with a mean absolute error of 1.82 beats per minute (BPM) relative to a ground-truth chest-strap sensor in 30s windows. Together, these results establish a future pathway toward a longitudinally worn, ultra-low-power, glasses-based physiological monitoring platform.

AI.tldr: GlassTENG embeds self-powered triboelectric nanogenerators into smart glasses to simultaneously capture arterial pulse, jaw kinematics, and facial activity at ultra-low power (1.36 μW/sensor), achieving 93.8% activity classification accuracy and 1.82 BPM heart rate error in a 20-participant study.
AI.motivation: Existing smart glasses for physiological sensing suffer from two key barriers to longitudinal daily use: (1) discomfort from prolonged sensor-skin contact requiring gels/adhesives, and (2) high sensor power consumption that increases battery size, weight, and charging burden.
AI.method: Three custom triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) are integrated into a glasses frame at anatomically strategic sites: the angular artery (nasal bridge), the superficial temporal artery (extended arm), and the temporalis muscle (temple). Each TENG is self-powered, converting mechanical deformation into electrical signals, with the analog front-end consuming only 1.36 μW per sensor. The system simultaneously captures arterial pulse waveforms, jaw kinematics (clenching, tapping, eating), and upper facial movements (blinking, eyebrow movement). A 20-participant user study evaluated both activity classification and heart rate estimation against a chest-strap ground truth.
AI.result: The system achieved 93.8% accuracy across six jaw and upper facial activity classes. Heart rate estimation yielded a mean absolute error of 1.82 BPM relative to a chest-strap sensor using 30-second windows.
AI.conclusion: GlassTENG demonstrates a viable pathway toward longitudinally wearable, ultra-low-power, glasses-based physiological monitoring, overcoming key comfort and power barriers that previously limited sustained daily deployment.

title: From Passive Retrieval to Active Memory Navigation: Learning to Use Memory as a Structured Action Space
summary: Long-term user memory is essential for personalized conversational agents, yet many memory systems still expose memory through passive retrieval interfaces, making the model a consumer of pre-selected evidence. We introduce NapMem, a framework for learning to use long-term user memory as a structured action space rather than passively retrieved context. NapMem organizes user history into a linked multi-granularity memory pyramid, where raw conversations, typed memory records, topic tracks, and user profiles are connected through provenance relations, and exposes these levels through memory tools. The agent is trained to select memory according to the query and intermediate evidence, allowing it to inspect different memory granularities before answering. Experiments on PersonaMem-v2, LongMemEval, and LoCoMo show that a NapMem agent trained with memory-tool reinforcement learning is competitive across diverse memory-intensive tasks, while evaluations on non-memory tasks suggest that the learned policy largely preserves general reasoning and tool-use abilities. Additional analyses examine storage, inference cost, tool-use behavior, and ablations over navigation, memory granularity, and RL training. Our results suggest that long-term user memory benefits from coupling structured storage with a learned policy for using memory at the appropriate granularity.

AI.tldr: NapMem proposes a framework where long-term user memory is treated as a structured action space for conversational agents, organizing memory into a multi-granularity pyramid (conversations, records, topics, profiles) with provenance links, and training agents via memory-tool reinforcement learning to actively select and inspect appropriate memory granularities rather than passively consuming retrieved evidence.
AI.motivation: Existing memory systems for conversational agents rely on passive retrieval interfaces, where the model merely consumes pre-selected evidence. This limits the agent's ability to actively reason about what memory to use and at what granularity, motivating a shift toward treating memory as an action space the agent learns to navigate.
AI.method: NapMem organizes user history into a linked multi-granularity memory pyramid with four levels: raw conversations, typed memory records, topic tracks, and user profiles — all connected via provenance relations. These levels are exposed as memory tools. The agent is trained using memory-tool reinforcement learning to select and inspect different memory granularities based on the query and intermediate evidence before generating an answer.
AI.result: Experiments on PersonaMem-v2, LongMemEval, and LoCoMo show that the NapMem agent is competitive across diverse memory-intensive tasks. Evaluations on non-memory tasks indicate that the learned policy largely preserves general reasoning and tool-use abilities. Additional analyses cover storage, inference cost, tool-use behavior, and ablations on navigation, memory granularity, and RL training.
AI.conclusion: Long-term user memory benefits from coupling structured storage with a learned policy that selects memory at the appropriate granularity, rather than relying on passive retrieval alone.

title: UCSC NLP at SemEval-2026 Task 10: Boundary-Aware Span Extraction and RoBERTa Classification for Conspiracy Detection
comment: 6 pages, 2 tables. System description paper for SemEval-2026 Task 10 (PsyCoMark: Psycholinguistic Conspiracy Marker Extraction and Detection)
summary: We present our systems for SemEval-2026 Task 10 (PsyCoMark), addressing conspiracy marker extraction (Subtask 1) and document-level conspiracy detection (Subtask 2). For marker extraction, we formulate the task as multi-label span classification over enumerated candidate spans, using IoU >= 0.95 positive labeling, hard-negative sampling, and containment-based non-maximum suppression (NMS) with boundary-aware span representations. Document classification is modeled independently using a sequence classifier with label smoothing and a stratified train-validation split. Analysis shows that entity-like roles (Actor, Victim) are detected robustly, while abstract roles (Action, Effect, Evidence) remain sensitive to boundary criteria. On the official test set, our systems rank 7th in Subtask 1 (0.2251 macro F1) and 11th in Subtask 2 (0.7694 weighted F1).

AI.tldr: The paper presents systems for SemEval-2026 Task 10 (PsyCoMark), addressing conspiracy marker extraction via multi-label span classification with IoU-based labeling and NMS, and document-level conspiracy detection via sequence classification. Their systems ranked 7th in Subtask 1 and 11th in Subtask 2.
AI.motivation: To develop effective systems for the PsyCoMark shared task, which involves extracting fine-grained conspiracy markers (roles like Actor, Victim, Action, Effect, Evidence) from text spans and detecting conspiracy documents at the document level.
AI.method: For Subtask 1 (marker extraction): multi-label span classification over enumerated candidate spans, using IoU ≥ 0.95 for positive labeling, hard-negative sampling, and containment-based non-maximum suppression (NMS) with boundary-aware span representations. For Subtask 2 (document classification): an independent sequence classifier trained with label smoothing and stratified train-validation splitting.
AI.result: Entity-like roles (Actor, Victim) were detected robustly, while abstract roles (Action, Effect, Evidence) remained sensitive to boundary criteria. Official test set results: Subtask 1 — 0.2251 macro F1 (7th place); Subtask 2 — 0.7694 weighted F1 (11th place).
AI.conclusion: The multi-label span classification approach is viable for conspiracy marker extraction, but abstract roles pose challenges due to boundary ambiguity. The document-level classifier performs reasonably but trails top systems, suggesting room for improvement in capturing subtle conspiracy signals.

title: $\mathbfλ$-VAE: Variance Equalization for Posterior Collapse
summary: Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) frequently suffer from posterior collapse, a failure mode in which the approximate posterior converges to the prior, rendering the latent code uninformative. Despite extensive research, a unified account of why collapse occurs has remained an open question. We identify and formalize two logically independent but coupled causes. \emph{Gradient imbalance} occurs when the decoder's reconstruction signal vanishes faster than the $\mathbb{KL}$ regularization pressure as the posterior widens. \emph{Information gap} occurs when the stochastic sampling step discards a substantial fraction of the encoder's computed representation, attenuating decoder sensitivity and making collapse inexpensive. Both causes share the same collapse trajectory, and we show that the information gap is algebraically equivalent to mismatch between the aggregate posterior and the prior, unifying two pathologies. Subsequently, we introduce $λ$-VAE, which resolves both causes through a single modification to the reparameterization step: the sampling noise is scaled by per-dimension exponent, while the $\mathbb{KL}$ penalty retains the original posterior variance. This asymmetry shifts the stable training attractor away from the degenerate collapsed state, driving all latent dimensions toward the same equilibrium -- a mechanism we term \emph{variance equalization}. A closed-form optimal exponent per dimension follows from a net information gain objective, with a single hyperparameter controlling the reconstruction-generation tradeoff. We validate on standard benchmarks (Binary MNIST, Binary Omniglot, CIFAR-10, CelebA-64), showing consistent reductions in collapsed dimensions, information capacity gains of up to $2.8\times$ nats, and reconstruction quality improvements of up to $+0.33$ BPD.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies two coupled causes of posterior collapse in VAEs—gradient imbalance and information gap—and proposes λ-VAE, which modifies the reparameterization step by scaling sampling noise with a per-dimension exponent while keeping the KL penalty on original variance, thereby shifting the training attractor away from collapse and achieving up to 2.8× information capacity gains.
AI.motivation: Despite extensive research, a unified account of why posterior collapse occurs in VAEs has remained elusive. The authors aim to formalize the underlying causes and provide a principled, minimally invasive solution that resolves collapse without architectural overhauls or auxiliary objectives.
AI.method: The authors first formalize two independent causes: (1) gradient imbalance, where the decoder reconstruction gradient vanishes faster than KL regularization pressure as posterior variance widens; and (2) information gap, where stochastic sampling discards encoder information, reducing decoder sensitivity. They show the information gap is algebraically equivalent to aggregate posterior–prior mismatch. Their proposed λ-VAE scales the reparameterization noise by a per-dimension exponent while the KL penalty retains the original posterior variance. This asymmetry drives all latent dimensions toward a non-degenerate equilibrium via variance equalization. A closed-form optimal exponent is derived from a net information gain objective, with a single hyperparameter controlling the reconstruction–generation tradeoff.
AI.result: On Binary MNIST, Binary Omniglot, CIFAR-10, and CelebA-64, λ-VAE consistently reduces collapsed dimensions, achieves information capacity gains of up to 2.8× nats, and improves reconstruction quality by up to +0.33 BPD.
AI.conclusion: Posterior collapse stems from two logically distinct but coupled causes, both resolved by the λ-VAE's asymmetric reparameterization. The method provides a simple, theoretically grounded fix that unifies prior pathological accounts and delivers consistent empirical improvements across standard benchmarks.

title: i-EXAM: Instructable and Explainable Attack Connectivity Graph Modeler
comment: In the Proceedings of the International Conference on Automated Planning and Scheduling (ICAPS 2026)
summary: i-EXAM is a planning-powered tool that helps system administrators to create security profiles of complex networks and perform what-if analyses to identify network hardening strategies. It leverages planning compilation that provides soundness and completeness guarantees to identify attack paths, evaluate security metrics, generate diverse hardening strategies, and explain these strategies in natural language using Large Language Models.

AI.tldr: i-EXAM is a planning-based tool for network security analysis that automatically identifies attack paths, computes security metrics, generates diverse hardening strategies, and provides natural language explanations via LLMs, all backed by formal soundness and completeness guarantees through planning compilation.
AI.motivation: System administrators face significant challenges in securing complex networks: manually identifying attack paths is tedious, evaluating security posture is subjective, and generating effective hardening strategies is non-trivial. Existing tools often lack formal guarantees or fail to provide interpretable, actionable recommendations. i-EXAM addresses these gaps by combining automated planning with LLM-based explanation.
AI.method: The core technique is planning compilation, which encodes the network (hosts, vulnerabilities, connectivity, attacker capabilities) as a classical planning problem. This allows off-the-shelf planners to: (1) find all valid attack paths with soundness and completeness guarantees, (2) compute quantitative security metrics by analyzing the planning state space, (3) generate diverse network hardening plans as plan-space exploration, and (4) feed these structured plans into Large Language Models to produce natural language explanations for administrators.
AI.result: i-EXAM produces security profiles of target networks, enumerates attack paths, calculates security metrics, proposes multiple diverse hardening strategies, and explains each strategy in human-readable natural language. The planning compilation approach ensures that all identified attack paths are valid (soundness) and no valid attack paths are missed (completeness).
AI.conclusion: i-EXAM demonstrates that planning compilation is an effective foundation for network security analysis tools, offering formal guarantees while enabling both automated reasoning and human-interpretable output through LLM integration. It bridges the gap between rigorous formal methods and practical usability for system administrators.

title: InfluMatch: Frontier-Quality KOL Search at 4B-Model Cost
summary: Matching influencers (KOLs) to free-form, multi-part Thai marketing criteria is today served either by keyword search over structured profiles, which misses semantic fit, or by prompting frontier LLMs over every candidate, which is accurate but slow and expensive. We present InfluMatch, a low-cost three-stage cascade -- retrieval $\rightarrow$ rerank $\rightarrow$ reason -- built entirely from small open-weight models: dense retrieval returns 50 candidates, a 4B pointwise reranker scores each by the log-probability of a single Yes token and keeps 10, and a 4B reasoner grades the shortlist per criterion on a rubric with a Thai rationale. The cascade is designed for cost: reasoning over a filtered top-10 halves token spend versus reasoning over all 50 while scoring 14 points higher. End-to-end against human relevance labels on an 11-query set with all 50 candidates labeled, the full cascade reaches 94.1% P@5, versus a retrieval-only baseline near random; it matches the frontier model Kimi-K2.6 (91.8%) while emitting ${\sim}35\times$ fewer output tokens and serving a 50-KOL query in ${\sim}20$ s on one A100. Notably, the only fine-tuning that pays off is pairwise: a SimPO-tuned reranker matches the frontier baseline's best-pick accuracy (78.0 EM), whereas fine-tuning the reasoner on pointwise per-criterion labels improves offline scores yet degrades end-to-end ranking -- an inversion we trace to the design of the absolute labeling task -- leaving the untuned base model as the strongest deployed reasoner. The result is a deployable, explainable KOL search system at a small fraction of frontier serving cost.

AI.tldr: InfluMatch is a low-cost, three-stage cascade (retrieval → rerank → reason) using small open-weight models to match Thai KOLs to free-form marketing briefs. It achieves 94.1% P@5, matching frontier LLM accuracy while emitting ~35× fewer tokens and serving queries in ~20s on a single A100. Notably, pairwise SimPO fine-tuning of the reranker is effective, but pointwise fine-tuning of the reasoner backfires due to flaws in the absolute labeling task design.
AI.motivation: Matching influencers to complex Thai marketing criteria is currently done via either keyword search (poor semantic fit) or prompting frontier LLMs over all candidates (accurate but slow and expensive). The authors aim to achieve frontier-level accuracy at a fraction of the cost using only small open-weight models.
AI.method: A three-stage cascade: (1) Dense retrieval returns 50 candidates; (2) a 4B pointwise reranker scores each by the log-probability of a "Yes" token, keeping the top 10; (3) a 4B reasoner grades the shortlist per criterion using a rubric and outputs a Thai rationale. The reranker is fine-tuned with SimPO (pairwise preference optimization), while the reasoner remains the untuned base model, as pointwise per-criterion fine-tuning was found to degrade end-to-end ranking performance.
AI.result: On an 11-query evaluation set with all 50 candidates labeled, the full cascade achieves 94.1% P@5, matching the frontier model Kimi-K2.6 (91.8%) while emitting ~35× fewer output tokens. Reasoning over the filtered top-10 halves token spend versus reasoning over all 50, while scoring 14 points higher. The retrieval-only baseline performs near random. The SimPO-tuned reranker matches the frontier baseline's best-pick accuracy (78.0 EM).
AI.conclusion: A cascade of small open-weight models can match frontier LLM accuracy for KOL matching at dramatically lower cost. Pairwise fine-tuning (SimPO) is effective for the reranker, but pointwise fine-tuning of the reasoner is counterproductive due to the design of the absolute labeling task. The result is a deployable, explainable, and cost-efficient KOL search system.

title: Hidden Amplifiers: Cross-Level Risk in Software Supply Chains
comment: In The 42nd International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME 2026)
summary: Modern software supply chains comprise hundreds of transitive dependencies, yet existing analysis tools operate at either the ecosystem level (dependency graphs) or the code level (static analysis within packages). This separation creates two failure modes. First, false-positive CVE alerts for unreachable code. Second, blind spots for structurally critical micro-dependencies. We introduce cross-level risk propagation, a framework that bridges code-level risk metrics with ecosystem-level dependency exposure through a unified risk formula. Preliminary evaluation on 50 packages across npm and PyPI reveals a class of hidden amplifiers -- micro-dependencies with fewer than 50 methods but over 50,000 dependents -- that carry outsized supply-chain risk invisible to all current Software Composition Analysis (SCA) tools. Without cross-level analysis, such packages can harbor exploitable code for years because no current tool considers both internal code structure and ecosystem position simultaneously. These results suggest that cross-level analysis opens a new design space for supply-chain security.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes cross-level risk propagation, a framework combining code-level risk metrics with ecosystem-level dependency graphs to identify "hidden amplifiers" — micro-dependencies with minimal code but massive transitive impact — that are invisible to current SCA tools.
AI.motivation: Current software supply chain analysis operates in silos: ecosystem-level tools (dependency graphs) miss unreachable code risks, while code-level tools (static analysis) miss structurally critical but tiny packages. This gap causes false-positive CVE alerts and blind spots for high-impact micro-dependencies.
AI.method: The authors introduce a unified risk formula that bridges code-level risk metrics (e.g., method count, code complexity) with ecosystem-level dependency exposure (transitive dependents). They evaluate 50 packages across npm and PyPI to quantify risk propagation.
AI.result: The evaluation reveals "hidden amplifiers" — packages with fewer than 50 methods but over 50,000 dependents — that carry outsized supply-chain risk. These packages are invisible to all current SCA tools because they require simultaneous analysis of internal code structure and ecosystem position.
AI.conclusion: Cross-level analysis opens a new design space for supply-chain security, suggesting that tools must jointly consider code-level and ecosystem-level signals to eliminate both false-positive fatigue and dangerous blind spots.

title: TurnOPD: Making On-Policy Distillation Turn-Aware for Efficient Long-Horizon Agent Training
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student policy by matching a stronger teacher on the student's own trajectories, offering a promising framework for language agent training. However, its application to long-horizon agentic tasks remains insufficiently explored. We identify two key inefficiencies in vanilla agent OPD: (1) full-horizon rollouts often waste wall-clock resources on tail turns that provide weak and noisy KL supervision, and (2) trajectory-level KL objectives concentrate most of the loss on shallow tokens, leaving deeper decision turns under-trained once initial behaviors are aligned. To address these challenges, we propose TurnOPD, a turn-level budgeting strategy for efficient on-policy distillation of long-horizon agents. TurnOPD consists of two budget controllers: adaptive rollout-depth budgeting, which uses probe-based turn statistics to determine rollout length, and progressive turn-normalized loss budgeting, which gradually shifts KL weighting from token-level to turn-balanced supervision. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Multi-Hop Search with task-specialized teacher models show that TurnOPD achieves superior validation accuracy under equal wall-clock training budgets and advances the accuracy--time frontier beyond vanilla OPD.

AI.tldr: TurnOPD introduces turn-level budgeting for on-policy distillation, addressing inefficiencies in long-horizon agent training through adaptive rollout-depth control and progressive turn-normalized loss weighting, outperforming vanilla OPD on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Multi-Hop Search.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation (OPD) is promising for training language agents, but when applied to long-horizon tasks, two key inefficiencies emerge: (1) full-horizon rollouts waste compute on tail turns with weak/noisy KL supervision, and (2) trajectory-level KL objectives disproportionately weight shallow tokens, leaving deeper decision turns under-trained. These issues limit the efficiency and effectiveness of vanilla OPD for complex agentic tasks.
AI.method: TurnOPD proposes two budget controllers: (1) Adaptive rollout-depth budgeting, which uses probe-based turn statistics to dynamically determine when to truncate rollouts, avoiding wasteful tail-turn computation. (2) Progressive turn-normalized loss budgeting, which gradually shifts the KL weighting scheme from token-level (where shallow tokens dominate) to turn-balanced supervision, ensuring deeper decision turns receive adequate training signal.
AI.result: Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Multi-Hop Search using task-specialized teacher models demonstrate that TurnOPD achieves superior validation accuracy under equal wall-clock training budgets and advances the accuracy-time frontier beyond vanilla OPD.
AI.conclusion: Turn-level budgeting via TurnOPD effectively addresses the core inefficiencies of vanilla OPD in long-horizon settings, enabling more efficient and accurate policy distillation for language agents by better allocating computational and supervisory resources across turns.

title: Where to cut, how deep: BPE and Unigram-LM on chemistry SMILES
summary: Every chemical language model reading SMILES begins with a tokenizer, yet the field has inherited byte-pair encoding (BPE) from natural language with little scrutiny. In natural language, BPE's principal alternative, Unigram-LM, is known to build structurally different vocabularies. Whether that contrast survives in chemistry was open. We report a controlled comparison of BPE and Unigram-LM over a fixed 165-token chemistry base, at the small vocabulary sizes where token embeddings are learnable, across three corpus typologies (diverse, drug-like, natural-products) and both pre-tokenization boundary policies. The two do not converge. In all 22 matched conditions they build near-disjoint subword vocabularies: cross-algorithm Jaccard overlap on the learned pieces never exceeds 0.161, and at most 0.05 once weighted toward the high-frequency pieces a model updates most. Unigram-LM also segments held-out molecules into 29-41% more tokens; the arms largely agree on where to cut but not how deeply, so BPE's segmentation is a strict coarsening of Unigram-LM's on 80-99% of molecules. The separation holds across corpus, boundary, and vocabulary size, persisting even at eight times that scale. The subword algorithm is therefore a modeling decision, not a free default. The study trains no language models.

AI.tldr: BPE and Unigram-LM tokenizers produce near-disjoint subword vocabularies for SMILES, with BPE segmenting more coarsely. Tokenizer choice is a consequential modeling decision, not a free default.
AI.motivation: The field of chemical language modeling inherited BPE tokenization from NLP without scrutiny. Since Unigram-LM is known to yield structurally different vocabularies in natural language, the authors investigated whether this divergence persists in the chemistry domain.
AI.method: Controlled comparison of BPE vs. Unigram-LM at a fixed 165-token chemical base across three corpus typologies (diverse, drug-like, natural-products), both pre-tokenization boundary policies, and small vocabulary sizes. Measured Jaccard overlap of learned subword pieces and segmentation depth on held-out molecules. No language models were trained.
AI.result: Across all 22 matched conditions, cross-algorithm Jaccard overlap never exceeded 0.161 (≤0.05 when weighted toward high-frequency tokens). Unigram-LM segments molecules into 29-41% more tokens. Both agree on cut locations but not depth; BPE segmentation is a strict coarsening of Unigram-LM on 80-99% of molecules. Results hold across all variables and persist at 8× vocabulary scale.
AI.conclusion: Subword algorithm choice is a consequential modeling decision for chemical language models, not a free default. BPE and Unigram-LM do not converge in the chemistry domain.

title: Self-Review Reinforcement Learning (SRRL) with Cross-Episode Memory and Policy Distillation
summary: Reinforcement Learning is commonly used to train large language models using environmental feedback. In applied settings, the environment usually provides sparse or delayed feedback. This makes it difficult for the model to pinpoint which actions in its reasoning led to success or failure. So, learning effectively from these signals is hard because the model must determine how each failure should inform meaningful behavioral corrections in subsequent iterations. We introduce a training framework, Self-Review Reinforcement Learning, that embeds an explicit self-review step into each RL episode. When a first-pass response fails, the model generates a self-review to identify what went wrong, which conditions an improved second attempt. Unlike inference-time reflection approaches, such as Reflexion, the framework optimizes self-review with policy gradients and internalizes improvements into the base policy via selective distillation, ensuring they persist across future episodes. A cross-episode memory keeps successful self-reviews for reuse when encountering similar tasks in future episodes during training. We evaluate SRRL against a standard RLVR baseline using the GRPO optimizer across two language models, Qwen 3-4B and OLMo-3- 7B, on GSM8K benchmark. SRRL consistently outperforms the RLVR in final reward performance and achieves greater learning efficiency by successfully transforming feedback into behavioral improvement.

AI.tldr: SRRL introduces an explicit self-review step into RL episodes for LLM training, where failed first-pass responses trigger a model-generated critique that conditions a second attempt. The framework optimizes self-reviews via policy gradients and distills successful corrections into the base policy, outperforming standard RLVR on GSM8K.
AI.motivation: In applied RL settings for LLMs, environmental feedback is often sparse or delayed, making it difficult for models to identify which specific reasoning actions led to success or failure. This credit assignment problem hampers effective behavioral learning from feedback signals.
AI.method: SRRL embeds self-review into each RL episode: when a first-pass response fails, the model generates a self-review diagnosing the failure, which conditions a second improved attempt. Unlike inference-time methods like Reflexion, SRRL optimizes self-reviews using policy gradients and internalizes improvements into the base policy via selective distillation. A cross-episode memory retains successful self-reviews for reuse on similar future tasks. The framework is evaluated using GRPO optimizer against a standard RLVR baseline.
AI.result: SRRL consistently outperforms the standard RLVR baseline in final reward performance and achieves greater learning efficiency on the GSM8K benchmark, evaluated across Qwen 3-4B and OLMo-3-7B models.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly incorporating self-review into RL training, combined with policy-gradient optimization of those reviews and selective distillation into the base policy, enables LLMs to more effectively transform sparse/delayed feedback into meaningful behavioral improvements.

title: Reproducible Validation of Voucher-Based L2 Interoperability: Diagnosing an ERC-4337 Compatibility Issue in an EIL SDK Implementation
summary:
Ethereum Layer-2 (L2) ecosystems improve scalability but also fragment users, liquidity, gas funding, and execution across rollups. Consequently, cross-rollup interoperability is not only a bridging problem but also a wallet, execution, and validation problem. Ethereum Interop Layer (EIL) proposes a voucher-based architecture in which users create voucher requests on an origin chain and redeem XLP-signed vouchers on a destination chain. When reproducing the evaluated SDK version in a controlled local environment, we observed a compatibility issue in the \texttt{UserOperation} path: paymaster-related data can differ after signing, preventing a stable comparison between the user-authorized representation and the representation later inspected by the local validation flow.
  This paper presents a reproducible two-L2 validation framework and a controlled compatibility mitigation for that issue. We build a deterministic local testbed over Arbitrum- and Optimism-style development chains, deploy the core paymaster and bridge-related components, implement mock bundlers and event-driven XLP providers, and introduce a sanitized paymaster-data handling path together with a compatible multichain account wrapper. Using this framework, we execute the core voucher lifecycle from request creation to destination-chain voucher redemption and asset release.
  The contribution is an empirical diagnosis of an implementation-level compatibility barrier, a bounded mitigation that restores controlled end-to-end execution, and an inspectable validation artifact for studying voucher-based interoperability. The work does not claim a new interoperability protocol, universal wallet compatibility, or production readiness; it identifies the remaining gaps toward standard-account validation, one-signature multichain authorization, and full dispute-settlement support.

AI.tldr: This paper diagnoses a paymaster data compatibility issue in Ethereum Layer-2 voucher-based interoperability and presents a reproducible local testbed with a bounded mitigation that restores end-to-end voucher lifecycle execution across Arbitrum- and Optimism-style chains.
AI.motivation: Ethereum L2 ecosystems fragment users, liquidity, and execution across rollups. The Ethereum Interop Layer (EIL) proposes voucher-based cross-rollup interoperability, but a compatibility issue arises: paymaster-related data in UserOperations can diverge after signing, breaking the stable comparison between user-authorized representations and those inspected during local validation. This paper aims to empirically diagnose and mitigate that specific implementation-level barrier.
AI.method: The authors construct a deterministic local testbed spanning Arbitrum- and Optimism-style development chains. They deploy core paymaster and bridge components, implement mock bundlers and event-driven XLP providers, and introduce a sanitized paymaster-data handling path with a compatible multichain account wrapper. The framework executes the full voucher lifecycle: request creation on the origin chain, XLP-signed voucher generation, and destination-chain redemption with asset release.
AI.result: The mitigation successfully restores controlled end-to-end execution of the voucher lifecycle. The paper delivers an empirical diagnosis of the paymaster data divergence issue, a bounded mitigation, and an inspectable validation artifact. However, the authors explicitly note remaining gaps in standard-account validation, one-signature multichain authorization, and full dispute-settlement support.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a concrete, reproducible contribution to studying voucher-based interoperability by isolating and mitigating a specific compatibility barrier, but does not claim a new protocol, universal wallet compatibility, or production readiness. It maps out remaining gaps for future work.

title: DynaKRAG: A Unified Framework for Learnable Evidence Control in Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Multi-hop retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) acquires evidence sequentially, with each new document potentially revealing missing facts, bridge entities, query defects, or sufficient support for answering. Existing methods provide useful operations such as iterative retrieval, query reformulation, evidence critique, and sufficiency judging, but typically organize them within method-specific pipelines or predefined control topologies. This leaves underexplored how to learn a shared state-conditioned policy that chooses among currently valid evidence operations. We introduce DynaKRAG, which formulates multi-hop evidence acquisition as state-conditioned control over atomic evidence operations. At each step, a validity layer constructs the executable action set, and a learned controller selects the next operation. The resulting transition updates the evidence state and may enable new operations at subsequent steps. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, DynaKRAG achieves F1 scores of 0.5998 on HotpotQA, 0.5340 on 2Wiki, and 0.3061 on MuSiQue, outperforming the strongest controlled baseline on all three benchmarks. Replacing the learned controller with a uniform-valid policy reduces F1 by 3.96--5.78 points, while removing sufficiency feedback hurts all three datasets. Controlled retrieval-cap experiments further show that additional retrieval is not uniformly beneficial. Together, these results demonstrate the benefit of coordinating retrieval, diagnosis, and gap-directed acquisition under an evolving evidence state.

AI.tldr: DynaKRAG frames multi-hop RAG as state-conditioned control over atomic evidence operations, learning a policy to dynamically choose among retrieval, query reformulation, critique, and sufficiency checking, achieving superior F1 on HotpotQA, 2Wiki, and MuSiQue.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-hop RAG systems prescribe rigid, method-specific pipelines or fixed control topologies for evidence acquisition, failing to explore how a shared, learned policy can adaptively select among available evidence operations based on evolving context.
AI.method: DynaKRAG models multi-hop evidence acquisition as a state-conditioned control problem. At each step, a validity layer determines the executable action set (retrieval, query reformulation, evidence critique, sufficiency judging), and a learned controller (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) selects the next operation. Each action transitions the evidence state, potentially unlocking new operations for subsequent steps.
AI.result: DynaKRAG achieves F1 scores of 0.5998 (HotpotQA), 0.5340 (2Wiki), and 0.3061 (MuSiQue), outperforming the strongest controlled baseline on all three benchmarks. Ablations show replacing the learned controller with a uniform-valid policy drops F1 by 3.96–5.78 points, removing sufficiency feedback hurts all datasets, and additional retrieval is not uniformly beneficial.
AI.conclusion: Learning to dynamically coordinate retrieval, diagnosis, and gap-directed acquisition under an evolving evidence state yields significant gains over static multi-hop RAG pipelines, demonstrating the value of flexible, state-conditioned evidence operations.

title: xDECAF: An Extensible Data Flow Diagram Analysis Framework for Information Security
comment: Accepted at ASE'26 Tools and Datasets
summary: xDECAF is an extensible tool for architecture-based data flow analysis with a focus on information security. It combines an extended data flow diagram metamodel of labeled flows and nodes, a domain-specific constraint language with different flow operations, and a browser-based editor backed by an analysis engine. In this paper, we present the xDECAF tool library and a curated catalog of over 20 example models with documented constraints and expected violations, intended as a reusable dataset for the community. The tool has already been adopted by several research lines, providing concrete evidence of its utility. The tool, dataset, and a hosted online editor are publicly available.

AI.tldr: xDECAF is a browser-based tool for architecture-level data flow analysis in information security, featuring an extended DFD metamodel, a constraint language, and an analysis engine. The paper presents the tool, along with a curated dataset of 20+ example models for community reuse.
AI.motivation: To provide an extensible, reusable tool and dataset for architecture-based data flow analysis in information security, addressing the need for standardized modeling and constraint checking in the community.
AI.method: xDECAF combines (1) an extended data flow diagram (DFD) metamodel with labeled flows and nodes, (2) a domain-specific constraint language supporting various flow operations, and (3) a browser-based editor with a backend analysis engine. The paper also introduces a catalog of over 20 curated example models with documented constraints and expected violations.
AI.result: The tool has been adopted by multiple research lines, providing concrete evidence of its utility. The tool, curated dataset, and a hosted online editor are all publicly available.
AI.conclusion: xDECAF fills a gap in architecture-based security analysis by offering both an extensible tool and a reusable benchmark dataset, demonstrating practical adoption and community value.

title: Onnes: A Physics-Grounded Multi-Agent LLM Simulator for Cryogenic Fault Diagnosis in Quantum Computing Infrastructure
comment: 18 pages, 14 figures, 10 tables. Code, data, and released run logs: https://github.com/Onnes-Research/onnes
summary: Dilution refrigerators are the enabling infrastructure of superconducting quantum computers, yet their fault diagnosis is still dominated by threshold alarms that report that something is wrong, not what. We present Onnes, a physics-grounded digital-twin simulator of a dilution refrigerator (a forward physics model with a learned real-fridge noise fingerprint) that drives a live multi-agent LLM operations layer, and use it for a controlled head-to-head between a zero-shot LLM agent panel and a supervised ML classifier on cryogenic fault diagnosis. The twin couples a real dilution-cooling floor, a noise-and-correlation fingerprint learned from real BlueFors logs, and six physics-grounded fault classes, three engineered to overlap on temperature but separate on flow and pressure. Across a 1000-turn evaluation the zero-shot panel shows no significant difference from the classifier on detection but trails on classification, its errors concentrating on the confusable faults. Curated contrastive few-shot demonstrations and self-consistency voting then raise classification accuracy from 0.685 to 0.990, matching the supervised classifier (0.985) with no parameter updates and six labeled demonstrations; an ablation attributes the gain almost entirely to the demonstrations. Run as a continuous monitor across a nine-run fault-by-seed sweep, the agent catches every developing fault within one poll interval, and a confidence gate suppresses pre-onset false alarms whose rate is backend-dependent. As a first sim-to-real check, a detector trained purely on real BlueFors telemetry posts a real-hardware false-alarm rate of 6.4% and 100% recall on physics faults injected onto real held-out windows. All numbers are drawn verbatim from released run logs.

AI.tldr: Onnes combines a physics-grounded digital twin of a dilution refrigerator with a multi-agent LLM operations layer for cryogenic fault diagnosis. Zero-shot LLM agents match supervised ML on fault detection but lag on classification of confusable faults; curated few-shot demonstrations and self-consistency voting boost classification accuracy from 0.685 to 0.990, matching the supervised baseline (0.985) with no parameter updates. A sim-to-real check shows 6.4% false-alarm rate and 100% recall on real hardware.
AI.motivation: Dilution refrigerator fault diagnosis is dominated by threshold alarms that indicate something is wrong but not what. The authors aim to replace vague threshold alerts with specific, interpretable fault diagnosis by leveraging LLM-based agents grounded in a physics-based digital twin, and to benchmark this approach against traditional supervised ML classifiers.
AI.method: The authors build Onnes, a physics-grounded digital-twin simulator of a dilution refrigerator that couples a real cooling-floor model, a noise-and-correlation fingerprint learned from real BlueFors logs, and six physics-grounded fault classes (three engineered to overlap on temperature but separate on flow and pressure). This twin drives a live multi-agent LLM operations layer. They conduct a controlled head-to-head between a zero-shot LLM agent panel and a supervised ML classifier over 1000 turns, then augment with curated contrastive few-shot demonstrations and self-consistency voting. Ablation studies attribute gains, and a sim-to-real check trains a detector purely on real BlueFors telemetry with faults injected onto held-out windows.
AI.result: Across 1000-turn evaluation, the zero-shot LLM panel shows no significant difference from the supervised classifier on detection but trails on classification, with errors concentrated on confusable faults. Curated few-shot demonstrations plus self-consistency voting raise classification accuracy from 0.685 to 0.990, matching the supervised classifier (0.985) with only six labeled demonstrations and no parameter updates. Ablation attributes the gain almost entirely to demonstrations. As a continuous monitor over a nine-run fault-by-seed sweep, the agent catches every developing fault within one poll interval, and a confidence gate suppresses pre-onset false alarms. Sim-to-real: detector trained on real telemetry achieves 6.4% false-alarm rate with 100% recall on injected physics faults.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based agents, when grounded in a physics-based digital twin and augmented with minimal few-shot demonstrations, can match or exceed supervised classifiers for cryogenic fault diagnosis while providing interpretable output, without requiring parameter updates or large labeled training sets.

title: SpanUQ: Span-Level Uncertainty Quantification for Large Language Model Generation
comment: The project page is available at https://damon-demon.github.io/SpanUQ.html
summary: Uncertainty estimation is essential not only for the trustworthy deployment of large language models (LLMs) but also as a foundation for self-refinement in LLM generation. However, existing approaches operate at suboptimal granularities: token-level scores lack semantic coherence, while sequence-level scores fail to localize errors. We formalize Span-Level Uncertainty Estimation (SLUE), a new task that targets the natural granularity for uncertainty: semantically coherent text spans, each conveying a single assessable unit of meaning. To address this task, we introduce SPANUQ, a lightweight probe that distills the uncertainty knowledge from expensive multi-sample inference into a single forward pass over LLM hidden states. SPANUQ employs a DETR-style span decoder to simultaneously detect spans and estimate their uncertainty via a Mixture of Beta distribution, trained with a principled combination of Beta NLL regression and contrastive ranking objectives. We construct SPANUQ-BENCH, the first span-level uncertainty benchmark comprising 20K prompts, 293K annotated spans, and continuous soft labels derived from multi-sample claim verification. Experiments on five LLM backbones show that SPANUQ consistently achieves the best span-level uncertainty quality, outperforming the strongest probe baseline and all sampling-based methods while being 10-20x faster. Its DETR-based span detector attains 0.910 F1, surpassing the best heuristic by 39.4%, enabling precise error localization that sequence-level methods cannot provide. The framework generalizes across five LLMs spanning two model families.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Span-Level Uncertainty Estimation (SLUE), a new task targeting semantically coherent text spans for uncertainty assessment, and proposes SPANUQ, a lightweight probe that distills multi-sample uncertainty knowledge into a single forward pass using a DETR-style decoder with Mixture of Beta distributions, achieving superior accuracy at 10-20x speedup over sampling methods.
AI.motivation: Existing uncertainty estimation for LLMs suffers from a granularity mismatch: token-level scores lack semantic coherence, while sequence-level scores cannot localize errors. There is a need for uncertainty estimation at the natural granularity of semantically coherent text spans — each conveying a single assessable unit of meaning — enabling both trustworthy deployment and targeted self-refinement.
AI.method: The authors formalize SLUE and introduce SPANUQ, a lightweight probe that distills uncertainty from expensive multi-sample inference into a single forward pass over LLM hidden states. It uses a DETR-style span decoder to simultaneously detect spans and estimate uncertainty via a Mixture of Beta distribution. Training combines Beta NLL regression and contrastive ranking objectives. They also construct SPANUQ-BENCH, a benchmark with 20K prompts, 293K annotated spans, and continuous soft labels from multi-sample claim verification.
AI.result: SPANUQ consistently achieves the best span-level uncertainty quality across five LLM backbones from two model families, outperforming the strongest probe baseline and all sampling-based methods. Its DETR-based span detector attains 0.910 F1, surpassing the best heuristic by 39.4%. The method is 10-20x faster than sampling-based alternatives.
AI.conclusion: Span-level uncertainty estimation fills a critical gap between token-level and sequence-level approaches. SPANUQ demonstrates that uncertainty knowledge from costly multi-sample inference can be effectively distilled into a single-pass probe, enabling both precise error localization and efficient, trustworthy LLM deployment across diverse model families.

title: Federated Physics-Grounded Reinforcement Learning for Distributed Stability Control in Smart Grids
comment: Accepted at IEEE SmartGridComm 2026. This is the accepted manuscript version. The final published version will appear in IEEE Xplore
summary: Transient stability control in smart grids requires rapid post-fault damping of generator frequency and rotor angle deviations to prevent cascading failures. This paper proposes FedPPO-PG, a Federated Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization framework with Physics-Grounded neighborhoods, which reformulates transient stability control as a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning problem optimized directly against closed-loop stability objectives. Each generator hosts an independent local actor augmented with the frequency deviations of its two most strongly coupled electrical neighbors, identified from the post-fault Kron-reduced susceptance matrix. A guided policy initialization phase warm-starts all actors from the classical decentralized controller, while a centralized critic guides advantage estimation under the centralized training--decentralized execution (CTDE) paradigm. Evaluated on a simulation of the IEEE 39-bus benchmark system across five training and three unseen fault contingencies, FedPPO-PG achieves 100% stabilization in all 24 trials, reduces mean stability time by 72.4%, and cuts the control power by 7-14 times compared to the centralized baseline. Each actor executes independently with no central coordinator at deployment, and the per-actor inference latency satisfies the IEEE/IEC 60255-118-1-2018 real-time reporting requirements.

AI.tldr: FedPPO-PG is a federated multi-agent PPO framework for transient stability control in smart grids. Each generator learns a local controller using only its own and two strongest neighbors' frequency deviations. It achieves 100% stabilization on IEEE 39-bus, reduces stabilization time by 72.4% and control power by 7-14× versus centralized baselines, while meeting real-time latency standards.
AI.motivation: Post-fault transient stability control in smart grids requires rapid damping of generator frequency and rotor angle deviations to prevent cascading failures. Existing centralized or fully decentralized approaches struggle with scalability, communication latency, and coordination. The paper aims to design a decentralized multi-agent control framework that achieves global stability using only local observations, trained in a privacy-preserving federated manner under CTDE.
AI.method: The paper proposes FedPPO-PG, which (1) reformulates transient stability control as a cooperative MARL problem; (2) equips each generator with an independent local PPO actor whose observation includes its own state plus frequency deviations of the two most strongly coupled electrical neighbors (identified via the post-fault Kron-reduced susceptance matrix); (3) uses a guided policy initialization phase that warm-starts all actors from a classical decentralized controller; (4) employs a centralized critic for advantage estimation under CTDE; and (5) evaluates on IEEE 39-bus with five training and three unseen fault contingencies.
AI.result: FedPPO-PG achieves 100% stabilization across all 24 trials (including unseen faults), reduces mean stabilization time by 72.4%, and reduces control power by 7–14 times compared to the centralized baseline. Each actor operates independently at deployment with no central coordinator, and per-actor inference latency satisfies IEEE/IEC 60255-118-1-2018 real-time reporting requirements.
AI.conclusion: The physics-grounded neighborhood selection (top-2 coupled neighbors via Kron-reduced susceptance) combined with federated multi-agent PPO under CTDE yields a highly effective, scalable, and deployable solution for real-time transient stability control. The approach meets stringent latency standards while dramatically outperforming centralized baselines in both speed and energy efficiency.

title: Beyond the Syntax: Do Security Experts Trust LLMs for NIDS Rule Engineering?
summary: As network threats evolve, manual NIDS rule engineering has become a critical operational bottleneck. While Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise for automating this process, their ability to produce production-ready rules remains unvalidated. This paper presents a human-centered investigation into LLM-based NIDS rule engineering, formalizing a grounded generation framework and evaluating it through a user study with 10 domain experts. Our evaluation reveals a syntax-semantics paradox: although LLMs generate syntactically correct rules, experts find them only partially deployable due to low specificity and logic hallucinations in 12% of cases. While the system received a favorable SUS score of 67, practitioners remain skeptical of its autonomous capabilities, viewing LLMs as support tools for drafting and verification rather than independent generators. Finally, our statistical analysis indicates that while large-scale models ($\geq 70B$) consistently produce syntactically valid rules, small models ($\leq 4B$) are largely ineffective for IDS rule generation.

AI.tldr: A user study with 10 experts finds LLMs generate syntactically correct NIDS rules but suffer from low specificity and logic hallucinations (12% of cases). Practitioners view LLMs as drafting/verification aids, not autonomous generators. Only models ≥70B produce consistently valid rules; small models (≤4B) are ineffective.
AI.motivation: Manual NIDS rule engineering has become a critical operational bottleneck as network threats evolve. While LLMs show promise for automation, their ability to produce production-ready rules remains unvalidated, motivating a rigorous human-centered investigation.
AI.method: The authors formalize a grounded generation framework for LLM-based NIDS rule engineering and evaluate it through a user study with 10 domain experts. They collect quantitative metrics (SUS score, syntax validity) and qualitative feedback, supplemented by statistical analysis comparing model scales.
AI.result: A syntax-semantics paradox emerges: LLMs generate syntactically correct rules, but experts deem them only partially deployable due to low specificity and logic hallucinations in 12% of cases. The system achieved a SUS score of 67 (marginally acceptable). Large models (≥70B) consistently produce valid rules; small models (≤4B) are largely ineffective.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are not yet suitable as autonomous NIDS rule generators. Their current value lies in assisting with drafting and verification. Model scale is a decisive factor, with a clear capability threshold around 70B parameters for meaningful rule generation.

title: Mitigating Errors in LLM-Generated Web API Invocations via Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Constrained Decoding
comment: 54 pages, 11 figures; supersedes arXiv:2509.20172v6, which is a discarded journal extension of our work
summary:
Integration of web APIs is a cornerstone of modern software systems, yet writing correct web API invocation code remains challenging due to complex and evolving API specifications. Although LLMs are increasingly used for code generation, previous work has empirically shown that their ability to generate correct web API integrations is limited. At the same time, mitigation techniques and their effectiveness for this setting remain insufficiently understood.
  In this paper, we propose and systematically evaluate retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and constrained decoding (CD) as two complementary approaches to improving LLM-generated web API invocation code. For RAG, we design a retriever that processes OpenAPI specifications and retrieves compact endpoint representations to inject into model prompts. For CD, we introduce an automatic translation from OpenAPI specifications to regex-based constraints enforced during generation.
  We evaluate both approaches on WAPIIBench's existing synthetic dataset and on a new real-world dataset derived from GitHub repositories. Our results show that RAG reduces hallucinations and improves correctness when generating full API invocations but reduces it when the endpoint is already provided as it encourages the generation of unnecessary parameters. In contrast, CD reliably prevents illegal URLs, HTTP methods, and arguments and substantially improves overall correctness for both starter codes.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and systematically evaluates Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and Constrained Decoding (CD) for improving LLM-generated web API invocation code.
