RAG retrieves compact endpoint representations from OpenAPI specs, while CD automatically translates OpenAPI specs into regex-based generation constraints. Results show RAG helps full API invocation generation but can harm when the endpoint is already given; CD reliably prevents illegal API elements and improves overall correctness.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle to generate correct web API invocation code due to complex and evolving API specifications. Prior work has empirically demonstrated these limitations, but mitigation techniques and their effectiveness for web API code generation remain insufficiently understood.
AI.method: Two complementary approaches are proposed: (1) RAG — a retriever that processes OpenAPI specifications to extract compact endpoint representations injected into prompts; (2) CD — an automatic translation pipeline from OpenAPI specifications to regex-based constraints that are enforced during token generation. Both are evaluated on WAPIIBench's synthetic dataset and a newly constructed real-world dataset from GitHub repositories.
AI.result: RAG reduces hallucinations and improves correctness for full API invocation generation but degrades performance when the endpoint is already provided in the prompt, as it encourages unnecessary parameter generation. CD reliably prevents illegal URLs, HTTP methods, and arguments, and substantially improves overall correctness across both starter code scenarios.
AI.conclusion: RAG and CD are complementary techniques with distinct strengths and failure modes for web API code generation. CD provides reliable, hard guarantees against malformed invocations, while RAG is context-dependent — beneficial for full generation but detrimental when the endpoint is pre-specified. A combined or context-aware strategy may yield optimal results.

title: Prompt Coach: An Empirical Evaluation of an Agentic Tutor for Learning Prompt Engineering in Software Development
comment: 7 pages. To be published in the proceedings of 41st International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE '26), October 12-16, 2026, Munich, Germany (Industry Showcase Track)
summary: Prompt engineering has emerged as a critical yet undertaught skill for software developers, one that traditional learning approaches are ill-equipped to support given its evolving, interactive, and context-dependent nature. In this paper, we introduce Prompt Coach (PC), an agentic tutor that helps developers learn how to craft high-quality code-generation prompts through Socratic guidance embedded in-flow within their IDE. PC evaluates prompt quality across multiple dimensions and surfaces targeted questions to guide self-correction, grounded in the developer's codebase and the behavior of the target LLM. We present an early empirical study with 15 professional developers combining quantitative prompt quality scoring with qualitative perception measures. Participants showed statistically significant improvements after a single 60-minute session, with the largest gains across dimensions commonly overlooked by developers. They also reported strong trust, high adoption readiness, and unanimous agreement that PC improved their prompt-writing skills.

AI.tldr: Prompt Coach is an IDE-integrated agentic tutor that uses Socratic questioning to help developers improve their code-generation prompts. An empirical study with 15 professional developers showed statistically significant improvements in prompt quality after a single 60-minute session, with strong user trust and adoption readiness.
AI.motivation: Prompt engineering is a critical yet undertaught skill for software developers. Traditional learning approaches fail because prompt engineering is evolving, interactive, and context-dependent — it cannot be effectively taught through static, decontextualized instruction.
AI.method: The authors built Prompt Coach (PC), an agentic tutor embedded in the IDE that evaluates prompt quality across multiple dimensions and surfaces targeted Socratic questions to guide self-correction. The evaluation is grounded in the developer's actual codebase and the behavior of the target LLM. An empirical study was conducted with 15 professional developers, combining quantitative prompt quality scoring with qualitative perception measures over a single 60-minute session.
AI.result: Participants showed statistically significant improvements in prompt quality, with the largest gains occurring in dimensions typically overlooked by developers. Users reported strong trust, high adoption readiness, and unanimous agreement that PC improved their prompt-writing skills.
AI.conclusion: An IDE-embedded, Socratic tutoring agent can effectively teach prompt engineering in situ, leveraging real codebase context and live LLM feedback to produce measurable skill improvements in a short time frame.

title: Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion: A Tri-Mode Language Model Unifying Autoregressive, Diffusion, and Self-Speculation Decoding
summary: We introduce Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion, a tri-mode language model (LM) that unifies AR, diffusion, and self-speculation decoding within a single architecture. Trained with a joint AR-diffusion objective, Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion can switch modes to sustain high throughput across deployment settings and concurrency levels. Our study shows that (1) AR and diffusion objectives are complementary: diffusion improves lookahead planning, while AR provides left-to-right linguistic priors. (2) In self-speculation mode, diffusion drafts while AR verifies, outperforming multi-token prediction (MTP) methods in both acceptance rate and real-device efficiency. (3) A speed-of-light analysis further demonstrates diffusion's long-term potential, with up to 76.5% more tokens per forward pass than self-speculation under an optimal sampler. Scaling to 3B, 8B, and 14B parameters, our Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion family, including base, instruct, and vision-language models, consistently outperforms state-of-the-art open-source AR and diffusion LMs in both accuracy and speed. For example, Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-8B decodes 6x more tokens per forward than Qwen3-8B with comparable accuracy, translating to 4x higher throughput on SPEED-Bench with SGLang on a GB200 GPU.

AI.tldr: Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion is a tri-mode language model that unifies autoregressive (AR), diffusion, and self-speculation decoding in one architecture, achieving up to 6× more tokens per forward pass and 4× higher throughput than comparable AR models while maintaining accuracy.
AI.motivation: Current language models are constrained by the sequential bottleneck of autoregressive decoding, which limits throughput. The authors aim to harness the complementary strengths of AR (linguistic priors) and diffusion (lookahead planning) in a single model, while also using self-speculation (diffusion drafts, AR verifies) to surpass existing speculative decoding methods like multi-token prediction.
AI.method: The authors train Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion with a joint AR-diffusion objective, enabling three operational modes within one architecture: pure AR generation, pure diffusion generation, and self-speculation mode where diffusion produces draft tokens that AR verifies. They scale the model to 3B, 8B, and 14B parameters across base, instruct, and vision-language variants.
AI.result: (1) AR and diffusion objectives are complementary. (2) Self-speculation mode outperforms multi-token prediction in acceptance rate and real-device efficiency. (3) A speed-of-light analysis shows diffusion can yield up to 76.5% more tokens per forward pass than self-speculation with optimal sampling. At 8B scale, the model decodes 6× more tokens per forward than Qwen3-8B at comparable accuracy, yielding 4× higher throughput on SPEED-Bench with SGLang on a GB200 GPU.
AI.conclusion: The tri-mode approach demonstrates that unifying AR and diffusion within a single model unlocks substantial throughput gains without sacrificing accuracy. Diffusion's long-term potential, combined with AR verification in self-speculation mode, positions this as a compelling direction for efficient LLM deployment across diverse concurrency settings.

title: EquiFiLM: Charge-Conditioned Equivariant Force Fields via Feature-wise Linear Modulation
summary: Foundation machine learning force fields (MLFFs) such as MACE-MP-0 and UMA cover broad chemical space at near density functional theory (DFT) accuracy. However, they assume equilibrium ground-state physics and do not natively handle externally induced changes to the electronic state, such as charging, applied fields, or electronic excitation, which limits their use for driven processes such as photoexcitation and charge injection. We propose EquiFiLM, a lightweight extension that adds continuous external conditioning to any equivariant foundation MLFF via a per-layer Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) block, learning externally driven changes to the potential energy surface from minimal training data. The block modulates only scalar channels and preserves E(3)-equivariance exactly. We demonstrate the recipe on charged liquid water with the foundation model MACE-MatPES as the backbone, yielding E-MACE. On the four training charges, E-MACE delivers a $3.1\times$ reduction in force RMSE ($21.3$ to $6.96$ meV/$\mathring{A}$) and a $61\times$ reduction in per-atom energy RMSE ($6.1$ to $0.1$ meV/atom) over a baseline without EquiFiLM trained on the same data, at indistinguishable inference cost. Across seven held-out interpolation and extrapolation charges, force RMSE stays within $18-61$ meV/$\mathring{A}$ and energy RMSE within $0.7-5.4$ meV/atom. The model runs stable molecular dynamics across the full range tested and predicts the charge-dependent first-shell response of the reduced pair distribution function probed by ultrafast electron diffraction. Adding this conditioning axis to the foundation requires only a few thousand DFT-labeled frames, against the $\approx 10^8$ structures of a charge-aware foundation trained from scratch. The recipe is backbone- and conditioning-agnostic: it applies without architectural change to any equivariant MLFF with scalar interaction-layer channels.

AI.tldr: EquiFiLM is a lightweight FiLM-based extension that adds external conditioning (e.g., charge, fields, excitation) to any equivariant foundation MLFF while preserving E(3)-equivariance. Demonstrated on charged water with MACE-MatPES, it achieves dramatic accuracy gains from minimal training data and enables stable molecular dynamics across interpolation and extrapolation regimes.
AI.motivation: Foundation MLFFs like MACE-MP-0 and UMA assume equilibrium ground-state physics and cannot natively handle externally driven changes to the electronic state (charging, applied fields, photoexcitation). This limits application to driven processes. Training a charge-aware foundation from scratch would require ~10^8 structures, which is prohibitive.
AI.method: EquiFiLM inserts per-layer Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) blocks into any equivariant MLFF. These blocks modulate only scalar interaction-layer channels, learning a continuous conditioning signal (e.g., net charge) via a lightweight network that outputs scaling and shifting parameters. E(3)-equivariance is preserved exactly since only scalar features are modulated. The approach is backbone-agnostic and demonstrated on MACE-MatPES (yielding E-MACE) trained on only a few thousand DFT-labeled frames.
AI.result: On four training charges, E-MACE achieves: 3.1× reduction in force RMSE (21.3→6.96 meV/Å) and 61× reduction in per-atom energy RMSE (6.1→0.1 meV/atom) vs. a baseline without EquiFiLM. Across seven held-out interpolation/extrapolation charges, force RMSE stays within 18–61 meV/Å and energy RMSE within 0.7–5.4 meV/atom. Stable MD runs across the full charge range and correctly predicts charge-dependent first-shell structural response in reduced pair distribution functions.
AI.conclusion: EquiFiLM provides a practical, data-efficient recipe for extending foundation MLFFs to driven electronic regimes without architectural changes or retraining from scratch. It is backbone- and conditioning-agnostic, applicable to any equivariant MLFF with scalar interaction-layer channels, and requires orders of magnitude less training data than a full charge-aware foundation model.

title: LibFHE: A Numba-Based CUDA-Python Library for Non-RNS CKKS-BGV Fully Homomorphic Encryption on GPUs
summary: It has been a decade since the fourth-generation FHE framework, CKKS, was proposed; yet, there is still no indicator pointing toward a fifth-generation successor; and in recent years, numerous studies have explored GPU acceleration to improve the efficiency of homomorphic computations. In this paper, we propose LibFHE, a high-performance GPU-accelerated framework that features CUDA-Python bindings to achieve both high-level programmability and bare-metal GPU performance for homomorphic workloads. A large majority of state-of-the-art implementations adopt the RNS-CKKS variant. In contrast, this work deliberately revisits the original (non-RNS) CKKS-BGV framework, and develops a GPU-based implementation along with corresponding optimizations. Experimental results demonstrate that optimized CUDA-Python implementations can achieve performance comparable to highly optimized C++ FHE libraries, while significantly reducing implementation complexity and improving programmability.

AI.tldr: LibFHE revisits the original (non-RNS) CKKS-BGV framework and implements it with GPU acceleration via CUDA-Python bindings, achieving performance comparable to optimized C++ FHE libraries while offering improved programmability and reduced complexity.
AI.motivation: Despite a decade since CKKS was proposed, no fifth-generation FHE framework has emerged. Meanwhile, GPU acceleration has been widely explored for homomorphic computation. The authors identify a gap: state-of-the-art implementations overwhelmingly adopt RNS-CKKS, but no GPU-accelerated framework revisits the original non-RNS CKKS-BGV variant with high-level Python programmability.
AI.method: The authors develop LibFHE, a GPU-accelerated framework using CUDA-Python bindings. They deliberately choose the original (non-RNS) CKKS-BGV scheme over RNS-CKKS and implement GPU-specific optimizations. The CUDA-Python interface provides bare-metal GPU performance while maintaining high-level Python usability.
AI.result: Optimized CUDA-Python implementations achieve performance comparable to highly optimized C++ FHE libraries, while significantly reducing implementation complexity and improving programmability.
AI.conclusion: Revisiting the original non-RNS CKKS-BGV framework with modern GPU acceleration and Python bindings is a viable approach — it can match the performance of optimized C++ FHE libraries while dramatically improving developer accessibility and reducing implementation overhead.

title: Large Language Models Have Unreliable Understanding of Software Engineering Terminology
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in software engineering (SE), yet there is no systematic study that determines to which degree these LLMs actually understand standardized SE terminology. Lack of such understanding can lead to miscommunication and misunderstanding, both by LLMs consuming text but also by human-developers acting on LLM-generated text. Within this paper, we investigate to which degree state-of-the-art LLMs are able to identify whether definitions from the ISO/IEC/IEEE 24765:2017 Systems and Software Engineering - Vocabulary are correct. We prompt LLMs both with correct definitions, as well as systematically falsified definitions. The falsifications are both semantic (substitution of key terms) and structural (removing critical information). We measure both classification accuracy and whether reasoning tokens generated by the LLMs make sense with respect to understanding the definition. While most LLMs detect falsified definitions with high accuracy, they also reject many correct definitions, indicating a systematic rejection bias rather than genuine discriminative understanding. Explicit reasoning does not consistently improve results and may even hinder performance through over-thinking. Our work demonstrates that while the performance of LLMs (including their agentic use) in many SE tasks is impressive, there are still fundamental issues to understand how this will impact SE, including the consistent use of terminology.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates whether LLMs genuinely understand standardized software engineering terminology (ISO/IEC/IEEE 24765:2017) by testing their ability to classify correct vs. systematically falsified definitions. Results reveal a systematic rejection bias — LLMs reject many correct definitions alongside falsified ones — and explicit reasoning often fails to improve or even harms performance due to over-thinking.
AI.motivation: LLMs are widely applied in software engineering, but no prior systematic study assesses whether they truly comprehend standardized SE terminology. Misunderstanding terminology can cause miscommunication between LLMs and human developers, undermining trust in LLM-generated SE artifacts.
AI.method: The authors use the ISO/IEC/IEEE 24765:2017 Systems and Software Engineering Vocabulary as ground truth. They construct a test set of correct definitions and systematically falsified variants — semantic falsifications (key term substitution) and structural falsifications (removing critical information). LLMs are prompted to classify definitions as correct or incorrect. Both classification accuracy and the quality of reasoning tokens are evaluated. Multiple state-of-the-art LLMs are tested, with and without explicit reasoning (chain-of-thought).
AI.result: LLMs detect falsified definitions with high accuracy but also incorrectly reject many correct definitions, indicating a rejection bias rather than genuine discriminative understanding. Explicit reasoning does not consistently improve classification and can degrade performance through over-thinking. Reasoning token analysis shows LLMs often produce plausible-sounding but flawed justifications.
AI.conclusion: Despite impressive SE task performance, LLMs exhibit fundamental weaknesses in understanding standardized terminology, raising concerns about their reliability in terminology-critical SE applications. The rejection bias and over-thinking phenomena suggest that current LLM evaluation metrics may overstate true comprehension.

title: Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development
comment: 5 pages. To be published in the proceedings of 41st International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE '26), October 12-16, 2026, Munich, Germany (New Ideas and Emerging Results Track)
summary: AI coding agents are rapidly reshaping how software is built, with developers increasingly delegating substantial coding tasks to autonomous agents in pursuit of higher productivity. While these gains are real, they come at the cost of incidental learning. Developers historically acquired informal knowledge through effortful problem-solving, and this has long shaped how software engineering expertise develops. However, with over-reliance on agentic coding, unpracticed skills could atrophy silently over time. As this learning pathway is short-circuited, developers risk silently accruing Knowledge Debt, a developer-level analogue of Technical Debt, where changes the agent executes that the developer cannot fully understand accrue over time. In this paper, we argue that incidental learning will not re-emerge on its own and must be consciously designed back into developer-agent interactions, and propose six design principles to guide such systems. We then present "SHIELD", a multi-agent system grounded in the notion of "agents that teach", that operationalizes these principles by leveraging the AI coding agent's own reasoning to surface contextual, out-of-band learning moments without disrupting developer flow. Through this work, we envision a path toward learning-aware development environments where productivity and learning are complementary, not competing.

AI.tldr: AI coding agents boost productivity but undermine incidental learning, causing developers to accumulate "Knowledge Debt" — a lack of understanding of agent-generated code. The paper proposes six design principles for integrating learning back into developer-agent interactions and presents SHIELD, a multi-agent system where agents teach developers in-context without disrupting workflow.
AI.motivation: The core concern is that as developers increasingly delegate coding tasks to autonomous AI agents, they lose the incidental, effortful problem-solving experiences that historically built deep software engineering expertise. This creates a silent atrophy of skills and accumulation of "Knowledge Debt," where developers cannot fully understand changes made by agents in their codebases.
AI.method: The authors first articulate the problem of Knowledge Debt and argue that incidental learning must be deliberately reintroduced. They propose six design principles for learning-aware developer-agent systems. They then build SHIELD, a multi-agent system implementing "agents that teach," which uses the coding agent's own reasoning capabilities to surface contextual, out-of-band learning moments — teaching interventions that occur at appropriate moments without interrupting the developer's flow state.
AI.result: The paper contributes a conceptual framework distinguishing Knowledge Debt from Technical Debt, six prescriptive design principles for integrating learning into AI-assisted development, and the SHIELD system as a proof-of-concept operationalizing those principles.
AI.conclusion: Incidental learning will not spontaneously re-emerge in AI-augmented workflows; it must be intentionally designed. SHIELD demonstrates a viable path toward learning-aware development environments where productivity gains and skill development coexist as complementary goals rather than trade-offs.

title: Uncovering Latent Depression Severity for Binary Depression Detection via Advantage-weighting Ranking
summary: Automatic depression detection using audio-visual data faces significant challenges, particularly in disentangling overlapping feature distributions and establishing robust decision boundaries. To address this, we propose a fine-grained multimodal framework featuring a temporal encoder and a mutual transformer to facilitate deep cross-modal fusion. Our core contribution is the Binary Advantage-weighting Ranking Loss, which optimizes the latent space distribution through two complementary mechanisms: Advantage-weighted Separation, which mines hard pairs by computing a pairwise prediction difference matrix and dynamically weighting them based on their difficulty; and Advantage-weighted Compactness, which minimizes intra-class variance to force features to cluster around their respective class centers. Extensive experiments on D-vlog and LMVD demonstrate that our model reconstructs the latent ordinal structure by prioritizing hard pairs, thereby achieving state-of-the-art performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a fine-grained multimodal depression detection framework using a temporal encoder and mutual transformer, with a novel Binary Advantage-weighting Ranking Loss that improves latent space organization through hard-pair mining and intra-class compactness, achieving state-of-the-art results on D-vlog and LMVD datasets.
AI.motivation: Automatic depression detection using audio-visual data suffers from overlapping feature distributions across classes and poorly defined decision boundaries, making reliable classification difficult. Existing methods lack effective mechanisms to separate ambiguous features while maintaining intra-class cohesion.
AI.method: The authors propose a fine-grained multimodal framework with: (1) a temporal encoder for sequence modeling; (2) a mutual transformer for deep cross-modal fusion between audio and visual streams; and (3) the Binary Advantage-weighting Ranking Loss, consisting of two components: Advantage-weighted Separation, which constructs a pairwise prediction difference matrix to identify hard pairs and weights them dynamically by difficulty; and Advantage-weighted Compactness, which reduces intra-class variance by pulling features toward class centers, reconstructing the latent ordinal depression structure.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on the D-vlog and LMVD benchmark datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, validating that the proposed ranking loss effectively reconstructs ordinal structure in the latent space by prioritizing hard pairs.
AI.conclusion: The Binary Advantage-weighting Ranking Loss successfully addresses the challenge of overlapping feature distributions in multimodal depression detection by jointly enforcing separation of difficult samples and compactness within classes, leading to superior performance over existing approaches.

title: When Should LLMs Search? Counterfactual Supervision for Search Routing
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures. Accepted at the FAGEN Workshop at ICML 2026
summary: Search-augmented language models can use external evidence to compensate for limitations in parametric knowledge, but search is not uniformly beneficial: models may call search for questions they can already answer, or rely on noisy evidence when correction, clarification, or abstention would be more appropriate. We formulate this as an instance-level search-routing problem: deciding whether search is needed to improve task success relative to a no-search execution. To derive supervision, we compare no-search and forced-search outcomes for the same question and construct an oracle over NO SEARCH, SEARCH, and UNSOLVED based on task-specific success. Using this oracle as both an evaluation criterion and a learning signal, we train search-routing policies with supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization, improving routing macro-F1 on oracle-eligible examples from 0.7082 to 0.8235 for Gemma E2B and from 0.7053 to 0.8365 for Qwen3.5-4B. Further analysis shows that the learned policies reduce model-specific routing failures: Gemma primarily learns no-search restraint, while Qwen further reduces missed search; residual UNSOLVED cases reveal heterogeneous bottlenecks involving model capacity, retrieval budget, evidence use, and policy behavior.

AI.tldr: Language models augmented with search don't always benefit from retrieval. This paper formulates search-routing as an instance-level decision problem—whether to search, not search, or declare a question unsolved—and trains routing policies using oracle-derived supervision, significantly improving routing accuracy for Gemma and Qwen models.
AI.motivation: Search-augmented LMs can compensate for parametric knowledge gaps, but indiscriminate search is suboptimal: models may unnecessarily search for known answers or blindly trust noisy retrieved evidence when they should instead correct, clarify, or abstain. There is a need for intelligent, instance-level routing that decides when search actually improves outcomes.
AI.method: The authors construct an oracle by comparing no-search and forced-search outcomes per question, labeling each instance as NO SEARCH, SEARCH, or UNSOLVED based on task-specific success criteria. This oracle serves both as an evaluation metric and a supervision signal. Search-routing policies are then trained using supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and preference optimization (e.g., DPO) on Gemma E2B and Qwen3.5-4B models.
AI.result: Routing macro-F1 on oracle-eligible examples improved from 0.7082 to 0.8235 for Gemma E2B and from 0.7053 to 0.8365 for Qwen3.5-4B. Analysis reveals model-specific failure patterns: Gemma primarily benefits from learning no-search restraint, while Qwen additionally reduces missed search. Residual UNSOLVED cases expose heterogeneous bottlenecks spanning model capacity, retrieval budget, evidence utilization, and policy behavior.
AI.conclusion: Instance-level search-routing can be effectively learned from oracle supervision, yielding substantial improvements over default search behavior. The approach surfaces distinct per-model failure modes and highlights that unsolved cases stem from multiple interacting bottlenecks rather than any single factor.

title: SafeImpute: Reliable Clinical Data Imputation via Conformal Selection
comment: Accepted at KDD 2026. Author accepted manuscript
summary: Clinical care often relies on key laboratory indicators, yet real-world patient visits are sparse and tests are ordered irregularly, leading to pervasive missingness. While many imputation methods improve average accuracy, they provide limited guidance on which imputed values are reliable enough for high-stakes downstream use. In this work, we study reliable clinical imputation, aiming to produce accurate imputations while selectively releasing the reliable results, with statistical control over clinically unacceptable errors. To achieve this goal, we propose SafeImpute, a reliable imputation framework for irregular and sparse clinical longitudinal records. SafeImpute constructs an event graph that captures both intra-patient temporal trajectories and inter-patient clinical similarity, and learns imputations with a two-relation GNN and adaptive fusion, regularized by an auxiliary masked reconstruction objective. For reliability guarantees, SafeImpute converts a proxy risk score into conformal p-values and applies the Benjamini--Hochberg procedure to control the false discovery rate (FDR) of unacceptable errors among released imputations at a user-specified tolerance. Experiments on our Mayo Clinic data, the public MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV datasets show that SafeImpute achieves strong imputation accuracy while providing reliable error control, outperforming diverse baselines in both standard imputation evaluation and FDR-controlled selective-release evaluation.

AI.tldr: SafeImpute is a reliable clinical imputation framework for irregular, sparse longitudinal data that uses a two-relation GNN with conformal prediction and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control to selectively release only trustworthy imputed values.
AI.motivation: Clinical lab data suffer from pervasive missingness due to irregular visits and test ordering, and existing imputation methods lack mechanisms to identify which imputed values are reliable enough for high-stakes downstream use — creating a need for imputation with statistical error guarantees.
AI.method: SafeImpute builds an event graph encoding intra-patient temporal trajectories and inter-patient clinical similarity, learns imputations via a two-relation GNN with adaptive fusion and auxiliary masked reconstruction, then converts proxy risk scores into conformal p-values and applies the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure to control FDR of unacceptable errors among released imputations at a user-specified tolerance.
AI.result: Experiments on Mayo Clinic data, MIMIC-III, and MIMIC-IV demonstrate that SafeImpute achieves strong imputation accuracy while providing reliable FDR-controlled error guarantees, outperforming diverse baselines in both standard imputation metrics and FDR-controlled selective-release evaluation.
AI.conclusion: SafeImpute offers a principled solution for clinical imputation with reliability guarantees, enabling safe downstream use by distinguishing trustworthy from untrustworthy imputed values with formal statistical error control.

title: From Regression to Prior-Aware Inference: Solving the ILWE Family in Randomness Leakage Attacks against ML-DSA
summary:
ML-DSA is a representative lattice-based signature scheme standardized by NIST. It relies on signing randomness and rejection sampling to ensure that released signatures are statistically independent of the secret key. Practical implementations, however, may leak partial information about this randomness, and such leakage can transform public signatures into ILWE-type problems, resulting in secret key disclosure risks.
  Such randomness leakage attack can be formulated as a two-stage key-recovery procedure, in which leaked partial information and public signatures are first transformed into an ILWE-family instance, and then a recovery solver is applied to recover the secret key. Existing work has mainly focused on the first stage by constructing such instances under different leakage models. By contrast, the role of solver in the subsequent instance-solving stage remains under-explored, and existing attacks often rely on ad-hoc model-specific solvers. To address this gap, we propose a unified framework to systematically evaluate different recovery solvers on leakage-derived ILWE-family instances. The framework covers three ILWE instances, including the ordinary ILWE, Fiat-Shamir ILWE (FS-ILWE) and Concealed ILWE (CILWE) under different scenarios.
  Within our framework, we explore three classes of solvers. Our experiments show that the solver has a significant impact on the secret-key recovery efficiency. In particular, on FS-ILWE, prior-aware discrete-inference reduces the number of informative relations by one to two orders of magnitude compared to the baselines: Compared with OLS, BP constitutes a reduction by a factor of 15.4x-64.9x in noise-free settings, and by a factor of 10.5x-73.9x in noisy settings. Overall, this work provides a systematic evaluation on different solvers in randomness leakage attacks, and presents new benchmarks for future analysis on ML-DSA.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a unified framework to systematically evaluate different solvers for recovering secret keys from ILWE-family instances derived from randomness leakage in ML-DSA signatures. The authors demonstrate that solver choice dramatically impacts recovery efficiency, with prior-aware discrete-inference reducing required informative relations by 1–2 orders of magnitude compared to baselines like OLS and BP.
AI.motivation: Existing work on randomness leakage attacks against ML-DSA has focused heavily on constructing ILWE-family instances (Stage 1), while the solver stage (Stage 2) remains under-explored. Prior attacks often use ad-hoc, model-specific solvers without systematic comparison, leaving a gap in understanding which solvers are most effective for key recovery under different leakage scenarios.
AI.method: The authors propose a unified two-stage framework covering three ILWE instance types: ordinary ILWE, Fiat-Shamir ILWE (FS-ILWE), and Concealed ILWE (CILWE). Within this framework, they systematically evaluate three classes of recovery solvers — Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), Belief Propagation (BP), and prior-aware discrete-inference — across both noise-free and noisy settings, measuring the number of informative relations required for successful secret-key recovery.
AI.result: The solver choice significantly impacts recovery efficiency. On FS-ILWE instances, prior-aware discrete-inference reduces the required number of informative relations by 1–2 orders of magnitude versus baselines: a 15.4×–64.9× reduction compared to OLS in noise-free settings, and 10.5×–73.9× reduction compared to OLS in noisy settings. The framework establishes new benchmarks for evaluating randomness leakage attacks on ML-DSA.
AI.conclusion: The solver stage is critical to the efficiency of randomness leakage attacks on ML-DSA, and systematic solver selection yields substantial improvements. Prior-aware discrete-inference consistently outperforms conventional approaches. This work provides a standardized evaluation framework and new benchmarks to guide future security analysis of lattice-based signature implementations.

title: Automating Quality Assessment with NLP of LLM-Generated Defeaters
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures. Author preprint version of a paper published at ICSRS 2025
summary: High-integrity systems, such as autonomous vehicle fleets and large-scale energy infrastructures, rely on structured assurance cases to justify safety claims. To remain valid under evolving operational conditions, such cases must be examined against potential challenges, known as defeaters. While large language models (LLMs) can support the scalable generation of candidate defeaters, assessing their quality remains largely manual and subjective process. This paper presents an automated approach for supporting the assessment of LLM-generated defeaters using natural language processing techniques. The method combines structural features from assurance case graphs with semantic embeddings and meta-classifiers trained on expert-assessed defeater annotations. We evaluate the approach through two case studies in the automotive and energy domains. The results show substantial human reviewer dissensus, with Cohen's kappa values below 0.442, highlighting the difficulty of consistent manual assessment. Against this background, the proposed classifiers achieve an average F1-score of 0.84 in validation and show improved alignment with individual expert ratings. The findings suggest that automated assessment can help reduce subjective variance and provide scalable decision support for assurance case review, while leaving final judgment to domain experts.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an automated NLP-based approach to assess the quality of LLM-generated defeaters (challenges to safety claims) in assurance cases. Using structural graph features, semantic embeddings, and meta-classifiers trained on expert annotations, the method achieves an average F1-score of 0.84. The study reveals high expert dissensus (Cohen's κ < 0.442), suggesting automated assessment can reduce subjective variance while supporting—not replacing—human judgment.
AI.motivation: High-integrity systems (e.g., autonomous vehicles, energy infrastructures) use assurance cases to justify safety claims, but these must be continuously challenged against potential defeaters to remain valid under evolving conditions. While LLMs can generate defeaters at scale, assessing their quality is currently manual, subjective, and inconsistent. There is a clear need for automated, scalable defeater quality assessment.
AI.method: The approach combines three feature sources: (1) structural features extracted from assurance case graphs (e.g., Goal Structuring Notation), (2) semantic embeddings of defeater text, and (3) meta-classifiers trained on expert-assessed defeater annotations. Evaluation is conducted through two case studies in the automotive and energy domains. Inter-rater agreement is measured via Cohen's kappa, and classifier performance via F1-score.
AI.result: Expert reviewers exhibited substantial dissensus, with Cohen's kappa values below 0.442, underscoring the inherent difficulty of consistent manual defeater assessment. The proposed classifiers achieved an average F1-score of 0.84 in validation and demonstrated improved alignment with individual expert ratings compared to aggregate labels.
AI.conclusion: Automated defeater assessment can reduce subjective variance and offer scalable decision support for assurance case review. However, the authors advocate a human-in-the-loop paradigm where final judgment remains with domain experts. The approach shows promise for practical deployment in safety-critical system assurance workflows.

title: PCBWorld: A Benchmark Environment for Engine-Grounded PCB Design Automation
comment: Accepted to the KDD 2026 Workshop on Evaluation and Trustworthiness of Agentic AI (non-archival). Main text with appendix
summary: PCB routing is the task of connecting the nets of a board with copper traces under strict design rules, yet learning-based methods still lag behind rule-based routers. We introduce PCBWorld, an open-source engine-grounded PCB routing environment built on the KiCad EDA engine. As a human engineer does, agents in PCBWorld interactively route a board through the engine's native operations, using its Design Rule Check (DRC) feedback to keep the routing within the design rules. The environment supports both RL policies and tool-using LLM agents. Alongside the environment, PCBWorld-Bench provides three dataset families in KiCad's native board format (.kicad_pcb), covering two types of controllable synthetic instances and 679 real open-source boards. It scores any completed board with eight engine-checked evaluation metrics, regardless of the routing method. In our experiments, agents in PCBWorld consistently outperformed grid-action RL policies and open-loop LLM baselines, and an RL policy trained only on synthetic boards transferred zero-shot to real boards, approaching rule-based routers. These results position the engine-grounded, interactive approach of PCBWorld as a promising foundation for advancing the routing ability of both RL and LLM agents.

AI.tldr: PCBWorld is an open-source, engine-grounded PCB routing environment built on KiCad that enables RL and LLM agents to interactively route boards using native engine operations with DRC feedback. It includes PCBWorld-Bench with synthetic and real-board datasets, plus eight engine-checked evaluation metrics. Agents trained in this environment outperformed baselines and transferred zero-shot from synthetic to real boards.
AI.motivation: Learning-based methods for PCB routing still lag behind traditional rule-based routers. Prior approaches lack realistic, interactive environments grounded in actual EDA engines, limiting agents' ability to learn from genuine design rule feedback and transfer to real-world boards.
AI.method: The authors built PCBWorld on top of the KiCad EDA engine, allowing agents to perform native routing operations and receive Design Rule Check (DRC) feedback interactively. The environment supports both RL policies and tool-using LLM agents. PCBWorld-Bench provides three dataset families (two synthetic, one with 679 real open-source boards) in KiCad's native .kicad_pcb format, with eight engine-checked evaluation metrics for scoring completed boards.
AI.result: Agents operating within PCBWorld consistently outperformed grid-action RL policies and open-loop LLM baselines. An RL policy trained solely on synthetic boards transferred zero-shot to real boards, achieving performance approaching that of rule-based routers.
AI.conclusion: The engine-grounded, interactive paradigm of PCBWorld provides a promising foundation for advancing PCB routing capabilities in both RL and LLM agents, demonstrating effective zero-shot transfer from synthetic to real boards.

title: A Coin Flip Per Token: Bernoulli Sparse Steering of Large Language Models
summary: Activation steering via sparse autoencoders (SAEs) enables behavioral control of large language models without task-specific fine-tuning, but standard methods apply the steering signal at every generated token, incurring constant per-token perturbation that risks degrading fluency. We ask: is dense intervention necessary? We introduce Stochastic Token Steering (STS), which gates each token independently with probability $p$, and Stochastic Block Steering (SBS), which gates a leading window once per sequence; neither requires a reward model or learned gating policy. Across two model families and two behavioral tasks, steering only 50% of the tokens recovers most of the dense-steering effect while preserving fluency, and steering as few as 30% surpasses prompt-based control. The optimal steering magnitude scales inversely with the intervention ratio, revealing that SAE-mediated control is rate-limited: the behavioral outcome depends on cumulative signal dosage across a sequence.

AI.tldr: Standard SAE-based activation steering applies a perturbation at every token, degrading fluency. The authors propose stochastic gating (token-level or block-level) and show that steering only 30–50% of tokens recovers most of the behavioral effect while preserving fluency, revealing that control is rate-limited and depends on cumulative signal dosage.
AI.motivation: Dense, per-token intervention in SAE-based activation steering imposes constant perturbation that risks degrading output fluency. The authors question whether this dense intervention is necessary for effective behavioral control.
AI.method: Two stochastic gating strategies: Stochastic Token Steering (STS), which independently applies the steering signal to each token with probability p, and Stochastic Block Steering (SBS), which applies steering to a leading window of tokens once per sequence. No reward model or learned gating policy is required. The relationship between steering magnitude and intervention ratio is also analyzed.
AI.result: Steering only 50% of tokens recovers most of the dense-steering effect while maintaining fluency. Steering as few as 30% surpasses prompt-based control. Optimal steering magnitude scales inversely with intervention ratio, indicating cumulative signal dosage determines behavioral outcome.
AI.conclusion: SAE-mediated behavioral control is rate-limited rather than requiring dense, per-token intervention. Sparse stochastic gating achieves comparable behavioral effects with better fluency, and the inverse scaling between optimal magnitude and intervention ratio suggests a cumulative dosage model of steering.

title: ProvICS: A Provenance-based Intrusion Detection for Industrial Control Systems
summary: The convergence of Information Technology and Operational Technology has exposed Industrial Control Systems (ICS) to multi-stage cyberattacks that traverse software, network, and physical process layers simultaneously. Although Provenance-based Intrusion Detection Systems (PIDS) are effective in Information Technology (IT) environments, their applicability to Industrial Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) remains largely unexplored because of the absence of datasets that jointly capture host-level causal behavior, industrial network semantics, and physical process state. To address this gap, we design an open-source, Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) CPS testbed that replicates an industrial chemical reactor control architecture across the Purdue model layers. Using this testbed, we propose ProvICS, a multimodal provenance dataset purpose-built for CPS intrusion detection, which synchronously captures four streams: whole-system provenance graphs from the supervisory host and the resource-constrained PLC, decoded Modbus deep-packet inspection records, and physical process telemetry. The collection comprises a 48-hour benign phase and a 22-hour attack phase across four campaigns covering 20 ICS ATT&CK techniques over 32 attack events, ranging from reconnaissance to physical process manipulation. Comparative analysis shows that ProvICS is among the few existing ICS/CPS benchmarks with multi-host kernel-level provenance, real PLC hardware-in-the-loop execution, decoded Modbus traffic, physical process-state measurements, and auxiliary raw PCAP traces in a time-synchronized collection. Baseline detection further confirms that cross-modal fusion can detect all 32 labeled attack events (F1 = 0.913, false-positive rate (FPR) = 1.40%), demonstrating the dataset's ability to expose complementary attack signals across modalities and addressing a gap not covered by prior benchmarks.

AI.tldr: ProvICS is a multimodal provenance dataset for CPS intrusion detection, synchronously capturing host-level provenance graphs, Modbus DPI records, and physical process telemetry from a HIL testbed. It covers 32 attack events across 20 ICS ATT&CK techniques, and baseline cross-modal fusion achieves F1=0.913 with 1.40% FPR, filling a critical gap in multimodal ICS security benchmarks.
AI.motivation: IT-OT convergence exposes ICS to multi-stage cyberattacks spanning software, network, and physical layers. Provenance-based IDS (PIDS) is effective in IT but unexplored in CPS due to the lack of datasets that jointly capture host-level causal behavior, industrial network semantics, and physical process state.
AI.method: The authors built an open-source HIL CPS testbed replicating an industrial chemical reactor control architecture across Purdue model layers. Using this testbed, they created ProvICS, which synchronously captures four data streams: whole-system provenance graphs (supervisory host and PLC), decoded Modbus DPI records, physical process telemetry, and raw PCAP traces. The dataset spans a 48-hour benign phase and a 22-hour attack phase with 32 events covering 20 ICS ATT&CK techniques. Baseline detection using cross-modal fusion was performed to validate the dataset's utility.
AI.result: ProvICS is among the few ICS/CPS benchmarks offering multi-host kernel-level provenance, real PLC HIL execution, decoded Modbus traffic, and physical process-state measurements in a time-synchronized manner. Baseline cross-modal fusion detected all 32 labeled attack events with F1=0.913 and FPR=1.40%, demonstrating complementary attack signals across modalities.
AI.conclusion: ProvICS successfully addresses the gap in multimodal, provenance-aware CPS intrusion detection benchmarks. The dataset enables research on cross-modal fusion for ICS security, and the open-source testbed provides a reproducible foundation for future CPS security experimentation.

title: SWE-Review: Closing the Loop on Issue Resolution with Agentic Code Review
summary: Coding agents increasingly generate pull requests (PRs) for real-world software issues, yet one-shot PR generation remains open-loop: the PR is proposed without systematic review, diagnosis, or revision. We introduce \textbf{SWE-Review}, a framework for closing this loop with agentic code review. Given an issue and an AI-generated PR, a reviewer agent explores the repository, decides whether the PR should be accepted, and provides structured feedback for revision. We evaluate this setting with our proposed \textbf{SWE-Review-Bench} to measure both review correctness and downstream revision usefulness. We further curate \textbf{SWE-Review-Traj} dataset to study broader applications of agentic review and fill the data-scarcity gap for open reviewer training. Experiments show that agentic review continuously improves PRs through a generate-review-revise loop, outperforms single-turn fixed-context review in both decision accuracy and resolve rate after revision, transfers beyond review to improve issue-resolution models, and enables effective and efficient test-time scaling. These results position agentic code review as a practical mechanism for moving AI coding agents from one-shot PR generation toward closed-loop issue resolution.

AI.tldr: SWE-Review introduces an agentic code review framework that closes the loop on AI-generated pull requests by having a reviewer agent explore the repository, evaluate PR correctness, and provide structured feedback. The authors provide a benchmark (SWE-Review-Bench), a trajectory dataset (SWE-Review-Traj), and demonstrate that iterative generate-review-revise cycles outperform single-turn approaches in both review accuracy and downstream issue resolution.
AI.motivation: Current AI coding agents generate PRs in a one-shot, open-loop manner — a PR is proposed without systematic review, diagnosis, or revision. This mirrors real-world software engineering where code review is essential, yet no framework exists for agentic, repository-aware review of AI-generated PRs. There is also a data-scarcity problem for training open reviewer models.
AI.method: The authors propose SWE-Review, a framework where a reviewer agent explores the repository, decides whether to accept/reject a PR, and provides structured feedback. They introduce SWE-Review-Bench to evaluate review correctness and revision usefulness, and curate SWE-Review-Traj to provide training data for open reviewer models. Experiments test the generate-review-revise loop against single-turn fixed-context review baselines.
AI.result: Agentic review in a generate-review-revise loop continuously improves PRs. It outperforms single-turn fixed-context review in both decision accuracy and resolve rate after revision. The approach transfers beyond review to improve issue-resolution models and enables effective and efficient test-time scaling.
AI.conclusion: Agentic code review is a practical mechanism for transitioning AI coding agents from one-shot PR generation to closed-loop issue resolution, with benefits in accuracy, revision usefulness, and scalability.

title: SearchEyes: Towards Frontier Multimodal Deep Search Intelligence via Search World Simulation
summary: Training multimodal search agents to perform multi-hop reasoning remains challenging due to a fundamental structural disconnect: existing pipelines construct training data, search environments, and reward signals independently, causing synthesized structural metadata to be discarded, environments to rely on irreproducible external engines, and RL rewards to remain sparse at the trajectory level. We present \textbf{SearchEyes}, which uses a typed knowledge graph as the backbone of a \emph{simulated search world} that unifies all three components. We propose \textbf{Perception-Knowledge Chains (PKC)} to sample constrained multi-hop paths over the visual-knowledge intersection of Wikidata5M, retaining hop-level entity metadata that simultaneously defines a self-contained search world and step-level reward anchors. We further propose \textbf{Hop-Anchored Policy Optimization (HaPO)}, which reuses these anchors for step-level credit assignment without a separately trained process reward model. Experiments on six multimodal knowledge-intensive benchmarks show that SearchEyes achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source multimodal search agents, with SearchEyes-27B improving over the strongest open-source baseline by 6.2 points on average.%

AI.tldr: SearchEyes unifies training data, search environment, and reward signals using a typed knowledge graph backbone. It introduces Perception-Knowledge Chains (PKC) for constrained multi-hop path sampling with step-level metadata, and Hop-Anchored Policy Optimization (HaPO) for step-level credit assignment without a separate reward model. The approach achieves SOTA among open-source multimodal search agents.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal search agent pipelines suffer from a structural disconnect: training data, search environments, and reward signals are constructed independently, leading to discarded structural metadata, irreproducible external search engines, and sparse trajectory-level RL rewards.
AI.method: SearchEyes uses a typed knowledge graph (Wikidata5M) as a simulated search world backbone. Two key innovations: (1) Perception-Knowledge Chains (PKC) sample constrained multi-hop paths over the visual-knowledge intersection, retaining hop-level entity metadata that defines the search world and provides step-level reward anchors; (2) Hop-Anchored Policy Optimization (HaPO) reuses these anchors for step-level credit assignment, eliminating the need for a separately trained process reward model.
AI.result: SearchEyes-27B achieves state-of-the-art performance among open-source multimodal search agents across six multimodal knowledge-intensive benchmarks, outperforming the strongest open-source baseline by an average of 6.2 points.
AI.conclusion: Unifying training data, environment, and reward design through a typed knowledge graph backbone effectively addresses the structural disconnect in multimodal search agent training, enabling more granular and efficient multi-hop reasoning.

title: CoPiT: Cognitive Pivot Translation for Digraphic Low-Resource Mongolian in the Traditional Script
summary: Low-resource languages remain challenging for machine translation, and Mongolian is a representative case. As a digraphic language, Mongolian is written in both Cyrillic and Traditional scripts, which exhibit a severe imbalance in data availability. While the Cyrillic script is relatively well-resourced, the Traditional script remains extremely data-scarce and orthographically ambiguous, leading to substantial performance degradation in direct translation. We propose CoPiT, a cognitively motivated pivot-based translation pipeline that exploits this internal resource hierarchy by routing translation through the Cyrillic script. The pipeline explicitly resolves script-induced ambiguity in the Traditional script before translation, enabling more stable and accurate meaning transfer. Across multiple backbone models and target languages, CoPiT consistently outperforms direct translation, achieving substantial absolute BLEU improvements together with consistent 1.5-1.6x COMET gains. These gains allow strong open-source models to match or outperform GPT-4.1 under comparable evaluation settings. Beyond inference-time improvements, CoPiT enables the construction of synthetic parallel data directly from Traditional-script text, mitigating data scarcity in realistic low-resource scenarios. We release a new multi-script parallel dataset covering Mongolian in both scripts alongside English, Korean, and Russian. All datasets and code are publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/anonymous_project-76C7.

AI.tldr: CoPiT proposes a pivot-based translation pipeline for low-resource Mongolian that routes Traditional-script input through Cyrillic script to resolve orthographic ambiguity, achieving substantial BLEU and COMET gains over direct translation, matching GPT-4.1 performance, and enabling synthetic parallel data construction.
AI.motivation: Mongolian is a digraphic language with severe data imbalance: Cyrillic script is relatively well-resourced while Traditional script is extremely data-scarce and orthographically ambiguous, causing significant performance degradation in direct machine translation. The authors seek to exploit this internal resource hierarchy rather than treating Traditional Mongolian as a separate low-resource language.
AI.method: CoPiT (Cognitively motivated Pivot-based Translation) is a pipeline that first converts Traditional Mongolian script to Cyrillic script, explicitly resolving script-induced orthographic ambiguity, then translates from Cyrillic to the target language. This cognitively motivated routing leverages the data-rich Cyrillic intermediate representation. The method also enables constructing synthetic parallel data directly from Traditional-script text to mitigate data scarcity. A new multi-script parallel dataset is released covering Mongolian (both scripts) with English, Korean, and Russian.
AI.result: CoPiT consistently outperforms direct translation across multiple backbone models and target languages, achieving substantial absolute BLEU improvements and 1.5–1.6× COMET gains. Strong open-source models using CoPiT match or outperform GPT-4.1 under comparable evaluation settings.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting internal resource hierarchies via script pivoting is an effective strategy for digraphic low-resource languages like Mongolian. CoPiT not only improves inference-time translation quality but also facilitates synthetic data generation, addressing data scarcity in realistic low-resource scenarios.

title: Safe Bayesian Optimization with Counterfactual Policies
summary: In many decision-making settings, new interventions are acceptable only if they do not reduce outcomes below some established threshold. For example, in clinical medicine, new treatments are often acceptable only if they do not worsen outcomes relative to an established standard of care. Safe Bayesian optimization maximizes an objective subject to safety constraints. In the setting that we consider here, safety is defined relative to a known baseline policy whose outcomes are counterfactual and therefore unobserved. Thus, the counterfactual outcomes of the baseline policy must be estimated and those (uncertain) estimates must be used to safely optimize the objective. We address this estimation problem by using conformal prediction to construct valid uncertainty intervals for counterfactual baseline outcomes, and we show how these intervals can be integrated into safe Bayesian optimization to ensure that constraint violations occur at or below a user-specified rate. We also show how to adapt these conformal estimates to different kinds of covariate shift. We provide a safety proof, experimental evidence, and a sensitivity analysis.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses safe Bayesian optimization when safety is defined relative to a baseline policy with unobserved counterfactual outcomes. The authors use conformal prediction to construct valid uncertainty intervals for these counterfactuals and integrate them into safe BO, ensuring constraint violations remain below a user-specified rate, with adaptations for covariate shift.
AI.motivation: In decision-making settings like clinical medicine, new interventions must not worsen outcomes relative to an established standard of care. However, the baseline policy's outcomes are counterfactual and unobserved, creating a fundamental estimation challenge: one must estimate counterfactual baseline outcomes under uncertainty and safely optimize without violating the unknown constraint.
AI.method: The authors employ conformal prediction to construct valid, distribution-free uncertainty intervals for counterfactual baseline outcomes. These conformal intervals are then integrated into a safe Bayesian optimization framework, allowing the optimizer to respect safety constraints probabilistically. The method also incorporates adaptations to handle covariate shift between the data-generating distribution and the optimization distribution. A user-specified violation rate controls the safety guarantee.
AI.result: The paper provides a formal safety proof demonstrating that constraint violations occur at or below the user-specified rate. Experimental evidence validates the approach empirically, and a sensitivity analysis examines robustness to assumptions such as unconfoundedness and the degree of covariate shift.
AI.conclusion: Conformal prediction offers a principled way to quantify uncertainty in counterfactual baseline estimates, enabling safe Bayesian optimization under counterfactual safety constraints. The framework is theoretically grounded, empirically validated, and flexible to various forms of covariate shift.

title: Bit2Watt: A Cyber-Physical Vulnerability Exploiting GPU Workloads Across Power and Computing Infrastructures
summary: Modern data centers increasingly rely on large-scale GPU clusters and on-site renewable energy resources, resulting in a tightly coupled cyber-physical system between computing workloads and power-electronic-dominated grids. In this paper, we reveal Bit2Watt, a previously unexplored vulnerability in which an adversary manipulates GPU workloads to induce controlled, high-frequency power modulations that destabilize local power infrastructure and propagate back to disrupt computing services. Unlike traditional attacks that compromise grid-side devices or communication channels, Bit2Watt operates entirely within the cyber layer as a legal tenant, which could amplify fluctuations, harmonic distortion, and damping degradation, particularly in high-DER-penetration scenarios. This risk is difficult to detect under routine cloud- and facility-side monitoring because it exploits legitimate workload execution paths and concentrates much of its distinctive behavior in high-frequency components that are weakly captured by common telemetry. We validate Bit2Watt through impedance-based analysis, power system simulations, and real-world experiments on GPUs and grid-connected PV inverters. Under the synchronized worst-case aggregation model studied in the paper, manipulating 1,000 GPUs in a 1-MW local power system with 90% DERs raises current THD to 46.8% and results in a damping ratio of -0.27. We further show that the resulting power-quality degradation can stress data-center power-delivery equipment, trigger protection mechanisms, and, in extreme simulated cases, induce cascading failures in transmission-scale systems. In addition, we analyze a plausible Watt2Bit feedback path, including denial-of-service risks and covert information exfiltration via EMI side channels. This work highlights the urgent need for cross-layer defenses that jointly consider workload scheduling and power electronics.

AI.tldr: Bit2Watt is a novel cyber-physical attack where an adversary manipulates GPU workloads to generate high-frequency power modulations that destabilize local power grids in data centers with high renewable penetration, potentially causing power-quality degradation, equipment stress, and cascading failures, while also enabling a feedback Watt2Bit path for DoS and covert exfiltration.
AI.motivation: Modern data centers increasingly integrate large GPU clusters with on-site renewable energy, creating a tightly coupled cyber-physical system. The authors identify a gap: existing attacks target grid-side devices or communication channels, but no prior work explores exploiting legitimate GPU workload execution to undermine power infrastructure stability from within the cyber layer.
AI.method: The authors propose Bit2Watt, where an adversary (as a legal tenant) modulates GPU workloads to produce controlled high-frequency power fluctuations. They validate the attack through: (1) impedance-based analytical modeling, (2) power system simulations, and (3) real-world experiments on GPUs and grid-connected PV inverters. A worst-case synchronized aggregation of 1,000 GPUs in a 1-MW system with 90% DERs is modeled. They also analyze a Watt2Bit feedback path for DoS and EMI-based covert exfiltration.
AI.result: Under the synchronized worst-case model, manipulating 1,000 GPUs in a 1-MW system with 90% DER penetration raises current Total Harmonic Distortion (THD) to 46.8% and yields a damping ratio of -0.27 (indicating instability). The power-quality degradation stresses data-center power-delivery equipment, triggers protection mechanisms, and in extreme simulations induces cascading failures in transmission-scale systems.
AI.conclusion: Bit2Watt represents a critical, previously unexplored cross-layer vulnerability that is difficult to detect via conventional cloud/facility monitoring because it exploits legitimate workload paths and concentrates anomalous behavior in high-frequency components. The work underscores the urgent need for cross-layer defenses integrating workload scheduling and power electronics governance.

title: Integrating knowledge graphs and multilingual scholarly corpora for domain-adaptive LLMs in SSH
comment: 8 pages, 4 tables, workshop LLMs4SSH of LREC 2026 conference
summary: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into scientific research workflows, particularly for bibliographic discovery and literature synthesis, raises significant methodological, epistemic and regulatory challenges for the Social Sciences and Humanities (SSH), especially with regard to disciplinary diversity, multilingual access to sources and the evaluation of results. This paper presents an on-going use case developed within the European project LLMs4EU and the ALT-EDIC infrastructure, aimed at adapting foundation models to SSH research practices and supporting tasks such as question answering, comparative document analysis and literature review. The evaluation framework follows the LLMs4EU protocol and encompasses both independent quantitative benchmarking (retrieval, summarisation, traceability and hallucination detection) and a qualitative assessment involving a panel of Digital Humanities experts. By embedding model adaptation within research infrastructures and a structured legal and ethical compliance framework, the use case explores how domain-sensitive and regulation-aware generative AI can support SSH scholarship while preserving reliability and epistemic responsibility.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a use case from the LLMs4EU project that adapts LLMs for Social Sciences and Humanities (SSH) bibliographic workflows, using a dual evaluation framework combining quantitative benchmarking and qualitative expert assessment, all within a structured legal-ethical compliance framework.
AI.motivation: LLMs integrated into scientific research workflows pose methodological, epistemic, and regulatory challenges for SSH disciplines — particularly regarding disciplinary diversity, multilingual source access, and result evaluation. There is a need for domain-sensitive, regulation-aware generative AI that respects SSH's specific scholarly practices.
AI.method: The authors develop a use case within the LLMs4EU project and ALT-EDIC infrastructure, adapting foundation models to SSH tasks (question answering, comparative document analysis, literature review). Evaluation follows the LLMs4EU protocol: independent quantitative benchmarking (retrieval, summarisation, traceability, hallucination detection) plus qualitative assessment by a Digital Humanities expert panel, all embedded in a structured legal and ethical compliance framework.
AI.result: The paper describes an on-going use case; no finalized experimental results are reported in the abstract. The contribution lies in the methodological design combining model adaptation, dual evaluation, and compliance infrastructure.
AI.conclusion: Embedding model adaptation within research infrastructures and a structured compliance framework enables domain-sensitive, regulation-aware generative AI to support SSH scholarship while preserving reliability and epistemic responsibility.

title: Mitigating Factual Hallucination in Large Reasoning Models via Mixed-Mode Advantage Regularization
summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) improve language model capabilities by generating explicit thinking traces before final answers. In factuality-oriented question answering (QA), such thinking often improves overall performance by helping the model recover relevant knowledge and refine its answers. However, we find that this benefit is not uniform at the instance level: explicit thinking can also overturn correct non-thinking answers and lead to factual drift. We refer to this failure mode as \emph{thinking-induced hallucination}. To explain this phenomenon, we formulate explicit thinking in factuality QA as a thinking residual over the model's direct-answer tendency, which can either recover missing knowledge or introduce unsupported associations. Based on this formulation, we propose MARGO, \underline{\textit{M}}ixed-Mode \underline{\textit{A}}dvantage \underline{\textit{R}}egularization for \underline{\textit{G}}rounded \underline{\textit{O}}ptimization, a reinforcement learning framework that uses non-thinking rollouts as same-model references in advantage estimation. By constructing mixed-mode rollout groups with both thinking and non-thinking trajectories, MARGO evaluates whether explicit thinking adds factual value beyond direct answering, thereby suppressing hallucination-prone thinking while preserving beneficial thinking behaviors. Experiments across multiple factuality-oriented QA benchmarks demonstrate that MARGO improves factual reliability over strong baselines, while evaluations on mathematical benchmarks show that it preserves general reasoning ability.

AI.tldr: Large reasoning models can produce thinking traces that improve factuality-oriented QA, but explicit thinking sometimes overturns correct answers, causing "thinking-induced hallucination." The authors propose MARGO, a reinforcement learning framework that uses mixed-mode (thinking + non-thinking) rollouts for advantage estimation, suppressing harmful thinking while preserving beneficial reasoning.
AI.motivation: While explicit thinking in LRMs generally improves QA performance, the benefit is non-uniform: thinking can override correct intuitive answers and introduce factual errors. This failure mode—thinking-induced hallucination—lacks a formal understanding and a targeted mitigation strategy.
AI.method: The authors formalize explicit thinking as a "thinking residual" over the model's direct-answer tendency. They propose MARGO (Mixed-Mode Advantage Regularization for Grounded Optimization), an RL framework that constructs mixed-mode rollout groups containing both thinking and non-thinking trajectories. The advantage estimation compares thinking-based answers against same-model non-thinking references, penalizing instances where thinking degrades factual accuracy and rewarding cases where it adds value.
AI.result: MARGO improves factual reliability over strong baselines across multiple factuality-oriented QA benchmarks while preserving general reasoning ability on mathematical benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Thinking-induced hallucination is a systematic failure mode in LRMs. By using non-thinking rollouts as references in RL-based advantage estimation, MARGO effectively suppresses hallucination-prone thinking without sacrificing beneficial reasoning, offering a principled solution for more reliable factuality-oriented QA.

title: Intuitionistic Fuzzy Graph Embedded Random Vector Functional Link with Multiview Learning
summary: Random Vector Functional Link (RVFL) networks are popular due to their fast training and universal approximation capabilities. However, RVFL models face challenges in preserving geometric relationships and utilizing multiple feature views effectively. To address these limitations we propose the Intuitionistic Fuzzy Graph Embedded Random Vector Functional Link with Multiview Learning (IFGRVFL-MV) model. The proposed approach comprises three key components: intuitionistic fuzzy sets for uncertainty handling, graph embedding to capture intrinsic geometric structures, and multiview learning to use complementary information from multiple feature spaces. The model assigns intuitionistic fuzzy membership and non-membership values to data points making it robust to outliers. Also, the graph embedding framework preserves topological structures, increasing the generalization performance. We performed experiments on benchmark datasets from UCI and KEEL repositories which concludes that IFGRVFL-MV outperforms existing models in classification accuracy. Our results establish that IFGRVFL-MV is a promising advancement in the domain of uncertainty and multiview environments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes IFGRVFL-MV, a novel model combining intuitionistic fuzzy sets, graph embedding, and multiview learning within the RVFL framework to improve classification accuracy on benchmark datasets.
AI.motivation: Standard RVFL networks fail to preserve geometric/topological relationships in data and cannot effectively leverage complementary information from multiple feature views. There is also a need for robustness against outliers and uncertainty.
AI.method: IFGRVFL-MV integrates three components: (1) intuitionistic fuzzy sets that assign both membership and non-membership values to handle uncertainty and outliers; (2) graph embedding to capture intrinsic geometric structures of data; (3) multiview learning to exploit complementary information across multiple feature spaces.
AI.result: Experiments on UCI and KEEL benchmark datasets demonstrate that IFGRVFL-MV outperforms existing models in classification accuracy.
AI.conclusion: IFGRVFL-MV represents a promising advancement for classification tasks in environments characterized by uncertainty and multiple feature views.

title: Context-to-Execution Integrity for LLM Agents
summary:
Language-model agents read attacker-writable context to solve tasks. Tool execution needs a separate authority check for protected sink fields, sink-interpreted payloads, and the invocation event. Context-to-Execution Integrity (CXI) is an execution-boundary system for this setting. Policies mark protected sink fields, typed releases carry narrow validated values from writable context to specific destinations, opaque data slots keep evidence as data, and a deterministic gate admits a call only after field authority, exact-effect authorization, and invocation authority all bind to the same action manifest.
  We evaluate CXI on open-weight field-projection runs, AgentDojo live episodes, a code-agent exact-effect benchmark, manifest-bound ledger faults, proposal-pressure controls, and hosted/API compatibility traces. AgentDojo covers 720 live episodes and 1,739 LLM calls; the code-agent benchmark covers 400 repository episodes with exact-effect authorization and lease-bound execution, yielding 231 safe task completions and zero observed field, effect, or invocation escapes. The accounting reports parser outcomes, authorization outcomes, and task-quality outcomes together with the admission-integrity result. Across the evaluated sinks, CXI admits execution only when field, effect, and invocation authority bind to the same action manifest.

AI.tldr: CXI (Context-to-Execution Integrity) is an execution-boundary system for LLM agents that enforces three-way authority binding — field authority, exact-effect authorization, and invocation authority must all align with a single action manifest before any protected sink operation is admitted, preventing unauthorized tool execution from agent-writable context.
AI.motivation: LLM agents read attacker-writable context (e.g., web pages, emails) to perform tool-calling tasks, creating a fundamental security gap: tool execution lacks separate authority checks for protected sink fields, sink-interpreted payloads, and invocation events. An adversary can inject malicious instructions into writable context that the agent reads and executes without proper authorization boundaries.
AI.method: CXI introduces four mechanisms: (1) policies that mark protected sink fields, (2) typed releases that carry narrow validated values from writable context to specific destinations, (3) opaque data slots that preserve evidence as non-interpretable data, and (4) a deterministic gate that admits tool calls only when field authority, exact-effect authorization, and invocation authority all bind to the same action manifest. The system operates at the execution boundary between context-reading and tool invocation.
AI.result: Evaluation across multiple benchmarks: AgentDojo (720 live episodes, 1,739 LLM calls), a code-agent exact-effect benchmark (400 repository episodes with exact-effect authorization and lease-bound execution), manifest-bound ledger fault tests, proposal-pressure controls, and hosted/API compatibility traces. Results: 231 safe task completions with zero observed field, effect, or invocation escapes. The accounting reports capture parser outcomes, authorization outcomes, task-quality outcomes, and admission-integrity results together.
AI.conclusion: CXI demonstrates that binding field authority, effect authority, and invocation authority to a unified action manifest at the execution boundary is both feasible and effective — the system admits execution only under this three-way binding and eliminates all observed escape categories across diverse benchmarks, providing a principled integrity guarantee for LLM-agent tool use.

title: Collaborative Multi-Agent Testing for Emergent Failure Discovery in Autonomous Driving Systems
summary: Autonomous Driving Systems (ADS) can fail because of faults within individual modules as well as from interactions across perception, planning, and control. Yet existing ADS testing research often treats key testing functions, such as perturbation generation, behavioural assessment, and test case selection and exploration, as loosely coupled steps rather than coordinated roles for discovering such failures. We present CREAD, a collaborative multi-agent testing framework for testing ADS that organises perturbation generation, behavioural validation, and search coordination through a shared blackboard and an orchestrator.
