In the current work-in-progress instantiation, the framework focuses on perception-oriented perturbation generation, while remaining extensible to other ADS modules, including planning and control. It currently comprises a Perception Fuzzer Agent, a Metamorphic Validator Agent, and an Orchestrator Agent. Respectively, they generate perturbations, assess behavioural consistency across related scenario pairs, and coordinate further exploration. Experiments in HighwayEnv simulator show that the collaborative configuration improves failure discovery in the highway environment and remains competitive in the roundabout setting. Across the two environments, it yields about 2.1x as many failures per 100 scenarios as the single-agent baseline on average, while gains over a non-collaborative two-agent baseline vary across environments. These results suggest that collaborative multi-agent testing is a promising research direction for emergent ADS behaviour discovery.

AI.tldr: CREAD is a collaborative multi-agent testing framework for Autonomous Driving Systems that uses a shared blackboard and orchestrator to coordinate perturbation generation, behavioural validation, and search, achieving ~2.1x improvement in failure discovery over single-agent baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing ADS testing approaches treat perturbation generation, behavioural assessment, and test case selection as loosely coupled steps rather than coordinated roles, limiting the discovery of emergent failures arising from cross-module interactions among perception, planning, and control.
AI.method: CREAD employs three agents — a Perception Fuzzer Agent for generating perturbations, a Metamorphic Validator Agent for assessing behavioural consistency across related scenario pairs, and an Orchestrator Agent for coordinating exploration — all connected via a shared blackboard architecture. The current implementation focuses on perception-oriented perturbation but is designed to be extensible to planning and control modules.
AI.result: In HighwayEnv simulator experiments, the collaborative configuration yielded approximately 2.1x as many failures per 100 scenarios as the single-agent baseline on average across highway and roundabout environments, though gains over a non-collaborative two-agent baseline varied by environment.
AI.conclusion: Collaborative multi-agent testing is a promising direction for discovering emergent ADS behaviours, with the coordinated approach outperforming isolated single-agent methods.

title: Auto-DSM Under the Lens: A Black-Box Evaluation Framework for LLM-Based DSM Generation
summary: This paper presents a black-box evaluation framework to systematically assess the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate Design Structure Matrices (DSMs) from structured technical documentation. Motivated by the closed-source nature of current Auto-DSM pipelines, the framework introduces a reproducible methodology that benchmarks generated DSMs (GEN-DSMs) against manually validated ground-truth matrices (GT-DSMs). The evaluation integrates both single-run and multi-run perspectives, combining structural metrics (Completeness, Correctness, Coupling Density), classification metrics (Selective Accuracy, Abstention Coverage), and stability measures (Entropy, Fleiss' $κ$). To synthesize these aspects, a Composite Quality Score (Q) is proposed. Controlled experiments are conducted on two datasets: a fictive abstract system and a real-world refrigerator decomposition, covering variations in phrasing, parameter-dataset alignment, and system complexity. Results show that LLMs can produce structurally plausible DSMs and achieve high reproducibility under well-structured inputs, but remain sensitive to ambiguity, inconsistent dependency definitions, and prompt formulation. The findings highlight systematic sources of hallucination and abstention failure, demonstrating both the potential and current limitations of LLM-driven DSM automation. The proposed framework provides a transparent benchmark for auditing Auto-DSM pipelines and establishes foundations for integrating LLM-based decomposition methods into model-based systems engineering (MBSE) workflows.

AI.tldr: A black-box evaluation framework benchmarks LLM-generated Design Structure Matrices (DSMs) against ground-truth matrices using structural, classification, and stability metrics, combined into a Composite Quality Score. Experiments on fictive and real-world datasets reveal LLMs produce plausible DSMs under well-structured inputs but suffer from ambiguity, hallucination, and prompt sensitivity.
AI.motivation: Current Auto-DSM pipelines are predominantly closed-source, making it difficult to audit their reliability, reproducibility, and failure modes. A transparent, reproducible benchmarking framework is needed to systematically assess LLM capabilities and limitations in generating DSMs from structured technical documentation.
AI.method: The authors propose a black-box evaluation framework that compares generated DSMs (GEN-DSMs) against manually validated ground-truth DSMs (GT-DSMs). It employs three families of metrics: (1) structural metrics (Completeness, Correctness, Coupling Density), (2) classification metrics (Selective Accuracy, Abstention Coverage), and (3) stability measures (Entropy, Fleiss' κ), all synthesized into a Composite Quality Score (Q). Controlled experiments span two datasets — a fictive abstract system and a real-world refrigerator decomposition — with variations in phrasing, parameter-dataset alignment, and system complexity.
AI.result: LLMs can generate structurally plausible DSMs with high reproducibility when inputs are well-structured. However, performance degrades under ambiguous phrasing, inconsistent dependency definitions, and suboptimal prompt formulation. Systematic sources of hallucination and abstention failure were identified, exposing current limitations in LLM-driven DSM automation.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a transparent, reproducible benchmark for auditing Auto-DSM pipelines and establishes foundational principles for integrating LLM-based decomposition into model-based systems engineering (MBSE) workflows. LLMs show promise but require careful handling of ambiguity and prompt engineering to be reliable in practice.

title: Is Domain Adaptation Always Helpful? A Frozen-Backbone Study of Cross-Domain Sentiment Transfer
summary: Sentiment analysis with frozen pre-trained language model (PLM) backbones has become a common paradigm, yet the practical benefit of explicit domain adaptation remains unclear, particularly when backbones encode varying degrees of target-domain knowledge. We present a preliminary case study evaluating a controlled family of frozen embedding backbones (Qwen3-Embedding 0.6B, 4B, 8B), alongside RoBERTa-base and FinBERT. We train a lightweight MLP adapter on consumer reviews using Domain-Adversarial Neural Networks (DANN), Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), and Supervised Contrastive Learning (SCL), and evaluate transfer to movie reviews (SST-2) and a heavily restricted subset of financial news (Financial PhraseBank). Within this constrained sample, we observe two distinct transfer patterns. On SST-2, domain adaptation provides negligible gain regardless of scale. On the financial subset, explicit domain adaptation appears to recover substantial performance for small general-purpose backbones. Notably, we find that adversarial alignment (DANN) is associated with degraded performance for domain-specialized backbones like FinBERT, consistent with erosion of pre-existing domain-specific structure, whereas supervised contrastive loss appears to preserve it. These preliminary findings suggest that the efficacy of explicit domain adaptation is highly contingent on whether the frozen backbone already possesses target-domain coverage.

AI.tldr: A case study evaluating domain adaptation techniques (DANN, MMD, SCL) on frozen PLM backbones of varying scales and domain specialization reveals that adaptation benefits depend critically on whether the backbone already encodes target-domain knowledge. Gains are negligible for in-domain transfers (SST-2) but substantial for out-of-domain financial text when using small general-purpose models. Adversarial alignment (DANN) degrades domain-specialized backbones like FinBERT, while supervised contrastive loss preserves domain-specific structure.
AI.motivation: Despite sentiment analysis commonly using frozen PLM backbones, the practical benefit of explicit domain adaptation remains unclear — particularly when backbones vary in scale and pre-existing target-domain knowledge. The authors aim to systematically probe when and for which backbones domain adaptation techniques actually help.
AI.method: A controlled family of frozen embedding backbones (Qwen3-Embedding at 0.6B, 4B, 8B scales, plus RoBERTa-base and FinBERT) is evaluated with a lightweight MLP adapter trained on consumer reviews. Three domain adaptation techniques are compared: Domain-Adversarial Neural Networks (DANN), Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), and Supervised Contrastive Learning (SCL). Transfer is evaluated on SST-2 (movie reviews) and a restricted subset of Financial PhraseBank (financial news).
AI.result: Two distinct transfer patterns emerge: (1) On SST-2, domain adaptation provides negligible gain regardless of backbone scale. (2) On the financial subset, explicit domain adaptation substantially recovers performance for small general-purpose backbones. DANN degrades performance for domain-specialized backbones like FinBERT (consistent with erosion of pre-existing domain-specific structure), whereas supervised contrastive loss preserves it.
AI.conclusion: The efficacy of explicit domain adaptation is highly contingent on whether the frozen backbone already possesses target-domain coverage. Domain adaptation is most beneficial when the backbone lacks target-domain knowledge and the target domain is sufficiently distinct from the source domain.

title: Domain-Adaptive Climate Downscaling Under Temporal Distribution Shift
summary: Deep-learning-based climate downscaling aims to learn relationships from historical low-resolution (LR) and high-resolution (HR) climate data to generate HR climate projections. However, this setting faces a temporal out-of-distribution (OOD) challenge: models trained on historical data are commonly applied to future projections whose distributions may differ substantially from the training period. This study investigates temporal OOD shift for daily temperature downscaling over the Continental United States using paired LR-HR model simulations. We propose a temporal domain-adaptive downscaling framework that combines supervised HR reconstruction on historical data with domain alignment between historical and future climate distributions. Experiments across future validation periods show that the proposed domain-adaptive model consistently outperforms statistical and deep-learning-based bias-correction methods, with the largest gains occurring when the temporal distribution shift is strongest. Spatial analyses indicate stronger improvements over high-elevation and topographically complex regions, along with higher spatiotemporal correlation with the HR target. The extreme analysis shows that domain adaptation also reduces upper-tail temperature bias relative to the non-adaptive model. These results demonstrate that temporal domain adaptation can improve the robustness of HR climate projections under non-stationary climate conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a temporal domain-adaptive deep-learning framework for climate downscaling that addresses the temporal out-of-distribution (OOD) problem — where models trained on historical data degrade when applied to future climate projections with different distributions. The method combines supervised HR reconstruction with domain alignment between historical and future distributions, demonstrating consistent improvements over conventional bias-correction methods, especially in topographically complex regions and under strong distribution shifts.
AI.motivation: Deep-learning-based climate downscaling models trained on historical data face a critical temporal out-of-distribution (OOD) challenge: future climate projections may exhibit substantially different distributions from the training period, causing model degradation. Addressing this distribution shift is essential for generating robust high-resolution climate projections under non-stationary climate conditions.
AI.method: A temporal domain-adaptive downscaling framework that jointly optimizes two objectives: (1) supervised high-resolution reconstruction using paired historical low-resolution (LR) and high-resolution (HR) climate data, and (2) unsupervised domain alignment between historical and future climate feature distributions. The framework is evaluated on daily temperature downscaling over the Continental United States using paired LR-HR model simulations, with experiments across multiple future validation periods experiencing varying degrees of distribution shift.
AI.result: The domain-adaptive model consistently outperforms both statistical and deep-learning-based bias-correction methods across all future validation periods. The largest performance gains occur when temporal distribution shift is strongest. Spatial analyses reveal stronger improvements over high-elevation and topographically complex regions, along with enhanced spatiotemporal correlation with the HR target. Extreme value analysis shows that domain adaptation reduces upper-tail temperature bias compared to the non-adaptive baseline.
AI.conclusion: Temporal domain adaptation significantly improves the robustness of deep-learning-based climate downscaling under non-stationary climate conditions, demonstrating its value for producing more reliable high-resolution climate projections, particularly for future periods and regions where distribution shifts are most pronounced.

title: Multi-Channel Spread-Spectrum Code Watermarking
summary: Attributing code to the large language model that produced it is essential for provenance, licensing, and misuse accountability, yet no deployed watermark meets this need. Generation-time schemes require access to the producing model and cannot be applied to third-party code, while post-hoc schemes work on any code but carry at most 4 bits of payload, far too few to distinguish the many deployed model configurations. We present multi-channel spread-spectrum watermarking, the first post-hoc, training-free code watermark with a 24-bit payload and formal robustness guarantees. The scheme encodes bits in variable naming conventions and in eight pairs of semantically equivalent code patterns, and a keyed pseudo-random permutation maps every site to a codeword bit so that each bit receives multiple independent votes. Majority voting absorbs distributed corruption, while an outer Reed-Solomon code recovers the identifier when concentrated channel attacks defeat the vote, yielding provable robustness bounds for formatting, syntactic, and structural attacks. Across 1,750 Python files from CodeNet and from GPT-4.1 and Llama-4 generations, the watermark achieves 100% clean-detection accuracy with zero false positives. Under 17 attack types, it recovers the identifier at 97.6% accuracy under 8 variable renames and 94.1% under 10% random per-site corruption, while the strongest post-hoc baseline collapses to 0% under any single-transform attack. Embedding and detection together take under 200 ms on CPU without training data or GPU.

AI.tldr: A post-hoc, training-free code watermarking method using multi-channel spread-spectrum techniques achieves 24-bit payload capacity with formal robustness guarantees, enabling attribution of code to specific LLM configurations across diverse attack types.
AI.motivation: Existing code watermarking schemes are inadequate: generation-time methods require model access and cannot apply to third-party code, while post-hoc methods are limited to ~4-bit payloads—insufficient to uniquely identify the many deployed LLM configurations. A high-capacity, universally applicable watermark is needed for provenance, licensing, and accountability.
AI.method: Multi-channel spread-spectrum watermarking encodes 24 bits across two channels: (1) variable naming conventions and (2) eight pairs of semantically equivalent code patterns. A keyed pseudo-random permutation maps each site to a codeword bit, providing multiple independent votes per bit. Majority voting absorbs distributed corruption, while an outer Reed-Solomon error-correcting code recovers the identifier under concentrated channel attacks. This yields provable robustness bounds against formatting, syntactic, and structural attacks.
AI.result: Evaluated on 1,750 Python files (CodeNet + GPT-4.1 + Llama-4), the watermark achieves 100% clean-detection accuracy with zero false positives. Under 17 attack types, it recovers identifiers at 97.6% accuracy under 8 variable renames and 94.1% under 10% random per-site corruption, while the strongest post-hoc baseline collapses to 0% under any single-transform attack. Embedding and detection combined run under 200 ms on CPU with no training data or GPU required.
AI.conclusion: The proposed scheme is the first post-hoc code watermark to deliver both high payload (24-bit) and formal robustness guarantees, enabling practical attribution of code to specific LLM configurations without model access, training data, or GPU resources.

title: AgoraSim: A Hybrid Agent-Based Modeling Framework
summary: LLM-agent simulations make natural-language social scenarios easy to instantiate, but their outputs can be overread as predictions and are often difficult to compare with explicit social dynamics. We present AgoraSim, a hybrid agent-based modeling framework for scenario-oriented social reaction analysis. AgoraSim resolves textual or multimodal artifacts into editable ABM configurations, runs ratio-controlled populations that mix LLM, vision-language, custom-endpoint, random, and classical agents, and compares the same scenario against matched classical reference dynamics. All agents emit a shared structured decision object, enabling common action spaces, interaction protocols, metrics, and audit records. Exposed through a local UI, Python SDK/CLI, and REST API, AgoraSim helps users inspect scenario trajectories, compare modeling assumptions, and identify cases that warrant empirical validation.

AI.tldr: AgoraSim is a hybrid agent-based modeling framework that integrates LLM, vision-language, and classical agents into ratio-controlled populations for scenario-oriented social reaction analysis, with structured decision outputs enabling consistent comparison against classical reference dynamics.
AI.motivation: LLM-agent simulations produce naturalistic social scenarios easily, but their outputs risk being over-interpreted as predictions and lack comparability with explicit social dynamics models. There is a need for a framework that bridges the gap between rich LLM-based simulation and the rigor of classical agent-based modeling.
AI.method: AgoraSim resolves textual or multimodal artifacts into editable ABM configurations. It supports ratio-controlled populations mixing LLM, vision-language, custom-endpoint, random, and classical agents. All agents emit a shared structured decision object, establishing common action spaces, interaction protocols, metrics, and audit records. The system exposes a local UI, Python SDK/CLI, and REST API.
AI.result: The framework enables users to inspect scenario trajectories, compare modeling assumptions across agent types, and identify cases warranting empirical validation. It provides a structured basis for comparing LLM-driven social simulations against matched classical reference dynamics.
AI.conclusion: AgoraSim provides a principled hybrid simulation environment that combines the expressiveness of LLM-based agents with the comparability and rigor of classical ABMs, making social simulation outputs more auditable and empirically grounded.

title: Umm... With Transformers? Insights from Filled Pause Use across Four Slavic Parliaments
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure. Accepted at InterSpeech 2026. Code published: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20766877
summary: Filled pauses (FPs) are a universal feature of spontaneous speech, yet most studies rely on small, single-language corpora, limiting the generalisability of their findings. We analyse ~4,000 hours of parliamentary speech across four related Slavic languages (Croatian, Czech, Polish, Serbian). FP occurrence is obtained via transformer-based automatic detection, while FP rate is modelled using Generalised Estimating Equations (GEE) with Mundlak correction to distinguish within- from between- speaker effects. We replicate a negative association of age and speech rate with FP rate, but find that gender effects are language-specific and directionally opposite to most prior literature. Novel analyses of sentiment, political orientation, and power status reveal a consistent positive association between sentiment and FP rate, alongside parliament-specific modulation by orientation and power status, with opposition speakers tending toward lower FP rates than governing coalition speakers.

AI.tldr: Analysis of ~4,000 hours of parliamentary speech across four Slavic languages (Croatian, Czech, Polish, Serbian) using transformer-based FP detection and GEE modeling reveals that age and speech rate negatively associate with filled pauses, gender effects are language-specific, and sentiment, political orientation, and power status significantly modulate FP rate — with opposition speakers showing fewer FPs than governing coalition members.
AI.motivation: Most filled pause research relies on small, single-language corpora, severely limiting the generalisability of findings across languages and contexts. The authors aim to overcome this by leveraging large-scale, cross-linguistic spontaneous speech data from comparable settings.
AI.method: (1) Corpus: ~4,000 hours of parliamentary speech from Croatian, Czech, Polish, and Serbian. (2) FP detection: Transformer-based automatic identification of filled pauses. (3) Statistical modeling: Generalised Estimating Equations (GEE) with Mundlak correction to disentangle within-speaker and between-speaker effects on FP rate.
AI.result: (1) Age and speech rate negatively associated with FP rate, replicating prior findings. (2) Gender effects were language-specific and directionally opposite to most previous literature. (3) Sentiment showed a consistent positive association with FP rate across languages. (4) Political orientation and power status modulated FP rate: opposition speakers tended toward lower FP rates than governing coalition speakers.
AI.conclusion: Filled pause production is shaped not only by well-established cognitive and demographic factors but also by sociolinguistic and political-contextual variables. Cross-linguistic, large-scale analysis reveals both universal patterns and language-specific effects, underscoring the need to move beyond small, monolingual corpora in disfluency research.

title: Orthogonal Dendritic Intrinsic Networks: An Architecture for Significance-Ordered, Orthogonal Latent Spaces
summary: Principal Component Analysis or PCA-like properties (orthogonality, variance ranking) are seldom realized in deep autoencoder architectures. In this work, we present ODIN (Orthogonal Dendritic Intrinsic Network), a novel autoencoder architecture that recovers PCA-like latent structure in a fully non-linear regime. By incorporating a set of geometric constraints directly into the training objective, ODIN encourages latent dimensions to be mutually orthogonal and ordered by explained variance, mirroring the interpretable decomposition of PCA while retaining the expressive power of deep networks. We provide theoretical grounding for these constraints and demonstrate their compatibility with standard encoder-decoder frameworks. We also establish empirical results for both synthetic and real world datasets, establishing a principled path toward interpretable, structured feature learning and dimensionality reduction.

AI.tldr: ODIN is a deep autoencoder architecture that recovers PCA-like properties (orthogonal, variance-ranked latent dimensions) in a fully non-linear setting by incorporating geometric constraints into the training objective, offering interpretable structured feature learning.
AI.motivation: Principal Component Analysis provides interpretable latent structure (orthogonality, variance ranking) but is limited to linear transformations. Deep autoencoders offer expressive non-linear representational power but sacrifice PCA's desirable structural properties. The authors aim to bridge this gap—achieving the best of both worlds.
AI.method: The authors propose ODIN (Orthogonal Dendritic Intrinsic Network), which imposes geometric constraints directly in the training objective to enforce: (1) mutual orthogonality of latent dimensions, and (2) ordering of latent dimensions by explained variance. These constraints are theoretically grounded and compatible with standard encoder-decoder architectures.
AI.result: Empirical results on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that ODIN successfully recovers PCA-like latent structure (orthogonal, variance-sorted dimensions) while maintaining the expressive, non-linear representational capacity of deep networks.
AI.conclusion: ODIN establishes a principled path toward interpretable, structured feature learning and dimensionality reduction, combining the interpretability of PCA with the power of deep non-linear autoencoders.

title: REAN: Reconstruction-aware ECG Anonymization Based on Privacy--Utility Orthogonality
summary: A shared electrocardiogram (ECG) is itself a biometric fingerprint that can re-identify a patient and reveal personal information. Recent ECG anonymizers transform the signal before sharing to reduce privacy leakage. However, existing methods still face a privacy--utility trade-off, in which preserving privacy often compromises utility while preserving utility reveals personal information. We propose \emph{REAN} (\emph{RE}construction-aware ECG \emph{AN}onymizer), a raw ECG signal anonymizer, to address this privacy--utility trade-off. REAN reconstructs the signal using a 1-D U-Net trained with losses from frozen privacy and utility classifiers to reduce privacy leakage while preserving utility. The privacy and utility gradients are near-orthogonal ($\approx$93.8$^\circ$), so reducing privacy leakage leaves utility almost unchanged. On four public PhysioNet databases, REAN achieves the strongest privacy--utility balance among raw ECG signal baselines. It drives re-identification to chance (0.96$\to$0.00), keeps arrhythmia macro-AUROC at the clean level (Clean 0.9982 vs.\ REAN 0.9991), and maintains re-identification protection under unseen privacy-classifier architectures.

AI.tldr: REAN is a raw ECG anonymizer that uses a 1-D U-Net trained with frozen privacy and utility classifiers to reconstruct ECG signals. It exploits near-orthogonal privacy/utility gradients (~93.8°) to reduce re-identification risk to chance while preserving arrhythmia classification performance, achieving state-of-the-art privacy–utility balance across four PhysioNet databases.
AI.motivation: Shared ECG signals act as biometric fingerprints, enabling patient re-identification and revealing personal information. Existing anonymization methods suffer from a privacy–utility trade-off: improving privacy degrades clinical utility and vice versa. The authors aim to break this trade-off.
AI.method: REAN employs a 1-D U-Net reconstruction architecture trained with loss signals from two frozen pre-trained classifiers — a privacy classifier (for re-identification) and a utility classifier (for arrhythmia detection). The key insight is that the gradients from these two classifiers are nearly orthogonal (~93.8°), meaning minimizing privacy leakage has negligible impact on utility preservation. The U-Net learns to transform raw ECG signals accordingly.
AI.result: On four PhysioNet databases, REAN drives re-identification accuracy from 0.96 to 0.00 (chance level), maintains arrhythmia macro-AUROC at 0.9991 versus 0.9982 for clean signals, and generalizes privacy protection to unseen classifier architectures.
AI.conclusion: REAN achieves the strongest privacy–utility balance among raw ECG anonymization baselines, effectively eliminating re-identification risk without sacrificing clinical diagnostic utility, thanks to the near-orthogonality of privacy and utility gradients.

title: Static Metrics Are Insufficient: Predicting Java Method Energy Usage with Execution Time
comment: Accepted for publication at the 19th International Conference on the Quality of Information and Communications Technology (QUATIC 2026)
summary: The increasing energy demand of software systems is raising concerns about their environmental impact and associated costs. Reasoning on energy usage early in the development flow has the potential to significantly reduce the overall energy usage of a software system, as it allows developers to make informed design and refactoring decisions before inefficiencies propagate. However, assessing energy usage without repeated profiling and direct measurement is difficult, which limits early reasoning in practice. This study investigates the limits of method-level energy prediction in Java, examining whether static source code metrics complemented with method-level execution time can estimate the energy consumption of Java methods. We profile 2,786 Java methods to extract 33 static features and measure execution time and energy, then train and compare eleven regression models. Our findings show that static source code metrics alone yield poor predictive performance, with average R2 values close to zero. Incorporating execution time as a lightweight dynamic input significantly improves accuracy, raising R2 to as high as 0.46. Execution time, internal method calls, and cyclomatic complexity consistently emerge as the strongest predictors of energy consumption.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates whether static source code metrics, combined with execution time, can predict method-level energy consumption in Java. Using 2,786 profiled methods and eleven regression models, results show static metrics alone perform poorly (R² ≈ 0), but adding execution time as a lightweight dynamic feature raises predictive accuracy to R² = 0.46. Execution time, internal method calls, and cyclomatic complexity are the strongest predictors.
AI.motivation: Rising energy demands of software systems create environmental and cost concerns. Early reasoning about energy consumption during development could enable informed design/refactoring decisions, but current approaches require repeated profiling and direct measurement, which is cumbersome and limits practical adoption in early development stages.
AI.method: The authors profiled 2,786 Java methods, extracting 33 static source code metrics along with execution time and energy measurements. They trained and compared eleven regression models to assess predictive performance, evaluating static metrics alone versus static metrics augmented with execution time as a lightweight dynamic feature.
AI.result: Static source code metrics alone yield near-zero predictive performance (average R² ≈ 0). Incorporating execution time dramatically improves accuracy to R² = 0.46. The top three predictors consistently identified are execution time, internal method calls, and cyclomatic complexity.
AI.conclusion: Early-stage energy prediction using purely static metrics is insufficient; however, adding lightweight dynamic data like execution time makes method-level energy estimation feasible. This suggests a practical middle ground between costly full profiling and ineffective static-only analysis for guiding energy-aware software development decisions.

title: Poster: Mind the Gap -- Characterizing the Temporal Blind Spot Between GSB and DNS Resolution
comment: To appear in the proceedings of the 23rd Conference on Detection of Intrusions and Malware & Vulnerability Assessment (DIMVA '26)
summary: Google Safe Browsing (GSB) and DNS resolution operate concurrently during browser navigation, yet their packet-level synchronization remains understudied. This work characterizes the timing gap (\(Δ_{time}\)) between GSB-related query close events and parallel DNS resolution responses, identifying a consistent temporal offset with potential security relevance. Using packet-capture analysis across general and CNAME-domain datasets, we observe positive timing gaps in approximately 79\% of measurements. In these instances, DNS responses lag behind GSB-related query closures with median delays of 67-79 ms and maximum delays surpassing 2,400 ms. These empirical results highlight a measurable window within the browsing workflow. We suggest that such temporal inconsistencies, particularly in complex CNAME-domain resolutions, may create a security-relevant timing precondition under DNS-manipulation threat models. These results provide a foundation for further research into timing-based risks and mitigations in browser safety mechanisms.

AI.tldr: Characterizes the timing gap between Google Safe Browsing query closures and parallel DNS resolution responses during browser navigation, finding DNS lags behind GSB in ~79% of cases with median delays of 67–79 ms and maximums exceeding 2,400 ms, suggesting a potentially exploitable security window.
AI.motivation: Although Google Safe Browsing and DNS resolution operate concurrently during browser navigation, their packet-level synchronization remains understudied. The authors aim to quantify the temporal relationship between these two parallel processes to identify any security-relevant timing conditions.
AI.method: Packet-capture analysis measuring the timing gap (Δtime) between GSB-related query close events and parallel DNS resolution responses, conducted across both general and CNAME-domain datasets.
AI.result: Positive timing gaps observed in ~79% of measurements, where DNS responses lag behind GSB query closures with median delays of 67–79 ms and maximum delays exceeding 2,400 ms. The effect is particularly pronounced in complex CNAME-domain resolutions.
AI.conclusion: The identified temporal inconsistency creates a measurable, security-relevant timing precondition under DNS-manipulation threat models. Findings provide a foundation for further research into timing-based risks and mitigations in browser safety mechanisms.

title: Evaluating Fine-Tuning and Metrics for Neural Decompilation of Dart AOT Binaries
comment: Under review at ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology (TOSEM)
summary: Neural decompilation is increasingly studied as a code-generation problem, yet its evaluation methodology remains underdeveloped for modern languages. We present a systematic empirical study of fine-tuning effectiveness and metric validity for Dart Ahead-of-Time (AOT) neural decompilation. We evaluate six fine-tuned model variants across three base architectures (4B-8B parameters) using three metrics: CodeBLEU, compile@k, and pass@k on a new 154-task HumanEval-Dart benchmark. Our study yields three principal findings grounded in paired task-level statistical tests. First, no fine-tuning configuration produces a statistically significant pass@k improvement. The sole positive case yields +0.71 pp (McNemar p=0.21), while fine-tuning the strongest base (Qwen3-8B) causes a highly significant regression of -5.65 pp (p<0.001). This capacity-dependent trend is consistent across architectures but needs broader scale sweeps. Second, cross-lingual interference from Swift training is highly significant at 4B (-2.66 pp, p<0.001) but statistically indistinguishable from zero at 8B, consistent with the scaling hypothesis. Third, we demonstrate metric divergence: CodeBLEU and compile@k can improve significantly while pass@k moves in the opposite direction. This has implications for any LLM code generation task where fine-tuning targets superficial similarity. Error analysis reveals assembly sequence length is the strongest predictor of task difficulty (p=0.001), with a capability cliff at 200 instructions. We contribute the HumanEval-Dart benchmark, a Dart-adapted CodeBLEU, and empirical evidence that pass@k must be the primary evaluation metric for neural decompilation.

AI.tldr: An empirical study on fine-tuning LLMs for Dart AOT neural decompilation reveals that fine-tuning produces no statistically significant pass@k improvement and can even cause regression in stronger models. The paper demonstrates metric divergence (CodeBLEU/compile@k vs. pass@k), identifies cross-lingual interference from Swift training, and finds assembly sequence length as the strongest predictor of task difficulty with a capability cliff at 200 instructions.
AI.motivation: Neural decompilation is increasingly framed as a code-generation problem, but evaluation methodology remains underdeveloped—particularly for modern languages like Dart. Existing metrics (CodeBLEU, compile@k) may not align with functional correctness (pass@k), and fine-tuning strategies lack rigorous statistical validation.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune six model variants across three base architectures (4B–8B parameters: CodeGemma, CodeQwen, Qwen3) and evaluate on a newly constructed 154-task HumanEval-Dart benchmark. Three metrics are compared: CodeBLEU, compile@k, and pass@k. Paired task-level statistical tests (McNemar) are used throughout. Error analysis examines predictors of task difficulty including assembly sequence length.
AI.result: (1) No fine-tuning configuration yields statistically significant pass@k improvement; the best case is +0.71 pp (p=0.21), while fine-tuning Qwen3-8B causes a significant -5.65 pp regression (p<0.001). (2) Cross-lingual interference from Swift training is significant at 4B (-2.66 pp, p<0.001) but negligible at 8B. (3) CodeBLEU and compile@k can significantly improve while pass@k worsens, demonstrating metric invalidity. Assembly sequence length is the strongest difficulty predictor (p=0.001) with a cliff at 200 instructions.
AI.conclusion: Pass@k must be the primary evaluation metric for neural decompilation. Fine-tuning offers no reliable gains and can harm stronger models. The paper contributes HumanEval-Dart, a Dart-adapted CodeBLEU, and empirical grounding for evaluation standards in the field.

title: PolyWorkBench: Benchmarking Multilingual Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have shown strong performance in long-horizon tasks that require planning, tool use, and interaction with external environments. However, most existing benchmarks implicitly assume a monolingual setting, where the entire execution process, including reasoning, tool invocation, and output generation, is conducted within a single language. In contrast, real-world applications often involve multilingual inputs and outputs within a unified workflow, yet the interaction between multilinguality and agentic execution remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce PolyWorkBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on multilingual long-horizon workplace workflows. PolyWorkBench consists of 67 tasks across five domains, including commerce, knowledge work, legal analysis, localization, and manufacturing, where agents must process heterogeneous multilingual inputs, perform iterative reasoning, invoke external tools, and produce structured outputs. To enable comprehensive evaluation, we propose a hybrid framework that combines structural grading, executable verification, and LLM-based semantic assessment. This design allows us to capture both functional correctness and linguistic consistency across complex workflows. Empirical results show that state-of-the-art LLM agents suffer significant performance degradation in multilingual workflow settings compared to monolingual counterparts. Our analysis suggests that multilinguality introduces compounding effects across reasoning and execution steps, highlighting the importance of jointly modeling language variation and procedural decision-making in agent evaluation.

AI.tldr: PolyWorkBench is a new benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on multilingual, long-horizon workplace workflows across five domains. Results reveal that state-of-the-art agents degrade significantly in multilingual settings due to compounding effects across reasoning and execution steps.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent benchmarks assume monolingual execution, but real-world workflows frequently involve multilingual inputs and outputs. The interaction between multilinguality and agentic execution remains underexplored, creating a gap between benchmark evaluation and practical deployment.
AI.method: The authors introduce PolyWorkBench, comprising 67 tasks across five domains (commerce, knowledge work, legal analysis, localization, manufacturing). Agents must process heterogeneous multilingual inputs, perform iterative reasoning, invoke tools, and produce structured outputs. A hybrid evaluation framework combines structural grading, executable verification, and LLM-based semantic assessment to capture both functional correctness and linguistic consistency.
AI.result: State-of-the-art LLM agents exhibit significant performance degradation in multilingual workflow settings compared to monolingual counterparts. The degradation stems from compounding effects where language variation impacts both reasoning quality and execution accuracy across multiple steps.
AI.conclusion: Multilinguality introduces compounding effects across reasoning and execution steps in agentic workflows. This highlights the need to jointly model language variation and procedural decision-making in future agent evaluation and development.

title: MemDefrag: Latent Memory Defragmentation for Large Language Models
summary: Latent memory, which stores past knowledge fragments as per-layer hidden states, has emerged as a promising paradigm (e.g., MemoryLLM and M+) for long-term memory in large language models (LLMs). However, the paradigm suffers from significant performance degradation during memory updates, due to positional encoding misalignment and the absence of any tracing mechanism to distinguish target memory fragments from irrelevant ones. To discover such a tracing mechanism, we probe the layer-wise attention density over stored memory fragments, and find that a small set of middle transformer layers consistently concentrates the highest density on the target fragment - exposing an inherent tracing signal. In light of this, we propose MemDefrag, a training-free and model-agnostic framework that (1) uses a middle-layer tracing signal to conduct memory defragmentation (rank, reorder, and filter memories), and (2) applies an informativeness-guided proportional forgetting mechanism once capacity is exceeded. Experiments show that MemDefrag substantially outperforms MemoryLLM and M+ on knowledge retention (e.g., 43.0% vs. 17.4%/17.6% after 50 memory updates) and long-context benchmarks, and generalizes well across various LLMs and latent-memory variants.

AI.tldr: MemDefrag is a training-free framework that leverages middle-layer attention density as a tracing signal to defragment and manage latent memory in LLMs, significantly improving knowledge retention and long-context performance over MemoryLLM and M+.
AI.motivation: Latent memory paradigms (e.g., MemoryLLM, M+) suffer severe performance degradation during memory updates due to positional encoding misalignment and the lack of a mechanism to distinguish relevant memory fragments from irrelevant ones. The authors seek to discover an inherent tracing signal within LLMs to address this.
AI.method: The authors probe layer-wise attention density and identify that middle transformer layers consistently concentrate highest attention on target memory fragments, revealing an inherent tracing signal. MemDefrag uses this signal to defragment memory (rank, reorder, filter) and employs informativeness-guided proportional forgetting when memory capacity is exceeded. The method is training-free and model-agnostic.
AI.result: MemDefrag substantially outperforms MemoryLLM and M+ on knowledge retention (43.0% vs. 17.4%/17.6% after 50 memory updates) and long-context benchmarks, while generalizing across diverse LLMs and latent-memory variants.
AI.conclusion: Middle-layer attention density provides an effective, intrinsic tracing signal for latent memory management, enabling MemDefrag to achieve significant improvements in memory update stability and long-context performance without requiring any training.

title: LLM-Driven Neural Network Generation with Same-Family Architecture Guidance: Disentangling Transfer and Adaptation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate neural-network modifications, but unrestricted generation is often invalid or harmful. This paper studies a narrower setting: improving a weak target model using a stronger same-family source model from a neural-network database. We propose a source-guided candidate-generation protocol with non-source controls, source-conditioned candidates, and a no-LLM hp_copy ablation under equal evaluation budgets. The protocol reports validity separately from accuracy and selects the best valid candidate only when it improves the target. On CIFAR-10, the strongest source-guided candidate reaches 0.5049 accuracy versus 0.2398 for the best non-source candidate, a +0.2651 advantage, while improving a weak target originally at 0.1254; a five-epoch check preserves the gain at 0.7686 versus 0.4839. On SVHN AlexNet with DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B, source-guided transfer reaches 0.7880 versus 0.2254, a +0.5626 advantage; a fresh repeat reaches 0.8069 versus 0.2509, a +0.5560 advantage. Direct source-recipe copy produces 0.1959 on SVHN AlexNet, matching the original target, while hp_transfer reaches 0.7880, showing that the LLM adapts rather than copies the source recipe. Family-level analysis shows the clearest positive signals for AlexNet, with 6/8 wins across SVHN, Imagenette, and CelebA-Gender, and alt_nn1, with 8/10 wins on CIFAR-10.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a controlled, source-guided protocol for using LLMs to generate neural-network modifications, where a stronger same-family source model guides improvements to a weak target model. On CIFAR-10 and SVHN benchmarks, source-guided candidates substantially outperform non-source candidates, and the LLM demonstrably adapts rather than copies source recipes. Family-level analysis reveals architecture-dependent effectiveness, with AlexNet and alt_nn1 showing the strongest positive signals.
AI.motivation: Unrestricted LLM-generated neural-network modifications are often invalid or harmful. The authors address this by studying a narrower, more controlled setting: leveraging a stronger source model from the same architectural family within a neural-network database to guide improvements to a weaker target model.
AI.method: The authors propose a source-guided candidate-generation protocol with: (1) non-source controls (candidates generated without source guidance), (2) source-conditioned candidates, and (3) a no-LLM hp_copy ablation (direct hyperparameter copy from source). All methods operate under equal evaluation budgets. The protocol separately reports validity and accuracy, and selects the best valid candidate only when it improves the target. Experiments use CIFAR-10 and SVHN (with AlexNet and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B), plus Imagenette and CelebA-Gender for family-level analysis.
AI.result: On CIFAR-10, the best source-guided candidate achieves 0.5049 accuracy vs. 0.2398 for non-source (a +0.2651 advantage), improving a target at 0.1254. A five-epoch check preserves gains (0.7686 vs. 0.4839). On SVHN AlexNet with DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B, source-guided transfer reaches 0.7880 vs. 0.2254 (+0.5626); a repeat yields 0.8069 vs. 0.2509 (+0.5560). Direct source-recipe copy yields only 0.1959 on SVHN AlexNet (matching the original target), while hp_transfer reaches 0.7880, confirming LLM adaptation rather than copying. Family-level analysis shows AlexNet with 6/8 wins across SVHN, Imagenette, and CelebA-Gender, and alt_nn1 with 8/10 wins on CIFAR-10.
AI.conclusion: Source-guided LLM candidate generation effectively improves weak target models when a stronger same-family source is available, with the LLM adapting rather than merely copying source recipes. Effectiveness varies by architecture family, with AlexNet and alt_nn1 showing the most consistent gains across benchmarks.

title: The Masks We (Think We) Wear: Privacy Threats of Browser-Extension Wallets in the Web3 Ecosystem
comment: Accepted at Proceedings on Privacy Enhancing Technologies (PoPETs) 2026
summary:
Cryptocurrency wallets are the primary interface for managing pseudonymous blockchain addresses, viewing balances, and interacting with Web3 applications. Although users typically assume that their addresses remain independent of each other unless intentionally revealed, modern wallets routinely communicate with both blockchain infrastructure and decentralized applications (dApps), generating network-side and web-side signals that may undermine this assumption.
  In this paper, we identify and formalize five privacy threats that arise directly from wallets interacting with the network and the web browser. Using large-scale dynamic measurements of 85 of the most popular Chrome Web Store browser-extension wallets (representing 35.16 million users), we observe that routine remote procedure call (RPC) operations leak structural links between a user's addresses; that the majority of Ethereum wallets implement permission revocation inconsistently and continue to expose previously revoked addresses across sessions; and that many wallets inject their provider interfaces into cross-origin iframes, enabling passive cross-site tracking beyond dApps and potentially real-world identity deanonymization without user interaction.
  Taken together, our results show that these wallet behaviors leak sensitive information that can be used to link multiple addresses to the same user, track wallet users across sessions and sites, and connect their browsing activity to their on-chain wealth.
  We discuss practical mitigations and show that many of these threats can be substantially reduced through improved wallet implementation, stronger privacy considerations in ecosystem standards, and stricter controls over provider exposure. Our results highlight the need for standardized, privacy-preserving wallet architectures.

AI.tldr: Browser-extension cryptocurrency wallets leak privacy-sensitive signals through routine RPC operations, inconsistent permission revocation, and cross-origin iframe injection, enabling address linking, cross-site tracking, and deanonymization of 35M+ users across 85 popular wallets.
AI.motivation: Users assume their blockchain addresses remain unlinkable unless intentionally revealed, but wallet software routinely interacts with blockchain infrastructure and dApps, generating network-side and web-side signals that may betray this assumption. The paper aims to systematically identify and formalize the privacy threats stemming from these wallet behaviors.
AI.method: Large-scale dynamic measurements of 85 popular Chrome Web Store browser-extension wallets (representing 35.16 million users), analyzing RPC traffic patterns, permission revocation consistency across sessions, and provider interface injection behavior in cross-origin iframes.
AI.result: (1) Routine RPC operations leak structural links between user addresses; (2) Most Ethereum wallets inconsistently implement permission revocation, continuing to expose previously revoked addresses across sessions; (3) Many wallets inject provider interfaces into cross-origin iframes, enabling passive cross-site tracking beyond dApps and potential real-world identity deanonymization without user interaction.
AI.conclusion: Wallet behaviors leak sensitive information enabling multi-address linking, cross-session tracking, and connection of browsing activity to on-chain wealth. Mitigations include improved wallet implementation, stronger privacy standards in ecosystem protocols, and stricter controls over provider exposure. Standardized, privacy-preserving wallet architectures are urgently needed.

title: Property-Driven Synthetic Data Engineering for Data-Scarce Software Systems: Reflections from the Breast Cancer Domain
summary: Modern software systems increasingly depend on data for analysis, prediction, testing, and decision-making. Yet many important domains, including medicine, safety-critical systems, and regulated industries, lack abundant, shareable, or representative data. Synthetic data generation is often proposed as a remedy, but our experience engineering software for intraoperative radiotherapy (IORT) in breast cancer treatment suggests that synthetic data shifts rather than solves the central engineering problem. The key challenge becomes deciding which properties synthetic data must preserve, how these properties should be elicited from stakeholders, how they can be validated under privacy constraints, and how they evolve. We call this problem property-driven synthetic data engineering. Drawing on a collaboration with oncologists and preliminary experiments with a sensitive IORT dataset, we identify challenges in requirements, validation, privacy, and pipeline evolution. We argue that automated software engineering research should develop methods and tools for eliciting, formalizing, checking, and evolving validity properties for synthetic data in data-scarce software systems.

AI.tldr: Synthetic data generation shifts rather than solves data-scarcity problems; the real challenge is property-driven synthetic data engineering—eliciting, formalizing, validating, and evolving the properties synthetic data must preserve, especially under privacy constraints.
AI.motivation: Modern software systems rely heavily on data, but many critical domains (medicine, safety-critical systems, regulated industries) lack abundant, shareable, or representative data. While synthetic data generation is commonly proposed as a remedy, the authors' experience with intraoperative radiotherapy (IORT) software for breast cancer treatment reveals that synthetic data merely relocates the engineering burden rather than eliminating it.
AI.method: The paper draws on a real-world collaboration with oncologists and preliminary experiments using a sensitive IORT dataset. Through this case study, the authors identify and articulate the core challenges of what they term "property-driven synthetic data engineering," focusing on four dimensions: requirements elicitation, validation, privacy, and pipeline evolution.
AI.result: The authors identify that the fundamental difficulty lies not in generating synthetic data per se, but in deciding which statistical and semantic properties must be preserved, how to elicit these properties from domain stakeholders, how to validate them under privacy constraints, and how to manage their evolution over time. They characterize this as a distinct engineering problem requiring dedicated ASE research.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that the automated software engineering (ASE) community should develop methods and tools specifically targeting property elicitation, formalization, checking, and evolution for synthetic data in data-scarce systems, framing this as an open research agenda.

title: Reward-Density Heuristic for Dynamic Multi-Vehicle Routing: Performance and Computational Efficiency
summary: The Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) and its variants represent some of the most practically consequential optimization challenges in modern logistics and urban mobility. In this study, we address a dynamic, online variant combining elements of the VRP and the Orienteering Problem (OP), in which a fleet of vehicles must maximise cumulative reward collected within a fixed time horizon while continuously replanning as new tasks arrive. We propose and evaluate a reward-density heuristic for dynamic multi-vehicle assignment, referred to as the Efficiency heuristic. We evaluate this formulation across two application domains: autonomous drone task allocation and urban taxi dispatch, across multiple fleet sizes and task scales. The proposed method is compared with four classical construction heuristics and three metaheuristic algorithms (Adaptive Large Neighbourhood Search, Genetic Algorithm, and Simulated Annealing), all evaluated under identical conditions. Across all tested configurations, the Efficiency heuristic matches the solution quality of the best metaheuristic algorithms while requiring two to three orders of magnitude less planning time, establishing Pareto dominance over all competing methods on the reward-versus-compute frontier. These findings suggest a practical design principle for real-time allocation and dispatch systems: in dynamic, time-constrained routing environments, carefully designed greedy heuristics can match the output of sophisticated search procedures at a fraction of the computational cost, making them preferable for online deployment.

AI.tldr: A reward-density greedy heuristic ("Efficiency heuristic") for dynamic multi-vehicle routing with online task arrivals achieves solution quality matching top metaheuristics (ALNS, GA, Simulated Annealing) while requiring 100–1000× less planning time, establishing Pareto dominance on the reward-versus-compute frontier across drone dispatch and taxi routing domains.
AI.motivation: Dynamic, online vehicle routing problems — where new tasks continuously arrive and replanning is required within a fixed time horizon — demand both high solution quality and extremely low computational latency. Existing metaheuristics (ALNS, GA, SA) produce strong solutions but are too computationally expensive for real-time deployment. The authors seek a principled, computationally efficient alternative suitable for online dispatch systems.
AI.method: The paper proposes a reward-density heuristic called the Efficiency heuristic for dynamic multi-vehicle task assignment. The approach greedily prioritizes tasks based on the ratio of expected reward to marginal travel cost (reward density). Evaluation spans two application domains (autonomous drone task allocation and urban taxi dispatch), across multiple fleet sizes and task volumes. The heuristic is benchmarked against four classical construction heuristics and three metaheuristics (Adaptive Large Neighbourhood Search, Genetic Algorithm, Simulated Annealing) under identical experimental conditions, with performance measured on both solution quality (cumulative reward) and planning time.
AI.result: Across all tested configurations, the Efficiency heuristic matched the solution quality of the best metaheuristic algorithms while requiring two to three orders of magnitude less planning time. It established Pareto dominance over all competing methods on the reward-versus-compute frontier — no competing method achieved higher reward without incurring greater computational cost.
AI.conclusion: In dynamic, time-constrained routing environments, carefully designed greedy heuristics can match or exceed the output of sophisticated metaheuristic search procedures at a fraction of the computational cost, making them preferable for online deployment. This serves as a practical design principle for real-time allocation and dispatch systems.

title: PluraMath: Extending Mathematical Reasoning Evaluation Beyond High-Resource Languages
summary: Mathematical reasoning has become a central task for evaluating and tuning reasoning Large Language Models (LLMs), yet existing benchmarks remain heavily biased toward high-resource languages, with English and Chinese dominating both pre-training corpora and evaluation suites. The recently released PolyMath (Wang et al., 2025) dataset represents a significant step forward, yet its coverage is still limited to 18 only high-resource languages. To address this gap, we introduce PluraMath, an extension of PolyMath to 18 additional {underrepresented languages spanning 6 language families -- ranging from mid-resource to extreme low-resource settings. We constructed the dataset through a human-curated pipeline, where native speakers thoroughly validated pre-computed translations. Using PluraMath, we then benchmark 27 reasoning LLMs across four model scales -- small, mid-size, large, and closed-source ensembles -- probing the multilingual mathematical reasoning capabilities of state-of-the-art models under diverse linguistic conditions. Our fine-grained analysis confirms a persistent gap in mathematical reasoning performance between high-resource and underrepresented languages, with stronger results largely associated with better instruction-following ability. We fully open-source our dataset, data acquisition pipeline, and evaluation framework, with the goal of lowering the barrier to multilingual benchmark development for underrepresented communities.

AI.tldr: PluraMath extends the PolyMath multilingual math reasoning benchmark from 18 high-resource languages to 18 additional underrepresented languages across 6 language families, using human-validated translations. Benchmarking 27 LLMs reveals a persistent performance gap tied to instruction-following ability.
AI.motivation: Existing mathematical reasoning benchmarks for LLMs are heavily biased toward high-resource languages (English, Chinese), and even the recent PolyMath dataset covers only 18 high-resource languages. There is a clear need to evaluate and understand LLM mathematical reasoning in mid-resource and extreme low-resource languages.
AI.method: The authors introduce PluraMath, extending PolyMath to 18 additional underrepresented languages spanning 6 language families. The dataset is constructed via a human-curated pipeline where native speakers validate pre-computed translations. Using this benchmark, 27 reasoning LLMs across four model scales (small, mid-size, large, closed-source) are evaluated to probe multilingual mathematical reasoning capabilities.
AI.result: Fine-grained analysis confirms a persistent performance gap in mathematical reasoning between high-resource and underrepresented languages. Stronger multilingual math reasoning performance is largely associated with better instruction-following ability in the target language.
AI.conclusion: The work highlights the ongoing disparity in multilingual mathematical reasoning and provides open-source dataset, pipeline, and evaluation framework to lower barriers for benchmark development in underrepresented language communities.

title: FourTune: Towards Fully 4-Bit Efficient Post-Training for Diffusion Models
summary: Diffusion models have become a dominant paradigm for high-quality generative modeling, while post-training is essential for adapting them to diverse downstream applications. However, post-training of large diffusion models is still challenging due to the prohibitive memory footprints and slow training speed, which existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods only partially address. To overcome these limitations, we propose FourTune, an efficient post-training framework for diffusion models based on an end-to-end W4A4G4 paradigm. FourTune introduces a triple-branch hybrid pipeline that augments the standard LoRA architecture with a frozen numerical stabilizer to isolate quantization-sensitive outliers, enabling stable training under native 4-bit computation. In addition, FourTune employs hardware-efficient block-wise quantization and customized fused kernels to support efficient quantized backpropagation and reduce memory bandwidth overhead. Across customization, reinforcement learning, and distillation tasks, FourTune matches the quality of full-precision fine-tuning. On FLUX.1-dev (12B), FourTune reduces memory overhead by 2.25$\times$ and increases end-to-end training throughput by 2.27$\times$ compared to BF16 LoRA.

AI.tldr: FourTune is an efficient post-training framework for diffusion models using end-to-end W4A4G4 (4-bit weights, activations, and gradients) quantization. It combines a triple-branch hybrid pipeline with LoRA and a frozen numerical stabilizer to handle quantization-sensitive outliers, plus hardware-efficient block-wise quantization and custom fused kernels. On FLUX.1-dev (12B), it matches full-precision fine-tuning quality while reducing memory by 2.25× and increasing throughput by 2.27× vs. BF16 LoRA.
AI.motivation: Post-training large diffusion models is hindered by prohibitive memory footprints and slow training speed. Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods (like LoRA) only partially address these issues, motivating a fully quantized 4-bit training paradigm that maintains quality.
AI.method: FourTune proposes an end-to-end W4A4G4 quantized post-training framework with three key components: (1) a triple-branch hybrid pipeline that augments standard LoRA with a frozen numerical stabilizer branch to isolate quantization-sensitive outliers, enabling stable native 4-bit training; (2) hardware-efficient block-wise quantization; and (3) customized fused kernels for efficient quantized backpropagation with reduced memory bandwidth overhead. The framework is evaluated across customization, reinforcement learning, and distillation tasks.
AI.result: FourTune matches the generation quality of full-precision fine-tuning across multiple downstream tasks. On FLUX.1-dev (12B), it achieves 2.25× memory reduction and 2.27× end-to-end training throughput improvement compared to BF16 LoRA.
AI.conclusion: FourTune demonstrates that end-to-end 4-bit quantization (W4A4G4) is viable for post-training large diffusion models without sacrificing quality, offering significant memory and speed gains over existing parameter-efficient methods.

title: Claimed or Attested? A Commit-Signature Dataset and Identity Trust Tiers across the World of Code
summary: An author string in a git commit is free text the committer typed, so identity resolution over a global commit corpus rests on a claim that nothing in the commit verifies. A cryptographically signed commit is different: it binds the commit to a key the committer controls, and when that key ties back to a real-world identity the git identity becomes attested rather than merely claimed. We release the first commit-signature axis for the World of Code (WoC), extracted for the V2604 collection. The signature travels in the commit object's gpgsig header and is already carried, unparsed, in the commit-message field of the WoC commit tables, so the axis is a scan over existing tables rather than a re-read of the object database. Over the V2604 corpus of 5,866,595,698 commits, 17.59% carry a signature (PGP dominant at 98.96%, with a growing minority of SSH and X.509/sigstore signatures), or 1,031,721,316 signed commits. We release the per-commit signature map c2sigFull, a key-to-author graph gated so that shared organization and continuous-integration keys are separated from person keys, and A2trust, a per-identity attestation tier (unsigned, signed, real-world-bound, cross-corpus attested) that extends the published A2cls identity-class dataset. The signature axis is a precision anchor, not a coverage layer: signed commits skew toward recent and security-conscious developers, a population that overlaps the scholarly authors a bibliography join targets. We use the person keys to build a cryptographically grounded alias gold that calibrates the heuristic WoC alias map independently of hand-labeled pairs, and to attach an attestation provenance to science-to-software identity links. All artifacts are released as a self-contained, in dependently hosted replication package keyed to the WoC V2604 collection.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a commit-signature axis for the World of Code (WoC) V2604 corpus, parsing existing gpgsig headers to map 1.03B signed commits (17.59% of 5.87B total). It releases three artifacts: c2sigFull (per-commit signature map), a key-to-author graph separating person keys from organizational/CI keys, and A2trust (an attestation tier extending A2cls). The signature axis serves as a cryptographically grounded precision anchor for identity resolution, alias calibration, and science-to-software provenance linking.
AI.motivation: Git commit author strings are unverified free text, making global identity resolution rely on unverifiable claims. Cryptographically signed commits bind code to a key the committer controls, and when that key links to a real-world identity, the git identity becomes attested. The authors aim to provide a precision anchor for identity resolution across the massive WoC corpus by extracting and structuring existing signature data that was already carried but unparsed in WoC tables.
AI.method: The authors scanned existing WoC commit tables (rather than re-reading the object database) to parse the gpgsig header from the commit-message field across the V2604 corpus of 5,866,595,698 commits. They classified signatures by type (PGP, SSH, X.509/sigstore), built a key-to-author graph with gating to separate person keys from shared organization/CI keys, and created A2trust — a per-identity attestation tier (unsigned, signed, real-world-bound, cross-corpus attested) that extends the existing A2cls identity-class dataset. They also used person keys to build a cryptographically grounded alias gold standard for calibrating the heuristic WoC alias map.
AI.result: 17.59% of commits (1,031,721,316) carry a signature. PGP dominates at 98.96%, with a growing minority of SSH and X.509/sigstore signatures. Signed commits skew toward recent, security-conscious developers, overlapping with the scholarly author population targeted by bibliography joins. The released artifacts include c2sigFull, the gated key-to-author graph, and A2trust. The alias gold standard enables independent calibration of the WoC alias map without hand-labeled pairs, and attaches attestation provenance to science-to-software identity links.
AI.conclusion: The signature axis is a precision anchor, not a coverage layer. By mining already-present but unparsed signature data, the work provides cryptographically grounded identity attestation at scale. The released artifacts — c2sigFull, the key-to-author graph, and A2trust — form a self-contained replication package that enhances identity resolution, alias mapping calibration, and provenance tracking for science-to-software links in the WoC ecosystem.

title: A Global Author-Identity Map for the World of Code:62.7M Developer Identities from 106.8M Author Strings over 5.87B Commits
summary: Mining software repositories at global scale founders on author identity: the same developer commits under many name/email strings, and the same string is reused by many developers. We release a curated author-identity map for World of Code (WoC) version V2604, covering all 5,866,595,698 commits. It ships four co-versioned artifacts: a global alias map (a2AFullSUG) folding 106,826,059 raw author/committer strings into canonical identities; a per-identity classification (A2clsFull) tagging each id good, bad-by-attribute, local, bot, or partial; a within-project table (P2aAFull) recovering low-quality ids inside the one project where their reuse is unambiguous; and a commit-to-identity table (c2AFull) tagging every commit with its resolution provenance. The map is mega-cluster free, its largest cluster 6,910 ids (one GitHub noreply identity), and it resolves 73.5% of six billion commits into multi-id identities, raising human-id commit coverage to 98.17%. The design problem is clumping, not recall: a naive transitive union over shared-attribute edges welds three million unrelated people into one cluster, an over-merge that recall-only benchmarks price at zero. We report both error families, splitting and clumping, and show the high precision claimed by global-scale union maps can be an artifact of never measuring the conflated region. Against the ALFAA human-rated gold set the map scores recall 0.70 / precision 0.88, where the prior WoC map's apparent 0.95 precision collapses to 0.52 once its 3,006,318-id mega-cluster is counted. A canonical software-author identity is also a cross-corpus join key to scholarly author graphs, where clumping is again the binding constraint. All artifacts ship with the WoC V2604 release and a self-contained replication package.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a curated global author-identity map for 5.8 billion commits in World of Code, resolving 106M raw name/email strings into canonical identities with 73.5% commit resolution, while demonstrating that prior global-scale union maps severely over-merge identities — a failure masked by recall-only evaluation.
AI.motivation: Mining software repositories at global scale is hindered by the author identity problem: developers use multiple name/email strings, and the same string is reused by different developers. Prior approaches using naive transitive closure over shared attributes (e.g., same email) create massive "mega-clusters" that conflate millions of distinct people. This over-merging (clumping) is invisible to recall-only benchmarks, creating a false sense of precision. The work aims to provide a high-quality, mega-cluster-free identity map with honest evaluation of both error types.
AI.method: The authors construct identity resolution for World of Code V2604 (5.86B commits) using a conservative disambiguation pipeline that avoids naive transitive union. They ship four co-versioned artifacts: (1) a2AFullSUG — a global alias map folding 106.8M raw strings into canonical IDs; (2) A2clsFull — per-identity classification (good, bad-by-attribute, local, bot, partial); (3) P2aAFull — within-project recovery of low-quality IDs; and (4) c2AFull — commit-to-identity mapping with resolution provenance. Evaluation uses the ALFAA human-rated gold set and introduces metrics accounting for both splitting and clumping errors.
AI.result: The map is mega-cluster free (largest cluster: 6,910 IDs, a GitHub noreply identity). It resolves 73.5% of 5.86B commits into multi-id identities, achieving 98.17% human-id commit coverage. Against ALFAA: recall 0.70, precision 0.88. Critically, the prior WoC map's apparent 0.95 precision collapses to 0.52 once its 3,006,318-id mega-cluster is counted, revealing that clumping — not recall — is the binding design constraint for global-scale author identity resolution.
AI.conclusion: Clumping is the dominant failure mode in global-scale software author identity resolution, and recall-only evaluation systematically hides this problem. Canonical author identities serve as cross-corpus join keys to scholarly author graphs, where clumping is likewise the critical constraint. All artifacts are released open-source with the WoC V2604 release and a replication package.

title: When do prophets profit in prediction markets?
summary: Prediction markets aggregate dispersed beliefs into prices that act as probabilistic forecasts of uncertain events. Classical theory establishes a clean equivalence between forecasting accuracy and trading profit, but only for the specific automated market maker (AMM) design. However, the largest exchanges today are based on central limit order books in which informed forecasters routinely lose money while uninformed strategies can profit on simple heuristics. We resolve this discrepancy by establishing a formal equivalence between predictive accuracy and profitability. For any strictly proper scoring rule $S$, we exhibit a "proper" betting strategy that depends only on the forecaster's prediction $\mathbf{p}$ and the market price $\mathbf{q}$, and earns positive expected profit whenever $\mathbf{p}$ outperforms $\mathbf{q}$ under $S$ and the market has sufficient liquidity. Moreover, this proper betting is essentially the only strategy with such robust profitability guarantee. The proof rests on a decomposition of expected profit that strictly generalizes the classical AMM guarantee and also explains how strategies can profit without an accuracy edge. Empirically, across thousands of forecasts by AI models, proper betting is the only strategy that reliably converts accuracy into profit, and we further identify systematic forecasting personas and show how the optimal proper strategy varies across them. A month-long live deployment on Kalshi achieves $+80.33\%$ return on investment with a Sharpe ratio of $3.35$.

AI.tldr: This paper bridges a gap between theory and practice in prediction markets by showing that, for any strictly proper scoring rule, there exists a "proper" betting strategy that converts predictive accuracy into positive expected profit, provided sufficient market liquidity. The authors prove this is essentially the unique strategy with such robustness, validate it empirically on AI forecasts, and demonstrate a live deployment on Kalshi achieving +80.33% ROI with a 3.35 Sharpe ratio.
AI.motivation: Classical theory (Hanson's LMSR/AMM) establishes equivalence between forecasting accuracy and trading profit, but real-world prediction markets use central limit order books (CLOBs) where this equivalence breaks — informed traders can lose money while naive heuristics can profit. The authors aim to resolve this discrepancy by establishing a formal accuracy-profitability equivalence that holds in CLOB-based markets.
AI.method: The authors derive a decomposition of expected profit for any betting strategy in a CLOB market. They construct a "proper betting" strategy parameterized solely by a forecaster's prediction p and the market price q, proving it yields positive expected profit whenever p outperforms q under any strictly proper scoring rule S, given sufficient liquidity. They further prove this is essentially the unique strategy with such a robustness guarantee. Empirical validation uses thousands of AI model forecasts, and a live month-long deployment on Kalshi tests real-world performance.
AI.result: Theoretically, the expected profit decomposition strictly generalizes the classical AMM guarantee and explains how strategies can profit without an accuracy edge. Empirically, proper betting is the only strategy that reliably converts accuracy into profit across diverse AI forecasting personas. The live Kalshi deployment achieved +80.33% ROI with a Sharpe ratio of 3.35.
AI.conclusion: Proper betting resolves the theory-practice gap in prediction markets by providing a universal, accuracy-linked betting strategy for CLOB-based exchanges. It offers both a theoretical foundation and practical tool for forecasters to monetize predictive skill in real-world markets.

title: From Blueprint to Reality: Modeling and Applying Putnam's Social Capital Theory with LLM-based Multi-agent Simulations
summary: Putnam's Social Capital Theory is a foundational framework for collective action and community prosperity. However, traditional empirical methods face practical limits on control and replication. Meanwhile, LLM-based social simulations are typically behavior-driven and lack theory-aligned environments for modeling Putnam's core propositions. To address these gaps, we introduce SocaSim, an LLM-based multi-agent simulation framework to study Putnam's Social Capital Theory from theoretical blueprint to simulated reality.
