  Crossroads relies on key encumbrance: a threshold signing committee holds encumbered keys controlling assets on each integrated chain, signing transactions only as authorized by smart contracts on the backend blockchain. Asset movements are fee-efficient, as ownership changes are recorded on the backend blockchain and users may set the transaction fee for withdrawals.
  Crossroads enables permissionless, modular integration of new blockchains using pluggable oracles with flexible design options (zkBridge, TEE-based, hybrid). Asset deposits into Crossroads benefit from strong, chain-specific finalization guarantees, minimizing the risk of reorg attacks. Unlike existing bridges, however, third-party smart contracts in Crossroads can provide fast, optimistic access to funds before finalization completes.
  We prove that Crossroads satisfies soundness: given an honest quorum of signing committee members, any user can unilaterally generate a withdrawal transaction transferring their net balance to an account on an integrated blockchain. We implement a proof of concept across multiple public blockchains: Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana. We catalog a range of applications enabled by Crossroads, including universal wallets, cross-chain staking and lending, privacy-preserving payments, and private management of public blockchain assets.

AI.tldr: Crossroads is a smart contract layer that unifies assets from multiple blockchains as ERC-20 tokens on a single backend chain, enabling cross-chain DeFi and privacy applications via threshold-encumbered keys and pluggable oracles, with formal soundness guarantees.
AI.motivation: The blockchain ecosystem suffers from fragmentation — assets are siloed on separate chains, making unified smart-contract-based exchange, lending, and privacy applications difficult. Existing cross-chain bridges offer only partial solutions. Crossroads aims to provide general-purpose chain abstraction where any asset can participate in a single unified platform.
AI.method: Crossroads employs (1) key encumbrance via a threshold signing committee that holds keys for each integrated chain and only signs transactions authorized by backend smart contracts; (2) ERC-20 representation of foreign chain assets on a backend blockchain; (3) pluggable oracles (zkBridge, TEE-based, hybrid) for permissionless modular chain integration; (4) chain-specific finalization guarantees with optional fast optimistic access via third-party contracts; (5) a formal soundness proof ensuring honest-quorum users can unilaterally withdraw their net balance.
AI.result: The authors prove Crossroads satisfies soundness — any user can unilaterally generate a withdrawal transaction to an integrated chain given an honest signing quorum. A proof-of-concept implementation spans Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana. The paper catalogs applications including universal wallets, cross-chain staking/lending, privacy-preserving payments, and private management of public blockchain assets.
AI.conclusion: Crossroads provides a general-purpose, sound, and modular chain-abstraction framework that goes beyond bridging by unifying assets on a single smart contract layer, enabling rich cross-chain applications with strong security guarantees and flexible oracle-based integration of new chains.

title: RuBench: A Repository-Level Agentic Coding Benchmark with Natively Authored Russian Task Specifications
comment: 16 pages, 1 figure, 7 tables. Benchmark: 25 natively Russian repository-level agentic coding tasks; 4 product agent configurations, 3 runs each. Data, full trajectories and harness: https://github.com/eugeneshilow/rubench
summary: Developers increasingly delegate real maintenance work to product-grade coding agents, and many state tasks in their native language, in the style of a customer request rather than a curated English issue. Existing repository-level agentic benchmarks do not measure this setting: their task statements are English by design. We introduce RuBench 1.0, a benchmark of 25 tasks mined from recent fix commits in five live open-source repositories (aiohttp, aiogram, Laravel, NestJS, Fastify; Python, PHP, TypeScript, JavaScript), where each task is specified natively in Russian -- written from scratch in the style of an actual customer request, not translated -- and judged by the upstream maintainer's regression tests, which we withhold from release. All 25 fix commits postdate the training-data cutoffs of every evaluated model, giving a contamination argument that holds task-by-task. We evaluate deployed product configurations (CLI agent + model + reasoning effort) -- Claude Code with Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, and Haiku 4.5, and Codex CLI with GPT-5.5 -- with three independent runs each, reporting pass@1 with task-level confidence intervals, paired comparisons, dollar cost, and token usage. The best configuration resolves 78.7% of tasks; at N=25 only the gaps to the weakest model are statistically resolvable, which we state explicitly. Auditing full trajectories of a fifth, hors-concours configuration (Claude Code + Fable 5, July 2, 2026 release), we caught the product silently substituting the model: on 5 of 25 tasks (20%) an official safeguard fallback re-routed routine HTTP-protocol fixes to Opus 4.8 -- direct, reproducible evidence that the deployed product, not the model, is the unit actually measured. We release task statements, metadata, full agent trajectories, and diffs; grading oracles are withheld, with a SHA-256 manifest committed at publication time.

AI.tldr: RuBench 1.0 is a benchmark of 25 repository-level coding tasks specified in Russian (not translated), mined from recent fix commits across five live open-source repositories. It evaluates deployed product-grade coding agents (Claude Code, Codex CLI) using upstream regression tests as oracles, with contamination-controlled task selection. A key finding: the deployed product, not just the model, is the unit of measurement, evidenced by silent model fallback substitution in 20% of tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing repository-level agentic benchmarks use English task statements by design, failing to reflect real-world scenarios where developers state tasks in their native language (e.g., Russian) as customer-style requests. The authors aim to measure how deployed product-grade coding agents handle this realistic, multilingual maintenance setting while addressing contamination concerns and product-vs-model measurement validity.
AI.method: The benchmark comprises 25 tasks sourced from fix commits in five open-source repositories (aiohttp, aiogram, Laravel, NestJS, Fastify) spanning Python, PHP, TypeScript, and JavaScript. Tasks are written from scratch in Russian in a customer-request style. All commits postdate training cutoffs of evaluated models, ensuring contamination-free evaluation. Grading uses upstream maintainer regression tests (withheld from release). Evaluated configurations include Claude Code (Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5, Haiku 4.5) and Codex CLI (GPT-5.5), with three independent runs each, reporting pass@1 with confidence intervals, paired comparisons, cost, and token usage.
AI.result: The best configuration resolves 78.7% of tasks. At N=25, only gaps to the weakest model are statistically significant. A hors-concours evaluation using Claude Code + Fable 5 revealed that the product silently substituted the model via a safeguard fallback to Opus 4.8 on 5 of 25 tasks (20%), demonstrating that the deployed product — not the model in isolation — is the actual unit of measurement.
AI.conclusion: RuBench provides a more ecologically valid evaluation of coding agents by using native-language, customer-style task specifications and contamination-controlled commits. The finding that products can silently substitute models underscores the importance of treating the full deployed system as the evaluation unit. All task statements, metadata, trajectories, and diffs are released; grading oracles are withheld with a SHA-256 manifest for integrity.

title: Task Decomposition-Guided Reranking for Adaptive Agent Skill Retrieval
summary: Skill usage can significantly enhance the ability of modern agent systems to complete complex tasks. However, the growing scale of skill libraries makes accurate skill selection increasingly challenging. In real-world scenarios, ambiguous semantic matching often arises between a specific task requirement and multiple generic yet semantically similar candidate skills. Moreover, existing methods tend to overlook the dynamic influence of task difficulty and skill applicability when selecting the optimal target skill set. To address these issues, we propose SkillReranker, an inference-time reranking framework for adaptive skill selection. Specifically, we first perform semantic decomposition on both the task and skill sides, yielding informative subtask and execution-state descriptions as well as transition-state descriptions that characterize each skill's functionality. These descriptions are then used to construct a directed acyclic execution graph, where intermediate task states are modeled as nodes and candidate skills as edges, thereby establishing a structured task-skill correspondence. On this basis, SkillReranker determines whether each state node satisfies the split condition to identify subtask intervals. For each task interval, we employ a cross-encoder to perform comprehensive scoring over candidate skills and select the most suitable ones to form the final target skill set. Experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld with three backbone LLMs show that SkillReranker effectively improves task performance, reduces environment interaction steps, and lowers token consumption compared with existing skill selection baselines.

AI.tldr: SkillReranker proposes an inference-time reranking framework that constructs a directed acyclic execution graph from semantic decomposition of tasks and skills, then uses a cross-encoder to score and select optimal skills per subtask interval, outperforming baselines on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld benchmarks.
AI.motivation: As skill libraries grow, two key challenges emerge: (1) ambiguous semantic matching between specific task requirements and multiple similar candidate skills, and (2) existing methods ignore the dynamic interplay between task difficulty and skill applicability during selection.
AI.method: SkillReranker operates in three stages: (1) semantic decomposition of tasks into subtask/execution-state descriptions and skills into transition-state descriptions; (2) construction of a directed acyclic execution graph with intermediate task states as nodes and candidate skills as edges; (3) split-condition checking on state nodes to define subtask intervals, followed by cross-encoder scoring over candidate skills within each interval to select the final target skill set.
AI.result: Experiments on ALFWorld and ScienceWorld with three backbone LLMs demonstrate that SkillReranker improves task performance, reduces environment interaction steps, and lowers token consumption compared to existing skill selection baselines.
AI.conclusion: SkillReranker effectively addresses the challenges of ambiguous skill matching and dynamic task-skill relationships through structured graph-based reranking, offering a practical inference-time solution for adaptive skill selection in agent systems.

title: LongCrafter: Towards Diverse Long-Context Understanding via Evidence-Graph-Guided Instruction Synthesis
summary: Synthesizing long-context supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data is a scalable way to enhance the long-context understanding of large language models (LLMs), yet existing approaches share three limitations: narrow task coverage, insufficient instruction difficulty, and a lack of faithfulness supervision. We propose \textbf{LongCrafter}, a structured synthesis framework that couples a hierarchical task taxonomy with an evidence-grounded pipeline. The taxonomy organizes long-context understanding into local/shallow and global/deep levels and yields 32 fine-grained task types that serve as a global generative prior. Guided by this taxonomy, LongCrafter constructs task-aligned long contexts, decomposes them into explicit evidence graphs that model cross-paragraph dependencies, and generates instruction--response pairs strictly grounded in the located evidence spans, ensuring both controllable difficulty and faithful, traceable reasoning. Models fine-tuned on LongCrafter data outperform all SFT baselines and even the official post-trained models on LongBench, LongBench~v2, and LooGLE across both Qwen2.5-7B and LLaMA-3.1-8B, with the largest gains on high-difficulty tasks. Further analysis shows that LongCrafter data is more diverse and better spread across difficulty levels, and that the trained models locate evidence robustly regardless of position, effectively mitigating the ``lost in the middle'' problem.

AI.tldr: LongCrafter is a structured framework for synthesizing long-context SFT data using a hierarchical task taxonomy (32 fine-grained types) and an evidence-grounded pipeline. It builds task-aligned contexts, constructs explicit evidence graphs for cross-paragraph dependencies, and generates faithful instruction-response pairs anchored in evidence spans. Models fine-tuned on LongCrafter surpass all SFT baselines and official post-trained models on LongBench, LongBench v2, and LooGLE, with strongest gains on hard tasks, and effectively mitigate the "lost in the middle" problem.
AI.motivation: Existing long-context SFT data synthesis methods suffer from three key shortcomings: (1) narrow task coverage limited to a few task types, (2) insufficient instruction difficulty that fails to stress deep/long-range understanding, and (3) a lack of faithfulness supervision, meaning generated responses may not be genuinely grounded in the provided context. These limitations hinder the effective enhancement of LLMs' long-context capabilities.
AI.method: LongCrafter employs a structured synthesis framework with two core components: (1) A hierarchical task taxonomy that partitions long-context understanding into local/shallow and global/deep levels, yielding 32 fine-grained task types that serve as a generative prior ensuring broad coverage. (2) An evidence-grounded pipeline that first constructs task-aligned long contexts, then decomposes them into explicit evidence graphs modeling cross-paragraph dependencies, and finally generates instruction-response pairs strictly grounded in located evidence spans. This ensures controllable difficulty scaling and faithful, traceable reasoning.
AI.result: Models fine-tuned on LongCrafter data (using Qwen2.5-7B and LLaMA-3.1-8B) outperform all SFT baselines and even official post-trained models across LongBench, LongBench v2, and LooGLE. The largest performance gains are observed on high-difficulty tasks. Ablation analysis confirms that LongCrafter data exhibits greater diversity and a more balanced spread across difficulty levels. Trained models also demonstrate robust evidence localization regardless of position, effectively mitigating the "lost in the middle" phenomenon.
AI.conclusion: LongCrafter demonstrates that structured, taxonomy-guided synthesis with explicit evidence grounding is an effective and scalable approach for improving long-context understanding in LLMs. The framework addresses coverage, difficulty, and faithfulness simultaneously, producing SFT data that yields superior and more robust long-context performance compared to both existing SFT methods and official post-training.

title: Decision-Focused Scenario Generation and Selection for Efficient and Robust Grid Dispatch
summary: The increasing uncertainty from flexible demand and renewable generation has made distributionally robust optimization (DRO) an important tool for robust power system dispatch. DRO relies on forecast scenarios to construct ambiguity sets, but conventional scenario generation pipelines are often trained in an accuracy-oriented manner and may neglect spatial correlations among uncertainties. This mismatch can produce ambiguity sets that are statistically plausible but suboptimal for downstream operation. This work proposes a decision-focused generative framework for correlated scenario generation in DRO-based dispatch. Instead of training generative models solely to fit the historical uncertainty distribution, the proposed framework optimizes generated scenarios according to their induced downstream operational cost. The proposed framework is tailored to mainstream generative models, including variational autoencoders, generative adversarial networks, and diffusion models, while capturing the joint distribution of uncertainties across buses. To improve computational tractability, we further develop a differentiable scenario selector that selects decision-relevant scenarios from a generated pool and can be trained within the same decision-focused pipeline. Case studies demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively reduces 0.80%-2.02% operational cost across different generative models compared to accuracy-oriented methods.

AI.tldr: A decision-focused generative framework is proposed for correlated scenario generation in DRO-based power dispatch, optimizing scenarios directly for downstream operational cost rather than distributional accuracy, achieving 0.80%–2.02% cost reduction.
AI.motivation: Conventional scenario generation for DRO is accuracy-oriented and neglects spatial correlations among uncertainties, leading to ambiguity sets that are statistically plausible but yield suboptimal dispatch decisions. The mismatch between generation objectives and downstream operational goals motivates a decision-focused approach.
AI.method: The authors propose a decision-focused generative framework that optimizes generated scenarios by minimizing induced downstream operational cost. The framework is adapted to three generative model families (VAEs, GANs, diffusion models) while capturing joint uncertainty distributions across buses. A differentiable scenario selector is developed to pick decision-relevant scenarios from a generated pool, enabling end-to-end training.
AI.result: Case studies show the proposed decision-focused framework reduces operational costs by 0.80%–2.02% across different generative models compared to conventional accuracy-oriented methods.
AI.conclusion: Training generative models with a decision-focused objective, rather than purely distributional accuracy, yields statistically meaningful and operationally superior ambiguity sets for DRO-based power system dispatch, with consistent improvements across multiple generative architectures.

title: Domain-Driven Design in Practice: A Large-Scale Empirical Characterisation of the Open-Source Ecosystem
summary: Context: Domain-Driven Design (DDD) is a leading paradigm for managing software complexity, yet research remains largely theoretical; our prior work found nearly 39% of DDD studies lack rigorous empirical evaluation, leaving practical adoption largely unexamined at scale. Objective: We provide the first large-scale characterisation of the DDD landscape on GitHub, a data-driven baseline for how the paradigm is implemented and sustained in practice. Method: Using a Mining Software Repositories (MSR) approach with a hybrid strategy (topics and README keywords), we identified 11,742 candidate repositories. To address label noise, we built a novel semantic validation pipeline using GPT-4o with a triplicate majority-vote strategy, yielding 2,502 verified repositories. Validation against a manually labelled sample showed substantial agreement with human experts (kappa = 0.77). Results: DDD adoption accelerated sharply after a 2017 inflection point, and the resulting projects are notably long-lived: their median lifespan exceeds the typical GitHub project by over an order of magnitude, indicating sustained, professional-grade engineering rather than short-lived experiments. Layered and Clean Architecture dominate, while CQRS and Event Sourcing recur in distributed, data-intensive systems. Notably, the data challenge the Java-centric assumption of much academic work: C# and TypeScript, not Java, lead practical adoption. Conclusions: DDD has matured into a stable, professional-grade practice adopted across diverse languages and domains. However, a quarter of projects (25.3%) record no explicit business context, revealing a persistent gap between how domain intent is designed and how it is preserved in version control. We call for lightweight architectural traceability standards and offer guidance for teams reusing these repositories as reference implementations.

AI.tldr: First large-scale empirical study of Domain-Driven Design adoption on GitHub, analyzing 2,502 verified repositories. DDD projects are notably long-lived (median lifespan >10x typical GitHub projects), with C# and TypeScript leading over Java. A persistent gap exists between domain intent design and its preservation in version control (25.3% lack explicit business context).
AI.motivation: Prior DDD research is largely theoretical, with nearly 39% of studies lacking rigorous empirical evaluation. There is no large-scale, data-driven baseline characterizing how DDD is actually implemented and sustained in practice, leaving a significant gap between academic understanding and real-world adoption.
AI.method: Mining Software Repositories (MSR) approach combining GitHub topic tags and README keyword searches to identify 11,742 candidate repositories. A novel semantic validation pipeline using GPT-4o with a triplicate majority-vote strategy was employed to filter label noise, yielding 2,502 verified repositories. Validation against a manually labeled sample achieved substantial inter-rater agreement (kappa = 0.77).
AI.result: DDD adoption accelerated sharply post-2017. Verified DDD repositories have a median lifespan exceeding typical GitHub projects by over an order of magnitude. Layered and Clean Architecture dominate; CQRS and Event Sourcing appear in distributed, data-intensive systems. C# and TypeScript lead practical adoption, not Java. 25.3% of projects lack explicit business context in version control.
AI.conclusion: DDD has matured into a stable, professional-grade practice across diverse languages and domains. The gap between designed domain intent and its traceability in repositories is a concern. The authors call for lightweight architectural traceability standards and offer guidance for teams using these repositories as reference implementations.

title: DT-Guard: Intent-Driven Reasoning-Active Training for Reasoning-Free LLM Safety Guardrail
summary: Large language models deployed in open-world applications require safety guardrails that are both robust to complex risks and efficient enough for low-latency runtime moderation. Existing guardrails face a practical trade-off between lightweight classification-based models, which are efficient but often struggle with concealed intent, ambiguous semantics, and borderline safety decisions, and reasoning-based guards, which improve judgment quality but introduce additional token generation and inference latency. We present DT-Guard, a content safety guardrail model based on a Reasoning-Active Training, Reasoning-Free Inference paradigm. The key idea is to use reasoning supervision during training while emitting only structured safety labels at inference time. DT-Guard formulates safety judgment as a progressive decision process, Intent - Category - Safety, and constructs an intent-driven dataset with intent labels, risk categories, safety labels, and structured reasoning trajectories. To further improve hard-case robustness, we propose Rollout-Guided Progressive Hard-Case Optimization (RG-PHO), which uses multi-rollout consistency to identify stably mastered, persistently failed, and preference-unstable samples, and applies targeted supervised and preference optimization accordingly. At inference time, DT-Guard directly generates structured labels without explicit reasoning traces, preserving deployment efficiency. Experiments on prompt-side and response-side safety benchmarks show that DT-Guard achieves average F1 scores of 0.886 and 0.870, respectively. With only a 4B backbone, it reaches a dual-side average F1 of 0.878, outperforming strong 8B guardrail baselines. These results demonstrate that reasoning supervision can be effectively internalized into low-latency safety discrimination.

AI.tldr: DT-Guard is a 4B safety guardrail model that uses reasoning supervision during training but outputs only structured safety labels at inference, achieving strong dual-side F1 (0.878) while avoiding the latency cost of reasoning-based approaches. It employs an Intent-Category-Safety progressive decision framework and Rollout-Guided Progressive Hard-Case Optimization to handle ambiguous and hard cases.
AI.motivation: Existing safety guardrails face a trade-off: lightweight classifiers are efficient but fail on concealed intent and borderline cases, while reasoning-based guards improve accuracy at the cost of inference latency. The authors aim to internalize reasoning capabilities into a model that remains efficient at deployment by decoupling training-time reasoning from inference-time execution.
AI.method: DT-Guard operates on a Reasoning-Active Training, Reasoning-Free Inference paradigm. During training, safety judgment is formulated as a progressive chain: Intent → Category → Safety, with an intent-driven dataset containing intent labels, risk categories, safety labels, and structured reasoning trajectories. Rollout-Guided Progressive Hard-Case Optimization (RG-PHO) uses multi-rollout consistency to classify samples as stably mastered, persistently failed, or preference-unstable, then applies targeted supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization accordingly. At inference, only structured safety labels are emitted without reasoning traces.
AI.result: On prompt-side and response-side safety benchmarks, DT-Guard achieves average F1 scores of 0.886 and 0.870 respectively. With a 4B backbone, it attains a dual-side average F1 of 0.878, outperforming strong 8B guardrail baselines.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning supervision can be effectively internalized into compact models for low-latency safety discrimination, enabling guardrails that combine the judgment quality of reasoning-based methods with the deployment efficiency of classification-based approaches.

title: Improving LLM-Generated Process Model Quality Through Reinforcement Learning: The Role of Reward Function Design
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate BPMN process models from natural-language descriptions, yet supervised fine-tuning (SFT) limits their output quality to the patterns present in the training data. Reinforcement learning (RL) can optimize beyond this ceiling using external quality measures, but how the reward function should be designed when quality is multi-dimensional remains unexplored. We present a systematic investigation of reward function design for RL-based process model generation, training two LLM families (Llama~3.1 8B, Qwen~2.5 14B) under 48 configurations using Group Sequence Policy Optimization with rewards derived from an automated evaluation framework comprising 38 metrics across syntactic, pragmatic, and semantic quality. Three findings emerge. First, RL significantly improves pragmatic and syntactic quality while preserving semantic fidelity, reducing output variability by more than sixfold. Second, equal reward weighting consistently outperforms targeted weighting: emphasizing a specific dimension fails to improve it and can collapse the model into a low-quality mode. Third, design choices interact with model architecture in non-trivial ways: the invalidity penalty is essential for one model but irrelevant for the other, and SFT initialization is indispensable for one architecture but counterproductive for another. These results demonstrate that reward composition is a primary determinant of optimization outcomes, with effects as large as the decision to apply RL itself. The findings generalize to any structured generation task where quality is assessed along multiple automated dimensions. We release our implementation and experimental code at https://github.com/chlauer99/RL_for_process_modeling.

AI.tldr: Investigating how reward function design affects RL-based BPMN process model generation from LLMs, finding that equal weighting of quality dimensions works best, design choices interact with model architecture, and reward composition matters as much as the decision to use RL itself.
AI.motivation: Supervised fine-tuning limits LLM-generated BPMN models to patterns in training data. While RL can optimize beyond this using external quality measures, no prior work has systematically studied how to design multi-dimensional reward functions for process model generation.
AI.method: Trained two LLM families (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 14B) under 48 configurations using Group Sequence Policy Optimization. Rewards derived from an automated evaluation framework with 38 metrics spanning syntactic, pragmatic, and semantic quality. Systematically varied reward weightings, SFT initialization, and invalidity penalties.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) RL significantly improves pragmatic and syntactic quality while preserving semantic fidelity, reducing output variability >6×; (2) equal reward weighting consistently outperforms targeted weighting — emphasizing one dimension fails and can collapse the model; (3) design choices interact with model architecture non-trivially, e.g., invalidity penalty is essential for one model but irrelevant for another, and SFT initialization is indispensable for one architecture but counterproductive for another.
AI.conclusion: Reward composition is a primary determinant of optimization outcomes, with effects as large as the decision to apply RL itself. Findings generalize to any structured generation task with multi-dimensional automated quality assessment.

title: AbICL: In-Context Learning for Antigen-Specific Antibody Affinity Ranking
summary: Accurate ranking of antibody candidates according to their binding affinity is essential for therapeutic antibody discovery. However, existing methods treat affinity comparisons independently and ignore the contextual information encoded in other labeled comparisons, limiting their ability to capture antigen-specific binding landscapes. For many target antigens, a small number of experimentally characterized affinity comparisons are often available. An important question is whether the model can exploit these existing comparisons to infer antigen-specific ranking patterns that facilitate subsequent affinity ranking. This form of learning from labeled demonstrations closely resembles the paradigm of In-Context Learning, motivating us to revisit antibody affinity ranking from an ICL perspective. To this end, we propose AbICL, an ICL framework for antigen-specific antibody affinity ranking. AbICL combines a pretrained structural encoder with a context ranking head and is trained with an episodic meta-training strategy that enables the model to leverage support demonstrations for test-time adaptation without gradient updates. Experiments on the AbRank benchmark demonstrate that AbICL consistently outperforms existing ranking baselines across almost all data splits and evaluation benchmarks. Further analysis shows that the value of contextual demonstrations depends on how well they match the target inference task, and becomes increasingly pronounced under distribution shift and fine-grained affinity discrimination. These findings highlight the potential of ICL as an effective paradigm for antigen-specific antibody affinity ranking, particularly in challenging settings where a single global ranking function is insufficient.

AI.tldr: AbICL proposes an In-Context Learning framework for antibody affinity ranking that leverages existing labeled comparisons as contextual demonstrations, enabling antigen-specific ranking without gradient updates. It combines a pretrained structural encoder with a context ranking head trained via episodic meta-training, consistently outperforming baselines on the AbRank benchmark, particularly under distribution shift.
AI.motivation: Existing antibody affinity ranking methods treat comparisons independently, ignoring contextual information from other labeled comparisons. Given that a small number of experimentally characterized affinity comparisons are often available for a target antigen, the authors ask whether models can exploit these to infer antigen-specific ranking patterns — a paradigm resembling In-Context Learning.
AI.method: AbICL consists of (1) a pretrained structural encoder for antibody-antigen complexes, (2) a context ranking head that processes support demonstrations alongside the query pair, and (3) an episodic meta-training strategy where each episode samples a support set of labeled comparisons and a query set, training the model to predict query rankings conditioned on the support set without gradient updates at test time.
AI.result: AbICL consistently outperforms existing ranking baselines across nearly all data splits and evaluation benchmarks in the AbRank benchmark. The value of contextual demonstrations depends on their match to the target inference task and becomes more pronounced under distribution shift and fine-grained affinity discrimination.
AI.conclusion: ICL is an effective paradigm for antigen-specific antibody affinity ranking, especially in challenging settings where a single global ranking function is insufficient. The approach shows particular promise when the support demonstrations align well with the target task distribution.

title: Industry Classification of GitHub Repositories Using the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS)
summary: GitHub hosts hundreds of millions of public repositories, but the platform exposes no native mapping from repositories to standardized industry sectors. This gap limits empirical work on the geography of innovation, the industrial composition of open-source production, and the diffusion of new technologies across economic sectors. We present NAICS-GH, a publicly released corpus of 6,588 GitHub repositories drawn from source pools covering the United States, the European Union, and Australia, each labeled with a 2-digit sector from the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS 2022). Labels are produced by a retrieve-and-verify pipeline that combines BAAI/bge-large-en embeddings, FAISS retrieval, and GPT-4.1 rubric scoring. The pipeline narrows about 1.37 million source repositories to 31,178 candidate repository-sector pairs and retains 6,588 high-confidence labels with score at least 8. Re-running the retrieval pipeline end to end reproduces the candidate set to within 0.03 percent. On a 2,421-repository human-validated random sample, the released labels attain 96.98 percent precision, with Wilson 95 percent confidence interval [96.23, 97.59]. We benchmark six pretrained encoders on the released corpus; RoBERTa-large reaches 86.45 percent F1 and 86.35 percent accuracy on a held-out 20 percent test set. The dataset, Croissant metadata, pipeline code, prompts, and fine-tuned checkpoint are released under CC-BY-4.0 and MIT licenses.

AI.tldr: NAICS-GH is a curated corpus of 6,588 GitHub repositories mapped to 2-digit NAICS industry sectors via a retrieve-and-verify pipeline (BGE embeddings + FAISS + GPT-4.1 scoring). It achieves 96.98% precision against human validation and enables benchmarking of encoder-based sector classification.
AI.motivation: GitHub lacks a native mapping of repositories to standardized industry sectors, which hinders research on the geography of innovation, the industrial composition of open-source software, and technology diffusion across economic sectors.
AI.method: A two-stage retrieve-and-verify pipeline: (1) candidate retrieval from ~1.37M source repositories (US, EU, Australia) using BAAI/bge-large-en embeddings and FAISS similarity search, yielding 31,178 candidate repository-sector pairs; (2) verification via GPT-4.1 rubric scoring, retaining 6,588 pairs with score ≥ 8. Pipeline reproducibility is validated (candidate set reproduced to within 0.03%). Six pretrained encoders are benchmarked on the corpus, with RoBERTa-large as the top performer.
AI.result: The released labels achieve 96.98% precision on a 2,421-repository human-validated random sample (Wilson 95% CI: [96.23, 97.59]). Reproducibility of candidate retrieval is within 0.03%. RoBERTa-large attains 86.45% F1 and 86.35% accuracy on a held-out 20% test set for sector classification.
AI.conclusion: NAICS-GH provides a high-quality, reproducible benchmark for industry-sector classification of GitHub repositories, with strong precision and solid fine-tuning baselines. All artifacts are openly released under CC-BY-4.0 and MIT licenses.

title: Driving the Wrong Way: Leveraging Interpretability in End2End Autonomous Driving Models
summary: The increasing adoption of end-to-end learning for autonomous driving introduces increased model complexity and opacity, raising the risk of learning undesired or erroneous behavior. In this work, we integrate unsupervised dictionary learning as a post hoc interpretability module within state-of-the-art driving models to decompose driving behavior into semantically meaningful concepts while demonstrating their causal influence on the model's driving decisions. We propose a stepwise framework for extracting and interpreting meaningful concepts from the end-to-end model and connecting them to the multifaceted model outputs, thereby revealing the underlying decision-making logic for the prediction of future trajectories. Furthermore, targeted interventions at the concept level allow us to manipulate and correct driving decisions, resulting in measurable improvements in overall driving performance. We thus demonstrate how interpretability can effectively be used to reduce model opacity, uncover erroneous behavior, and enable targeted mitigation, ultimately boosting model performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a post hoc interpretability framework using unsupervised dictionary learning to decompose end-to-end autonomous driving model behavior into semantically meaningful concepts, enabling causal intervention that improves driving performance.
AI.motivation: End-to-end learning for autonomous driving increases model complexity and opacity, raising the risk of learning undesired or erroneous behaviors. There is a need for interpretability methods that not only explain but also enable correction of these models.
AI.method: A stepwise framework integrating unsupervised dictionary learning as a post hoc interpretability module: (1) decomposes driving behavior into semantically meaningful concepts, (2) connects these concepts to multifaceted model outputs to reveal decision-making logic for trajectory prediction, and (3) performs targeted concept-level interventions to manipulate and correct driving decisions.
AI.result: Concept-level interventions successfully manipulate and correct driving decisions, yielding measurable improvements in overall driving performance. The approach reduces model opacity and uncovers erroneous behavior.
AI.conclusion: Interpretability can be effectively leveraged not merely for explanation but also for targeted mitigation of errors, ultimately boosting end-to-end driving model performance.

authors: Tom Wei-cyuan Lin Kashyap Ramanandula Manjusha
title: Pluralis v0.1: Towards a Multicultural, Multimodal, Multilingual Benchmark for AI Risk and Reliability
summary: Current AI safety evaluation and benchmarking frameworks predominantly rely on Western-centric culture-agnostic defaults that mask critical regional laws, socio-linguistic nuances, and cultural taboos, leaving Vision-Language Models (VLMs) vulnerable in global deployments. We introduce Pluralis v0.1: a novel multimodal, multi-regional, and multilingual dataset built from a culture-first perspective. Spanning 6,448 prompts across six Asia-Pacific countries (Bangladesh, India, Korea, Pakistan, Singapore, Taiwan) and eight languages, Pluralis diverges from prior work by natively sourcing localized safety hazards rather than adapting Western datasets. Crucially, it introduces a multimodal evaluation paradigm: user text (e.g., "Should I gift this?") and an image referring to "this" (e.g., a clock) - both innocuous in isolation, but synergistically triggering specific legal or cultural violations. Pluralis disentangles universal safety violations from localized cultural appropriateness, establishing the latter as a first-class evaluation axis. To operationalize this, we present Judge-Pluralis, an agreement-gated LLM-as-a-Judge ensemble trained on examples classified in an empirically derived cultural taxonomy. Observing VLM behavior on a subset of the Pluralis surfaces recurring, locale-specific failure modes such as image misidentifications with downstream harm, missed item-context-locale interactions, and inadequate refusals. These failure modes vary systematically across locales and languages, exposing blind spots that globally averaged metrics conceal. Ultimately, Pluralis is not presented as a solved evaluation framework for cultural alignment, but rather as a first step and catalyst for future innovation. We call upon the research community to utilize this foundation to advance the science of multilingual, multicultural evaluation to better support AI cultural alignment globally.

AI.tldr: Pluralis v0.1 is a multimodal, multi-regional, multilingual safety dataset (6,448 prompts, 6 Asia-Pacific countries, 8 languages) that evaluates VLMs on localized cultural safety hazards using a novel image+text synergy paradigm, revealing systematic locale-specific failure modes masked by Western-centric benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current AI safety benchmarks are Western-centric and culture-agnostic, failing to capture regional laws, socio-linguistic nuances, and cultural taboos. This leaves VLMs vulnerable to safety failures when deployed globally, as violations that are innocuous in one culture may be severe in another.
AI.method: The authors construct Pluralis v0.1 by natively sourcing localized safety hazards from six Asia-Pacific countries rather than adapting Western datasets. The dataset introduces a multimodal evaluation paradigm where individually innocuous text prompts (e.g., "Should I gift this?") and images (e.g., a clock) combine synergistically to trigger specific legal/cultural violations. They develop Judge-Pluralis, an agreement-gated LLM-as-a-Judge ensemble trained on an empirically derived cultural taxonomy, and use it to evaluate VLM behavior on a curated subset to surface locale-specific failure modes (image misidentifications, missed item-context-locale interactions, inadequate refusals).
AI.result: VLM evaluation reveals recurring failure modes — image misidentifications leading to downstream harm, missed item-context-locale interactions, and inadequate refusals — that vary systematically across locales and languages, exposing blind spots that globally averaged metrics conceal.
AI.conclusion: Pluralis is positioned as a first step and catalyst, not a solved framework. The authors call on the research community to build upon this foundation to advance multilingual, multicultural AI safety evaluation and better support cultural alignment globally.

title: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection of Information Operations Users via Behavioral and Language Patterns
summary: Information Operations on social media networks have been identified as a significant threat to democracy and modern society, but they are challenging and expensive to detect by humans. Existing supervised IO detection methods fail to capture the dynamic nature of evolving IO user behavior, while existing unsupervised approaches rely on oversimplified assumptions of coordination among IO users that may not exist in practice. To overcome the limitations of existing methods, we formulate IO user detection as an anomaly detection problem and propose a novel unsupervised IO user detection approach called Temporal-bEhavior-laNguage Signals for information Operation Recognition (TENSOR), which leverages multimodal data, including temporal online user behavior, such as message posting activities, and the textual content of the messages. The motivation is that IO users are typically a very small fraction of all online users and have unique temporal behavioral and language patterns. Specifically, we train a Temporal Point Process (TPP) to capture abnormal temporal behavioral patterns of IO users because they are known to behave in a coordinated manner for IO campaigns. We further introduce a novel evidence function that converts LLM responses, which are generated from user post timelines, into quantitative scores to adjust the TPP outputs for better IO user detection. Experimental results show that TENSOR outperforms the baselines on five real-world IO datasets. Code is available at https://github.com/xiuzhenzhang/TENSOR.

AI.tldr: TENSOR is an unsupervised anomaly detection framework for identifying Information Operation (IO) users on social media. It combines a Temporal Point Process (TPP) to model abnormal coordinated posting behavior with an LLM-based evidence function that scores user post timelines, jointly capturing temporal and linguistic signals. Experiments on five real-world IO datasets show it outperforms existing baselines.
AI.motivation: Information Operations on social media threaten democracy but are costly to detect manually. Supervised methods cannot adapt to evolving IO behavior, and existing unsupervised methods rely on oversimplified coordination assumptions that often fail in practice. The authors are motivated by two observations: IO users constitute a very small fraction of all users (anomaly detection framing), and they exhibit distinctive temporal behavioral and language patterns that can be exploited jointly.
AI.method: The paper formulates IO user detection as an anomaly detection problem and proposes TENSOR. It has two core components: (1) a Temporal Point Process (TPP) trained to capture abnormal temporal behavioral patterns of IO users, exploiting their known coordinated activity; (2) a novel evidence function that converts LLM-generated responses from user post timelines into quantitative scores, which then adjust the TPP outputs to improve detection. The approach is fully unsupervised and multimodal, leveraging both temporal behavior and textual content.
AI.result: Experimental results on five real-world IO datasets demonstrate that TENSOR outperforms all baseline methods in IO user detection.
AI.conclusion: TENSOR effectively addresses the limitations of prior IO detection methods by combining temporal behavior modeling via TPPs with LLM-driven language analysis in an unsupervised anomaly detection framework, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple real-world datasets.

title: TopoBrick: Agentic Topology Sampling of Exogenous Variables for Zero-Shot Building IoT Forecasting
summary: Building sensors are embedded in physical topology, spatial hierarchy, and operational context, yet existing forecasters often treat them as isolated time series or rely on fixed covariate sets. We present TopoBrick, a training-free framework for zero-shot building IoT (Internet-of-Things) forecasting. TopoBrick uses building knowledge graphs to construct a compact structural skeleton and employs an agentic topology sampler to select target-specific exogenous variables. The selected variables are organized by deployment-time availability, separating past-known sensor states from future-known calendar, schedule, and meteorological exogenous variables. Across three real-world buildings, TopoBrick outperforms strong zero-shot foundation-model baselines and remains competitive with fully trained building-specific models. Ablations show that topology-aware sampling is more reliable than random, ontology-only, or fixed-hop selection, especially for physically coupled HVAC and weather-driven sensing variables.

AI.tldr: TopoBrick is a training-free, zero-shot building IoT forecasting framework that uses knowledge graphs and agentic topology sampling to select target-specific exogenous variables, outperforming zero-shot baselines and rivaling fully trained models across three real-world buildings.
AI.motivation: Existing building forecasting methods treat sensors as isolated time series or rely on fixed covariate sets, ignoring the rich physical topology, spatial hierarchy, and operational context in which building sensors are embedded. This limits generalization and adaptability across different buildings.
AI.method: TopoBrick constructs a compact structural skeleton from building knowledge graphs (Brick/Brick+ schema) and employs an agentic topology sampler to select target-specific exogenous variables. Variables are organized by deployment-time availability: past-known sensor states (lagged) vs. future-known exogenous variables (calendar, schedule, meteorological). The framework requires no training.
AI.result: Across three real-world buildings, TopoBrick outperforms strong zero-shot foundation-model baselines and remains competitive with fully trained building-specific models. Ablations demonstrate that topology-aware sampling is more reliable than random, ontology-only, or fixed-hop selection, especially for physically coupled HVAC and weather-driven sensing variables.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging building knowledge graphs for topology-aware variable selection enables effective zero-shot forecasting in smart buildings, bridging the gap between training-free approaches and building-specific trained models.

title: Spider 2.0-AIFunc: Extending Real-World Text-to-SQL to AI-Native SQL Workflows
summary: Major cloud data platforms now expose large language model capabilities as native SQL functions, enabling analysts to perform classification, filtering, sentiment analysis, extraction, similarity search, and aggregation within ordinary SQL queries. Yet existing text-to-SQL benchmarks evaluate only conventional SQL and provide no signal on whether models can generate such AI-native SQL. We introduce Spider 2.0-AIFunc, a benchmark of 465 verified instances across 125 real-world databases covering six types of AI functions on the Snowflake platform. Starting from an existing enterprise text-to-SQL benchmark, we construct Spider 2.0-AIFunc through an agent-based pipeline that rewrites source tasks into AI-native form, simultaneously transforming target queries and refining natural language instructions to make the intended AI-native solution explicit and reduce ambiguity. All instances pass a multi-round repeated execution protocol across temporally separated windows to confirm result stability before release. Evaluating ten state-of-the-art language models, we find that the strongest proprietary models reach 67-70% execution accuracy while the best open-source model achieves 58.1%, a gap driven primarily by errors in predicate specification, schema grounding, and AI function parameterization. Agent frameworks designed for traditional text-to-SQL challenges, such as schema retrieval and relevant table selection, do not transfer effectively to AI-native SQL: a minimal agent setup consistently matches or outperforms more elaborate alternatives, suggesting that the strategies these frameworks employ are less critical in this setting. Data are available at https://github.com/Leolty/Spider2-AIFunc .

AI.tldr: Spider 2.0-AIFunc is a new benchmark with 465 verified instances across 125 databases for evaluating how well language models generate SQL queries that invoke AI functions (classification, sentiment analysis, extraction, etc.) on Snowflake. Top proprietary models achieve 67–70% execution accuracy vs. 58.1% for the best open-source model, with errors concentrated in predicate specification, schema grounding, and AI function parameterization. Traditional text-to-SQL agent frameworks fail to transfer effectively to this AI-native SQL setting.
AI.motivation: Cloud data platforms now expose LLM capabilities as native SQL functions, but existing text-to-SQL benchmarks evaluate only conventional SQL, providing no signal on model performance for AI-native SQL generation. There is a gap in benchmarking infrastructure for this emerging paradigm.
AI.method: Starting from an enterprise text-to-SQL benchmark, the authors use an agent-based pipeline to rewrite source tasks into AI-native form — transforming target queries and refining NL instructions to make intended AI-native solutions explicit. All 465 instances pass a multi-round repeated execution protocol across temporally separated windows to verify result stability. Ten SOTA LMs are evaluated, including both proprietary and open-source models.
AI.result: Top proprietary models reach 67–70% execution accuracy; best open-source model hits 58.1%. Primary error categories are predicate specification, schema grounding, and AI function parameterization. Agent frameworks designed for traditional text-to-SQL (schema retrieval, table selection) do not transfer effectively; a minimal agent setup matches or outperforms more elaborate alternatives.
AI.conclusion: AI-native SQL generation poses distinct challenges from conventional text-to-SQL, and existing agent strategies do not generalize well. The benchmark reveals a significant proprietary vs. open-source performance gap and identifies key failure modes, providing a foundation for future research on AI function integration in SQL generation.

title: Strategic Bargaining in Multi-Buyer Markets: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards for LLM Negotiations
summary:
Negotiation is a fundamental strategic interaction in management science, characterized by agents attempting to reach agreements while protecting private information, such as reservation costs and hidden valuations. A prevalent yet complex scenario involves a single seller negotiating concurrently with multiple buyers, each possessing heterogeneous, private budgets. In such settings, constrained by a limited number of communication turns, the seller must balance exploring the broader market to discover the highest valuation with concentrating sufficient turns on a single target buyer to secure the best possible outcome. Our analysis reveals a significant gap in standard Large Language Models (LLMs): while these models are linguistically proficient, they fail to act as effective economic decision-makers. Specifically, they exhibit a failure to explore the buyer pool, often fixating on the current highest bid rather than strategically investigating the market to discover latent high valuations.
  In this paper, we propose a specialized training recipe using Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR). By anchoring the reward function to objective economic outcomes, the strategic balance between market discovery and surplus extraction emerges natively through the learning process. Our results demonstrate that the trained seller undergoes a multi-stage strategic evolution, learning to leverage price anchoring and strategic probing to identify more profitable counterparties. The agent extracts a substantially higher surplus than frontier models by both improving its persuasive bargaining skills and consistently closing deals with high-value buyers. Finally, we show that our seller strategies generalize robustly to unseen buyer negotiation styles and budget distributions.

AI.tldr: Standard LLMs fail at multi-buyer negotiation because they fixate on the current highest bid instead of exploring the market. The authors propose RLVR training tied to objective economic outcomes, producing a seller agent that learns multi-stage strategies (price anchoring, strategic probing), extracts higher surplus, and generalizes to unseen buyer styles and budget distributions.
AI.motivation: In multi-buyer seller negotiations with limited communication turns, agents must balance market exploration (discovering latent high valuations) with exploitation (securing deals). Standard LLMs, despite linguistic ability, fail as economic decision-makers: they exhibit insufficient exploration of the buyer pool and prematurely fixate on the current highest bidder, leaving surplus uncaptured.
AI.method: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), where the reward function is directly anchored to objective, verifiable economic outcomes (i.e., surplus extracted), rather than human preferences or demonstrations. This allows strategic behaviors like market discovery vs. surplus extraction balance to emerge natively from the learning process.
AI.result: The RLVR-trained seller undergoes multi-stage strategic evolution, learning price anchoring and strategic probing to identify high-value buyers. It extracts substantially higher surplus than frontier LLMs by combining improved persuasive bargaining with consistent deal-closing with the most profitable counterparties. Strategies generalize robustly to unseen buyer negotiation styles and budget distributions.
AI.conclusion: LLMs lack innate economic reasoning for strategic multi-agent settings. RLVR with outcome-based rewards enables the emergence of sophisticated negotiation strategies, outperforming frontier models and demonstrating strong generalization, suggesting a viable path toward competent AI economic agents.

title: Auditing of Unlearning Algorithms
summary: Evaluating whether unlearning algorithms truly remove training data influence remains an open challenge. We propose a practical auditor that computes data-dependent lower bounds on the unlearning parameter $\varepsilon$ using membership inference attacks. Evaluating multiple unlearning algorithms, we find a sharp separation: algorithms with rigorous guarantees, such as model clipping and rewind-to-delete, achieve very small $\varepsilon$ bounds that do not falsify their unlearning guarantees, whereas empirical methods such as Hessian-based unlearning, interleaved ascent-descent, ascent on the forget set, and fine-tuning on the retain set exhibit large bounds, indicating poor unlearning. Our auditor provides a practical tool for empirically falsifying unlearning claims through a hypothesis-testing framework, and we validate it on CIFAR-100 and Shakespeare text.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a practical auditor that uses membership inference attacks to compute data-dependent lower bounds on the unlearning parameter ε, revealing a sharp divide: rigorous unlearning methods achieve small ε bounds while empirical/heuristic methods exhibit large bounds, indicating poor unlearning.
AI.motivation: Evaluating whether machine unlearning algorithms truly eliminate the influence of training data remains an open and challenging problem. There is a need for a practical, empirical tool to audit and potentially falsify unlearning claims.
AI.method: The authors design an auditor based on membership inference attacks (MIAs) that computes data-dependent lower bounds on the unlearning parameter ε within a hypothesis-testing framework. The auditor tests whether the unlearned model can be distinguished from a model retrained from scratch on the retain set.
AI.result: A sharp separation emerges: algorithms with rigorous guarantees (model clipping, rewind-to-delete) yield very small ε bounds that do not falsify their claims, while empirical methods (Hessian-based unlearning, interleaved ascent-descent, ascent on the forget set, fine-tuning on the retain set) produce large ε bounds, signaling poor unlearning. Validated on CIFAR-100 and Shakespeare text.
AI.conclusion: The proposed auditor serves as an effective, practical tool for empirically falsifying unlearning claims. The results highlight a significant gap between theoretically-grounded unlearning algorithms and heuristic empirical approaches, underscoring the need for rigorous unlearning methods.

title: A Definition and Roadmap for World Models
summary: World models -- internal simulators that learn the structure and dynamics of an environment -- have become one of the most actively debated concepts in AI. From model-based reinforcement learning and video generation to embodied robotics and ultimately, physical AI, researchers across AI subfields are building systems that they call "world models", yet there is no consensus on what a world model fundamentally is, what it should predict, or how it should be built. This perspective article provides a scientific definition of world models, discussions of their key technical aspects, and a staged roadmap for developing effective world models.

AI.tldr: This perspective article proposes a scientific definition of "world models," clarifies their key technical aspects, and presents a staged roadmap for their development, addressing the current lack of consensus across AI subfields.
AI.motivation: Despite the widespread use of the term "world models" across model-based RL, video generation, embodied robotics, and physical AI, there is no agreed-upon definition of what a world model is, what it should predict, or how it should be constructed.
AI.method: This is a perspective/position paper that synthesizes insights across AI subfields to propose a scientific definition, analyze key technical dimensions (e.g., what to predict, how to build), and outline a staged developmental roadmap.
AI.result: The paper delivers a unified scientific definition of world models, identifies and discusses critical technical considerations, and proposes a staged roadmap for progressing toward effective world model development.
AI.conclusion: Establishing a shared scientific definition and a clear developmental roadmap is essential for coherent progress in building effective world models, which serve as internal simulators of environmental structure and dynamics across diverse AI applications.

title: Early Language Learning via Spreading Activation and Category Exploration in Complex Networks
summary: Is word acquisition in children uneven with respect to semantic and lexical categories? To answer this question, we model early language learning as a search on a graph-based mental lexicon, driven by two interacting processes: spreading activation and an enforced exploration (rather than exploitation) of lexical categories. We evaluate model performance on four languages (German, English, Dutch, and Rioplatense Spanish), using CDIs as ground-truth data for lexical categories, normative ages derived from the Wordbank repository, and state-of-the-art resources for reconstructing graphs of word similarities. We find that spreading activation outperforms a shortest path baseline in simulating normative word acquisition. At the category level, we highlight complex transitions between CDIs. By studying their sequences in terms of burstiness and average persistence time within the same CDI, we find that spreading activation better captures the exploration dynamics observed empirically. Overall, our findings suggest that vocabulary development can be understood through the non-trivial interplay between activation dynamics and some degree of constraints regulating the visiting of lexical categories in complex networks.

AI.tldr: This paper models early word acquisition as a graph search on a mental lexicon using spreading activation with enforced category exploration. Evaluated across four languages against CDI norms, the model outperforms shortest-path baselines and captures empirical exploration dynamics such as burstiness and category persistence, revealing vocabulary development as an interplay between activation dynamics and constraints on lexical category traversal.
AI.motivation: To determine whether children's word acquisition is uneven across semantic and lexical categories, and to provide a mechanistic, process-based account of vocabulary development beyond descriptive analyses.
AI.method: The authors model early language learning as a search process on a graph-based mental lexicon, driven by two interacting mechanisms: (1) spreading activation from already-acquired words to neighboring nodes, and (2) an enforced exploration strategy that biases the learner toward sampling new lexical/semantic categories rather than exploiting familiar ones. They evaluate using CDI data from Wordbank for four languages (German, English, Dutch, Rioplatense Spanish), normative acquisition ages, and word-similarity graphs from state-of-the-art resources. Performance is compared against a shortest-path baseline, and category-level dynamics are analyzed via burstiness and average persistence time metrics.
AI.result: Spreading activation significantly outperforms the shortest-path baseline in simulating normative word acquisition trajectories. At the category level, the model reveals complex transition patterns between CDI categories. Analysis of category sequences shows that spreading activation better captures the burstiness and average persistence time observed in empirical data, indicating it more faithfully reproduces the exploration dynamics of real vocabulary development.
AI.conclusion: Vocabulary development can be understood as emerging from the interplay between spreading activation dynamics and constraints that regulate the visiting of lexical categories within a complex network structure, supporting a process-oriented view of early word learning.

title: Differentially Private Natural Gradient Descent
summary:
Under a fixed privacy budget, the utility of differentially private (DP) training is ultimately determined by its optimization efficiency. Standard first-order DP optimizers such as DP-SGD rely solely on local gradients and ignore the underlying loss curvature. This geometric blindness causes severe zigzagging in ill-conditioned landscapes, squandering precious privacy budgets on inefficient iterations. Practitioners are thus trapped in a bind: either stop training prematurely or inject massive per-step noise, both of which critically compromise final model utility. Natural Gradient Descent (NGD) resolves this by preconditioning gradients with curvature, aligning updates with the loss geometry and extracting more efficient signal from every noisy step, offering a principled pathway to break the privacy-utility bottleneck.
  Despite its theoretical appeal, directly integrating NGD with DP introduces fundamental challenges: curvature estimation itself consumes prohibitive privacy budgets, isotropic DP operations conflict with the anisotropic scaling of NGD, and the inverse curvature catastrophically amplify parameter updates in flat directions, causing training instability. We propose DP-NGD, a practical framework that systematically addresses these obstacles by decoupling curvature estimation from private data, reconciling isotropic DP constraints with anisotropic second-order optimization via a whitened-space mechanism, and dynamically clamping the curvature to stabilize training. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that DP-NGD achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, breaking through the utility ceilings of first-order baselines while delivering up to a $10\times$ convergence speedup under the same privacy budget.

AI.tldr: DP-NGD integrates Natural Gradient Descent with differential privacy by decoupling curvature estimation from private data, using a whitened-space mechanism to reconcile isotropic DP noise with anisotropic NGD scaling, and dynamically clamping curvature. It achieves SOTA accuracy and up to 10× convergence speedup over first-order DP optimizers under the same privacy budget.
AI.motivation: First-order DP optimizers like DP-SGD ignore loss curvature, causing inefficient zigzagging in ill-conditioned landscapes that wastes privacy budgets. NGD theoretically resolves this via curvature-aware preconditioning, but directly combining NGD with DP faces three challenges: curvature estimation consumes prohibitive privacy budgets, isotropic DP operations conflict with NGD's anisotropic scaling, and inverse curvature amplifies updates in flat directions, destabilizing training.
AI.method: DP-NGD addresses the three challenges through: (1) decoupling curvature estimation from private data to avoid privacy budget consumption; (2) a whitened-space mechanism that reconciles isotropic DP constraints with anisotropic second-order optimization; and (3) dynamic curvature clamping to stabilize training by preventing catastrophic amplification in flat directions.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks show DP-NGD achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, breaks through the utility ceilings of first-order baselines, and delivers up to 10× convergence speedup under the same privacy budget.
AI.conclusion: DP-NGD provides a principled and practical framework for curvature-aware differentially private training, breaking the privacy-utility bottleneck that constrains first-order DP optimizers.

title: ExplAIner: A Declarative Query Language for Explaining Classification Models
summary: The XAI community has studied a wide range of queries and scores for explaining predictions of ML models. From a data management perspective, this proliferation of explanation notions calls for declarative query languages in which such notions can be specified, combined, and analyzed uniformly. In this paper, we develop such a framework for Boolean models. We first revisit FOIL, an interpretability query language for black-box models, and show that it has two fundamental limitations: it cannot express central optimality-based explanation queries, and its evaluation problem over decision trees is hard for every level of the polynomial hierarchy. We then introduce ExplAIner, a query language based on FOIL with an extended vocabulary and a layered structure. We show that ExplAIner can express a broad family of explanation notions, including abductive, contrastive, feature-based, and distance-based queries. We also prove that the evaluation problem for each query in ExplAIner belongs to the Boolean hierarchy over every class of Boolean models for which some basic predicates can be evaluated in polynomial time. In particular, that property holds for deterministic and decomposable Boolean circuits. Finally, we introduce Opt-FOIL, an optimization-oriented fragment of ExplAIner for computing explanations that are minimal with respect to strict partial orders, and prove that its evaluation problem is in $\mathrm{FP}^{\mathrm{NP}}$ under the same tractability assumptions. These complexity results have a direct algorithmic consequence: a fixed ExplAIner query can be evaluated with a fixed number of calls to a SAT solver, while a notion of explanation specified in Opt-FOIL can be computed with a polynomial number of such calls. This is particularly relevant in formal XAI, where SAT solvers have been successfully used to compute explanations for several classes of ML models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ExplAIner, a declarative query language for specifying and evaluating explanation notions in Boolean ML models. It overcomes limitations of the prior FOIL language by supporting optimality-based explanations, achieving evaluation within the Boolean hierarchy (not the full polynomial hierarchy), and offering Opt-FOIL for computing minimal explanations in FP^NP.
AI.motivation: From a data management perspective, the proliferation of XAI explanation notions (abductive, contrastive, feature-based, distance-based, etc.) demands a unified declarative framework to specify, combine, and analyze them. Existing language FOIL has two critical limitations: (1) inability to express optimality-based explanation queries, and (2) evaluation hardness spanning every level of the polynomial hierarchy, even over decision trees.
AI.method: The authors first formally analyze FOIL's limitations. They then design ExplAIner, a layered query language extending FOIL with enriched vocabulary to express optimality. They characterize the evaluation complexity of ExplAIner queries within the Boolean hierarchy, assuming polynomial-time evaluation of basic predicates — a property satisfied by deterministic and decomposable Boolean circuits. They further introduce Opt-FOIL, an optimization fragment for minimal explanations under strict partial orders, and prove its evaluation complexity as FP^NP.
AI.result: ExplAIner subsumes a broad range of explanation types. Each ExplAIner query evaluates within the Boolean hierarchy (rather than arbitrary levels of PH), and Opt-FOIL queries are in FP^NP, both under the assumption that basic predicates are polytime computable. Concretely, a fixed ExplAIner query requires only a fixed number of SAT solver calls, while Opt-FOIL explanations require a polynomial number.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a practical path for implementing XAI explanations via SAT solvers, directly connecting complexity-theoretic results to algorithmic deployment. The work positions explanation specification as a data management problem and advances formal XAI by taming the complexity of diverse explanation notions through careful language design.

title: From Sinhala to Dhivehi: Cross-Lingual Transfer Learning for Low-Resource Speech Recognition
comment: 7 pages, 1 figure, 8 tables, Accepted paper at the 12th International Moratuwa Engineering Research Conference (MERCon) 2026
summary: Dhivehi, the national language of the Maldives, is currently under-resourced for automatic speech recognition (ASR) and other NLP tasks. This study investigates whether cross-lingual transfer learning from Sinhala, a linguistically related, relatively well-resourced Insular Indo-Aryan language, can improve Dhivehi ASR. We conduct seventeen experiments across five transfer learning paradigms: Dhivehi-only baselines, sequential fine-tuning, multilingual fine-tuning, continual pre-training, and a control using Turkish as an unrelated language. The strongest system, continual pre-training on Sinhala followed by fine-tuning on Dhivehi with KenLM, achieves 12.89% WER and 2.70% CER, outperforming the Dhivehi-only baseline by 13.50% WER and 3.02% CER. However, the adaptation strategy and decoding configuration are equally critical for a successful transfer learning experiment. We conduct seventeen controlled experiments spanning five transfer learning paradigms: Dhivehi-only baselines, sequential fine-tuning, multilingual fine-tuning, continual pre-training, and a control experiment using Turkish as an unrelated language. The strongest system, continual pre-training on Sinhala followed by fine-tuning on Dhivehi with KenLM, achieves 12.89% WER and 2.70% CER, outperforming the Dhivehi-only baseline by 13.50% WER and 3.02% CER. The Turkish control experiment confirms that observed improvements stem from linguistic relatedness; adaptation strategy and decoding configuration are also critical.

AI.tldr: Cross-lingual transfer learning from Sinhala significantly improves Dhivehi ASR, with continual pre-training achieving 12.89% WER (a 13.50% absolute improvement). Linguistic relatedness drives the gains, but adaptation strategy and decoding configuration are equally critical.
AI.motivation: Dhivehi, the national language of the Maldives, is severely under-resourced for automatic speech recognition (ASR) and other NLP tasks. Since Sinhala is a linguistically related, relatively well-resourced Insular Indo-Aryan language, the authors hypothesize that cross-lingual transfer learning from Sinhala can compensate for the scarcity of Dhivehi ASR resources.
AI.method: The study conducts 17 controlled experiments across five transfer learning paradigms: (1) Dhivehi-only baselines, (2) sequential fine-tuning (Sinhala → Dhivehi), (3) multilingual fine-tuning (joint training), (4) continual pre-training on Sinhala followed by Dhivehi fine-tuning, and (5) a control experiment using Turkish (an unrelated language) to isolate linguistic relatedness effects. Decoding is tested with and without KenLM language model integration.
AI.result: The best-performing system — continual pre-training on Sinhala followed by fine-tuning on Dhivehi with KenLM — achieves 12.89% WER and 2.70% CER, outperforming the Dhivehi-only baseline by 13.50% absolute WER and 3.02% absolute CER. The Turkish control experiment confirms that improvements are attributable to linguistic relatedness rather than general multilingual effects. Adaptation strategy and decoding configuration are shown to be equally critical factors for successful transfer.
AI.conclusion: Cross-lingual transfer from a linguistically related language (Sinhala) substantially improves under-resourced Dhivehi ASR. However, careful selection of transfer learning strategy and decoding configuration is essential — linguistic relatedness alone is insufficient without proper methodological choices.

title: No Subspace to Track: Non-Identifiability and Optimizer State in Low-Rank Training
summary: Memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore train large language models by projecting gradients onto a rank-r subspace recomputed every T steps, assuming this subspace is a slowly drifting object that can be tracked. We show that beyond a small reproducible core, there is no such object. Two estimates of the top-r subspace computed at the same step from disjoint minibatches disagree as much as estimates computed T steps apart (0.73 vs 0.74 of the maximal chordal distance sqrt(2r), at Pythia-160M with r=128): the apparent rotation at each refresh is dominated by estimator noise. This holds across four model families in three architecture classes from 70M to 6.9B parameters, strengthening with scale, and more weakly in a vision transformer. Only ~39 of 128 directions are reproducible across minibatches, and averaging cannot recover the rest: under N-fold averaging the gradient's spectral tail shrinks as N^(-1/4) rather than the N^(-1/2) of pure noise, so no averaging budget makes the subspace well defined. What helps instead follows from treating each refresh as a change of coordinates for Adam's state. Carrying the second moment blindly is provably about (r-k*)/2 worse than the best rotation-blind estimator, while the first moment transports exactly through the rotation, the optimal linear map under isotropic gradients and the rule LDAdam uses. At 1B over 40k steps (3 seeds), full LDAdam reaches 18.7 perplexity at beta2=0.999, beating untransported GaLore after its best beta2 fix (19.3); shortening the second-moment memory to beta2=0.99 helps the refreshing optimizers, though for canonical GaLore the effect is small and a full-rank control reverses it. One measurable fact, subspace non-identifiability, clarifies why GaLore works, which patches work, and what to check before trusting a low-rank assumption: the reproducible rank k*.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the core assumption behind memory-efficient optimizers like GaLore — that gradient subspaces drift slowly and can be tracked. The authors demonstrate that gradient subspaces are fundamentally non-identifiable across minibatches, with estimator noise dominating any true rotation. They propose LDAdam, which correctly transports Adam's state through subspace refreshes, outperforming GaLore.
AI.motivation: Memory-efficient optimizers like GaLore reduce training costs by projecting gradients onto low-rank subspaces recomputed periodically, relying on the assumption that these subspaces drift slowly.
