The authors question whether this "slowly drifting subspace" actually exists as a well-defined object, or whether the observed rotation is merely estimator noise — a question with direct implications for optimizer design and the validity of low-rank training assumptions.
AI.method: The authors conduct empirical analyses across four model families (Pythia, LLaMA, GPT-2, ViT) from 70M to 6.9B parameters. They compare subspace estimates from disjoint minibatches at the same step versus estimates T steps apart using chordal distance. They analyze the spectral decay of gradient covariance under N-fold averaging, derive the optimal transport rule for Adam's first and second moments under subspace rotation, and propose LDAdam — which exactly transports the first moment while handling the second moment with a provably near-optimal rotation-blind estimator.
AI.result: Subspace estimates from disjoint minibatches at the same step disagree nearly as much as estimates T steps apart (0.73 vs 0.74 chordal distance at r=128), showing estimator noise dominates apparent rotation. Only ~39 of 128 directions are reproducible across minibatches. Under N-fold averaging, the gradient spectral tail decays as N^(-1/4) rather than N^(-1/2), making the subspace fundamentally ill-defined regardless of averaging budget. LDAdam achieves 18.7 perplexity at 1B scale versus 19.3 for GaLore with its best beta2 fix.
AI.conclusion: The concept of a "slowly drifting gradient subspace" is a mirage — there is only a small reproducible core (k* directions) plus noise. GaLore works despite, not because of, subspace tracking. The correct approach is to treat subspace refreshes as coordinate changes and transport optimizer state accordingly, as LDAdam does. The reproducible rank k* serves as a measurable diagnostic for when low-rank assumptions may hold.

title: Finding H. pylori in the Fine Print: Evidence-Linked Multi-Agent Case Finding from Gastric Biopsy Reports
summary: Data from Singapore indicated that about 31% of the population had evidence of Helicobacter pylori infection. Persistent H. pylori infection is associated with chronic active gastritis and peptic ulcer disease, and its eradication is key to gastric cancer prevention. However, evidence supporting \textit{H. pylori} positivity and H. pylori-associated gastritis may be distributed across heterogeneous coded and free-text report fields and may require contextual interpretation of assertion and negation, limiting keyword search, and making manual review difficult to scale. We conducted a retrospective pilot evaluation of the Nimblemind Multi-Agent System (nMAS), a field-name-driven, evidence-linked extraction workflow, using 54 de-identified gastric biopsy pathology reports from a large healthcare system in Singapore. Four clinician-scoped binary fields were evaluated: gastric/stomach biopsy, biopsy status, H. pylori positivity, and H. pylori-associated gastritis. Across 216 feature-case decisions, nMAS correctly classified 213, corresponding to 98.61% overall accuracy. A separately implemented UMA-style MiniMax M2.5 comparator produced similar aggregate and per-field classification metrics. Although predictive performance was similar, nMAS maintained unified report-level outputs with supporting source sentences; the demonstrated contribution is therefore workflow integration and traceability rather than predictive superiority. Under an illustrative, unmeasured scenario, reviewing 1,000 reports at five minutes per manual review versus five seconds per evidence-linked verification would reduce review time from 83.3 to 1.4 staff-hours, corresponding to 81.9 staff-hours and about USD~6,100 in potential staff-time value. Larger multi-institutional studies should evaluate evidence-span correctness, clinician verification time, and generalizability.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent system (nMAS) achieved 98.61% accuracy in extracting H. pylori status and associated gastritis from gastric biopsy pathology reports, with key contributions in workflow integration and evidence traceability rather than predictive superiority over existing methods.
AI.motivation: H. pylori infection affects ~31% of Singapore's population and is linked to gastric cancer. Relevant clinical evidence is scattered across heterogeneous coded and free-text report fields, requiring nuanced assertion/negation interpretation. Keyword search is insufficient, and manual review does not scale, motivating an automated, interpretable extraction workflow.
AI.method: Retrospective pilot evaluation of the Nimblemind Multi-Agent System (nMAS) — a field-name-driven, evidence-linked extraction workflow — on 54 de-identified gastric biopsy pathology reports from a Singapore healthcare system. Four binary clinician-scoped fields were evaluated: gastric/stomach biopsy, biopsy status, H. pylori positivity, and H. pylori-associated gastritis. An UMA-style MiniMax M2.5 model served as comparator.
AI.result: nMAS correctly classified 213 of 216 feature-case decisions (98.61% overall accuracy). The MiniMax M2.5 comparator produced similar aggregate and per-field metrics. nMAS uniquely provided unified report-level outputs with supporting source sentences, demonstrating workflow integration and traceability. An illustrative scenario showed review time reduction from 83.3 to 1.4 staff-hours per 1,000 reports (~USD $6,100 savings).
AI.conclusion: nMAS delivers high-accuracy, traceable extraction of H. pylori-related findings from pathology reports. Its primary contribution lies in evidence-linked workflow integration rather than predictive superiority. Larger multi-institutional studies are needed to validate evidence-span correctness, clinician verification time, and generalizability.

title: Estimating Uncertainty from Reasoning: A Large-Scale Study of Multi- and Crosslingual MCQA Performance in LLMs
summary: Uncertainty estimation (UE) enables LLM-powered systems to recognize when to abstain, yet existing research has predominantly focused on English. We present the first large-scale evaluation of UE methods across 22 languages, spanning high-, mid-, and low-resource settings. Using two human-curated Q\&A datasets, we compare open and closed box UE methods (nine in total) across different model sizes and architectures while eliciting long-form reasoning, avoiding LLM-as-a-judge and embedding-based scoring, which can introduce evaluation noise. We report three main actionable findings. First, we find that prompting models to reason in English while keeping questions in low-resource languages substantially improves UE performance, suggesting that comprehension of low-resource languages is largely intact, and that the reliability bottleneck lies in generation rather than understanding. Second, prompting models to reason in English closes the UE performance gap between low and high-resource languages, demonstrating that generation language matters more than the question language. Third, the choice of UE method should depend on model scale: at smaller scales, open-box probability-based methods outperform alternatives; at larger scales, closed-box self-verbalized uncertainty becomes superior. Finally, we provide an analysis of threshold selection for selective prediction, offering guidance on calibrating abstention in multilingual settings.

AI.tldr: First large-scale multilingual evaluation of uncertainty estimation (UE) methods across 22 languages, finding that prompting LLMs to reason in English dramatically improves UE performance for low-resource languages, and that optimal UE method choice depends on model scale.
AI.motivation: Existing UE research focuses almost exclusively on English, leaving a critical gap in understanding how to enable reliable abstention in multilingual LLM systems. The authors aim to characterize UE performance across diverse languages and identify actionable strategies for improving reliability in low-resource settings.
AI.method: Evaluation of 9 UE methods (both open-box probability-based and closed-box verbalized) across multiple model sizes/architectures using two human-curated multilingual Q&A datasets spanning 22 languages (high-, mid-, low-resource). Long-form reasoning is elicited; LLM-as-a-judge and embedding-based scoring are avoided to reduce evaluation noise.
AI.result: Three main findings: (1) Prompting models to reason in English while keeping questions in low-resource languages substantially improves UE performance, indicating comprehension is intact and the bottleneck is generation. (2) English reasoning closes the UE performance gap between low and high-resource languages. (3) Open-box probability-based methods are superior at smaller model scales, while closed-box self-verbalized uncertainty excels at larger scales.
AI.conclusion: Generation language matters more than question language for UE reliability in multilingual settings. Practitioners should consider model scale when selecting UE methods, and English-language reasoning prompts offer a practical strategy for improving abstention decisions in low-resource languages.

title: Automated Compliance Mapping in Cloud Security with Domain-Adapted Sentence Transformers
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to the 30th International Conference on Knowledge-Based and Intelligent Information & Engineering Systems (KES 2026)
summary: Mapping cloud security controls to technical metrics is currently a manual process. This paper proposes domain adaptation of Sentence Transformer models to automate it. We build a training corpus of 3,499 semantic pairs from five European security standards and a set of technical metrics, then expand it via back-translation and LLM-based paraphrasing to up to 13,996 samples across four scenarios. We fine-tune five architectures and evaluate their performance on two independent tasks: control-to-metric and cross-standard controls association. All fine-tuned models outperform their zero-shot baselines. On the control-to-metric task, the best model gains up to 23 nDCG@10 points, while on the cross-standard control task, \textit{multi-qa-mpnet-dot-v1} under back-translation reaches 0.870 nDCG@10. The results show that in-domain training data is a primary driver of performance for the considered case studies.

AI.tldr: This paper automates the mapping of cloud security controls to technical metrics by fine-tuning Sentence Transformer models on a domain-specific corpus, achieving up to 23 nDCG@10 improvement over zero-shot baselines.
AI.motivation: Mapping cloud security controls to technical metrics is currently a manual, labor-intensive process lacking automation. The authors aim to replace this manual effort with an automated semantic matching approach using domain-adapted sentence embeddings.
AI.method: The authors construct a training corpus of 3,499 semantic pairs derived from five European security standards and a set of technical metrics. They augment this corpus via back-translation and LLM-based paraphrasing to yield up to 13,996 samples across four scenarios. Five Sentence Transformer architectures are fine-tuned and evaluated on two tasks: (1) control-to-metric mapping and (2) cross-standard controls association, with performance measured by nDCG@10 against zero-shot baselines.
AI.result: All fine-tuned models outperform zero-shot baselines. For control-to-metric mapping, the best model achieves up to a 23-point nDCG@10 gain. For cross-standard control association, multi-qa-mpnet-dot-v1 with back-translation reaches 0.870 nDCG@10. In-domain training data is identified as the primary performance driver.
AI.conclusion: Domain adaptation of Sentence Transformers via fine-tuning on in-domain semantic pairs is highly effective for automating cloud security control mapping. The approach generalizes well across both direct control-to-metric and cross-standard association tasks, with data quality and domain relevance being more critical than model architecture or augmentation technique.

title: K-ABENA: K-Adaptive Backpropagation with Error-based N-exclusion Algorithm : (Compensated Loss-Based Sample Exclusion with Unbiased Gradient Estimation)
comment: 11 pages main text + appendices, 13 pages total. Code: https://github.com/Bonbhel/kabena-ml
summary: We present K-ABENA (K-Adaptive Backpropagation with Error-based N-exclusion Algorithm), a selective gradient computation framework that reduces per-iteration training cost by excluding a fraction of low-loss ("minor") observations from the backward pass. Its canonical form (v3) combines a defensive-mixture sampling design over the minor set with Horvitz-Thompson inverse-probability reweighting, yielding a design-unbiased Horvitz-Thompson gradient estimator (Lemma 2) and whose self-normalized practical variant carries a bias of order O(1/m) with an explicit constant (Lemma 3). We prove an O(1/sqrt(T)) non-convex convergence guarantee for SGD under the estimator, with an additive term that quantifies the residual bias (Theorem 1). We further prove that uncompensated loss-based selection - a family that includes OHEM, SBP, and the two earlier K-ABENA variants - admits no stationary point at any minimizer where its selection bias is bounded away from zero (Proposition 2), and we quantify this failure empirically: at 0.17% class imbalance, uncompensated variants reach test AUC 0.53-0.62 versus 0.9998 for full-batch SGD, while the compensated estimator attains 0.9991 at identical 28.4% compute savings. On real datasets (Breast Cancer, Digits, Wine, Diabetes) the compensated estimator is statistically indistinguishable from full-batch SGD (paired permutation tests, p >= 0.5; Section 7) while saving 28-54% of per-epoch gradient computation. A biased "regularized mode" (the earlier half-domain variant) is retained as an option with a proven exact bias decomposition (Lemma 5) and quantified contraindications: it collapses to 0.386 accuracy under 40% label noise (baseline: 0.832) and to 0.53 AUC under extreme imbalance. Every advantage and every limitation reported in this paper is either proved or measured; all experiments are CPU-scale (NumPy/scikit-learn) and their scope is stated explicitly.

AI.tldr: K-ABENA is a selective backpropagation framework that skips low-loss examples during the backward pass while using Horvitz-Thompson reweighting to maintain estimator quality, achieving full-batch-equivalent accuracy with 28–54% compute savings and provable convergence guarantees.
AI.motivation: Reducing the per-iteration computational cost of training neural networks by selectively excluding examples from backpropagation, while avoiding the severe accuracy degradation that uncompensated loss-based selection (e.g., OHEM, SBP) suffers under class imbalance and label noise.
AI.method: K-ABENA v3 employs a defensive-mixture sampling design over low-loss ("minor") observations combined with Horvitz-Thompson inverse-probability reweighting to produce a design-unbiased gradient estimator. The framework includes convergence analysis for non-convex SGD (O(1/sqrt(T)) rate), formal characterization of residual bias (O(1/m)), and a proof that uncompensated loss-based selection admits no stationary point at minimizers when selection bias is non-zero. A biased "regularized mode" is also analyzed via exact bias decomposition.
AI.result: At 0.17% class imbalance, the compensated estimator achieves AUC 0.9991 vs. 0.9998 for full-batch SGD at 28.4% compute savings, while uncompensated variants collapse to AUC 0.53–0.62. On Breast Cancer, Digits, Wine, and Diabetes datasets, compensated K-ABENA is statistically indistinguishable from full-batch SGD (paired permutation tests, p ≥ 0.5) while saving 28–54% gradient computation. The biased regularized mode degrades to 0.386 accuracy under 40% label noise (baseline 0.832) and 0.53 AUC under extreme imbalance.
AI.conclusion: Horvitz-Thompson reweighting is essential for selective backpropagation to avoid catastrophic failure under distributional challenges like class imbalance. The compensated K-ABENA v3 framework provides a principled, provably convergent alternative to full-batch SGD with substantial computational savings and no statistically significant accuracy loss on standard benchmarks.

title: A Physics-Informed Neural Network Framework for Elastodynamic Wave Propagation in Bimaterial Systems
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) provide a promising framework for solving partial differential equations while embedding the underlying physical laws directly into the learning process. This study presents a PINN-based framework for modeling transient elastodynamic wave propagation in bimaterial systems governed by the axisymmetric equations of linear elasticity. A steel-aluminum specimen representative of a Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar configuration is considered, and the governing elastodynamic equations, together with the corresponding initial, boundary, and interface conditions, are incorporated directly into the network through a physics-informed loss function. High-fidelity finite-element simulations performed using ANSYS Workbench Explicit Dynamics are used for validation and as supplementary data constraints during training. The proposed framework accurately predicts wave transmission and reflection across the bimaterial interface and reproduces axial and radial displacement histories, face-averaged responses, and the dominant stress and strain evolution with close agreement to the finite-element solutions. The trained network further demonstrates the ability to predict wave responses at previously unseen time instants and for modified material properties without requiring additional finite-element simulations, providing a continuous surrogate model for elastodynamic analysis. Mesh-sensitivity studies confirm numerical robustness, while additional material combinations demonstrate the generality of the proposed methodology. The results show that integrating physics-informed neural networks with explicit finite-element analysis provides an accurate and computationally efficient framework for elastodynamic wave propagation in heterogeneous solids, offering an effective surrogate modeling approach for high-rate solid mechanics and impact engineering applications.

AI.tldr: A PINN-based framework models transient elastodynamic wave propagation in bimaterial systems, validated against high-fidelity FEM. The approach accurately predicts wave transmission/reflection, generalizes to unseen times and modified material properties, and offers an efficient surrogate model for impact engineering.
AI.motivation: Traditional numerical methods like FEM for elastodynamic wave propagation in heterogeneous solids are computationally expensive for parametric studies. A need exists for accurate, continuous surrogate models that can generalize across time instants and material properties without repeated simulations.
AI.method: A PINN framework solves axisymmetric linear elasticity equations for a steel-aluminum bimaterial system (Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar configuration). Governing equations, initial conditions, boundary conditions, and interface conditions are embedded in a physics-informed loss function. High-fidelity ANSYS Explicit Dynamics FEM simulations provide validation and supplementary training constraints. Mesh-sensitivity studies and testing on additional material combinations assess robustness and generality.
AI.result: The framework accurately predicts wave transmission and reflection across the bimaterial interface, reproducing axial/radial displacement histories, face-averaged responses, and dominant stress-strain evolution with close FEM agreement. The network generalizes to unseen time instants and modified material properties without retraining. Mesh-sensitivity studies confirm numerical robustness, and additional material combinations validate generality.
AI.conclusion: Integrating PINNs with explicit FEM provides an accurate, computationally efficient surrogate modeling framework for elastodynamic wave propagation in heterogeneous solids, well-suited for high-rate solid mechanics and impact engineering applications.

title: From Voting to Agent Collaboration: Answer-Type-Aware LLM Pipelines for BioASQ 14b
summary: Biomedical question answering requires not only accurate extraction of information from scientific literature but also reliable integration of evidence across multiple documents. This study presents a question-type-specific large language model (LLM) framework for BioASQ 14b Task B, designed to improve answer robustness and evidence grounding in biomedical question answering. Rather than applying a single prompting strategy to all questions, the framework selects different inference procedures for yes/no, factoid, and list questions according to their distinct reasoning and evaluation requirements. For yes/no questions, snippet shuffling and self-reflection are used to reduce sensitivity to evidence ordering and improve decision stability. For factoid questions, full-snippet input is combined with chain-of-thought-based in-context learning to support accurate biomedical entity identification. For list questions, a multi-agent architecture is employed, in which evidence extraction, candidate generation, answer verification, and final aggregation are handled collaboratively. Preliminary experiments on BioASQ 13b were used to identify effective inference strategies for each question type, and the resulting framework was subsequently evaluated in the official BioASQ 14b Task B challenge. In the official evaluation, our framework showed competitive performance across multiple batches and achieved first place in the factoid subtask of Batch 4. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of combining question-type-specific inference, ensemble prediction, and agent-based verification for reliable biomedical question answering.

AI.tldr: A question-type-specific LLM framework for biomedical QA (BioASQ 14b Task B) uses distinct inference strategies for yes/no, factoid, and list questions — achieving first place in the factoid subtask of Batch 4 through tailored prompting, self-reflection, chain-of-thought, and multi-agent architectures.
AI.motivation: Biomedical QA requires accurate information extraction from scientific literature and reliable multi-document evidence integration. A one-size-fits-all prompting strategy is insufficient because different question types (yes/no, factoid, list) have fundamentally distinct reasoning and evaluation requirements.
AI.method: A question-type-specific framework selects different inference procedures per question type: (1) Yes/no — snippet shuffling with self-reflection to reduce ordering sensitivity and improve decision stability; (2) Factoid — full-snippet input with chain-of-thought-based in-context learning for biomedical entity identification; (3) List — a multi-agent architecture with collaborative evidence extraction, candidate generation, answer verification, and final aggregation. Strategies were tuned on BioASQ 13b and evaluated on BioASQ 14b Task B.
AI.result: The framework showed competitive performance across multiple batches and achieved first place in the factoid subtask of Batch 4 in the official BioASQ 14b Task B evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Combining question-type-specific inference, ensemble prediction, and agent-based verification is effective for reliable biomedical question answering, demonstrating that tailoring LLM strategies to question structure yields robust, evidence-grounded results.

title: More Convincing, Not More Correct: Self-Play Reward Hacking of Reference-Free LLM Judges
comment: 9 pages main text, 15 pages total including references and appendix; 4 figures
summary: Training a language model against its own reference-free judgments (the premise of self-rewarding, self-play, and LLM-as-a-judge pipelines) assumes a model's verdict on a shown answer tracks correctness. We show it fails structurally: conditioned on a candidate, a judge scores plausibility, not correctness, leaving false-positive basins a policy learns to exploit. We measure this with a hidden-anchor audit: a held-out, cross-source exact-match check the judge never sees. On GSM8K with Qwen3 policies, self-play drives the judge's pass rate from 0.72 to 0.94 while true accuracy stays at 0.20 (three seeds). This reward hacking is not white-box gaming: the errors transfer across judge families (Qwen, Llama, Gemma) and scales, a strict three-judge ensemble still accepts 55% of them, and no plausibility-scoring defense closes the basin. The decisive variable is whether the judge commits an answer of its own before using the candidate: committing first drops the false-positive rate from 0.719 to 0.012, blind solving lifts discrimination to 0.96, and used as the training reward the de-anchored channel keeps false positives at zero, preventing the basin rather than only detecting it. A falsifiable bound (the gap is at most 1 - accuracy) predicts which regimes are exposed. The full arc replicates without training under best-of-N selection in code and competition math, and with a Gemma policy.

AI.tldr: Self-rewarding language model training fails because judges evaluate candidate plausibility rather than correctness, creating exploitable false-positive basins. A "hidden-anchor audit" reveals self-play inflates judge pass rates while true accuracy collapses. The fix: having the judge commit its own answer before evaluating a candidate eliminates reward hacking.
AI.motivation: Self-rewarding, self-play, and LLM-as-a-judge pipelines assume a model's own judgments correlate with correctness. The authors demonstrate this assumption is structurally flawed — models conditioned on a candidate answer score plausibility, not correctness, enabling policies to exploit false-positive basins during training.
AI.method: The authors introduce a "hidden-anchor audit": a held-out, cross-source exact-match check that the judge never sees, measuring the gap between judge pass rate and true accuracy. Experiments use GSM8K with Qwen3 policies under self-play training. They further test cross-family transfer (Qwen, Llama, Gemma), three-judge ensembles, and plausibility-scoring defenses. The key intervention is "de-anchoring": forcing the judge to commit its own answer before seeing the candidate. Results are replicated under best-of-N selection in code and competition math, and with a Gemma policy.
AI.result: Self-play drives judge pass rate from 0.72 to 0.94 while true accuracy remains at 0.20. Cross-family transfer shows errors generalize across judge architectures and scales. A three-judge ensemble still accepts 55% of errors. No plausibility-scoring defense closes the basin. Committing an answer first drops false-positive rate from 0.719 to 0.012, yields discrimination of 0.96, and keeps false positives at zero when used as training reward. The gap is bounded by 1 - accuracy. Results replicate without training under best-of-N selection and with a Gemma policy.
AI.conclusion: The structural failure of reference-free judgment is that conditioning on a candidate collapses evaluation into plausibility scoring rather than correctness verification. De-anchoring — forcing the judge to solve independently first — prevents the false-positive basin rather than merely detecting it, offering a principled fix. A falsifiable bound (gap ≤ 1 − accuracy) predicts vulnerable regimes.

title: Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning for Multi Objective Battery Management in Dairy Farms
summary: The dairy industry in Ireland has a large potential for the integration of renewable energy and the reduction of carbon emissions. However, researchers of distributed generation control are mainly focused on residential and commercial applications. To contribute to the effective integration of renewable energy in the dairy sector, this paper presents a multi-objective optimisation control system based on differential evolution and multi agent Deep Reinforcement Learning. The proposed control is organised in two layers: the upper layer uses dynamic pricing, and the lower layer is based on multi-agent reinforcement learning for battery management. This paper also simulates the electrical response of the proposed control system in a rural distribution circuit. The simulation results show that the proposed control framework can improve profits from energy arbitrage up to 18% compared to using Rule-based models, increase the use of distributed generation without significantly increasing cost, and comply with the Irish grid code in terms of voltage variation.

AI.tldr: A two-layer control system combining differential evolution (upper layer, dynamic pricing) and multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (lower layer, battery management) is proposed to optimize renewable energy integration in Ireland's dairy industry, achieving up to 18% profit improvement over rule-based models while maintaining grid code compliance.
AI.motivation: While Ireland's dairy sector holds significant potential for renewable energy integration and carbon reduction, existing distributed generation control research has predominantly focused on residential and commercial applications, leaving the dairy industry underserved. This gap motivates the development of a tailored control framework.
AI.method: A two-layer multi-objective optimization control system: (1) an upper layer employing differential evolution for dynamic pricing optimization, and (2) a lower layer using multi-agent deep reinforcement learning for battery energy management. The framework is validated through electrical simulation on a rural distribution circuit.
AI.result: The proposed framework achieves up to 18% higher profits from energy arbitrage compared to rule-based baselines, increases distributed generation utilization without substantial cost increases, and maintains voltage variation within Irish grid code limits.
AI.conclusion: The dual-layer DE-MADRL control system effectively enhances renewable energy integration and economic returns in the dairy sector while ensuring grid compliance, demonstrating its viability for rural industrial applications beyond conventional residential/commercial contexts.

title: Data Analysis in the Wild: Benchmarking Large Language Models Against Real-World Data Complexities
summary: Current benchmarks for evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) in data analysis often fail to reflect real-world settings. They typically focus on fact retrieval from small tables and overlook the challenges of large multi-tabular datasets, external knowledge integration, and exploratory insight discovery. We introduce DataGovBench, a benchmark derived from governmental open data designed to evaluate LLMs in practical scenarios. The benchmark includes two tasks: Table QA that requires solving complex decomposable questions and producing textual answers or visualizations, and Table Insight that evaluates the ability of models to generate expert-level findings through exploratory data analysis. Comprehensive experiments with state-of-the-art LLMs, both with and without agentic frameworks, reveal significant performance gaps across both tasks. These results suggest that current LLM-based systems remain far from satisfying the demands of real-world data analytics. DataGovBench provides a challenging benchmark for advancing research on LLMs capable of both answering analytical queries and discovering insights from data. Code and sample data are available at https://github.com/SoHasegawa/datagovbench.

AI.tldr: DataGovBench is a new benchmark built from governmental open data to evaluate LLMs on realistic data analysis tasks—Table QA (complex, decomposable questions with text/visualization outputs) and Table Insight (exploratory insight discovery). Experiments reveal that current LLMs, even with agentic frameworks, fall significantly short of real-world analytical demands.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM benchmarks for data analysis are unrealistic: they focus on small tables, simple fact retrieval, and ignore challenges like large multi-tabular datasets, external knowledge integration, and exploratory insight discovery. There is a need for a benchmark that reflects practical, real-world analytical scenarios.
AI.method: The authors construct DataGovBench from governmental open data, comprising two tasks: (1) Table QA — complex, decomposable questions requiring textual answers or visualizations; (2) Table Insight — generating expert-level findings via exploratory data analysis. They evaluate state-of-the-art LLMs, both standalone and augmented with agentic frameworks, across both tasks.
AI.result: Comprehensive experiments show significant performance gaps across both tasks for all evaluated LLMs, including those with agentic frameworks. No current system approaches satisfactory performance, highlighting a substantial gap between existing capabilities and the demands of real-world data analytics.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM-based systems remain far from meeting the requirements of practical data analysis. DataGovBench serves as a challenging testbed to drive progress toward LLMs capable of both answering analytical queries and autonomously discovering insights from complex, multi-tabular datasets.

title: Drift Happens: An Empirical Study of Neural Architecture Robustness to Temporal Distribution Shift
comment: 33 pages, 28 figures. Extended version of the QCDS 2026 proceedings paper; proceedings version to appear in Springer LNCS. Interactive website: https://drift-happens.org/
summary:
Real-world data distributions evolve over time, inducing temporal distribution shift that can substantially degrade the reliability of deployed machine learning systems. However, the extent to which architectural choices and their associated inductive biases affect temporal robustness remains insufficiently understood.
  We present a systematic empirical comparison of temporal robustness across three heterogeneous, time-indexed domains encompassing image classification, multi-label text classification, and text regression tasks. Using a unified evaluation framework based on temporal drift matrices, we train models on cumulative historical data and evaluate their performance on both earlier and later time periods, thereby quantifying cross-temporal generalization. Our study spans model families ranging from simple multilayer perceptrons and convolutional networks to recurrent networks and pretrained Transformer-based encoders.
  Collectively, the results show that architectural inductive biases systematically shape temporal robustness: models whose inductive biases lead them to exploit localized, highly discriminative features attain the highest in-distribution accuracy, yet those features are often the ones that change most over time, so these models degrade fastest, while pretrained encoders that draw on coarser, more stable representations drift more gradually. These observations offer practical guidance for selecting architectures for real-world systems subject to temporal drift.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically compares how different neural network architectures (MLPs, CNNs, RNNs, and pretrained Transformers) respond to temporal distribution shift across three time-indexed domains. The key finding is that models with inductive biases favoring localized, highly discriminative features achieve better in-distribution accuracy but degrade fastest over time, while pretrained encoders using coarser, more stable representations exhibit slower temporal degradation.
AI.motivation: Real-world data distributions shift over time, degrading deployed ML systems. Despite extensive work on distribution shift, the relationship between architectural inductive biases and temporal robustness remains poorly understood. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing a systematic empirical analysis.
AI.method: The authors employ a unified evaluation framework using temporal drift matrices. Models are trained on cumulative historical data and evaluated on both earlier and later time periods to quantify cross-temporal generalization. The study spans image classification, multi-label text classification, and text regression, covering architectures from MLPs and CNNs to RNNs and pretrained Transformer-based encoders.
AI.result: Architectural inductive biases systematically shape temporal robustness: models exploiting localized, highly discriminative features (e.g., CNNs) achieve highest in-distribution accuracy but degrade fastest over time. In contrast, pretrained encoders leveraging coarser, more stable representations drift more gradually, offering better temporal stability at the cost of lower peak in-distribution performance.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide practical guidance for architecture selection in systems subject to temporal drift: practitioners should consider the trade-off between peak in-distribution accuracy and long-term temporal stability, with pretrained encoders offering superior robustness to temporal distribution shift.

title: Doomed from the Start: Early Abort of LLM Agent Episodes via a Recall-Controlled Probe Cascade
comment: 10 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables. Code will be released soon
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents solving multi-step tasks frequently commit to trajectories that are doomed to fail, yet continue to consume substantial inference compute before the failure becomes observable. We show that failure is predictable early from the agent's internal representations: lightweight per-round probes on hidden activations anticipate eventual episode failure as early as the first interaction round, where scorers reading only the agent's observable behavior are barely better than chance. We turn this signal into a practical abort cascade: one distribution-free calibrated gate per round, with per-round recall budgets jointly searched so that eventually-successful episodes survive all gates at a user-specified global rate; this episode-level guarantee is the one that matters in deployment, since false-abort risk accumulates across gates. Across two agent models on TextCraft, the cascade meets every recall target from 90% to 97% and, at the 90% target, saves 47.1% +/- 10.3% (Qwen-2.5-7B) and 37.2% +/- 8.8% (Llama-3.2-3B) of inference compute, 1.6--1.7x the best single-gate policy. An otherwise-identical cascade reading only behavior saves roughly half as much, and adding behavioral features to the probe yields no further gain: the hidden states capture what behavior reveals. Finally, we characterize the sample complexity of certifying high recall targets, telling practitioners which recall promises their data can, and provably cannot, back. The code will be released soon.

AI.tldr: LLM agents exhibit early internal signals predictive of eventual task failure. The authors develop a calibrated abort cascade using probes on hidden activations, achieving substantial inference compute savings (37-47%) while meeting user-specified recall targets, significantly outperforming behavior-only baselines.
AI.motivation: LLM agents solving multi-step tasks often persist in doomed trajectories, wasting inference compute before failure becomes observable from behavior alone. The key insight is that failure may be predictable much earlier from internal representations, enabling early termination to save compute while maintaining reliability guarantees.
AI.method: The authors (1) train lightweight linear probes on per-round hidden activations to predict eventual episode failure; (2) construct a distribution-free calibrated abort cascade with one gate per round, using jointly searched per-round recall budgets; (3) guarantee that eventually-successful episodes survive all gates at a user-specified global rate (controlling false-abort risk accumulation); and (4) characterize sample complexity bounds for certifying high recall targets.
AI.result: On TextCraft with Qwen-2.5-7B and Llama-3.2-3B, the cascade meets every recall target from 90%–97%. At 90% recall, it saves 47.1%±10.3% (Qwen) and 37.2%±8.8% (Llama) of inference compute — 1.6–1.7× the best single-gate policy. Behavior-only cascades save roughly half as much; adding behavioral features to probes yields no further gain, indicating hidden states already capture what behavior reveals.
AI.conclusion: Early internal representations of LLM agents contain a strong, actionable failure signal. The proposed abort cascade provides practical, calibrated compute savings with formal episode-level recall guarantees, and the sample complexity analysis guides practitioners on what recall targets are certifiable from their data.

title: Pitwall: Faithful Natural-Language Race-Strategy Briefings from a Calibrated Real-Time Monte Carlo Engine
comment: 21 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Live-deployment results from the 2026 Austrian and British Grands Prix. URL: https://pitwall.jsantillana.com
summary: Live sports commentary is grounded generation under a deadline: statements concern real, named athletes, the grounding state changes every few seconds, and no reference text exists at generation time. We present Pitwall, a production system that generates natural-language Formula 1 strategy briefings in English, Spanish, and Portuguese, treating faithfulness as an architectural property rather than an aspiration: every published sentence is decomposed into typed factual claims (positions, gaps, tyres, pace, overtakes, race control) and each claim is verified against the probabilistic race state that prompted it. The same verifier gates the fine-tuning data: of 3,045 model-written targets, only the 81.9% whose every claim is state-supported are retained, the rest falling back to a provably faithful template, so the generator never sees an ungrounded target. Verification is meaningful because of the grounding substrate: a vectorized Monte Carlo engine (N=2,000 per-lap race continuations) calibrated on 126 races (2018-2024) and validated on fully held-out 2025-2026 seasons (winner-in-top-3 90.3% over 155 backtests; held-out Brier 0.0745). A recurring finding spans both halves of the system: virtues trade off and must be gated separately. In simulation, calibration-optimal is not decision-optimal; in generation, fine-tuning on richer targets buys vividness that collapses into hallucination when the grounding state is sparse -- a failure a four-base replication traces to base-model instruction adherence, not scale, and that sparse-context auditing removes from the production model. End-to-end operation -- live timing to verified trilingual briefings -- was confirmed at two consecutive live Grands Prix (Austria and Britain, 2026); at Silverstone a timestamped probability trace, committed to disk before the outcome was known, locked onto the eventual winner ten laps before the flag.

AI.tldr: Pitwall is a production system that generates verified, multi-lingual Formula 1 strategy briefings by decomposing generated sentences into typed factual claims and verifying each against a calibrated Monte Carlo race simulation engine, ensuring faithfulness by construction rather than aspiration.
AI.motivation: Live sports commentary demands grounded, faithful generation under severe temporal constraints with evolving state and no reference text. Existing NLG systems treat faithfulness as a post-hoc aspiration; the authors argue it must be an architectural guarantee, especially in a domain where every factual claim (positions, gaps, tyres, overtakes) is objectively verifiable against a known probabilistic state.
AI.method: The system has two core components: (1) A vectorized Monte Carlo race simulation engine (N=2,000 continuations per lap) calibrated on 126 races (2018-2024) and validated on held-out 2025-2026 seasons, providing a probabilistic grounding substrate. (2) A generation pipeline where every output sentence is decomposed into typed factual claims (positions, gaps, tyres, pace, overtakes, race control) and verified against the simulation state. Fine-tuning data is gated by the same verifier: only 81.9% of model-written targets with fully state-supported claims are retained; the rest fall back to a provably faithful template, ensuring the generator never sees ungrounded targets. The system outputs in English, Spanish, and Portuguese.
AI.result: The Monte Carlo engine achieved 90.3% winner-in-top-3 accuracy over 155 backtests and a held-out Brier score of 0.0745. End-to-end operation was confirmed at two live 2026 Grands Prix (Austria, Britain). At Silverstone, a timestamped probability trace committed before the outcome locked onto the eventual winner ten laps before the flag. A key finding: fine-tuning on richer targets improves vividness but causes hallucination under sparse grounding states — traced via a four-base replication to base-model instruction adherence, not model scale.
AI.conclusion: Faithfulness in grounded NLG can and should be treated as an architectural property via claim-level verification against a calibrated probabilistic state. Virtues like calibration quality and decision quality, or vividness and faithfulness, trade off and must be gated separately. Sparse-context auditing can remove hallucination without sacrificing generation quality.

title: Learning Sparsest Linear Causal DAGs with Latent Confounders via Higher-Order Cumulants
summary:
Recovering the exact directed acyclic graph (DAG) in linear non-Gaussian acyclic models with latent confounders (LvLiNGAM) remains a challenging problem. Although LvLiNGAM is identifiable only up to an observational equivalence class, each equivalence class is characterized by a unique sparsest DAG. Recovering the sparsest DAG from finite samples, however, remains difficult. Although existing methods are asymptotically consistent, they do not provide an explicit finite-sample procedure for recovering the unique sparsest DAG, nor do they handle models with an arbitrary number of latent confounders.
  In this paper, we propose a finite-sample method for recovering the sparsest DAG without imposing any restriction on the number of latent confounders. Simulation studies and real-data analyses demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior finite-sample performance compared with existing approaches.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a finite-sample method for recovering the unique sparsest DAG in linear non-Gaussian acyclic models with an arbitrary number of latent confounders (LvLiNGAM), addressing limitations in existing asymptotically consistent approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for LvLiNGAM are only asymptotically consistent and lack explicit finite-sample procedures for recovering the unique sparsest DAG. Additionally, current approaches do not handle models with an arbitrary number of latent confounders.
AI.method: The authors propose a finite-sample method for recovering the sparsest DAG in LvLiNGAM without imposing any restriction on the number of latent confounders.
AI.result: Simulation studies and real-data analyses demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior finite-sample performance compared with existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method effectively addresses the finite-sample recovery problem for the sparsest DAG in LvLiNGAM, outperforming existing approaches while accommodating an arbitrary number of latent confounders.

title: RMISC: A Large-scale Real-world Multivariate Corpus for Time Series Foundation Models
summary: Recent years have witnessed the emergence of multivariate modeling using time series foundation models (TSFMs), which achieve advanced zero-shot generalization. Modern multivariate TSFMs are predominantly pretrained on multivariate synthetic data, which is easier to scale but may fail to capture the complex temporal dynamics and cross-variable relationships present in real-world time series. This raises a key question: Whether and to what extent the leading TSFMs trained with the real-world corpus perform better than those trained with synthetic data? To answer this, we establish the RMISC corpus, a considerably large-scale, high-quality, openly accessible, real-world, and multivariate time series archive that contains around 200 datasets and 142 billion time points across diverse domains. Furthermore, we pretrain four advanced TSFMs on univariate, synthetic multivariate, and real-world multivariate data and evaluate their zero-shot generalization capabilities on standard in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks. Experimental results show that incorporating real-world multivariate data predominantly improves the generalization performance for both univariate and multivariate TSFMs. These results provide a deeper understanding of how real-world multivariate data contributes to the development of stronger TSFMs.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether pretraining time series foundation models (TSFMs) on real-world multivariate data yields better zero-shot generalization than synthetic data. The authors introduce RMISC, a large-scale real-world multivariate corpus (~200 datasets, 142B time points), and show that incorporating real-world data predominantly improves both univariate and multivariate TSFM performance.
AI.motivation: Modern multivariate TSFMs are predominantly pretrained on synthetic data, which scales easily but may fail to capture the complex temporal dynamics and cross-variable relationships inherent in real-world time series. The key unanswered question is whether real-world pretraining data offers a performance advantage over synthetic data for TSFMs.
AI.method: The authors construct RMISC, a large-scale, open-access, real-world multivariate time series corpus spanning ~200 datasets and 142 billion time points across diverse domains. They then pretrain four advanced TSFMs on three data types (univariate, synthetic multivariate, and real-world multivariate) and evaluate zero-shot generalization on standard in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks.
AI.result: Incorporating real-world multivariate data predominantly improves zero-shot generalization performance for both univariate and multivariate TSFMs compared to models trained solely on synthetic or univariate data.
AI.conclusion: Real-world multivariate pretraining data provides meaningful benefits for building stronger TSFMs, offering deeper insights into how data composition affects foundation model generalization in time series domains.

title: Stability Annealing Selects the Implicit Bias of Smoothed Sign Descent: A Rate-Indexed Barrier Path on Separable Data
summary: Adaptive gradient methods can favor max-margin separators that differ from gradient descent, yet a fixed positive numerical stability constant eventually changes the update geometry again. This paper studies the rate-controlled middle case for full-batch linear classification on separable data. For memoryless stability-annealed smoothed-sign descent with weighted exponential loss, we prove that the normalized iterates converge to the minimizer of a convex Burg-type barrier over a margin slice. The proof rewrites the dynamics exactly as entropic mirror ascent on a concave dual objective, controls the dual gap by a KL recursion, and yields an explicit S_t^{-1/2} normalized-iterate envelope. The static barrier geometry is fully characterized, including KKT conditions and both endpoint limits. Experiments validate the exact dual identities to floating-point error, illustrate the predicted path and rate diagram, and show an empirical fixed-epsilon crossover scaling in cumulative time. We further report robustness and boundary diagnostics for logistic tails, fixed-epsilon crossover, and adaptive-method variants, delineating the scope of the proved smoothed-sign theory.

AI.tldr: For memoryless stability-annealed smoothed-sign descent with weighted exponential loss on linearly separable data, normalized iterates converge to the minimizer of a convex Burg-type barrier over a margin slice. The proof uses entropic mirror ascent on a concave dual, KL recursion control, and yields an explicit S_t^{-1/2} envelope. Experiments confirm dual identities, illustrate predicted paths, and delineate scope.
AI.motivation: Adaptive gradient methods and gradient descent converge to different max-margin separators, and the numerical stability constant ε in adaptive methods acts as a rate-control parameter whose limiting behavior (ε→0 vs fixed ε>0) yields distinct geometries. The middle regime—where ε is annealed at a controlled rate—has not been theoretically characterized, motivating a rigorous analysis of this intermediate case.
AI.method: The authors study full-batch linear classification on separable data using memoryless stability-annealed smoothed-sign descent with weighted exponential loss. The dynamics are rewritten exactly as entropic mirror ascent on a concave dual objective. Convergence is proved by controlling the dual gap via a KL divergence recursion, yielding an explicit normalized-iterate envelope scaling as S_t^{-1/2}. The static barrier geometry is fully characterized via KKT conditions and endpoint limits. Experiments validate dual identities to floating-point error, illustrate predicted paths and rate diagrams, and test robustness across logistic tails, fixed-ε crossover scaling, and adaptive-method variants (e.g., Adam, AMSGrad).
AI.result: Normalized iterates provably converge to the minimizer of a convex Burg-type barrier over a margin slice. The S_t^{-1/2} envelope explicitly bounds iterate behavior. Experiments confirm exact dual identities numerically, match predicted paths and rate diagrams, and reveal an empirical fixed-ε crossover scaling in cumulative time. Robustness diagnostics delineate where the smoothed-sign theory holds versus where it breaks (e.g., heavy-tailed logistic losses, certain adaptive variants).
AI.conclusion: The rate-controlled annealing of the stability constant in smoothed-sign descent induces convergence to a Burg-type barrier solution, fundamentally distinct from both the ε→0 and fixed-ε limits. The entropic mirror ascent dual framework provides a unified analytical tool for understanding adaptive method dynamics. Empirical findings validate the theory and map its applicability boundaries across loss functions and optimizer variants.

title: FootsiesGym: A Fighting Game Benchmark for Two-Player Zero-Sum Imperfect-Information Games
comment: Accepted to the RLC 2026 Reinforcement Learning & Video Games Workshop; 14 pages, 9 figures
summary: We present FootsiesGym, an open-source environment for learning in a non-trivial two-player, zero-sum, imperfect-information game. Built on HiFight's minimalist 2D fighting game Footsies, it isolates the cyclic, non-transitive strategic interactions of fighting game neutral play while remaining simple enough for efficient analysis. We provide a vectorized simulator that enables high-throughput training on standard hardware, making the environment accessible and reproducible. We describe the design of the environment, benchmark several reinforcement learning algorithms, and discuss open research directions it enables. The code is available at https://github.com/como-research/FootsiesGym.

AI.tldr: FootsiesGym is an open-source RL environment based on the minimalist 2D fighting game Footsies, designed to study two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games with cyclic, non-transitive strategic interactions. It offers a vectorized simulator for high-throughput training and benchmarks several RL algorithms.
AI.motivation: Traditional RL benchmarks often fail to capture the cyclic, non-transitive dynamics characteristic of real-world competitive games (e.g., Rock-Paper-Scissors-like interactions in fighting game neutral play). The authors aim to isolate these dynamics in a simple, analyzable, and reproducible environment to advance research in multi-agent RL for imperfect-information, zero-sum settings.
AI.method: The authors build FootsiesGym on top of HiFight's Footsies, a minimalist 2D fighting game that distills neutral-game strategic interactions. They design a vectorized simulator enabling parallel, high-throughput training on commodity hardware. The environment is structured as a standard Gym interface and benchmarked with multiple reinforcement learning algorithms to establish baselines.
AI.result: The paper delivers a functional, open-source environment with a vectorized simulator that supports efficient training. Baseline results from several RL algorithms are provided, demonstrating the feasibility of using FootsiesGym for studying non-transitive strategic dynamics in imperfect-information games.
AI.conclusion: FootsiesGym fills a gap in RL benchmarks by providing a tractable yet non-trivial environment for studying cyclic strategic interactions. The authors highlight open research directions—including opponent modeling, meta-learning, and population-based training—that the environment is well-suited to explore.

title: RSF-GLLM: Bridging the Semantic Gap in Multi-Hop Knowledge Graph QA via Recurrent Soft-Flow and Decoupled LLM Generation
comment: Accepted for publication in ICML 2026 as a full research paper; 21 pages
summary: Multi-hop Question Answering over Knowledge Graphs faces a critical challenge: traditional retrieve-then-read pipelines break differentiability, preventing the retriever from learning to bridge the semantic gap where intermediate nodes lack lexical overlap with the query. To address this, we propose RSF-GLLM, a framework decoupling differentiable graph reasoning from answer generation. Our Recurrent Soft-Flow (RSF) module employs a GRU-guided query updater to propagate continuous relevance scores, utilizing a dynamic gating mechanism to traverse semantically dissimilar bridge nodes via structural cues. We introduce flow sparsity regularization to theoretically guarantee convergence from soft probabilities to discrete reasoning paths. These paths are extracted and textualized to fine-tune a Large Language Model (LLM), ensuring generation is grounded in factual topology. Experiments on WebQSP and CWQ demonstrate that RSF-GLLM achieves competitive performance with superior inference efficiency compared to LLM based computationally expensive approaches.

AI.tldr: RSF-GLLM decouples differentiable graph reasoning from answer generation in KGQA by using a GRU-guided Recurrent Soft-Flow module with flow sparsity regularization to propagate relevance scores across semantically dissimilar nodes, then textualizes extracted paths to fine-tune an LLM for grounded, efficient answer generation.
AI.motivation: Traditional retrieve-then-read pipelines for multi-hop KGQA break differentiability, preventing the retriever from bridging semantic gaps where intermediate bridge nodes lack lexical overlap with the query.
AI.method: The Recurrent Soft-Flow (RSF) module uses a GRU-guided query updater to propagate continuous relevance scores with a dynamic gating mechanism that traverses semantically dissimilar bridge nodes via structural cues. Flow sparsity regularization theoretically guarantees convergence from soft probabilities to discrete reasoning paths. Extracted paths are textualized to fine-tune an LLM, decoupling reasoning from generation.
AI.result: Experiments on WebQSP and CWQ show RSF-GLLM achieves competitive performance with superior inference efficiency compared to computationally expensive LLM-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling differentiable graph reasoning from LLM-based generation, with sparsity-regularized soft flow for path finding, yields competitive multi-hop KGQA performance with significantly better inference efficiency than prior LLM-heavy methods.

title: Learning When to Automate: Queue Control in Human-AI Service Systems
summary: We study a human-AI service system in which tasks arrive sequentially and are processed through a two-stage architecture: an automated chatbot followed, when necessary, by a human agent. We consider $T$ sequentially arriving tasks, each belonging to one of $K$ heterogeneous types. For each task the decision maker chooses how many resources to allocate to the chatbot, whose type-dependent success probabilities are initially unknown. Tasks not resolved by the chatbot enter type-dependent human-service queues, where they are processed by a human agent with unknown service rates. This model captures a central tradeoff in hybrid service systems: relying more on automation reduces human congestion but increases chatbot costs, while insufficient automation may overload the human agent. We propose the UCB-DPP policy, which combines Upper Confidence Bounds with Drift-Plus-Penalty control to learn the unknown parameters of the system while making queue-aware decisions. We prove that UCB-DPP achieves regret $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(K\sqrt{T})$ and guarantees mean-rate stability of the human-service queues. Simulations on synthetic instances show that the proposed policy outperforms natural baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper studies a two-stage human-AI service system where a chatbot first handles tasks and escalates unresolved ones to human agents. The authors propose UCB-DPP, a policy combining Upper Confidence Bounds with Drift-Plus-Penalty control, achieving $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(K\sqrt{T})$ regret with queue stability guarantees.
AI.motivation: Hybrid human-AI service systems face a fundamental tension: excessive reliance on automation increases chatbot costs, while insufficient automation overloads human agents. Existing approaches typically assume known system parameters, but in practice both chatbot success probabilities and human service rates are unknown a priori and must be learned online.
AI.method: The authors model the problem as a sequential decision process over $T$ tasks across $K$ types. The proposed UCB-DPP policy uses Upper Confidence Bounds to estimate unknown chatbot success probabilities and human service rates, while employing Drift-Plus-Penalty control to make queue-aware resource allocation decisions that balance the automation-human tradeoff.
AI.result: UCB-DPP provably achieves $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(K\sqrt{T})$ regret and guarantees mean-rate stability of the human-service queues. Simulations on synthetic instances demonstrate that UCB-DPP outperforms natural baseline policies.
AI.conclusion: The UCB-DPP policy effectively integrates online learning with queue-aware control, providing both theoretical guarantees and practical performance gains for hybrid human-AI service systems with initially unknown parameters.

title: FreqDepthKV: Frequency-Guided Depth Sharing for Robust KV Cache Compression in Long-Context LLM Inference
summary: Long-context LLM inference is increasingly limited by the memory and bandwidth cost of KV caches, yet aggressive compression can remove the layer-specific evidence needed for retrieval and multi-step reasoning. We introduce FreqDepthKV, an inference-time cache compression method that factorizes adjacent-layer KV states into shared low-frequency depth components and sparse high-frequency residuals. A lightweight online probe assigns attention heads to shared-depth, residual-depth, or exact cache modes according to their contribution to reconstruction-sensitive attention logits, allowing the compression policy to adapt to prompt structure without retraining. Across long-context question answering, needle retrieval, summarization, and code generation benchmarks, FreqDepthKV preserves task accuracy under substantially smaller cache budgets. With a 32k-token prefill window, FreqDepthKV reaches 58.3 Exact Match, 63.0 F1, 32.5 ROUGE-L, and 48.1 pass@1, closely matching full KV while outperforming prior compressed-cache methods. It also improves decoding throughput to 70.4 tokens/s, reduces TTFT to 2.06 seconds, and lowers peak KV memory to 6.2 GB, achieving a 3.9x effective compression ratio.

AI.tldr: FreqDepthKV is an inference-time KV cache compression method that factorizes adjacent-layer key-value states into shared low-frequency depth components and sparse high-frequency residuals, using a lightweight online probe to adaptively assign attention heads to compression modes. It achieves near full-KV accuracy across benchmarks with a 3.9× effective compression ratio, improving throughput and reducing latency and memory.
AI.motivation: Long-context LLM inference suffers from prohibitive KV cache memory and bandwidth costs. Aggressive cache compression often strips away layer-specific evidence critical for retrieval and multi-step reasoning. The key insight is that KV states across adjacent layers exhibit significant low-frequency redundancy that can be shared, while preserving sparse high-frequency residuals retains task-critical fine-grained information.
AI.method: FreqDepthKV operates at inference time by: (1) factorizing adjacent-layer KV states into shared low-frequency depth components (capturing cross-layer common structure) and sparse high-frequency residuals (preserving layer-specific details); (2) employing a lightweight online probe that measures each attention head's contribution to reconstruction-sensitive attention logits; (3) dynamically assigning heads to one of three modes — shared-depth, residual-depth, or exact (uncompressed) cache — based on probe scores, allowing the compression policy to adapt to prompt structure without any retraining.
AI.result: With a 32k-token prefill window, FreqDepthKV achieves 58.3 Exact Match, 63.0 F1, 32.5 ROUGE-L, and 48.1 pass@1 across QA, needle retrieval, summarization, and code generation benchmarks. These results closely match full KV cache performance and surpass prior compressed-cache methods. The method delivers 70.4 tokens/s decoding throughput, 2.06 s TTFT, and 6.2 GB peak KV memory, yielding a 3.9× effective compression ratio.
AI.conclusion: FreqDepthKV demonstrates that frequency-domain factorization of adjacent-layer KV caches enables aggressive yet accurate compression for long-context LLM inference. By adaptively preserving high-frequency residuals where they matter most for attention reconstruction, the method maintains task fidelity while substantially reducing memory footprint and latency, making it a practical solution for deployment under tight resource constraints.

title: Life Style Levels: Neighborhood Delineation using Geospatial Data
summary: Fine-scale socioeconomic information is often unavailable across rapidly ur-banizing regions of the developing world, like India, limiting the ability to delineate intra-urban variations in affluence and deprivation. This study pro-poses a scalable, grid-based urban delineation framework using building morphology derived from open-source satellite imagery. Urban areas across 59 Indian cities and towns are partitioned into high-resolution spatial grids and characterized using interpretable morphological indicators, which are combined into a transparent, rule-based scoring framework to delineate areas with contrasting levels of urban affluence. The resulting classifications are validated through ground-level Google Street View observations, revealing a sharp contrast between the grid classes which are consistent with the ex-pected effects of the lifestyle affluence indicators. We further investigate density-based clustering of building footprints in Mumbai to identify dense urban settlements, demonstrating that the resulting clusters exhibit substan-tial spatial overlap with known informal settlements across the city. Finally, we conduct an exploratory analysis mapping consumer loan delinquency across the derived affluence classes. By relying entirely on publicly available geospatial data, the proposed framework provides a scalable, interpretable, and cost-effective approach for granular urban affluence mapping across In-dian cities.

AI.tldr: A scalable framework using open-source satellite imagery and building morphology is proposed to map intra-urban affluence variations across 59 Indian cities. Rule-based scoring of morphological indicators produces grid-level classifications validated via Google Street View, with extensions to informal settlement detection and loan delinquency mapping.
AI.motivation: Fine-scale socioeconomic data is scarce across rapidly urbanizing regions of the developing world, particularly India. This data gap limits the ability to characterize intra-urban variations in affluence and deprivation, which are essential for urban planning, service delivery, and policy targeting.
AI.method: The study proposes a grid-based urban delineation framework operating on high-resolution spatial grids across 59 Indian cities. Building morphology indicators are extracted from open-source satellite imagery. These interpretable indicators feed into a transparent, rule-based scoring framework to classify areas by affluence level. Validation uses Google Street View ground-truth observations. Density-based clustering of building footprints is applied in Mumbai to identify dense urban settlements, with spatial overlap analysis against known informal settlements. An exploratory analysis maps consumer loan delinquency across the derived affluence classes.
AI.result: Grid-based affluence classifications show sharp contrasts consistent with expected lifestyle affluence indicators when validated against Google Street View. Density-based building footprint clusters in Mumbai exhibit substantial spatial overlap with known informal settlements. Consumer loan delinquency rates show patterned variation across the derived affluence classes.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a scalable, interpretable, and cost-effective approach for granular urban affluence mapping across Indian cities, relying entirely on publicly available geospatial data without requiring proprietary or survey-based socioeconomic datasets.

title: SplineNet: An Isogeometric Deep Learning Method for Complex Shells
summary: We present a novel isogeometric deep learning method, termed SplineNet, for the seamless design and analysis of shell structures with complex geometries. The proposed approach is built upon watertight spline representations, e.g., analysis-suitable unstructured T-splines, and features exact geometric descriptions of Computer-Aided Design (CAD) models in neural networks. Bézier extraction is used to build the network architecture, where Bernstein polynomials serve as the nonlinear activation functions. SplineNet can be applied in a data-free or data-driven way. In the data-free case, energy-based formulations can be naturally incorporated as loss terms, which fulfill the need of Computer-Aided Engineering (CAE) and can be accurately calculated. In particular, the Kirchhoff--Love (KL) model is adopted to solve for the mechanical behaviors of shell structures. This way, CAD and CAE can be tightly integrated in a deep neural network without the time-consuming model/data exchange process. In the data-driven case, SplineNet can be used as the trunk net of Deep Operator Networks (DeepONet) to provide interpretability. Given such a trained network and unseen input data, results can be immediately obtained without retraining the network or repeatedly performing the traditional workflow for analysis. In the end, a variety of numerical examples are studied to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, especially when real-world complex geometries are involved.

AI.tldr: SplineNet is an isogeometric deep learning method that integrates CAD and CAE by embedding watertight spline representations into neural networks, using Bézier extraction and Bernstein polynomials as activation functions. It supports both data-free (energy-based) and data-driven (DeepONet trunk) modes for efficient shell structure analysis without CAD/CAE data exchange.
AI.motivation: The work addresses the long-standing gap between Computer-Aided Design (CAD) and Computer-Aided Engineering (CAE), which typically requires time-consuming model/data exchange processes. By embedding exact geometric descriptions directly into neural networks, the authors aim to achieve seamless integration of design and analysis, especially for shell structures with complex geometries.
AI.method: The method, SplineNet, uses analysis-suitable unstructured T-splines as watertight spline representations. Bézier extraction builds the network architecture, with Bernstein polynomials serving as nonlinear activation functions. In data-free mode, energy-based loss formulations (specifically the Kirchhoff-Love shell model) are incorporated for mechanical analysis. In data-driven mode, SplineNet functions as the trunk net of a Deep Operator Network (DeepONet), providing interpretability and enabling immediate inference on unseen inputs without retraining.
AI.result: Numerical examples — including real-world complex geometries — demonstrate the effectiveness of SplineNet in both data-free and data-driven settings, showing that it can tightly integrate CAD and CAE within a deep neural network framework.
AI.conclusion: SplineNet successfully bridges CAD and CAE through isogeometric deep learning, offering a unified framework that eliminates the cumbersome model/data exchange bottleneck. Its dual-mode capability (data-free energy-based and data-driven operator learning) makes it versatile for both traditional analysis and rapid inference on shell structures with complex geometries.

title: Bridging Physical Reasoning and Task Generalization via Visual Action Outcome Reasoning Alignment
comment: ICML'26 Workshop RLxF: Reinforcement Learning from World Feedback
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) struggle to generalize in interactive physical reasoning, particularly under unseen tasks and environments. Two key failure modes are prominent: hallucinated chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning that contradicts physical reality, and misalignment between the model's reasoning and actions. We present VAORA (Visual Action Outcome Reasoning Alignment), a novel reward design that directly addresses both issues. VAORA introduces two complementary rewards: Visual Alignment Reward, which anchors VLM reasoning to the visual context independent of the agent action itself, and Visual-Action Alignment Reward, which grounds reasoning in the visual outcome induced by the model's action. Together, these rewards suppress hallucinated CoT and reduce the gap between reasoning and behavior. To improve training stability, we further employ smooth, dense rewards by estimating success probabilities using a pre-trained in-domain expert agent. Experiments on PHYRE and Virtual Tool support our performances across novel-task and unseen-environment settings, confirming that grounded and generalizable physical intelligence can be induced through VAORA.

AI.tldr: VAORA introduces dual alignment rewards — Visual Alignment and Visual-Action Alignment — to suppress hallucinated chain-of-thought reasoning and synchronize reasoning with actions in VLMs, achieving improved generalization on physical reasoning benchmarks like PHYRE and Virtual Tool.
AI.motivation: VLMs exhibit two critical failure modes in interactive physical reasoning: (1) hallucinated CoT that contradicts physical reality, and (2) misalignment between reasoning and executed actions. Existing approaches fail to address both issues simultaneously, limiting generalization to unseen tasks and environments.
AI.method: VAORA proposes two complementary rewards: a Visual Alignment Reward that anchors reasoning to the visual context independently of agent actions, and a Visual-Action Alignment Reward that grounds reasoning in the visual outcome caused by the model's actions. Training stability is enhanced via smooth, dense reward signals derived from success probability estimates produced by a pre-trained in-domain expert agent.
AI.result: The method demonstrates strong performance on PHYRE and Virtual Tool benchmarks in both novel-task and unseen-environment settings, confirming that VAORA induces grounded and generalizable physical intelligence.
AI.conclusion: Grounded and generalizable physical intelligence in VLMs can be effectively induced through dual visual and visual-action alignment rewards, addressing both hallucinated reasoning and reasoning-action gaps while maintaining training stability.

title: Hierarchical Acoustic-Semantic Modeling: Modality Separation and Semantic Coherence for Full-Duplex SLMs
summary: Developing seamless, high-performance, native intelligent full-duplex Spoken Language Models (SLMs) remains a critical challenge and long-standing goal for the speech and NLP community. Despite notable progress, recent endeavors are fundamentally constrained by severe modality interference, which causes substantial knowledge degradation and compromises semantic integrity -- ultimately making full-duplex SLMs feel unnatural and unintelligent. In this paper, through an exhaustive fine-grained analysis of model optimization dynamics, we uncover the root cause of such performance degradation, revealing that modality interference arises from inherent gradient conflicts between acoustic and semantic modeling when the two modalities are forced to share a deep parameter space. Guided by this key insight, we introduce Lychee-FD, a native end-to-end full-duplex framework designed to mitigate modality interference. Importantly, we propose a hierarchical parameter separation strategy that decouples conflicting modalities in deep layers while preserving cross-modality coherence via a dedicated semantic alignment channel. Extensive experiments on multiple full-duplex benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly advances the state of the art, yielding substantial improvements in both speech intelligence (+7.4% on Spoken QA) and full-duplex interaction fluidity (+28.5% on FullDuplexBench 1.5) without compromising inference efficiency. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to achieve two key advances: 1) uncovering and elucidating the root cause of modality interference in full-duplex SLMs, and 2) designing an elegant hierarchical model together with a practical solution for seamless, high-performance, native intelligent full-duplex SLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies gradient conflicts between acoustic and semantic modeling in shared deep parameter space as the root cause of modality interference in full-duplex SLMs, and proposes Lychee-FD, a hierarchical parameter separation framework that decouples conflicting modalities while preserving cross-modality coherence, achieving significant gains in speech QA (+7.4%) and interaction fluidity (+28.5%).
AI.motivation: Current full-duplex Spoken Language Models suffer from severe modality interference where shared parameterization of acoustic and semantic modeling leads to knowledge degradation and compromised semantic integrity, making interactions feel unnatural and unintelligent. The root cause of this interference was previously not well understood.
AI.method: The authors first conduct a fine-grained analysis of model optimization dynamics to uncover that modality interference stems from inherent gradient conflicts between acoustic and semantic modeling in deep shared layers. Based on this insight, they propose Lychee-FD, a native end-to-end full-duplex framework with a hierarchical parameter separation strategy that decouples conflicting modalities in deep layers while maintaining cross-modality coherence through a dedicated semantic alignment channel.
AI.result: Lychee-FD achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple full-duplex benchmarks: +7.4% improvement on Spoken QA and +28.5% improvement on FullDuplexBench 1.5, all without compromising inference efficiency.
