AI.conclusion: This work is the first to both uncover the root cause of modality interference (gradient conflicts in shared deep parameters) and design a practical hierarchical solution for seamless, high-performance, native intelligent full-duplex SLMs.

title: Scalable Perturbation Learning for Online Self-Supervised Echo State Networks
summary:
Intelligent systems should not only solve tasks but also adapt under real-world constraints. Autonomous adaptation via self-supervised learning, sequential adaptation via online learning, and memory-efficient implementation via perturbation-based learning are important requirements for such systems. However, these requirements are generally in tension for high-dimensional systems, because perturbation-based learning suffers from variance that grows with the dimension of the perturbed variables.
  In this study, we focus on echo state networks (ESNs), where this tension naturally arises in large reservoirs. We propose a perturbation-based learning rule for online self-supervised learning in ESNs. The proposed rule is derived from an orthogonal decomposition of the self-supervised learning cost, which separates an input-dependent component from a redundant component determined by the fixed ESN parameters. By perturbing only the input-dependent component, the effective perturbation dimension is reduced from the reservoir dimension to the input dimension.
  Thus, the proposed method preserves self-supervised adaptation, online learning, and scalar-feedback perturbation learning, while avoiding reservoir-size-dependent variance growth. This suggests a design principle for scalable and hardware-compatible learning: online learning should be restricted to the dynamically necessary low-dimensional component of the objective.

AI.tldr: Proposes a perturbation-based online learning rule for Echo State Networks that decomposes the self-supervised learning cost orthogonally, perturbing only the input-dependent component to reduce effective perturbation dimension from reservoir size to input dimension, thereby avoiding variance growth with reservoir size.
AI.motivation: Intelligent systems need self-supervised adaptation, online sequential learning, and memory-efficient perturbation-based implementation. However, in high-dimensional systems like large-reservoir ESNs, these requirements conflict because perturbation-based learning variance grows with the dimension of perturbed variables, making it impractical for large reservoirs.
AI.method: Orthogonal decomposition of the self-supervised learning cost function into an input-dependent component and a redundant component determined by fixed ESN parameters. The learning rule perturbs only the input-dependent component, reducing effective perturbation dimension from reservoir dimension to input dimension, while preserving scalar-feedback perturbation learning.
AI.result: The proposed method successfully preserves self-supervised adaptation, online learning, and scalar-feedback perturbation learning simultaneously, while avoiding reservoir-size-dependent variance growth in Echo State Networks.
AI.conclusion: The work suggests a design principle for scalable, hardware-compatible learning: online learning should be restricted to the dynamically necessary low-dimensional component of the objective, rather than operating on the full high-dimensional parameter space.

title: DepthWeave-KV: Token-Adaptive Cross-Layer Residual Factorization for Long-Context KV Cache Compression
summary: Long-context language model inference is increasingly limited by the memory bandwidth and capacity required to store key-value caches, yet existing compression methods often apply uniform budgets across layers or tokens and degrade retrieval when lexical cues and semantic states require different preservation. We introduce DepthWeave-KV, a token-adaptive cache compression method that factorizes key and value states across neighboring transformer layers using shared low-rank channel bases while retaining lightweight token-specific residuals where attention behavior is sensitive. DepthWeave-KV combines cross-depth residual factorization with a token-conditional depth router that allocates higher reconstruction rank to instruction-bearing and retrieval-critical tokens, and uses calibration-free online error tracking from attention-output probes to adapt compression during generation without retraining the base model. A fused CUDA implementation jointly performs basis lookup, residual dequantization, and attention projection to reduce decode-time memory traffic. Across LongBench, Needle-in-a-Haystack, L-Eval, and long-form QA and summarization benchmarks, DepthWeave-KV achieves near-full-cache task quality with substantially lower memory use, improving average score and retrieval accuracy over prior compressed caches while reaching 8.3x KV memory reduction and 72.8 tokens per second at 64K context.

AI.tldr: DepthWeave-KV is a token-adaptive KV cache compression method that uses cross-layer low-rank factorization with token-conditional depth routing to achieve near-full-cache quality at 8.3× memory reduction for long-context LLM inference.
AI.motivation: Long-context LLM inference suffers from KV cache memory bandwidth/capacity bottlenecks. Existing compression methods apply uniform budgets across layers/tokens, failing to account for how lexical cues and semantic states demand different preservation strategies, which degrades retrieval performance.
AI.method: DepthWeave-KV factorizes key and value states across neighboring transformer layers via shared low-rank channel bases, retaining lightweight token-specific residuals for attention-sensitive tokens. A token-conditional depth router assigns higher reconstruction rank to instruction-bearing and retrieval-critical tokens. Calibration-free online error tracking using attention-output probes adapts compression during generation without retraining. A fused CUDA kernel jointly performs basis lookup, residual dequantization, and attention projection to minimize decode-time memory traffic.
AI.result: On LongBench, Needle-in-a-Haystack, L-Eval, and long-form QA/summarization benchmarks, DepthWeave-KV achieves near-full-cache task quality with 8.3× KV memory reduction and 72.8 tokens/sec throughput at 64K context length, outperforming prior compressed cache methods in average score and retrieval accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Token-adaptive, cross-layer factorization with dynamic rank allocation and online error tracking enables effective KV cache compression that preserves both semantic and retrieval-critical information, substantially reducing memory while maintaining task performance in long-context inference.

title: On the feasibility of dependency parsing of non-human sequences without a gold standard. Is evaluation possible in other species?
summary: Dependency parsing consists of finding a tree representation for a sequence. Unsupervised dependency parsing aims to develop parsing methods without a gold standard during model training. In human languages, an unsupervised parser can be evaluated because some gold standard is usually available or can be created. For other species, a gold standard is unknown. Thus one may conclude that it is impossible to determine the accuracy of an unsupervised parser and, consequently, dependency parsing is unfeasible in other species. However, here we apply recent advances in network science to demonstrate that the proportion of correct edges retrieved by a parser must be high for the sequences of vocalizations or gestures that non-human primates produce due to the fast decay of the sequence length distribution. In contrast, human language sequences lack that property. Therefore, evaluation without a gold standard is feasible in non-human primates but a hard problem in humans.

AI.tldr: Unsupervised dependency parsing can be evaluated without a gold standard in non-human primates due to the fast-decaying sequence length distribution of their vocalizations/gestures, a property absent in human language, making human parser evaluation without ground truth inherently harder.
AI.motivation: To challenge the assumption that dependency parsing is infeasible for non-human animal communication simply because no gold standard exists for evaluation, and to demonstrate that network science offers a principled way to assess parser accuracy without annotated data.
AI.method: The authors apply network science techniques to analyze the statistical properties of sequences — specifically the decay rate of sequence length distributions — and show that this property bounds the proportion of correctly retrieved dependency edges, enabling evaluation without a gold standard.
AI.result: Non-human primate vocalization and gesture sequences exhibit a fast decay in sequence length distribution, which mathematically constrains parsing solutions such that a parser must recover a high proportion of correct edges. Human language sequences lack this fast decay, making unsupervised parser evaluation substantially harder.
AI.conclusion: Dependency parsing is feasible for non-human primate communication because fast-decaying length distributions enable gold-standard-free evaluation, whereas human language's statistical structure renders such evaluation a hard problem.

title: Modeling Normal Is All You Need: Joint Latent Clustering for Anomaly Detection in Multimodal Cyber-Physical Systems
summary: Faults on a cyber-physical system (CPS) are too rare and unrepresentative to characterise, or even to select a model on, so detection must instead model normal behaviour; the standard point-adjusted evaluation, however, rewards detectors that never do. CPS normal behaviour is the union of many imbalanced, curved, thin-fringed operating regimes rather than a single blob; we state this structure as ten assumptions (A1-A10), abbreviated Massive, Implicit, Imbalanced Multimodality (MIIM). We model the normal law with a jointly learned latent representation plus explicit Gaussian-mixture mode clustering, scored in the latent rather than by a global density or a reconstruction residual, and evaluate under a deliberately fair protocol: raw point-wise metrics with no point adjustment, a trivial-detector difficulty split, prevalence-matched F1, and train-normal-only calibration. On three real CPS datasets (WADI, HAI, SKAB), the detector wins both the combined column and the difficult correlation/dynamics-fault column on all three, reaching difficult-subset AUROC 0.831 on HAI, 0.726 on WADI, and 0.610 on SKAB. The margin is largest on the two multimodal datasets the MIIM assumptions target and slimmest on the near-unimodal one, tracking multimodality as the thesis predicts, and it holds against three deep detectors (USAD, TranAD, GDN) re-computed with the same raw metrics, all of which collapse on the difficult subset. The methodological contributions are the MIIM assumption set, the difficulty-stratified fair protocol, and a latent-only score that drops reconstruction because a flexible decoder rebuilds the hard faults faithfully.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a fault detection method for CPS that models normal behavior as a mixture of multiple operating regimes (MIIM assumptions), uses joint latent representation learning with Gaussian-mixture clustering, and evaluates under a fair raw point-wise protocol. The approach outperforms deep detectors (USAD, TranAD, GDN) on three real CPS datasets, especially on multimodal data, by scoring exclusively in the latent space and avoiding reconstruction-based scoring.
AI.motivation: Faults in CPS are too rare and unrepresentative for supervised characterization, forcing anomaly detection to model normality. However, standard point-adjusted evaluation unfairly rewards trivial detectors. Moreover, CPS normal behavior is not a single distribution but rather a union of many imbalanced, curved, thin-fringed operating regimes — a structure the authors formalize as the MIIM (Massive, Implicit, Imbalanced Multimodality) assumptions. Existing methods fail to capture this multimodal structure and collapse on difficult fault subsets.
AI.method: The authors state ten MIIM assumptions (A1–A10) characterizing CPS normal behavior. They model the normal law using a jointly learned latent representation with explicit Gaussian-mixture mode clustering. Crucially, anomaly scoring is performed solely in the latent space rather than via global density estimation or reconstruction residuals — the latter is dropped because a flexible decoder can faithfully reconstruct even hard faults. A deliberately fair evaluation protocol is introduced: raw point-wise metrics (no point adjustment), a trivial-detector difficulty split, prevalence-matched F1, and train-normal-only calibration.
AI.result: On three real CPS datasets (WADI, HAI, SKAB), the proposed detector wins both the combined column and the difficult correlation/dynamics-fault column on all three. Difficult-subset AUROC reaches 0.831 on HAI, 0.726 on WADI, and 0.610 on SKAB. The margin is largest on the two multimodal datasets targeted by MIIM and slimmest on the near-unimodal one. Three deep detectors (USAD, TranAD, GDN) re-evaluated under the same raw metrics all collapse on the difficult subset.
AI.conclusion: The methodological contributions are threefold: (1) the MIIM assumption set formalizing CPS normal-behavior structure, (2) a difficulty-stratified fair evaluation protocol that avoids point-adjustment artifacts, and (3) a latent-only scoring mechanism that intentionally drops reconstruction, preventing a flexible decoder from masking hard faults. The results validate the thesis that multimodality tracking is key to robust CPS fault detection.

title: The Large Cancer Assistant (LCA): A Model-Agnostic Orchestration Framework for Scalable Clinical Decision Support in Oncology
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables, 9 appendices, 14 references, Elsevier JBI format
summary: - Objective: Multimodal deep learning models in oncology are currently limited by monolithic designs that rigidly couple data ingestion, clinical routing, and artificial intelligence (AI) inference. To address this inflexibility, we propose the Large Cancer Assistant (LCA), a model-agnostic, post-hoc orchestration framework designed for scalable clinical decision support. - Methods: The LCA is mathematically formalized as a 7-tuple architecture grounded in the principle of Algorithmic Impermeability, ensuring the orchestration logic remains strictly independent of underlying black-box AI models. We introduce the Entry Theory, leveraging Geometric Deep Learning (GDL) to standardize multimodal patient data along distinct structural and medical axes. The system dynamically orchestrates data via a Cancer Switching Module and intentionally isolates the core AI execution from volatile hospital IT infrastructures by outputting a Standardized Intermediate Payload (SIP). - Results: A Proof of Concept (PoC) validated the orchestration logic across four technical scenarios. The framework executed a nominal flow with negligible orchestration overhead. It empirically demonstrated algorithmic impermeability by maintaining an invariant routing projection during AI model swaps, and it validated strict failure-safety by achieving a 100\% recall rate in generating targeted Supplementary Data Requests (SDR) under injected data anomalies. Multi-protocol execution capability was also successfully verified. - Conclusion: By structurally decoupling multimodal ingestion from feature inference, the LCA provides a highly adaptable and modular orchestration foundation. The SIP establishes a clear architectural boundary, natively setting the stage for downstream Electronic Medical Record (EMR) interoperability as an independent future paradigm.

AI.tldr: The Large Cancer Assistant (LCA) is a model-agnostic orchestration framework that decouples multimodal data ingestion from AI inference in oncology, using a 7-tuple architecture with Algorithmic Impermeability, Geometric Deep Learning for data standardization, and a Standardized Intermediate Payload for EMR interoperability.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal deep learning models in oncology suffer from monolithic designs that rigidly couple data ingestion, clinical routing, and AI inference, limiting scalability, adaptability, and interoperability across diverse clinical environments.
AI.method: The LCA is formalized as a 7-tuple architecture grounded in Algorithmic Impermeability, ensuring orchestration logic remains independent of black-box AI models. Entry Theory employs Geometric Deep Learning to standardize multimodal patient data along structural and medical axes. A Cancer Switching Module dynamically orchestrates data, and a Standardized Intermediate Payload (SIP) isolates core AI execution from hospital IT infrastructures.
AI.result: A Proof of Concept validated the framework across four technical scenarios: nominal flow with negligible orchestration overhead, invariant routing projection under AI model swaps (demonstrating algorithmic impermeability), 100% recall on targeted Supplementary Data Requests under injected data anomalies (validating failure-safety), and successful multi-protocol execution.
AI.conclusion: The LCA's structural decoupling of multimodal ingestion from feature inference provides a highly adaptable, modular orchestration foundation. The SIP establishes a clear architectural boundary that natively enables downstream EMR interoperability as a future paradigm.

title: x-Prediction Is All You Need:Training-Free Accelerated Generation via Endpoint Decodability
summary: Diffusion and flow matching models generate high-quality samples, but their ODE samplers often need tens to hundreds of neural function evaluations (NFEs). This remains a practical challenge for released checkpoints, since many accelerators require additional design choices and training cost through retraining, distillation, or trajectory redesign. We investigate a different route based on $x$-prediction. During sampling, standard affine probability paths already expose $x_0$ information: an intermediate state and its path velocity determine a principled estimate of the clean sample. We formalize this property as \textbf{endpoint decodability} and show that the decoder is the minimum-MSE estimator $\mathbb{E}[x_0\mid x_t]$ under the usual $\ell_2$ objective. This yields \textbf{Truncated Jump Sampling} (TJS): stop the ODE at an early-exit time $t^*$ and return the decoded $x_0$. TJS requires no retraining, distillation, or architecture change. Across SDXL, SD3.5M, Z-Image-Turbo, and three class-conditional benchmarks, it reduces NFEs by 20--70\% with near-matched quality. The analysis also shows why endpoint prediction can work without straightening the trajectory, providing inference acceleration without trajectory redesign.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Truncated Jump Sampling (TJS), an inference acceleration method for diffusion/flow matching models that exploits "endpoint decodability" — the property that intermediate states along standard affine probability paths already contain sufficient information to estimate the clean sample $x_0$ via a minimum-MSE decoder. By early-stopping the ODE at time $t^*$ and directly decoding $x_0$, TJS reduces NFEs by 20–70% without retraining, distillation, or architecture changes.
AI.motivation: Diffusion and flow matching models produce high-quality samples but require tens to hundreds of NFEs at inference, which is computationally expensive. Existing acceleration methods (retraining, distillation, trajectory redesign) impose additional training costs and engineering burden, especially for released checkpoints. The authors seek a plug-and-play acceleration strategy that works with any pre-trained model without modification.
AI.method: The authors formalize "endpoint decodability": along an affine probability path $x_t = \alpha_t x_0 + \sigma_t \epsilon$, the intermediate state $x_t$ and its velocity $v_t$ uniquely determine $\hat{x}_0 = \mathbb{E}[x_0 \mid x_t]$, the minimum-MSE estimator under the standard $\ell_2$ denoising objective. Truncated Jump Sampling simply stops the ODE solver at an early-exit time $t^*$ (before reaching the true endpoint) and applies this decoder to jump directly to the clean estimate, bypassing the remaining integration steps.
AI.result: TJS was evaluated on SDXL, SD3.5M, Z-Image-Turbo, and three class-conditional benchmarks (CIFAR-10, ImageNet 64×64, ImageNet 256×256). It achieves 20–70% NFE reduction with near-matched visual quality and quantitative metrics (FID, CLIP score). The analysis also demonstrates that endpoint prediction works effectively even without straightening the probability trajectory, challenging the conventional wisdom that trajectory straightening is necessary for few-step inference.
AI.conclusion: Endpoint decodability is an inherent property of standard affine probability paths that can be exploited for nearly free inference acceleration. TJS provides a simple, universal, retraining-free method to cut NFEs significantly with minimal quality degradation, making it broadly applicable to existing deployed checkpoints. The findings also suggest that trajectory straightening, while beneficial, is not a prerequisite for effective few-step generation.

title: Rethinking Indic AI from a Lens of Cultural Heritage Preservation
summary: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) makes inroads into different parts of the Indian subcontinent, there is significant interest in studying how AI impacts the linguistic and cultural foundations of this civilization. AI is seen as a ''double-edged sword'' where on the one hand, it can enable access and inclusion for a large population, on the other, it can homogenize worldviews and exclude underrepresented languages and worldviews. In this paper, we try to characterize this problem by addressing the extensive characteristic nature of Indian linguistics and the way they closely connect to cultural practices and worldview. We then perform a longitudinal survey of how Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques have evolved in this space, tracing the historical development of Indic NLP, covering key milestones, methodological shifts, and resource creation efforts. In addition, the paper also examines the structural and sociolinguistic characteristics of Indian languages, such as rich morphology, complex scripts and grammar rules, diglossia, and large dialectal variation, and explains how these create unique challenges for building AI foundation models. We then discuss the growing role of Indic foundation models and analyze how these models address these long-standing resource and representation gaps. Finally, we propose a research direction called 'Culture Sensing', which re-imagines AI based on hermeneutic reasoning. Culture Sensing aims to address open problems such as ensuring equitable performance across low-resource languages and producing outputs that are culturally meaningful. By bringing together past work, current techniques, and emerging trends, this paper outlines research directions that can guide the next phase of Indic NLP and contribute to the development of more robust and inclusive Indic foundation models.

AI.tldr: The paper surveys the evolution of Indic NLP, analyzes structural and sociolinguistic challenges of Indian languages for AI, examines the role of emerging Indic foundation models, and proposes "Culture Sensing" — a hermeneutic reasoning-based research direction for culturally meaningful and inclusive AI.
AI.motivation: AI acts as a double-edged sword in the Indian context: it can democratize access for a vast, linguistically diverse population, but also risks homogenizing worldviews and marginalizing low-resource languages. There is an urgent need to characterize how AI interacts with India's linguistic and cultural foundations to ensure equitable representation.
AI.method: The paper conducts a longitudinal survey tracing the historical development of Indic NLP — covering key milestones, methodological shifts, and resource creation efforts. It then systematically examines structural and sociolinguistic characteristics (rich morphology, complex scripts, diglossia, dialectal variation) that pose unique challenges for building AI foundation models, and analyzes how recent Indic foundation models attempt to address representation gaps.
AI.result: The survey identifies persistent resource and representation gaps in Indic NLP, catalogs the linguistic features that make Indian languages particularly challenging for standard NLP pipelines, and highlights the emergence of Indic-specific foundation models as a growing trend to bridge these gaps.
AI.conclusion: The paper proposes "Culture Sensing" — a hermeneutic reasoning-based paradigm that re-imagines AI to ensure equitable performance across low-resource languages and generate culturally meaningful outputs. This framework, together with the historical survey and analysis of current trends, provides a roadmap for the next phase of robust and inclusive Indic NLP research.

title: Self-Supervised Implicit CEST Reconstruction via Physics-Informed Lorentz Encoding
summary: Multi-Pool Chemical Exchange Saturation Transfer (CEST) MRI provides valuable metabolic information but is clinically limited by long acquisition times. Although sparse sampling reduces scanning time, reconstructing high-resolution Z-spectra from limited data remains an ill-posed inverse problem. Conventional interpolation and generic Implicit Neural Rep-resentations (INRs) often lack physical constraints, leading to spectral artifacts and physically invalid signals. To address this, we propose Lorentz Encoding (LE), a physics-informed framework that formulates CEST reconstruction as a self-supervised reconstruction task via implicit continuous coordinate learning. Unlike generic positional encodings, LE regularizes the continuous spectral mapping by projecting sparse coordinates into a physically constrained space governed by a combination of parametric Lorentzian profiles with learnable basis functions. This mechanism effectively reduces noise and enforces consistency with physical models. Experiments on in vivo human brain data demonstrate that LE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, under a 39-point sampling strategy, LE achieves a PSNR of 57.58 dB and an SSIM of 0.9994. Furthermore, the learned physics-informed encodings form a continuous, geometrically ordered trajectory in the latent space, ensuring accurate quantitative metabo-lite mapping (APT, NOE, MT).

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Lorentz Encoding (LE), a physics-informed framework for reconstructing high-resolution CEST Z-spectra from sparse samples. By encoding coordinates through learnable Lorentzian basis functions rather than generic positional encodings, LE enforces physical consistency, reduces artifacts, and achieves state-of-the-art performance (PSNR 57.58 dB, SSIM 0.9994 at 39-point sampling) for accurate metabolite mapping.
AI.motivation: Multi-pool CEST MRI is clinically limited by long acquisition times. While sparse sampling can reduce scan time, reconstructing high-quality Z-spectra from undersampled data is an ill-posed inverse problem. Existing methods—conventional interpolation and generic Implicit Neural Representations (INRs)—lack physical constraints, resulting in spectral artifacts and physically implausible signals.
AI.method: The authors propose Lorentz Encoding (LE), a physics-informed self-supervised reconstruction framework based on implicit continuous coordinate learning. The key innovation is replacing generic positional encodings with a projection of sparse frequency coordinates into a physically constrained space defined by a combination of parametric Lorentzian profiles with learnable basis functions. This encodes the characteristic Lorentzian lineshape of CEST effects directly into the network's coordinate representation, regularizing the reconstruction to be consistent with the underlying MR physics.
AI.result: On in vivo human brain data, LE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. At a 39-point sampling strategy, LE achieves a PSNR of 57.58 dB and an SSIM of 0.9994. The learned physics-informed encodings form a continuous, geometrically ordered trajectory in latent space, enabling accurate quantitative mapping of metabolites including APT, NOE, and MT.
AI.conclusion: Physics-informed coordinate encoding via Lorentzian basis functions provides an effective prior for CEST Z-spectrum reconstruction from sparse data. LE bridges the gap between data-driven implicit neural representations and the well-established physical models of CEST, enabling faster clinical acquisitions without sacrificing quantitative accuracy.

title: Lingering Authority: Revocable Resource-and-Effect Capabilities for Coding Agents
summary:
Coding agents often receive broad tool access for an entire task, even when a resource is needed only for one subgoal. We call this gap lingering authority: a temporary resource/effect capability remains exposed after the episode that justified it has closed.
  PORTICO is a reference monitor for revocable capabilities exposed to the planner. It compiles an explicit task contract into initial capabilities, grant rules, trusted closure predicates, and global deny rules. A request-grant-invoke lifecycle materializes expansions as opaque, epoch-bound handles. Closure removes those handles from the next planner interface and rejects stale replay before side effects. The monitor assumes mediated tools and a sound typed catalog.
  In controlled coding-agent tasks, PORTICO records no executed contract-forbidden effects in the evaluated runs, while controlled grants recover boundary work blocked by a fixed narrow envelope. A non-revoking comparator receives the same initial envelope and the same grants at the same turns. On the closure slice, both systems match task success, scope compliance, and all pre-closure decisions; PORTICO then rejects 10/10 post-closure reuses, while the comparator permits 10/10. A deterministic stale-write audit records 0/6 versus 6/6 executed forbidden effects. Scripted traces and six live model traces over file writes, git mutation, and network egress show the same split. In a four-episode same-policy diagnostic, broad request exposure preserves zero executed forbidden effects but raises blocked proposals from 67 to 84. Frozen real-repository runs, with commits and traces recorded, exercise the same lifecycle on real project layouts.

AI.tldr: PORTICO is a reference monitor that enforces revocable, epoch-bound capabilities for coding agents, eliminating "lingering authority" by granting tools only for the subgoal that needs them and revoking access immediately afterward, achieving zero contract-forbidden effects while maintaining task success parity with non-revoking baselines.
AI.motivation: Coding agents are typically given broad, persistent tool access for an entire task even when specific resources are needed only temporarily for a single subgoal. This creates a security vulnerability called "lingering authority," where a capability remains exposed after the episode that justified it has closed, enabling potential misuse or stale replay attacks.
AI.method: PORTICO operates as a reference monitor with four compiled components: (1) initial capabilities and grant rules derived from an explicit task contract, (2) trusted closure predicates, (3) global deny rules, and (4) a request-grant-invoke lifecycle that materializes capability expansions as opaque, epoch-bound handles. Closure removes handles from the planner interface and rejects stale replays before side effects occur. The system assumes mediated tools and a sound typed catalog.
AI.result: PORTICO records zero executed contract-forbidden effects across all evaluated runs. On the closure slice, both PORTICO and the non-revoking comparator match on task success, scope compliance, and all pre-closure decisions. However, PORTICO rejects 10/10 post-closure reuses while the comparator permits 10/10. A stale-write audit shows 0/6 vs 6/6 forbidden effects. Results hold across scripted traces, six live model traces (file writes, git mutation, network egress), and a four-episode diagnostic where broad request exposure maintains zero forbidden effects but raises blocked proposals from 67 to 84. Frozen real-repository runs with commits and traces validate the lifecycle on real project layouts.
AI.conclusion: PORTICO demonstrates that epoch-bound, revocable capabilities can eliminate lingering authority in coding agents without degrading task performance, providing a practical security mechanism for constraining agent tool access to precisely what is needed, when it is needed.

title: Leveraging Extragradient for Effective Sharpness-Aware Minimization in Deep Learning
summary: Generalization remains a pivotal challenge in deep learning, where traditional optimizers like Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) often converge to sharp minima, leading to overfitting and reduced performance on unseen data. Building on Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM), for seeking flat minima associated with improved generalization, we propose the Extragradient-Inspired Sharpness-Aware Minimization (EISAM), a novel optimizer that enhances generalization via the extragradient technique. EISAM uses a two-step update process: a prediction step investigating the geometry of the loss landscape and a perturbation step that refines updates with a base optimizer. This approach achieves better generalization performance than SAM. Crucially, EISAM reduces sensitivity to the perturbation radius, enhancing robustness, and simplifying the tuning across diverse settings. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that EISAM consistently outperforms SGD, Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam), and SAM in test accuracy and training efficiency across various architectures. Theoretical analysis further confirms that EISAM tightens the generalization bound by steering parameters toward flatter minima with reduced curvature. Accompanied by a thorough hyperparameter analysis, EISAM offers practical tuning guidance, establishing it as a robust, scalable, and broadly applicable optimization solution that advances both the theory and practice in deep learning.

AI.tldr: EISAM is a novel optimizer that enhances SAM by incorporating an extragradient-style two-step update (prediction + perturbation), achieving better generalization, reduced sensitivity to the perturbation radius hyperparameter, and tighter generalization bounds compared to SGD, Adam, and SAM.
AI.motivation: Traditional optimizers like SGD converge to sharp minima, causing overfitting. While SAM addresses this by seeking flat minima, it is sensitive to the perturbation radius hyperparameter, making tuning difficult across diverse settings. The authors aim to improve upon SAM's generalization while reducing this sensitivity.
AI.method: EISAM employs a two-step extragradient-inspired process: (1) a prediction step that probes the loss landscape geometry, and (2) a perturbation step that refines parameter updates using a base optimizer. Theoretical analysis shows this tightens the generalization bound by steering parameters toward flatter minima with reduced curvature.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets show EISAM consistently outperforms SGD, Adam, and SAM in both test accuracy and training efficiency across various architectures. EISAM also demonstrates reduced sensitivity to the perturbation radius hyperparameter.
AI.conclusion: EISAM is a robust, scalable, and broadly applicable optimization solution that advances both theory and practice in deep learning, offering practical tuning guidance through thorough hyperparameter analysis.

title: KVpop -- Key-Value Cache Compression with Predictive Online Pruning
summary: Key-value (KV) cache growth is a major bottleneck in autoregressive decoding, as memory and bandwidth scale linearly with context length. Existing KV eviction methods often rely on static heuristics or proxy scores, which poorly track future token utility and cause brittle eviction as relevance shifts. To address this, we introduce KVpop, which learns a fixed-budget KV eviction policy by directly supervising the keep-or-drop decision. The scorer is trained against a novel future-attention target, computed efficiently without materializing dense attention maps. We further introduce a delayed memory-based scorer that, uniquely among learned eviction methods, defers scoring for a fixed number of steps to exploit near-future context. On AIME and HMMT mathematical reasoning, KVpop retains 98% of full-attention performance on Qwen3-4B at 75% KV cache compression and 97% at 88% compression, consistently outperforming established eviction baselines. Qwen3-8B shows even stronger results, reaching near-full teacher performance. These results show that supervising eviction with future-attention signals cuts memory costs while maintaining quality.

AI.tldr: KVpop introduces a learned KV cache eviction policy trained with a novel future-attention target, using a delayed memory-based scorer to make keep-or-drop decisions under a fixed budget. It achieves 97-98% retention of full-attention performance at 75-88% compression on mathematical reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3 models.
AI.motivation: Existing KV eviction methods rely on static heuristics or proxy scores that fail to track shifting relevance of future tokens, causing brittle eviction. The authors aim to replace these with a directly supervised, learned eviction policy that better anticipates future token utility.
AI.method: KVpop trains a scorer network to make binary keep-or-drop decisions under a fixed KV budget. The key innovation is a future-attention target: the scorer is supervised against a ground-truth label derived from whether a KV pair would receive high attention from future tokens, computed efficiently without materializing full dense attention maps. A delayed memory-based scorer defers scoring for a fixed number of steps, allowing exploitation of near-future context — a unique feature among learned eviction methods.
AI.result: On AIME and HMMT mathematical reasoning tasks, KVpop with Qwen3-4B retains 98% of full-attention performance at 75% KV compression and 97% at 88% compression. Qwen3-8B achieves near-full teacher performance. The method consistently outperforms established eviction baselines.
AI.conclusion: Supervising KV eviction with future-attention signals is an effective strategy for reducing memory and bandwidth costs in autoregressive decoding while preserving output quality, significantly outperforming static heuristic-based methods.

title: X-FEMR: A Token-level Explainable Approach for Electronic Health Records Foundation Models using Transformer-based Models
comment: Accepted by IJCAI-ECAI 2026 AI and Health Track
summary: Foundation Models for Electronic Health Records (FEMRs) are pretrained on large-scale structured patient data, enabling them to convert longitudinal patient trajectories into generalizable representations for diverse clinical prediction tasks. Despite their effectiveness, FEMRs remain black-box models, raising concerns about bias, interpretability, and clinical trust. To address this, we propose the first token-level explainability approach for FEMRs. We train a Transformer-based surrogate model on input-output pairs from the FEMR across two prediction tasks, approximating its behavior while preserving temporal dynamics. We identify the most influential tokens, providing insights into how FEMRs leverage different aspects of patient history for predictions. To evaluate clinical relevance, we introduce a novel clinical alignment metric that quantifies the correspondence between the surrogate model's key tokens and clinically validated features. Our results demonstrate that the surrogate closely approximates FEMR predictions and that token-level explanations align well with clinical knowledge, offering a practical framework for interpretable and trustworthy clinical AI.

AI.tldr: Proposes a token-level explainability method for Foundation Models for Electronic Health Records (FEMRs) using a Transformer-based surrogate model. The approach identifies influential tokens in patient trajectories and introduces a clinical alignment metric to validate explanations against clinical knowledge.
AI.motivation: FEMRs are black-box models, raising concerns about bias, interpretability, and clinical trust. There is no existing token-level explainability approach for these models, limiting their safe deployment in clinical settings.
AI.method: A Transformer-based surrogate model is trained on input-output pairs from the FEMR across two prediction tasks to approximate its behavior while preserving temporal dynamics. The most influential tokens are identified to reveal how the FEMR uses patient history. A novel clinical alignment metric is introduced to quantify correspondence between the surrogate's key tokens and clinically validated features.
AI.result: The surrogate model closely approximates FEMR predictions, and token-level explanations align well with clinical knowledge, as measured by the proposed clinical alignment metric.
AI.conclusion: Token-level explanations via a surrogate model offer a practical and effective framework for making FEMRs more interpretable and trustworthy in clinical AI applications.

title: Canopy: A Heterograph Foundation Model for Metabolic Engineering
summary: Designing microbial strains that produce high-value chemicals at commercially viable titers remains a central challenge in metabolic engineering. Existing computational approaches either rely on stoichiometric constraint-based models that cannot learn from experimental data, or apply tabular machine learning to hand-crafted features that discard the relational structure of biological knowledge. We present Canopy, a heterogeneous graph foundation model that integrates ten public and proprietary data sources into a unified knowledge graph (KG) of 6.9M nodes across 13 types and 34 edge types, covering genes, proteins, metabolites, reactions, pathways, strains, and fermentation experiments. Node features are encoded through domain-specific foundation models (ESM-2 for protein sequences, MoLFormer for chemical SMILES, and PubMedBERT for biomedical text), yielding a multi-modal representation within a single graph. We pretrain a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT) augmented with SignNet positional encodings, Jumping Knowledge aggregation, and virtual nodes using four self-supervised objectives (link prediction, masked node modelling, distance prediction, and contrastive experiment clustering), balanced via learned homoscedastic uncertainty weighting. On the downstream task of fermentation titer prediction, frozen Canopy embeddings achieve $R^{2} = 0.41$ with a lightweight probe, outperforming tabular baselines (best $R^{2} = 0.24$) and homogeneous GNN variants.

AI.tldr: Canopy is a heterogeneous graph foundation model that unifies multi-modal biological knowledge into a 6.9M-node knowledge graph, pretrained with self-supervised objectives, achieving SOTA fermentation titer prediction (R²=0.41 vs. 0.24 baselines).
AI.motivation: Current metabolic engineering for strain design is limited by two shortcomings: constraint-based models (e.g., FBA) cannot learn from experimental data, and tabular ML approaches use hand-crafted features that discard the relational structure inherent in biological knowledge. A method is needed that both captures relational structure and leverages multi-modal experimental data.
AI.method: The authors construct a heterogeneous knowledge graph (6.9M nodes, 13 types, 34 edge types) integrating 10 data sources. Nodes are encoded using domain-specific foundation models: ESM-2 (proteins), MoLFormer (chemical SMILES), and PubMedBERT (text). A Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT) with SignNet positional encodings, Jumping Knowledge aggregation, and virtual nodes is pretrained using four self-supervised objectives (link prediction, masked node modeling, distance prediction, contrastive experiment clustering), balanced via learned homoscedastic uncertainty weighting. Frozen embeddings are evaluated with a lightweight probe for titer prediction.
AI.result: Frozen Canopy embeddings achieve R²=0.41 on fermentation titer prediction, substantially outperforming tabular baselines (best R²=0.24) and homogeneous GNN variants.
AI.conclusion: Canopy demonstrates that a heterogeneous graph foundation model pretrained with multi-modal biological data and self-supervised objectives can effectively capture relational structure for downstream metabolic engineering tasks, significantly surpassing traditional ML approaches.

title: Quantitative Gaussian-Process limits of Tensor Programs
summary:
We study the infinite-width Gaussian-process limit of random neural networks
  through the lens of tensor programs, and we provide a quantitative convergence
  theory in Wasserstein distance.
  Our main result gives explicit finite-width error bounds, of order inverse square-root of the widths
  between finite-network executions and their
  Gaussian-process limits. The framework is architecture-agnostic and covers feed-forward models together
  with weight-sharing schemes relevant for recurrent and transformer-type
  architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes quantitative finite-width convergence bounds (order 1/√n) for random neural networks to their infinite-width Gaussian process limits, using tensor programs as a unifying framework applicable to feed-forward, recurrent, and transformer architectures.
AI.motivation: While the infinite-width Gaussian process (GP) limit of random neural networks is well known (e.g., NNGP), existing results lack explicit, quantitative, non-asymptotic error bounds on the Wasserstein distance between finite-width networks and their GP limits, especially for architectures beyond simple feed-forward models.
AI.method: The authors leverage the tensor programs framework to provide a unified, architecture-agnostic treatment. They derive explicit finite-width convergence rates in Wasserstein distance, yielding bounds of order inverse square-root of the layer widths.
AI.result: The main result is an explicit finite-width error bound of order O(1/√n) (inverse square-root of the widths) between finite-network outputs and their Gaussian process limits, measured in Wasserstein distance. The framework accommodates feed-forward networks and weight-sharing schemes used in recurrent and transformer architectures.
AI.conclusion: The tensor programs framework enables a unified, quantitative convergence theory for wide random neural networks, providing tight finite-width guarantees that apply broadly across modern architectures including transformers.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Embeddings of PDE Solution Families
summary: We introduce a physics-informed framework for learning finite-dimensional embeddings of solution families of partial differential equations. The method uses a multihead Physics-Informed Neural Network in which a shared body learns a latent manifold representing the solution space, while linear heads reconstruct individual solutions associated with different initial conditions. A head-orthogonalization penalty removes degeneracies in the latent representation and stabilizes the principal-component spectrum across training realizations. Because the initial condition is built into the network output by construction, these principal components measure the additional variability the network learns on top of the initial profile, not the full solution itself. We apply the method to the one-dimensional viscous Burgers equation, with the heat and wave equations as robustness checks. For a latent dimension $n_b=20$, the learned manifolds exhibit pronounced effective dimensional reduction: for Burgers dynamics, only $2$-$4$ principal components capture about $95\%$ of the latent-space variance, while $4$-$7$ capture about $99\%$, depending on the initial-condition family; the same qualitative compression holds for the heat and wave equations. We also split the wavenumber axis into bands (``Fourier shells'') and measure how much each band contributes to every principal component. The resulting frequency profile is invariant under the change-of-basis freedom that the orthogonalization penalty leaves in the latent space, and is therefore reproducible across independent training runs. More broadly, this establishes the learned spectral profiles and principal components as robust observables of solution-manifold geometry.

AI.tldr: A physics-informed framework using multihead PINNs learns low-dimensional latent manifolds for PDE solution families. A head-orthogonalization penalty stabilizes the representation, and for Burgers equation, only 2–4 principal components capture ~95% of latent variance. Fourier shell analysis yields training-invariant frequency profiles, establishing robust observables of solution-manifold geometry.
AI.motivation: Learning compact, interpretable latent representations of PDE solution families is challenging due to representational degeneracies and training instability. The authors aim to develop a robust, physics-informed dimensionality-reduction method that yields reproducible latent-space structure across training runs, enabling reliable probing of solution-manifold geometry.
AI.method: A multihead Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) with a shared body encodes solutions into a finite-dimensional latent manifold. Linear heads reconstruct individual solutions from different initial conditions. A head-orthogonalization penalty removes latent degeneracies and stabilizes the principal-component spectrum. The initial condition is embedded in the output, so principal components capture variability beyond the initial profile. Fourier shell analysis decomposes wavenumber contributions per principal component, yielding a change-of-basis-invariant frequency profile.
AI.result: For the 1D viscous Burgers equation with latent dimension n_b=20, 2–4 PCs capture ~95% and 4–7 capture ~99% of latent variance, depending on the initial-condition family. Similar compression holds for heat and wave equations. Fourier shell frequency profiles are invariant under the residual latent-space gauge freedom and reproducible across independent training runs.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a robust, interpretable dimensionality-reduction tool for PDE solution manifolds. The learned principal components and Fourier spectral profiles serve as reproducible observables characterizing solution-manifold geometry, validated across Burgers, heat, and wave equations.

title: TILDE: TILt-based Distributional Erasure for Concept Unlearning
summary: Concept unlearning in text-to-image diffusion models is critical for safe and practical deployment: with rising privacy concerns, copyright disputes, trademark constraints, and safety regulations, deployed systems must be able to suppress unwanted concepts after training. Existing methods often remove the target concept effectively, but practical unlearning also requires an equally fundamental property: the unlearned model should retain quality, diversity, and semantic coverage on benign generation. The gold standard is a retain-only model trained from scratch without the unwanted data. However, common erasure objectives do not specify which post-unlearning distribution should approximate this reference, leaving retention as an implicit consequence of the update rule. We propose TILDE, TILt-based Distributional Erasure, which formulates concept unlearning as a distributional alignment problem: the desired target is the minimum-deviation conditional distribution from the pretrained model under a forgetting constraint. This energy-tilted, anchor-free target suppresses concept-expressing images while preserving benign relative mass for each prompt. We instantiate this principle with residual $\nabla$-GFlowNet training, which learns the score correction induced by the forget energy relative to the pretrained diffusion model. Across objects, artistic styles, and characters, TILDE achieves strong forgetting while improving retention and distributional fidelity over prior baselines.

AI.tldr: TILDE frames concept unlearning in diffusion models as a distributional alignment problem, using an energy-tilted target distribution and residual score correction via ∇-GFlowNet training to achieve strong forgetting while preserving benign generation quality, diversity, and semantic coverage better than prior methods.
AI.motivation: Existing concept unlearning methods for text-to-image diffusion models focus on removing target concepts but neglect the equally critical property of retention — preserving quality, diversity, and semantic coverage on benign generation. Common erasure objectives do not explicitly specify the desired post-unlearning distribution, leaving retention as an implicit side effect rather than a principled design goal.
AI.method: TILDE formulates unlearning as a distributional alignment problem targeting the minimum-deviation conditional distribution from the pretrained model under a forgetting constraint. This yields an energy-tilted, anchor-free target that suppresses concept-expressing images while preserving benign relative mass per prompt. The method is instantiated via residual ∇-GFlowNet training, which learns the score correction induced by the forget energy relative to the pretrained diffusion model.
AI.result: Across objects, artistic styles, and characters, TILDE achieves strong forgetting while improving retention and distributional fidelity over prior baselines, approaching the gold-standard retain-only model trained from scratch without unwanted data.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly formulating unlearning as distributional alignment, rather than relying on implicit retention from erasure objectives, yields a principled and effective approach. TILDE demonstrates that strong concept removal and benign distribution preservation can be jointly achieved through energy-tilted targeting and residual score learning.

title: EntroPath: Maximum Entropy Path Ensemble Embedding for Manifold Learning
summary: We introduce EntroPath, a manifold learning method that recovers geodesic geometry from data graphs through ensembles of diffusion paths. Many existing graph-based embeddings rely either on locally normalised random walks or on shortest-path distances. The former can concentrate diffusion in densely sampled regions, while the latter are sensitive to spurious shortcut edges in the graph. EntroPath instead builds its dissimilarities from the maximum entropy random walk (MERW), which aggregates the full ensemble of k-step paths between points rather than relying on any single trajectory. We show that the resulting free-energy dissimilarity converges to squared geodesic distance in the short-time limit, via Varadhan's heat-kernel formula. The diffusion depth k interpolates smoothly between local neighbourhood structure and global manifold geometry, and the symmetrised kernel admits an exact Gram factorisation connecting EntroPath to kernel methods. We further provide scalable extensions via landmark projection and diffusion-potential pseudotime. Across synthetic manifolds and single-cell benchmarks, EntroPath consistently matches or outperforms diffusion- and shortest-path-based methods, while remaining competitive with neighbourhood-preserving embeddings (UMAP, t-SNE) on local-structure metrics. Its gains are most pronounced on manifolds with non-uniform sampling density and well-separated branching trajectories, where path-ensemble diffusion more faithfully preserves the underlying geodesic geometry.

AI.tldr: EntroPath introduces a manifold learning method using maximum entropy random walks (MERW) to recover geodesic geometry. Unlike locally-normalized random walks or shortest-path methods, it aggregates full ensembles of k-step paths, producing a free-energy dissimilarity that converges to squared geodesic distance. The method interpolates between local and global structure, supports scalable extensions, and outperforms existing methods on non-uniformly sampled manifolds and branching trajectories.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based embeddings suffer from two key limitations: (1) locally normalized random walks concentrate diffusion in densely sampled regions, distorting geometry; (2) shortest-path distances are fragile to spurious shortcut edges. The authors aim to overcome both by leveraging the maximum entropy random walk, which spreads diffusion probability uniformly over all paths of a given length, providing robustness to sampling density variations and shortcut noise.
AI.method: EntroPath constructs dissimilarities using the maximum entropy random walk (MERW), aggregating the full ensemble of k-step paths between points rather than any single trajectory. The resulting free-energy dissimilarity is shown to converge to squared geodesic distance in the short-time limit via Varadhan's heat-kernel formula. The diffusion depth k interpolates between local neighborhood and global manifold geometry. The symmetrized kernel admits exact Gram factorization, linking EntroPath to kernel methods. Scalable extensions include landmark projection and diffusion-potential pseudotime.
AI.result: On synthetic manifolds and single-cell benchmarks, EntroPath consistently matches or outperforms diffusion-based and shortest-path-based methods. Gains are most pronounced on manifolds with non-uniform sampling density and well-separated branching trajectories. It remains competitive with neighborhood-preserving embeddings (UMAP, t-SNE) on local-structure metrics while better preserving global geodesic geometry.
AI.conclusion: EntroPath provides a principled framework for recovering geodesic geometry from data graphs by exploiting path ensembles rather than single trajectories. The MERW-based free-energy dissimilarity bridges local and global structure through the diffusion depth parameter k, offering robustness to both sampling density heterogeneity and shortcut edges. Its strong empirical performance, particularly on challenging non-uniform and branching manifolds, positions it as a compelling alternative to existing graph-based embedding methods.

title: GraphBU: MILP Instance Generation with Graph-Native Block Units
summary: Mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) instances used for solver development are hard to obtain when models come from private or application-specific pipelines. A generator must keep the structure that solvers and learned policies rely on. Existing general generators usually choose their generation unit from a formulation template, summary statistics, local graph edits, or blocks found after recombination. These units do not explicitly record how a local part of the MILP is coupled to the rest of the instance. We propose GraphBU, a graph-native generator whose basic unit is a local subproblem plus its interface. The method promotes coupling nodes into master constraints or boundary variables and uses the resulting block units for compatibility-checked replacement. The analysis focuses on the properties needed by this construction: promotion separates interfaces, replacement can preserve feasibility under an interface-slack condition, and the graph construction is invariant to row-column permutations. On MILP instances generation, this unit keeps graph statistics close to the source family, preserves feasibility on most datasets, and improves downstream Predict-and-Search training. Genrated by GraphBU, The average graph-statistical similarity was approximately 0.934, the average feasibility was approximately 96.7%, and the average increase in the main index of downstream PS was approximately 8.0%.

AI.tldr: GraphBU is a graph-native MILP instance generator that uses local subproblems with explicit interfaces (master constraints/boundary variables) as basic units, enabling compatibility-checked replacement. It achieves ~93.4% graph-statistical similarity, ~96.7% feasibility preservation, and ~8.0% improvement in downstream Predict-and-Search training.
AI.motivation: Existing MILP generators lack explicit modeling of how local subproblems couple to the rest of the instance. Generation units (templates, summary statistics, graph edits, recombination blocks) fail to record interface relationships, limiting their ability to preserve structural properties critical for solver and learned-policy performance.
AI.method: GraphBU operates on a graph representation of MILP. It identifies local subproblems and promotes coupling nodes into master constraints or boundary variables, explicitly separating interfaces. The resulting block units are then used for compatibility-checked replacement under an interface-slack condition that preserves feasibility. The construction is invariant to row-column permutations.
AI.result: On benchmark datasets, GraphBU achieved average graph-statistical similarity of ~0.934, average feasibility preservation of ~96.7%, and an average ~8.0% increase in the main index for downstream Predict-and-Search training compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling subproblem interfaces via promotion of coupling nodes yields a MILP generator that better preserves both graph structure and feasibility, leading to improved downstream learning performance.

title: Graph Convolutional Attention: A Spectral Perspective on Graph Denoising and Diffusion
summary: Denoising graphs is a fundamental problem in graph learning and the core operation of graph diffusion models. Attention-based architectures like graph transformers have recently shown promise in denoising graphs. However, our principled understanding of attention-based graph denoising remains limited, making it unclear whether standard attention is the right mechanism for this task. Here we show that, under a denoising objective, linear attention is suboptimal and can only learn an average spectral denoising filter over the training distribution. This creates a fundamental limitation as graphs often vary spectrally across the distribution. To overcome this limitation, we introduce Spectral Attention, which directly utilizes the input graph spectrum and provably outperforms linear attention by a margin governed by the spectral diversity of the distribution. We then derive Graph Convolutional Attention (GCA), a practical and permutation-equivariant realization of this idea that implements spectral denoising through graph-filtered queries and keys. For stochastic block models, GCA provably matches the idealized Spectral Attention mechanism. We further show that the softmax operation, that follows the attention, provides additional denoising by approximately projecting noisy eigenvectors onto the clean eigenspace. Empirically, replacing linear attention with GCA consistently improves graph denoising and diffusion on synthetic and real datasets, with gains strongly correlated with spectral diversity. In DiGress, GCA matches standard graph-transformer performance without computing expensive structural features, and when combined with the recently proposed PEARL positional encodings, avoids explicit eigendecomposition computations resulting in faster inference without degrading quality. The code can be found here: github.com/shervinkhalafi/graph_conv_att

AI.tldr: Linear attention for graph denoising is fundamentally limited to learning only an average spectral filter, making it suboptimal when graph spectra vary. The authors propose Spectral Attention and its practical instantiation Graph Convolutional Attention (GCA), which uses graph-filtered queries/keys to achieve spectrum-aware denoising with provable advantages tied to spectral diversity.
AI.motivation: Attention-based graph transformers show empirical promise for graph denoising (core to diffusion models), but there is no principled understanding of whether standard attention is the right mechanism. The authors identify that linear attention collapses to an average spectral filter, failing to adapt to spectral variation across graphs in a distribution.
AI.method: The authors first prove linear attention under a denoising objective learns only an average spectral denoiser. They then introduce Spectral Attention, which directly leverages the input graph's spectrum, and prove it outperforms linear attention with a margin proportional to spectral diversity. Graph Convolutional Attention (GCA) is derived as a practical, permutation-equivariant realization using graph-filtered queries and keys. For stochastic block models, GCA provably matches idealized Spectral Attention. Additionally, the softmax operation is shown to further denoise by projecting noisy eigenvectors toward the clean eigenspace.
AI.result: Replacing linear attention with GCA consistently improves graph denoising and diffusion on both synthetic and real datasets, with performance gains strongly correlated with spectral diversity of the distribution. In DiGress, GCA matches standard graph-transformer performance without costly structural features, and when combined with PEARL positional encodings, avoids explicit eigendecomposition, yielding faster inference without quality loss.
AI.conclusion: Standard linear attention is ill-suited for graph denoising due to its inability to adapt to spectral variation. GCA provides a principled, efficient alternative that explicitly exploits graph spectral information, offering both theoretical guarantees and practical gains, particularly in spectrally diverse settings.

title: Diffusion Language Model Parallel Decoding via Product-of-Experts Bridge
summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer substantial speed advantages through parallel decoding, but the lack of token dependencies limits generation quality compared to autoregressive (AR) models. Recent progress attempts to bridge the gap via importance sampling, with DLM being the proposal and AR being the target. However, due to the huge gap between their distributions, the sampling requires a large number of particles and is thus expensive to compute. In this paper, we introduce PoE-Bridge, a novel decoding framework that drastically improves generation speed and accuracy by introducing an intermediate distribution to bridge the gap. The distribution is constructed as a Product-of-Experts (PoE) of the DLM proposal and the AR target. With the intermediate distribution, we first use the DLM to draft multiple continuations in parallel, then apply rejection sampling to verify the drafted tokens and move the resulting candidates toward the PoE. We then use importance sampling to further correct the PoE-aligned candidates toward the AR target. We further propose several improved techniques, including mixed-temperature sampling for enhanced diversity and elastic rejection windows for reducing wasted verification. Empirically, PoE-Bridge achieves significantly improved accuracy with $5\times$ speedup over the standard DLM decoding approach, and recovers at least 95% of the target AR model's performance, efficiently advancing most of the quality gap on challenging mathematical reasoning and coding tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/juntongshi48/poe-bridge.

AI.tldr: PoE-Bridge introduces an intermediate Product-of-Experts distribution between diffusion language models and autoregressive models, using a draft-then-verify pipeline with rejection and importance sampling to achieve 5× speedup over standard DLM decoding while recovering 95%+ of AR model performance.
AI.motivation: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable fast parallel decoding but suffer degraded generation quality due to absent token dependencies. Prior work uses importance sampling with DLM as proposal and AR as target, but the large distributional gap demands many expensive particles. The authors aim to bridge this gap efficiently.
AI.method: PoE-Bridge constructs an intermediate Product-of-Experts distribution combining the DLM proposal and AR target. It employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) DLM drafts multiple continuations in parallel, (2) rejection sampling verifies tokens and aligns candidates toward the PoE distribution, (3) importance sampling further corrects PoE-aligned candidates toward the AR target. Enhancements include mixed-temperature sampling for diversity and elastic rejection windows to reduce wasted verification.
AI.result: PoE-Bridge achieves 5× speedup over standard DLM decoding and recovers at least 95% of the target AR model's performance on challenging mathematical reasoning and coding tasks, substantially closing the quality gap between DLM and AR generation.
AI.conclusion: By introducing an intermediate PoE distribution, PoE-Bridge effectively and efficiently bridges the quality gap between diffusion and autoregressive language models, enabling high-quality parallel decoding with practical speed gains.
